chunks.heading: Store the energy. Release it clean. Let gravity do its part.
chunks.text: A bow is a spring, an arrow is a projectile, and the 10-ring at 70 m is a tenth of a degree wide. Take the challenge, learn the science with an Arrow Lab, then find coaching, competitions and academies in India at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First arrows International ≈ 330 m How far an arrow from a 40 lb bow could fly at 45°. Why ranges keep clear zones well behind the targets. ≈ 32.6 J The energy in an arrow from a 40 lb bow. That's why ranges have strict rules. 18 kg Holding a 40 lb bow at full draw, on three fingers. Hold with your back and bones, not just your arms. 0.1° How wide the 10-ring looks from 70 m.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Store the energy. Release it clean. Let gravity do its part.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Nock and draw only on the line. And only towards the targets, at a supervised range. Wait for the signal. Nobody goes forward of the line until every archer has stopped. Never dry-fire a bow. Releasing without an arrow sends the energy into the limbs and can break them. Ask before you book a taster session → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of archery?
chunks.text: 15 questions on bow energy, arrow flight and gravity, spine and fletching, aiming and scoring, holding and breathing, and wind and range safety: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Arrow Lab to see how draw weight, arrow mass and distance change the flight. Interactive · Arrow Lab

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set the bow, the draw and the arrow, then pick a distance and see how far the arrow falls
chunks.text: A simple model: stored energy ≈ ½ × draw force × power stroke (draw length minus an 8.75-inch brace height), with 75% of it going into the arrow. Flight ignores air drag, so real arrows arrive a little slower and lower. These are illustrative values for learning, not tuning advice. Draw weight 40 lb Draw length 28 in Arrow mass 20 g Distance 18 m 30 m 50 m 70 m 90 m Energy stored in the limbs 43.5 J Ch 1 · ½ × force × stroke Arrow speed 57.1 m/s Ch 1 · ½ m v² Arrow energy 32.6 J Ch 6 · why ranges have rules Flight time 1.23 s Ch 2 · distance ÷ speed Drop if shot level 7.37 m Ch 2 · ½ g t² Launch angle needed 6.1° Ch 2 · ½ asin(g d ÷ v²) Bar = arrow speed on a 0–80 m/s scale.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set the bow, the draw and the arrow, then pick a distance and see how far the arrow falls
chunks.text: Try a heavier arrow, then a longer distance. Only ever shoot at a supervised range (Ch 6). CH 1

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How a bow stores energy
chunks.text: A bow is a spring you load with your back muscles. Drawing the string does work: force × distance. If the force rose evenly from zero to the draw weight F over the power stroke s (from brace height to full draw), the stored energy would be E ≈ ½ F s . Real bows store somewhat more because of their force–draw curve. Not all of it reaches the arrow: some stays in the limbs and string as vibration and sound.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How a bow stores energy
chunks.text: Worked example · 28-inch draw, 8.75-inch brace height, 75% of stored energy to the arrow (illustrative) Draw weight Arrow Stored energy Arrow energy Arrow speed 30 lb (133 N) 20 g ≈ 32.6 J ≈ 24.5 J ≈ 49.5 m/s 40 lb (178 N) 20 g ≈ 43.5 J ≈ 32.6 J ≈ 57.1 m/s 40 lb (178 N) 25 g ≈ 43.5 J ≈ 32.6 J ≈ 51.1 m/s 50 lb (222 N) 20 g ≈ 54.4 J ≈ 40.8 J ≈ 63.9 m/s 40 lb × 4.448 = 177.9 N; power stroke (28 − 8.75) × 0.0254 = 0.489 m; ½ × 177.9 × 0.489 ≈ 43.5 J; × 0.75 ≈ 32.6 J; v = √(2 × 32.6 ÷ 0.020) ≈ 57.1 m/s. ✋ Feel the number Holding 40 lb at full draw is like holding an 18 kg bag on three fingers, steady enough to aim at a 12 cm circle 70 m away.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How a bow stores energy
chunks.text: A longer draw (30 in) on the same 40 lb bow: what stored energy? Power stroke (30 − 8.75) × 0.0254 ≈ 0.54 m; ½ × 177.9 × 0.54 ≈ 48 J . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Arrow flight & gravity
chunks.text: From the moment it leaves the string, the arrow is falling. Ignoring drag, an arrow flies at constant horizontal speed and falls under gravity: flight time t = d ÷ v and drop ½ g t² below the line it was launched along. To land on target you launch slightly upward, at θ = ½ asin(g d ÷ v²) . Worked example · 20 g arrow at 57.1 m/s, no drag (from our Arrow Lab) Distance Flight time Drop if shot level Launch angle 18 m ≈ 0.32 s ≈ 0.49 m ≈ 1.6° 30 m ≈ 0.53 s ≈ 1.35 m ≈ 2.6° 50 m ≈ 0.88 s ≈ 3.76 m ≈ 4.3° 70 m ≈ 1.23 s ≈ 7.37 m ≈ 6.1° 90 m ≈ 1.58 s ≈ 12.2 m ≈ 7.9° 70 m: t = 70 ÷ 57.1 ≈ 1.23 s; ½ × 9.81 × 1.23² ≈ 7.4 m.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Arrow flight & gravity
chunks.text: World Archery's standard distances are 70 m for recurve and 50 m for compound, with competition distances of up to 90 m. Why the sight moves Drop grows with t², so it more than doubles from 30 m to 50 m. Archers set the sight lower for longer distances, which raises the bow arm and the launch angle. Drag slows the arrow along the way, adding a little more drop than this model shows. What launch angle would 57.1 m/s need at 30 m? ½ asin(9.81 × 30 ÷ 57.1²) ≈ 2.6° . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Spine, the archer's paradox & fletching
chunks.text: The arrow bends around the bow and still flies straight. That's no accident. On release, the string drives the back of the arrow forward while the front sits beside the riser. The shaft bends and oscillates as it clears the bow: the archer's paradox . An arrow with the right stiffness ( spine ) for the bow's draw weight recovers and flies true; too stiff or too weak and it leaves at an angle. What a spine number means "Spine" is measured, not guessed.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Spine, the archer's paradox & fletching
chunks.text: The industry test (ASTM F2031, used by makers such as Easton ; ASTM withdrew the written standard in 2023 but the method is still the reference) rests the shaft on two supports 28 inches apart, hangs a 1.94 lb (880 g) weight from the middle and measures how far it sags. The sag in thousandths of an inch is the spine number, so a lower number is a stiffer arrow . Simple beam theory turns that sag into a bending stiffness: EI = F L³ ÷ (48 δ) .

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Spine, the archer's paradox & fletching
chunks.text: Worked example · spine number to bending stiffness (F = 8.63 N, L = 0.711 m) Spine Sag δ Bending stiffness EI Typical use (rule of thumb) 700 17.8 mm 3.6 N·m² Light recurve draw weights 600 15.2 mm 4.2 N·m² ↓ 500 12.7 mm 5.1 N·m² ↓ 400 10.2 mm 6.4 N·m² Heavier draw weights, longer draws 500 spine: δ = 0.500 in = 12.7 mm; EI = 8.63 × 0.711³ ÷ (48 × 0.0127) ≈ 5.1 N·m². Going from 700 to 400 makes the shaft about 75% stiffer. The right spine for you also depends on arrow length, point weight and your release, which is why makers publish selection charts and coaches tune arrows by test-shooting.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Spine, the archer's paradox & fletching
chunks.text: Fletching keeps the point forward Vanes or feathers at the back move the centre of drag behind the centre of mass. If the arrow turns sideways, the extra drag on the tail swings it back in line, like a weathervane. Slightly angled vanes also spin the arrow, averaging out small flaws. Worked example · the same energy, different arrows (40 lb, 28 in) Arrow mass Speed Momentum Drop if shot level at 70 m 20 g ≈ 57.1 m/s ≈ 1.14 kg·m/s ≈ 7.4 m 25 g ≈ 51.1 m/s ≈ 1.28 kg·m/s ≈ 9.2 m Same 32.6 J: the heavier arrow is slower but carries more momentum (m × v), which helps it hold its line in wind. 25 g: t = 70 ÷ 51.1 ≈ 1.37 s; drop ≈ 9.2 m. A 30 g arrow from the same bow (32.6 J): what speed?

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Spine, the archer's paradox & fletching
chunks.text: v = √(2 × 32.6 ÷ 0.030) ≈ 46.6 m/s . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Aiming, angles & scoring
chunks.text: At 70 m, the 10-ring is a tenth of a degree wide. World Archery's recurve face at 70 m is 122 cm across with a 12.2 cm 10-ring; the compound face at 50 m is 80 cm with an 8 cm 10-ring. The angle a ring covers is angle ≈ size ÷ distance (in radians). Worked example · how small the 10 really is Division Distance 10-ring Angle covered Recurve 70 m 12.2 cm ≈ 1.74 mrad ≈ 0.10° Compound 50 m 8 cm ≈ 1.60 mrad ≈ 0.09° 0.122 ÷ 70 ≈ 0.00174 rad. A sight pin 0.8 m from your eye that drifts 1 mm moves the impact about 1 × 70 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 88 mm at 70 m. The five-colour target Ten scoring zones: yellow 10 and 9, red 8 and 7, blue 6 and 5, black 4 and 3, white 2 and 1; a miss scores 0.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Aiming, angles & scoring
chunks.text: On the compound face the outer four rings are usually removed, leaving yellow, red and blue. What angle does the compound 10-ring cover, in degrees? 0.08 ÷ 50 = 0.0016 rad × 57.3 ≈ 0.09° . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Holding, breathing & let-off
chunks.text: The steadiest bow is held by bones and back, not by arm muscles alone. A recurve archer holds the full draw weight while aiming. A compound bow's cams give let-off : the holding weight at full draw is only a fraction of the peak. Either way, small movements at the bow become big misses at the target (Ch 4), so archers build a repeatable posture: bow arm extended, drawing with the back, a consistent anchor point and a settled breath. Worked example · what you hold at full draw Bow Peak draw weight Let-off Holding force Recurve 40 lb none ≈ 178 N Compound 60 lb 80% ≈ 53 N 20% of 60 lb = 12 lb × 4.448 ≈ 53 N. Let-off values vary by bow; 80% is illustrative.

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Holding, breathing & let-off
chunks.text: Breathing and the shot sequence Settle the breath before the final aim: chest movement shifts the bow arm. Hold only as long as it's steady. If you start to shake, let down safely and start again. Clean release: relax the string fingers so the string leaves smoothly, and keep the bow arm still through the follow-through. A 50 lb compound with 75% let-off: what's the holding weight? 25% of 50 lb = 12.5 lb (about 56 N). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, drag & range safety
chunks.text: An arrow is a projectile with real energy. Ranges are designed around that. A crosswind pushes the arrow sideways for its whole flight. Light arrows are pushed around more by the same force, and slow arrows are exposed for longer, so both drift further. Drag also slows every arrow, so the drop at long range is a little more than the no-drag model. Worked example · energy an arrow carries Bow Arrow Speed Energy 30 lb 20 g ≈ 49.5 m/s ≈ 24.5 J 40 lb 20 g ≈ 57.1 m/s ≈ 32.6 J ½ × 0.020 × 57.1² ≈ 32.6 J. Launched at 45°, a no-drag arrow from this bow could fly about v² ÷ g ≈ 330 m: one reason ranges need clear zones well behind the targets. How much drag, really?

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, drag & range safety
chunks.text: A wind-tunnel answer Miyazaki and colleagues measured an Easton A/C/E target arrow in Japan's JAXA magnetic-suspension wind tunnel (the arrow floats in a magnetic field, so no support disturbs the air) and in free flight ( Sports Engineering, 2013 ). With a smooth, laminar boundary layer the drag coefficient was about 1.5 ; once the flow along the shaft turned turbulent , at higher speeds and depending on the point and vanes, it rose to about 2.6 . A typical target arrow at 57 m/s sits right in the speed range where that switch happens.

chunks.text: Worked example · our 20 g arrow at 57.1 m/s, 5.5 mm shaft (illustrative), sea-level air Distance Speed left (Cd 1.5 / 2.6) Extra flight time vs no drag Drift in a 3 m/s crosswind 30 m 55.3 / 54.0 m/s 0.009 / 0.015 s ≈ 3 / 4 cm 50 m 54.1 / 52.0 m/s 0.024 / 0.042 s ≈ 7 / 13 cm 70 m 53.0 / 50.2 m/s 0.047 / 0.083 s ≈ 14 / 25 cm 90 m 51.9 / 48.3 m/s 0.078 / 0.139 s ≈ 23 / 42 cm Drag force F = ½ ρ v² C d A, with A = π × (0.00275 m)² ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ m²: at launch about 0.07 N (laminar) or 0.12 N (turbulent). Speed falls as v = v₀ e −kx with k = ρ C d A ÷ 2m. For drift we use the "lag time" rule from ballistics: sideways drift ≈ wind speed × (real flight time − flight time with no drag).

chunks.title: Archery · Physics of Bows, Arrows & Aim · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, drag & range safety
chunks.text: It assumes the fletching keeps the arrow pointing along its flight path; gusts, vane shape and spin all add their own effects. At 70 m a 25 cm drift is two 10-rings wide, which is why archers read flags and aim off. Safety Range rules Shoot only at a supervised range. Nock and draw only on the shooting line and only towards the targets. Nobody goes forward of the line until every archer has stopped and the signal is given. Never "dry-fire" a bow (release without an arrow): the energy goes into the limbs and can break them. Doubling arrow speed multiplies its energy by how much? E ∝ v², so by 4 . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The archery ladder

chunks.heading: When the sea stands up eight storeys tall.
chunks.text: No Indian school or governing body found as of Oct 2026. Big-wave surfers ride the energy of distant storms, focused by the seabed into faces taller than buildings. Learn why energy grows with height squared, how canyons focus swell, why surfers get towed in and why whitewater won't hold you up. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science 3 m 26 m 25× The energy in a 15 m wave compared with a 3 m one. Energy grows with height squared. ≈ 49 km/h How fast a 15 m wave moves as it breaks. Too fast to paddle into, so surfers are towed in. −40% Lift lost from a float in whitewater that's 40% air. Foam is part air, and air doesn't hold you up.

chunks.heading: Before you consider it
chunks.text: It takes years of surfing first. Big waves come after you're at home in heavy surf, not instead of it. It's a team sport. chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Scale a wave up and watch the energy and speed run away from you
chunks.text: Textbook linear wave theory: energy per square metre of sea ⅛ρgH², deep-water wavelength gT² ÷ 2π, energy travelling at half the crest speed, a rule-of-thumb breaking depth of height ÷ 0.78 and wave speed √(g × depth) there. Real big waves are steeper and messier than this theory. For learning only.

chunks.heading: Scale a wave up and watch the energy and speed run away from you
chunks.text: Big-wave surfing is learned with a tow and rescue team, never from a lab. CH 1

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How big is big: measuring a wave
chunks.text: The biggest wave ever recorded as surfed stood 26.21 m from trough to crest: taller than an eight-storey building. Big-wave records measure the face from the trough in front of the wave to its crest . Guinness World Records lists the largest wave surfed (unlimited, male) as 26.21 m (86 ft), ridden by Sebastian Steudtner at Praia do Norte, Nazaré, Portugal, on 29 October 2020, authenticated by the World Surf League. Guinness notes that the accuracy of a wave measurement depends on things like the weather and the camera angles, and that frames were extracted and corrected geometrically for the camera's position and tilt.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How big is big: measuring a wave
chunks.text: Worked example · how wave height scales (example 3 m per storey) Face height About this many storeys Energy vs a 3 m wave 3 m 1 1 × 10 m 3 ≈ 11 × 15 m 5 25 × 26.21 m (record) ≈ 9 ≈ 76 × Energy grows with height squared ( Ch 2 ): (15 ÷ 3)² = 25; (26.21 ÷ 3)² ≈ 76. Why measuring is hard Moving reference: the trough and crest move and change shape every second. Photos, not tape measures: heights come from images, corrected for where the camera was. Surfers as a scale: analysts use the rider's known size in the frame. A 12 m wave versus a 3 m wave: how much more energy? (12 ÷ 3)² = 16 times . Sources: Guinness World Records · Guinness: how the wave was measured ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy grows with height squared
chunks.text: A 15 m face carries about 25 times the energy of a 3 m one. In linear wave theory the energy stored in each square metre of sea is E = ⅛ ρ g H² (ρ ≈ 1,025 kg/m³ for seawater). Double the height and the energy quadruples. Breaking big waves are steeper and more chaotic than this theory assumes, so treat it as a guide to scale, not an exact figure. Worked example · energy per square metre of sea Height E = ⅛ρgH² vs 3 m 3 m ≈ 11 kJ 1 × 6 m ≈ 45 kJ 4 × 15 m ≈ 283 kJ 25 × 20 m ≈ 503 kJ ≈ 44 × 15 m: 1,025 × 9.81 × 225 ÷ 8 ≈ 282,800 J per m². That's the energy in every square metre of sea surface the wave covers.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy grows with height squared
chunks.text: What that energy does Impact: a falling lip and the whitewater behind it hit with far more force than "a bit bigger" suggests. Distance: the energy pushes surfers and boards a long way underwater and towards the rocks. Equipment: boards, leashes and rescue sleds all have to survive it. ✋ Feel the number 283 kJ is roughly the energy of a one-tonne car at about 85 km/h, stored in every square metre of a 15 m wave. A 9 m wave grows to 18 m. How much more energy per square metre? 2² = 4 times . Physics: linear (Airy) wave theory, E = ⅛ρgH². ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Long-period swell from distant storms
chunks.text: Giant surf starts as a storm far out at sea, days before it reaches the coast. Big-wave days need powerful, long-period swell. In deep water, linear theory gives wavelength L = gT² ÷ 2π and crest speed c = gT ÷ 2π ; the energy travels at the group speed, half of c. Longer periods mean longer, faster waves that reach deeper into the sea and feel the seabed sooner.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Long-period swell from distant storms
chunks.text: Worked example · deep-water swell by period Period Wavelength Crest speed Energy travels at 1,000 km takes 12 s ≈ 225 m 18.7 m/s 33.7 km/h ≈ 30 h 16 s ≈ 400 m 25.0 m/s 45.0 km/h ≈ 22 h 20 s ≈ 625 m 31.2 m/s 56.2 km/h ≈ 18 h T = 16 s: L = 9.81 × 256 ÷ 6.283 ≈ 400 m; c ≈ 25.0 m/s; group speed 12.5 m/s = 45 km/h; 1,000 km ÷ 45 km/h ≈ 22 h. Reading a big-wave forecast Period matters: long-period swell carries more power for the same height and travels faster. Direction matters: a spot only "turns on" when swell arrives from the angle its seabed focuses ( Ch 4 ).

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Long-period swell from distant storms
chunks.text: Calls are made days ahead: the WSL issues a Yellow Alert up to 72 hours before a possible Nazaré event day, then a Green Alert when it's on within 24 hours. An 18-second swell: how long are the waves in deep water? L ≈ 1.56 × 18² ≈ 506 m . Physics: linear wave theory. Event calls: WSL: TUDOR Nazaré Big Wave Challenge ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Seabed shape: why some spots grow giants
chunks.text: Waves bend towards shallow water. Shape the seabed right and it focuses a swell onto one stretch of coast. Once a wave feels the bottom, its speed depends on depth: slower in shallow water, faster in deep. Where part of a crest runs over deeper water it gets ahead, and the crest swings round towards the shallower side: refraction , the same bending that light does in a lens.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Seabed shape: why some spots grow giants
chunks.text: At Nazaré, Portugal's Instituto Hidrográfico describes a submarine canyon whose head, a few hundred metres off the beach, reaches about 150 m deep while the seabed beside it is no more than 20 m, and attributes the wave amplification near the coast to refraction caused by the canyon combined with the nearshore dynamics near its head. Worked example · wave speed over different depths (full linear dispersion relation) Depth 16 s swell 18 s swell 20 m (shelf beside the canyon) ≈ 13.3 m/s ≈ 13.4 m/s 50 m ≈ 19.2 m/s ≈ 19.8 m/s 150 m (canyon head) ≈ 24.6 m/s ≈ 27.0 m/s Solved from ω² = g k tanh(k d), with ω = 2π ÷ T.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Seabed shape: why some spots grow giants
chunks.text: For an 18 s swell the same crest runs about twice as fast over the canyon as over the shelf beside it, which bends it sharply. What refraction does Focusing: energy that was spread along a long crest gets squeezed onto a shorter stretch, so the waves there grow. Direction-sensitive: only swell from certain angles is focused, which is why forecasters watch direction as closely as size. Shoaling: as the wave reaches shallow water it slows and grows taller before breaking ( Ch 5 ). In shallow water, wave speed is about √(g × depth). How fast is a wave over 10 m of water? √(9.81 × 10) ≈ 9.9 m/s (about 36 km/h). Sources: Instituto Hidrográfico: Hidromar 113 (Portuguese, PDF) .

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tow-in: matching the wave's speed
chunks.text: A breaking giant moves at motorway speed. To catch one, many big-wave surfers get towed in behind a jet ski. A wave breaks roughly when its height reaches about 0.78 times the water depth (a beach rule of thumb), and its speed there is about c ≈ √(g d) . The bigger the wave, the deeper it breaks and the faster it moves. In tow-in surfing a jet ski driver pulls the surfer up to speed and lets go on the wave. The WSL's TUDOR Nazaré Big Wave Challenge is a one-day tow-in event, run only when the swell is 25 feet or more; the WSL says every team member must be able to tow in and rescue their partner.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tow-in: matching the wave's speed
chunks.text: Worked example · speed of a breaking wave (rule of thumb H ≈ 0.78 d) Wave height Breaks in about Wave speed there Dropping the full face, no friction 3 m 3.8 m ≈ 22 km/h ≈ 28 km/h 10 m 12.8 m ≈ 40 km/h ≈ 50 km/h 15 m 19.2 m ≈ 49 km/h ≈ 62 km/h 20 m 25.6 m ≈ 57 km/h ≈ 71 km/h 15 m: d ≈ 15 ÷ 0.78 ≈ 19.2 m; √(9.81 × 19.2) ≈ 13.7 m/s ≈ 49 km/h. Drop: √(2 × 9.81 × 15) ≈ 17.2 m/s ≈ 62 km/h, an upper bound because water drag and the moving face cut it. How the team works Driver and surfer: in the WSL tow-in format, each team pairs riders with a jet ski driver. Speed and timing: the driver matches the swell, the surfer lets go at the right moment, and the driver circles back to pick them up.

chunks.heading: Tow-in: matching the wave's speed
chunks.text: Rescue is part of the job: Jet Resgate's tow-in course in Nazaré covers waves and oceanography, towing and piloting technique, and rescue and basic life support. A wave breaks in 16 m of water. Roughly how fast is it moving? √(9.81 × 16) ≈ 12.5 m/s ≈ 45 km/h . Sources: WSL: TUDOR Nazaré Big Wave Challenge format · Jet Resgate courses ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wipeouts, foam & rescue
chunks.text: Whitewater is part air, and air doesn't hold you up. Archimedes: the upward push on you equals the weight of the water you displace. Breaking waves churn air into the water, so the mixture is less dense, and anything floating in it, you, a board or a flotation vest, gets less lift. lift ∝ density of the water–air mix . Worked example · lift from a float that gives 10 kg of lift in solid seawater Air in the water (by volume) Mix density Lift from the same float 0% 1,025 kg/m³ 10 kg 20% ≈ 820 kg/m³ ≈ 8 kg 40% ≈ 615 kg/m³ ≈ 6 kg Mix density ≈ (1 − air fraction) × 1,025. Lift scales the same way: 10 × 0.6 = 6 kg at 40% air. The air fractions are examples to show the effect, not measurements.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wipeouts, foam & rescue
chunks.text: Rescue standards ISA/ILS water safety: the ISA and the International Life Saving Federation run a two-day surf rescue course with a run-swim-run fitness test (100 m run, at least 100 m swim through the surf, 100 m run, within five minutes), an unconscious board rescue, first aid and CPR. The accreditation lasts two years. Jet ski rescue: Jet Resgate's Nazaré course trains rescue with jet skis and basic life support, with up to 10 people per course. Team first: the WSL says safety is paramount and every big-wave team member must be able to rescue their partner.

chunks.title: Big-wave surfing · Physics of Giant Waves, Canyons & Tow-in · Kinetic by Curiosta

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Fall, stretch, bounce, glide. Gravity does the work; the cord and the cable do the catching.
chunks.text: A bungee jump is free fall followed by an elastic catch; a zip line is gravity on a slope against friction and air. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Bungee & Zip Lab, then see the standards operators follow and where to take your first zip, jump or swing. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First zip Swings & big jumps ≈ 2 s Free fall before a 20 m cord starts to pull. You reach about 71 km/h before it takes hold. 3.6× Your body weight: the harness pull at the very bottom. The hardest moment is the lowest point, not the fall. 5.8 m Ground clearance left for a 110 kg jumper; 40 kg leaves 22.9 m. Why operators weigh every rider before rigging.

chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Bungee & Zip Lab to see how your weight, the cord and the slope change the ride. Interactive · Bungee & Zip Lab

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick your weight, the cord's length and stiffness, the platform height and a zip line's slope, then see the free fall, the stretch, how much room is left at the bottom, the peak pull and your top speed on the zip
chunks.text: A simple model: free fall with no air drag until the cord goes tight; an ideal Hooke's-law cord (real cords aren't, Ch 2); energy is conserved to the lowest point. The zip line is a straight slope long enough to reach top speed, with trolley friction μ = 0.01 and a rider drag area of 0.5 m² in air of 1.2 kg/m³. Learning values only (illustrative): real operators choose cords, rigging and lines by weighing every rider, never with a calculator.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick your weight, the cord's length and stiffness, the platform height and a zip line's slope, then see the free fall, the stretch, how much room is left at the bottom, the peak pull and your top speed on the zip
chunks.text: Your weight 70 kg Cord length (unstretched) 20 m Cord stiffness k 100 N/m Platform height 60 m Zip line slope 6° Free fall before the cord bites 2.02 s Ch 1 · t = √(2L/g) Speed as the cord goes tight 71 km/h Ch 1 · v = √(2gL) Maximum stretch 24.8 m Ch 2 · m g (L + x) = ½ k x² Room left at the bottom 15.2 m Ch 4 · platform − (L + x) Peak pull of the cord 3.6 × body weight Ch 3 · k x ÷ m g Top speed on the zip line 53 km/h Ch 5 · gravity vs friction + drag Bar = how much of the platform height the jump uses. Try 110 kg on the same cord, then a 10 m cord with k = 200 N/m, then a 30 m cord. On the zip line, compare 40 kg and 110 kg riders (Ch 5). CH 1

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall: the first few seconds
chunks.text: Until the cord goes tight, a bungee jump is pure free fall. When you leave the platform, the cord is slack. For the first L metres (the cord's unstretched length) the only big force on you is gravity, so you speed up at about g = 9.81 m/s² . With no air drag, the time to fall that far is t = √(2L / g) and your speed when the cord starts to pull is v = √(2 g L) . Air drag trims a little off those speeds; our Skydiving page shows what happens when you fall long enough for drag to win.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall: the first few seconds
chunks.text: Worked example · free fall for different cord lengths (no drag, from our Bungee & Zip Lab) Cord length L Free-fall time Speed when it goes tight 10 m 1.43 s 14.0 m/s (50 km/h) 20 m 2.02 s 19.8 m/s (71 km/h) 30 m 2.47 s 24.3 m/s (87 km/h) 40 m 2.86 s 28.0 m/s (101 km/h) For 20 m: √(2 × 20 ÷ 9.81) ≈ 2.02 s and √(2 × 9.81 × 20) ≈ 19.8 m/s; × 3.6 ≈ 71 km/h. Doubling the cord length doesn't double the speed: it multiplies it by √2 ≈ 1.41. 🪂 Feel the number Jumpin Heights says its Rishikesh platform is about 83 m high and its Goa platform about 60 m. Even on a 20 m cord, you'd be doing motorway speed before the cord takes hold. How fast are you falling, with no drag, when a 15 m cord goes tight?

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall: the first few seconds
chunks.text: √(2 × 9.81 × 15) ≈ 17.2 m/s , about 62 km/h. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hooke's law & elastic energy
chunks.text: The cord catches you by storing your falling energy, then gives most of it back. An ideal elastic cord obeys Hooke's law : stretched by x, it pulls back with F = k x , where k (in N/m) is its stiffness. The energy it stores is E = ½ k x² , so twice the stretch stores four times the energy. At the lowest point you've stopped, so all the height you lost, L + x, has turned into stretch energy: m g (L + x) = ½ k x² . Solving that quadratic gives the maximum stretch: x = [m g + √((m g)² + 2 k m g L)] ÷ k .

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hooke's law & elastic energy
chunks.text: Worked example · one cord (20 m, k = 100 N/m), different jumpers, a 60 m platform (illustrative, from our Lab) Jumper Maximum stretch Lowest point below the platform Room left 40 kg 17.1 m 37.1 m 22.9 m 70 kg 24.8 m 44.8 m 15.2 m 90 kg 29.6 m 49.6 m 10.4 m 110 kg 34.2 m 54.2 m 5.8 m For 70 kg: m g = 686.7 N; x = [686.7 + √(686.7² + 2 × 100 × 686.7 × 20)] ÷ 100 = (686.7 + 1,794) ÷ 100 ≈ 24.8 m. Check: 686.7 × 44.8 ≈ 30,770 J and ½ × 100 × 24.8² ≈ 30,780 J. Real bungee cords are bundles of rubber strands, and they are not ideal springs.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hooke's law & elastic energy
chunks.text: Their stiffness changes as they stretch, so the force doesn't rise in a straight line, and rubber turns some of the energy into heat on every stretch (it unloads along a different curve than it loads — hysteresis ). That lost energy is why each rebound is a little lower than the last (Ch 3).

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hooke's law & elastic energy
chunks.text: Order of magnitude · energy at the bottom for our 70 kg / 20 m / k = 100 N/m example What Number Note Potential energy lost (mg × 44.8 m) ≈ 30.8 kJ Mostly stored as stretch at the bottom If 20% is lost to rubber heat on the way down ≈ 6.2 kJ Illustrative hysteresis; real cords vary with age and temperature Energy left for the rebound ≈ 24.6 kJ Enough to rise to about 9 m below the platform (Ch 3), not all the way back India's adventure guidelines ask operators to buy rubber from recognised sources, record its shelf life, store it cool, dark and away from UV light, and inspect it regularly, with cords made and certified by the jump masters. A cord stretched 10 m stores 5,000 J.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hooke's law & elastic energy
chunks.text: How much does it store stretched 20 m? E grows with x², so twice the stretch stores four times the energy: 20,000 J . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Peak g, rebound & damping
chunks.text: The hardest pull comes at the very bottom, when you've stopped for an instant. At the lowest point the cord pulls up with k x. What you feel is that pull compared with your weight, k x ÷ m g : "3.6 g" means the harness is pulling on you with 3.6 times your body weight. Your fastest moment isn't when the cord goes tight: you keep speeding up until the cord's pull equals your weight, at a stretch of m g ÷ k , and only then start to slow down.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Peak g, rebound & damping
chunks.text: Worked example · peak pull on a 20 m cord (illustrative, from our Lab) Jumper & cord Maximum stretch Peak pull Top speed 40 kg, k = 100 N/m 17.1 m 4.3 × body weight 75 km/h 70 kg, k = 100 N/m 24.8 m 3.6 × body weight 77 km/h 110 kg, k = 100 N/m 34.2 m 3.2 × body weight 80 km/h 70 kg, k = 200 N/m (stiffer) 15.6 m 4.6 × body weight 74 km/h For 70 kg: 100 × 24.8 ≈ 2,480 N ÷ 686.7 N ≈ 3.6. Top speed comes 686.7 ÷ 100 ≈ 6.9 m into the stretch: v² = 2 × 9.81 × 26.9 − (100 ÷ 70) × 6.9² ≈ 460, so v ≈ 21.4 m/s ≈ 77 km/h. A stiffer cord stops you in a shorter distance, so it must pull harder; a light jumper on a cord meant for a heavier one gets a harder stop. Then you rebound .

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Peak g, rebound & damping
chunks.text: With no losses, energy conservation would fling you straight back up to the platform. Real jumps lose energy to air drag and to heat in the rubber ( damping ). If, say, 20% of the stored energy were lost on the first stretch (an illustrative figure), the 70 kg jumper above would rise to about 9 m below the platform instead of all the way, and each bounce would be smaller until they hang still where the pull equals their weight, about 20 + 6.9 ≈ 26.9 m down.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Peak g, rebound & damping
chunks.text: Safety Who shouldn't jump India's adventure guidelines list medical restrictions for bungee jumping that include heart problems, high blood pressure, neurological disorders, spondylitis and back problems, a recent fracture, surgery or hospital stay, epilepsy, osteoporosis and pregnancy. Jumpin Heights lists similar conditions. Tell the crew about anything relevant, and follow the jump master's decision. A 70 kg jumper's cord stretches 30 m with k = 100 N/m. What's the peak pull in body weights? 100 × 30 = 3,000 N; 3,000 ÷ 686.7 ≈ 4.4 × body weight. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cord length vs jump height
chunks.text: The cord has to be long enough to thrill you and short enough to miss the ground. The lowest point is L + x below the platform, and it must stay well above the ground or water. Chapter 2 showed that a heavier jumper on the same cord goes lower, which is why operators weigh every jumper and have weight limits: India's adventure guidelines give 40–110 kg and an age range of 12–45 years for bungee jumping, and Jumpin Heights and AJ Hackett publish their own limits for each site. There's a neat result for cords made of the same rubber. A longer piece is softer in proportion to its length, k = E A ÷ L (E A is a property of the rubber and its cross-section).

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cord length vs jump height
chunks.text: Put that into the energy balance and L cancels: the stretch is always the same fraction of the cord's length, and the peak pull is the same whatever the length. Longer cords give a longer fall and a lower bottom, not a harder stop. Worked example · a 70 kg jumper on one type of rubber (E A = 2,000 N, illustrative) Cord length k Stretch Lowest point Room left: 60 m platform Room left: 83 m platform 10 m 200 N/m 12.4 m 22.4 m 37.6 m 60.6 m 20 m 100 N/m 24.8 m 44.8 m 15.2 m 38.2 m 25 m 80 N/m 31.0 m 56.0 m 4.0 m 27.0 m 30 m 67 N/m 37.2 m 67.2 m too long 15.8 m Each stretch is 1.24 × the cord length and every row has the same 3.6 × body-weight peak pull.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cord length vs jump height
chunks.text: On a 60 m platform the 30 m cord would reach 7 m below the ground. The 60 m and 83 m heights are the ones Jumpin Heights gives for Goa and Rishikesh; the cords are made up to show the idea. Same rubber, a 15 m cord, 70 kg jumper: how far below the platform is the lowest point? Stretch = 1.24 × 15 ≈ 18.6 m, so 15 + 18.6 ≈ 33.6 m . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Zip lines: slope, sag, friction & drag
chunks.text: On a zip line, gravity pulls you down the slope and the air pushes back. EN 15567-1, the European standard for ropes courses, defines a zip line as an activity in which the participant glides under gravity in a sloping direction. On a line sloping at θ, gravity pulls you along it with m g sin θ ; the trolley's wheels resist with about μ m g cos θ , and the air with ½ ρ C d A v² . You speed up until they balance, at a top speed of v = √(2 m g (sin θ − μ cos θ) ÷ (ρ C d A)) . Gravity's pull grows with your mass but drag doesn't, so heavier riders go faster .

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Zip lines: slope, sag, friction & drag
chunks.text: Worked example · top speed on a straight line (μ = 0.01, C d A = 0.5 m², illustrative, from our Lab) Slope 40 kg rider 70 kg rider 110 kg rider 3° 27 km/h 35 km/h 44 km/h 6° 40 km/h 53 km/h 66 km/h 10° 53 km/h 70 km/h 87 km/h 70 kg at 6°: sin 6° − 0.01 × cos 6° ≈ 0.0946; 2 × 70 × 9.81 × 0.0946 ÷ (1.2 × 0.5) ≈ 216.5, so v ≈ 14.7 m/s ≈ 53 km/h. Real lines sag, so the slope is steep at the start and flattens (or rises) towards the end, and many are too short to reach top speed. Operators say Jumpin Heights' Flying Fox reaches up to 140 km/h and Jais Flight in the UAE up to 160 km/h — those speeds are the operators' claims, not independent measurements on this page.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Zip lines: slope, sag, friction & drag
chunks.text: A cable can never be perfectly straight. Under its own weight it hangs in a curve called a catenary , and a rider pulls a V into it. Near the start the local slope is steeper than the average tower-to-tower angle (hard acceleration); near a rising finish the slope can turn against you and act as a soft brake. At mid-span, the two halves of the cable hold your weight W between them, so the tension is about T ≈ W L ÷ (4 s) for a span L and a sag s: the tighter the line, the bigger the tension. Designers trade sag against tension: too little sag means huge cable loads; too much means a deep, slow middle.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Zip lines: slope, sag, friction & drag
chunks.text: That's why anchors are built so strong; India's guidelines ask that rock anchors hold at least four times the load put on them. Worked example · a 300 m span with a 100 kg rider at mid-span (ignoring the cable's own weight, illustrative) Sag Sag as % of span Cable tension 18 m 6% 4.1 kN 9 m 3% 8.2 kN 4.5 m 1.5% 16.4 kN 981 N × 300 m ÷ (4 × 9 m) ≈ 8.2 kN, more than eight times the rider's weight. Halving the sag doubles the tension. 300 m is the length Flying Fox gives for its longest zip at Mehrangarh Fort. Same line at 6°: a 110 kg rider's top speed is 66 km/h. Roughly why is it higher than a 70 kg rider's 53 km/h? Top speed grows with √m: √(110 ÷ 70) ≈ 1.25, and 53 × 1.25 ≈ 66 km/h .

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Brakes, trolleys & harness load paths
chunks.text: Every gram of you hangs from one chain of parts. Each link has to hold. At the end of the line, your kinetic energy ½ m v² has to go somewhere. Stopping from speed v over a distance d needs an average deceleration of a = v² ÷ (2 d) , so a short, sharp stop means big forces. EN 15567-1 requires a passive braking system to always be in place on a zip line (one that works without anyone acting, such as gravity, a bungee, a net or impact absorbers), a primary brake to control deceleration in the arrival area, and an emergency brake where a failure of the primary brake could cause serious injury.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Brakes, trolleys & harness load paths
chunks.text: Riders who must brake actively need training and equipment, and if the landing can't be seen from the start, departures must be controlled. Worked example · stopping a rider arriving at 53 km/h (14.7 m/s) Braking distance Average deceleration In g 20 m 5.4 m/s² 0.55 g 10 m 10.8 m/s² 1.1 g 5 m 21.7 m/s² 2.2 g 3 m 36.1 m/s² 3.7 g 14.7² ÷ (2 × 5) ≈ 21.7 m/s² ÷ 9.81 ≈ 2.2 g. Spreading the stop over a longer distance is the whole job of a good brake. The load path runs from your body through the harness, the lanyards and karabiners, the trolley's pulley wheels, the cable and finally the anchors or towers.

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Brakes, trolleys & harness load paths
chunks.text: India's guidelines for zip wires ask for a sit harness (with a chest or full-body harness where appropriate), two points of attachment such as lanyards with screwgate karabiners, equipment that meets UIAA or EN/CE standards, a guide's check of the fit before use, and a full inspection by an inspector at least every 12 months. At least one guide per course must be able to bring a stuck rider back to the ground from mid-span within 30 minutes. Our Rock Climbing page works through rope forces and anchors in more detail. A rider arrives at 10 m/s and the brake stops them in 4 m. What's the average deceleration? 10² ÷ (2 × 4) = 12.5 m/s², about 1.3 g .

chunks.title: Bungee & Zipline · Physics of Free Fall, Elastic Cords & Zip Lines · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: No body certifies bungee jumpers or zip-line riders. Instead, standards bodies (ACCT, ERCA, EN 15567, AS/NZS 5848) write the rules operators build and run to, and in India the Ministry of Tourism and the ATOAI publish minimum adventure-safety guidelines for operators to adopt. Those guidelines are not a public “accredited operator” directory. We checked each body on an official source; operator claims about following them are labelled on the cards below.

chunks.heading: How we built this calendar
chunks.text: Peak means a cited source calls those months the best, peak or ideal time, or every source we cite agrees on the season. Where one source gives a narrower peak, the narrower one wins. Possible means the activity runs but it's a shoulder or part month, it depends on the weather, or our sources disagree. Off means closed, banned, or outside every season we found. Year-round rows, like indoor rinks, pools and ranges, say so. When sources disagree, we show the more cautious option and say so in the month's note. Monsoon timings come from the India Meteorological Department's normal onset and withdrawal dates. A normal date is an average, so any given year can run early or late.

chunks.heading: No straight way up: dive by the numbers.
chunks.text: No Indian school or governing body found as of Oct 2026. Cave divers plan every breath, because the only way out is back the way they came. Learn why gas use climbs with depth, how the rule of thirds works, why silt hangs in the water for hours and how buoyancy behaves under a ceiling. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Cavern Full cave ⅓ Of your gas for the swim in: the rule of thirds. A buddy's out-of-gas exit uses the other two-thirds. ≈ 4× Gas each breath takes at 30 m vs the surface. A 2-hour tank up top lasts about 30 min there. ≈ 46 min For stirred-up silt to settle just 1 m. One careless fin kick can blind a passage for hours.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Before you consider it
chunks.text: Open water isn't cave training. Don't enter a cavern, even “just to look”, without cave training and a guideline. It's a ladder, not a leap. TDI's cavern course asks for an open-water card and 25 logged dives first. Buoyancy comes first. Get your buoyancy and trim rock-steady in open water; everything in a cave builds on it. See the training ladder first → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of cave diving?
chunks.text: 15 questions on the overhead, pressure and gas use, the rule of thirds, silt and guidelines, depth and buoyancy: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Gas & Thirds Lab to plan a turn pressure and see whether a shared exit adds up. Interactive · Gas & Thirds Lab

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Plan the swim in, the turn, and a shared swim out
chunks.text: Boyle's law in fresh water (about 1 bar more every 10.2 m), a 200-bar fill and the rule of thirds. Breathing rates are examples you choose; real rates rise with cold, effort and stress. For learning only; it is not a dive plan.

chunks.text: Depth 20 m Your breathing at the surface 20 L/min Buddy's breathing at the surface 20 L/min Your cylinders (200 bar) Single 12 L Twin 2 × 12 L Pressure at depth 2.96 bar Ch 2 · 1 + depth ÷ 10.2 Your gas use there 59 L/min Ch 2 · surface rate × pressure Gas in your cylinders 2,400 L Ch 2 · litres × 200 bar Turn at 134 bar Ch 3 · a third used (66 bar) Time to the turn 13.4 min Ch 3 · a third ÷ gas use Shared exit needs 1,584 L Ch 3 · both of you, same time out You have left 1,608 L Ch 3 · two-thirds at the turn Shared exit 24 L spare Ch 3 · if the buddy loses all gas at the turn Bar = how much of your remaining two-thirds a shared exit would take. chunks.text: Real plans also allow for different cylinder sizes, decompression, flow and stress. Learn gas planning from a cave instructor, not this lab. CH 1

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The overhead: no straight way up
chunks.text: In open water, a problem can end with a slow swim to the surface. In a cave, the only way out is the way you came in. Cave divers call any place with rock or ice above them an overhead environment . The cavern is the entrance zone you can still see daylight from; beyond it is the cave , with no natural light at all. Training agencies set firm limits for each zone. TDI's Cavern Diver course, for example, limits graduates to 61 linear metres (200 ft) from the surface, a maximum depth of 40 m, a continuous guideline, and no restrictions or areas too small for two divers to swim side by side.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The overhead: no straight way up
chunks.text: Worked example · how far "out" really is (example swim speed 10 m per minute) Distance inside Swim out at 10 m/min At 5 m/min (zero visibility, on the line) 30 m 3 min 6 min 61 m (TDI cavern limit) ≈ 6 min ≈ 12 min 200 m 20 min 40 min Time = distance ÷ speed: 61 ÷ 10 ≈ 6 min. Halving your speed doubles the time, and every one of those minutes uses gas at depth ( Ch 2 ). The swim speeds are examples, not standards. Why cave divers train in steps Accident analysis: the NSS Cave Diving Section says analysing accidents produced safety rules that greatly improved survival, published in Sheck Exley's Basic Cave Diving: Blueprint for Survival (1979).

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The overhead: no straight way up
chunks.text: The results: the same NSS-CDS history records cave-diving deaths falling from an all-time high of 26 in 1974 to fewer than five a year after its training programme began. Step by step: TDI's path runs Cavern → Intro to Cave → Full Cave, each with its own limits (see the ladder below). Safety Open-water training isn't cave training An open-water card doesn't cover overhead diving. Don't swim into a cavern or cave, even "just to look", without cave training and a guideline. You're 120 m inside a cave and visibility drops to zero, halving your speed from 8 to 4 m per minute. How long is the swim out? 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes , instead of 15 at normal speed.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pressure & gas use
chunks.text: At 30 m every breath takes about four times the gas it does at the surface. Water pressure adds about 1 bar for every 10 m of sea water, or about 10.2 m of fresh water (many caves are fresh). Your regulator delivers gas at the surrounding pressure, so by Boyle's law each lungful holds more gas the deeper you are: gas use at depth = surface rate × absolute pressure , with P ≈ 1 + depth ÷ 10.2 bar in fresh water.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pressure & gas use
chunks.text: Worked example · gas use in fresh water (example surface rate 20 L/min) Depth Absolute pressure Gas use Minutes from a 12 L cylinder at 200 bar (2,400 L) Surface 1.0 bar 20 L/min 120 min 10 m ≈ 2.0 bar ≈ 40 L/min ≈ 60 min 20 m ≈ 3.0 bar ≈ 59 L/min ≈ 41 min 30 m ≈ 3.9 bar ≈ 79 L/min ≈ 30 min 40 m ≈ 4.9 bar ≈ 98 L/min ≈ 24 min 30 m: P = 1 + 30 ÷ 10.2 ≈ 3.94 bar; 20 × 3.94 ≈ 79 L/min; 2,400 ÷ 79 ≈ 30 min. That's the whole cylinder: with the rule of thirds ( Ch 3 ) you'd turn after about 10. Treating gas as ideal is a small simplification at 200 bar. What changes your gas use Depth: the biggest factor, straight from the pressure.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pressure & gas use
chunks.text: Effort and cold: swimming against flow, task loading and shivering all raise your breathing rate. Stress: fast, shallow breathing burns gas when you can least afford it. TDI's courses include stress management and breathing techniques. ✋ Feel the number A 12 L cylinder at 200 bar holds about 2,400 litres of air. At the example rate of 20 L/min that lasts two hours at the surface, but only about half an hour at 30 m. Your surface rate is 15 L/min. How much gas do you use per minute at 25 m in fresh water? P ≈ 1 + 25 ÷ 10.2 ≈ 3.45 bar; 15 × 3.45 ≈ 52 L/min . Physics: Boyle's law and hydrostatic pressure (ρ g h with fresh water at 1,000 kg/m³).

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rule of thirds
chunks.text: One third in, one third out, one third for the problem you didn't plan for. By 1968 Sheck Exley had proposed the rule of thirds , which the NSS Cave Diving Section says is still used today: you turn the dive when you've used a third of your starting gas. TDI's cavern and intro-to-cave limits write it as penetration limited to "the rule of thirds," or 1/6th if using doubles; its Full Cave level keeps the rule of thirds. The third you keep in reserve is for emergencies, most of all a buddy who loses their gas.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rule of thirds
chunks.text: Worked example · turn pressures and the shared exit Start A third (rounded down) Turn at Left at the turn 200 bar 66 bar 134 bar 134 bar (two-thirds) 230 bar 76 bar 154 bar 154 bar Shared exit, same depth and same time out: you used one third getting in. If your buddy loses all their gas at the turn and breathes exactly as you do, two of you need 2 × ⅓ = ⅔ for the exit: everything you have left, with nothing spare. If your buddy breathes 25% faster, you'd need ⅓ × (1 + 1.25) = 0.75 of your gas: more than you have. That's why thirds is a minimum, and why dissimilar cylinder sizes need their own sums (TDI teaches gas management "to include dissimilar volumes").

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rule of thirds
chunks.text: Using the rule Turn on the first signal: whoever reaches their turn pressure first turns the whole team. Round in the safe direction: round the third down, so the turn pressure is higher. Watch the flow: thirds assumes the swim out takes as long as the swim in. If you swim in with the flow, the exit is against it and takes longer, so the same gas buys less distance home. Safety Thirds assumes things go to plan on the way out Lost line, silt-out and stress all slow the exit and raise breathing. The reserve is there for those, not for extending the dive. You start at 210 bar. What's your turn pressure on thirds? 210 ÷ 3 = 70, so turn at 140 bar .

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Guidelines, silt & zero visibility
chunks.text: One careless fin kick can turn crystal-clear water into brown fog that takes hours to settle. Cave floors are often covered in fine silt and clay. Stirred up, the particles sink very slowly. Stokes' law gives the settling speed of a small grain in still water: v = 2 (ρ grain − ρ water ) g r² ÷ 9μ . Because v depends on the radius squared, a grain ten times smaller sinks a hundred times slower.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Guidelines, silt & zero visibility
chunks.text: Worked example · settling speed in still water at about 20 °C (mineral grains, 2,650 kg/m³) Grain diameter Settling speed Time to fall 1 m 200 µm (fine sand) ≈ 3.6 cm/s* ≈ 30 s 20 µm (silt) ≈ 0.36 mm/s ≈ 46 min 2 µm (clay) ≈ 3.6 µm/s ≈ 3 days 20 µm: r = 10 µm; v = 2 × 1,650 × 9.81 × (10⁻⁵)² ÷ (9 × 0.001) ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ m/s; 1 m ÷ 0.00036 m/s ≈ 2,800 s ≈ 46 min. *Stokes' law only holds for slow, tiny grains; it overestimates the fine-sand speed. Cold water is more viscous, so everything settles even more slowly.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Guidelines, silt & zero visibility
chunks.text: How cave divers deal with it A continuous guideline to open water: TDI requires it at every cave level; divers practise following the line with their eyes closed and sharing air by touch in the dark. Line markers: the NSS-CDS history describes how arrow-shaped markers on the line came to point the way to the nearest exit. Anti-silting finning: TDI's courses train finning and trim that keep water moving up and back, not down into the floor. Lights: TDI's skills include simulating a primary light failure and exiting on a backup light. ✋ Feel the number Clay-sized silt falls about a third of a metre a day. Stir up a passage and the next team may find it still cloudy.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Guidelines, silt & zero visibility
chunks.text: Grain A is 40 µm across, grain B is 4 µm. How much faster does A settle? Speed ∝ r², so (40 ÷ 4)² = 100 times faster . Physics: Stokes' law (water viscosity ≈ 1.0 mPa·s at 20 °C). Courses and history: TDI Full Cave Diver · NSS-CDS history ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Depth: dense gas & the 40 m limit
chunks.text: Deeper gas is thicker gas: harder to breathe, and with more nitrogen pressing on your brain. Air at the surface has a density of about 1.2 kg/m³ (the NASA standard atmosphere gives 1.225 at 15 °C). Compress it and density rises with pressure: at 40 m in fresh water (≈ 4.9 bar) your air is nearly five times as dense, so every breath takes more work. The partial pressure of each gas rises too: p gas = fraction × absolute pressure . TDI's cavern, intro and full cave levels all set a maximum depth of 40 m, and Tech Dive Thailand's deep cave course uses trimix because, in its words, narcosis is an issue to avoid in this kind of overhead environment.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Depth: dense gas & the 40 m limit
chunks.text: Worked example · breathing air in fresh water Depth Absolute pressure Air density Nitrogen partial pressure (79%) Oxygen partial pressure (21%) Surface 1.0 bar ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ 0.79 bar 0.21 bar 20 m ≈ 3.0 bar ≈ 3.6 kg/m³ ≈ 2.3 bar ≈ 0.62 bar 40 m ≈ 4.9 bar ≈ 6.0 kg/m³ ≈ 3.9 bar ≈ 1.03 bar 40 m: P = 1 + 40 ÷ 10.2 ≈ 4.92 bar; density ≈ 1.225 × 4.92 ≈ 6.0 kg/m³; pN₂ ≈ 0.79 × 4.92 ≈ 3.9 bar; pO₂ ≈ 0.21 × 4.92 ≈ 1.03 bar. Why depth limits matter more in caves Clear thinking: following a line, counting gas and solving problems all need a clear head; nitrogen narcosis dulls it. Harder breathing: denser gas means more effort per breath, which raises breathing rate and gas use.

chunks.text: Decompression: deeper and longer dives need decompression stops; TDI's Full Cave course needs separate decompression training if decompression dives are part of it. What's the oxygen partial pressure of air at 30 m in fresh water? P ≈ 3.94 bar; 0.21 × 3.94 ≈ 0.83 bar . Sources: NASA Glenn: Earth atmosphere model · TDI Full Cave Diver · Tech Dive Thailand ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & trim under a ceiling
chunks.text: Rise a few metres too fast in open water and you surface. In a cave you hit the roof. Archimedes: you float when the water you displace weighs as much as you and your kit. A buoyancy compensator (BC) adds lift with a bubble of gas, and by Boyle's law that bubble shrinks as you go down and grows as you go up. Near the surface the change is largest: the bubble doubles in size between 10 m and the surface. Worked example · 2 litres of gas in the BC, fresh water Start depth Rise to Volume becomes Extra lift 30 m (3.94 bar) 20 m (2.96 bar) ≈ 2.7 L ≈ 0.7 kg 10 m (1.98 bar) Surface (1 bar) ≈ 4.0 L ≈ 2 kg P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: 2 × 3.94 ÷ 2.96 ≈ 2.66 L. Each extra litre displaces about 1 kg of fresh water.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & trim under a ceiling
chunks.text: Unless you vent as you rise, a small ascent speeds itself up. Trim and drag Horizontal trim: a flat, streamlined body presents less frontal area, so water drag (∝ area × speed²) is lower and your fins stay off the floor. Stay neutral: small, early adjustments beat big corrections. TDI's skills include buoyancy control, proper trim and propulsion techniques. No dangling kit: anything hanging can snag the line or the rock. ✋ Feel the number Half a litre of extra gas is about half a kilogram of lift: enough to drift you up into the ceiling in a minute if you don't notice. 1 litre of gas in your BC at 20 m (2.96 bar). What's its volume at 5 m (1.49 bar)?

chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Cave diving has no Olympic-style federation. Its rules come from the world underwater federation's standards, training agencies' course standards and cave-diving organisations' safety work. We checked each on its own official website.

chunks.title: Cave diving · Physics of Gas, Thirds & Silt · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: World federation CMAS, the World Underwater Federation Publishes international diver-training standards, including Cave Diver Level II (Apprentice Cave Diver) and three cave-diving instructor levels. cmas.org Training agency Technical Diving International (TDI) Runs the Cavern Diver, Intro to Cave Diver and Full Cave Diver courses, each with published prerequisites and limits. tdisdi.com Cave-diving organisation NSS Cave Diving Section (NSS-CDS) Founded in 1973 by cave-diving members of the US National Speleological Society. Its accident analysis produced the safety rules published in Basic Cave Diving: Blueprint for Survival (1979). nsscds.org
