chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Every watt goes somewhere. Learn where.
chunks.text: On the flat you fight the air; uphill you fight gravity; off-road you fight the ground. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Power Lab, then find rides, brevets, courses and races in India at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Sunday ride MTB race ≈ 24 m To stop from 40 km/h, counting a 1-second reaction. Almost half is covered before you even brake. ≈ 4 g Landing a 1 m drop with only 25 cm of give. Absorb 40 cm with arms and legs and it's 2.5 g. ≈ 92% Of your power goes into lifting you on an 8% climb. Shift to an easy gear before it gets steep. ≈ 80% Of your effort on the flat goes into pushing air. Riding into a headwind can feel like hitting a wall.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Check brakes and tyres before every ride. Two thin contact patches handle every turn and every stop. Be predictable on the road. Ride with the traffic, wear a helmet, and use front and rear lights after dark. Group rides set a pace. Ask the group's average speed, and whether a sweep rider stays at the back. Ask before you book a group ride → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of cycling?
chunks.text: 15 questions on power, air drag and drafting, climbing, gears and cadence, cornering and braking, and trail riding: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Power Lab to see where your watts go on the flat, uphill and off-road. Interactive · Power Lab

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set your watts, the slope, the surface and your position, and see where every watt goes
chunks.text: A simple model: your power is shared between rolling resistance (C rr × weight), climbing (weight × sin θ) and air drag (½ρC d Av², with sea-level air and no wind). It ignores drivetrain losses, so real speeds are a little lower. Drag areas and rolling coefficients are illustrative. For learning only.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set your watts, the slope, the surface and your position, and see where every watt goes
chunks.text: Your power 200 W Gradient 0% Rider + bike mass 85 kg Position Upright (MTB) Hands on the hoods Low, on the drops Surface Smooth road Gravel Dirt trail Steady speed 33.9 km/h Ch 1 · power = force × speed Watts per kilo 2.35 W/kg Ch 3 · what climbing rewards Power to air drag 80% Ch 2 · grows with v³ Power to climbing 0% Ch 3 · m g sin θ × v Power to rolling 20% Ch 6 · tyres and surface Time for 10 km 17.7 min at this steady speed Height gained per hour 0 m/h Ch 3 · climbing rate Bar = speed on a 0–50 km/h scale. Try 8% with each mass, then flat with each position, then the dirt trail. Ride at speeds that suit the road, the traffic and your brakes (Ch 5). CH 1

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Every watt you make goes into rolling, climbing or pushing air. Power is force × speed: P = F × v . On a bike, three forces resist you: rolling resistance ( C rr × m g , from tyres squashing), gravity on a slope ( m g sin θ ), and air drag ( ½ ρ C d A v² ). Rolling and gravity grow in step with speed in power terms; drag power grows with v³ . Worked example · 85 kg rider + bike, flat smooth road, C rr 0.005, C d A 0.32 m², ρ 1.2 kg/m³ Speed Rolling power Drag power Total 20 km/h ≈ 23 W ≈ 33 W ≈ 56 W 30 km/h ≈ 35 W ≈ 111 W ≈ 146 W 40 km/h ≈ 46 W ≈ 263 W ≈ 309 W At 30 km/h (8.33 m/s): rolling = 0.005 × 85 × 9.81 × 8.33 ≈ 35 W; drag = ½ × 1.2 × 0.32 × 8.33³ ≈ 111 W.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Doubling speed from 20 to 40 km/h needs more than five times the power. Drag areas and C rr are typical illustrative values. ✋ Feel the number A bright household LED bulb uses about 10 W. Cruising at 30 km/h on the flat takes about 150 W: fifteen of them, from your legs, for as long as you ride. Rolling resistance, more closely C rr isn't a fixed property of "a bike". It comes mostly from the tyre casing flexing and springing back (hysteresis), so it depends on the tyre's construction, width, pressure and the surface. Because the force is C rr × m g, the power it costs grows only in step with speed, unlike drag.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Worked example · rolling power at 30 km/h, 85 kg rider + bike (illustrative C rr values) Tyre and surface (typical range) C rr Rolling force Rolling power Fast road tyre, smooth tarmac 0.003 ≈ 2.5 N ≈ 21 W Everyday road tyre (our lab's "smooth road") 0.005 ≈ 4.2 N ≈ 35 W Heavy commuter tyre or worn surface 0.008 ≈ 6.7 N ≈ 56 W Gravel (lab) 0.012 ≈ 10 N ≈ 83 W Force = C rr × 85 × 9.81; power = force × 8.33 m/s. At 200 W on the hoods, swapping C rr 0.005 for 0.003 lifts steady speed from about 33.9 to 35.0 km/h; going to 0.008 drops it to about 32.4 km/h.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Why harder tyres aren't always faster: roughness resistance On a perfectly smooth drum, more pressure means less casing flex and lower C rr . Real roads have bumps. A very stiff tyre passes those bumps into the bike and your body, where the vibration is soaked up as heat: that's lost power too. A 2024 model of this "roughness resistance" (Turner, Dublin City University, arXiv:2405.00019) finds it depends mainly on how rough the road is and how stiff the bike-plus-tyre is vertically. On moderately rough roads it can be larger than rolling resistance, and wider, softer tyres (or a more compliant frame) cut it.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: On very smooth roads, the stiff, narrow set-up still wins slightly because it has less drag. The practical lesson: there's a best pressure for each surface, and on Indian secondary roads it's usually lower than the number printed on the sidewall's maximum. Stay within the tyre and rim maker's limits. The crossover: when does air beat the ground? Drag force (½ρC d A v²) and rolling force (C rr m g) are equal at v = √(2 C rr m g ÷ (ρ C d A)) . Above that speed, air is your biggest enemy; below it, the ground is.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Worked example · crossover speed, 85 kg, ρ 1.2 kg/m³ Set-up C rr C d A Drag = rolling at Road bike, hoods, smooth road 0.005 0.32 m² ≈ 17 km/h Upright MTB on gravel 0.012 0.60 m² ≈ 19 km/h Upright MTB on a dirt trail 0.025 0.60 m² ≈ 27 km/h Road bike: √(2 × 0.005 × 85 × 9.81 ÷ (1.2 × 0.32)) ≈ 4.7 m/s ≈ 17 km/h. On a trail, the ground dominates at almost any speed you'll actually ride, which is why tyre choice matters more than an aero tuck off-road. The chain takes its cut Our Power Lab assumes every pedal watt reaches the back wheel. In reality the chain and sprockets lose a little.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Laboratory tests at Johns Hopkins University (Spicer and colleagues, Journal of Mechanical Design , 2001) measured derailleur chain-drive efficiencies from about 81% to 98.6%, with bigger sprockets and higher chain tension scoring better. Lubricant made no measurable difference on a new, clean chain in the lab; the researchers think its real job outdoors is keeping dirt out, and a dirty chain is a different story. A clean drivetrain in a sensible gear (not the smallest sprockets) should sit at the high end.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Power & the three resistances
chunks.text: Worked example · 200 W at the pedals, 85 kg, hoods, flat smooth road Drivetrain efficiency Watts at the wheel Steady speed 100% (lab model) 200 W ≈ 33.9 km/h 98% 196 W ≈ 33.7 km/h 95% 190 W ≈ 33.3 km/h Because drag power grows with v³, losing 5% of your power costs under 2% of your speed. Same model as the lab, with the wheel power reduced. You hold 300 W against 30 N of total resistance. How fast are you going? v = P ÷ F = 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m/s = 36 km/h . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: Your body, not the bike, makes most of the drag. How you sit changes everything. The drag area C d A combines how big you look from the front and how streamlined you are. Sitting upright on a mountain bike, you're a parachute; low on the drops of a road bike, you slice through. The same power then gives very different speeds. Worked example · 200 W, 85 kg, flat smooth road (from our Power Lab) Position C d A (illustrative) Steady speed 10 km takes Upright (MTB) 0.60 m² ≈ 27.9 km/h ≈ 21.5 min Hands on the hoods 0.32 m² ≈ 33.9 km/h ≈ 17.7 min Low, on the drops 0.27 m² ≈ 35.7 km/h ≈ 16.8 min Solve 200 = v(0.005 × 85 × 9.81) + ½ × 1.2 × C d A × v³ for v.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: With C d A 0.32: v ≈ 9.42 m/s ≈ 33.9 km/h; about 80% of the 200 W goes into drag. Drafting A rider ahead pushes the air aside and leaves a wake of slower-moving air. Ride in it and your drag falls, which is why groups ride in lines and take turns at the front. The cost: you're centimetres from another wheel, with little time to react. Ride close only with riders you trust, never on a busy road, and always signal hazards. How much does it help? Earlier studies of small single-file groups found the following riders' drag falling to roughly 70% to 50% of a rider alone.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: Inside a big, tightly packed race peloton the shelter is far greater: a 2018 study by Blocken and colleagues (CFD simulations of 121 riders, checked in four wind-tunnel campaigns; Journal of Wind Engineering and Industrial Aerodynamics ) found riders in the middle and rear of the bunch facing only 5% to 10% of the drag of a rider alone.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: Worked example · power to hold 35 km/h, 85 kg, C d A 0.32 m², smooth road Where you ride Drag vs riding alone Power needed Alone, or on the front 100% ≈ 217 W Second wheel in a small line (upper estimate) ≈ 70% ≈ 164 W Well sheltered in a small line (lower estimate) ≈ 50% ≈ 129 W Mid-pack in a 121-rider race peloton (Blocken et al.) ≈ 10% ≈ 58 W Rolling power (≈ 41 W) doesn't change; only the drag term is scaled. The peloton figure is for tightly packed professional racing on closed roads, not a Sunday group ride. Don't try to recreate it in traffic. Thin air, hot air and wind Drag is proportional to air density ρ, and ρ falls with heat and altitude.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: Same 200 W, same position: Worked example · 200 W, 85 kg, hoods, flat smooth road (standard-atmosphere densities) Where Air density Steady speed Sea level, 15 °C 1.23 kg/m³ ≈ 33.7 km/h Sea level, 35 °C 1.15 kg/m³ ≈ 34.4 km/h About 920 m (Bengaluru's height) 1.12 kg/m³ ≈ 34.7 km/h About 2,200 m (Shimla's height) 0.99 kg/m³ ≈ 36.0 km/h About 3,500 m (Leh's height) 0.86 kg/m³ ≈ 37.5 km/h ρ = p ÷ (R T) from the International Standard Atmosphere. The catch: thinner air also carries less oxygen, so most riders can't hold the same 200 W high up, and the heat that thins the air also makes hard efforts harder. The lab's 1.2 kg/m³ is a round sea-level value.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: Wind changes the airspeed, and drag follows the airspeed. Riding at 25 km/h over the ground into a 15 km/h headwind, the drag power is ½ρC d A × (airspeed)² × (ground speed): about 194 W in total instead of about 93 W in still air. A tailwind does the opposite, which is why out-and-back routes rarely average out the way you hope. ✋ Feel the number Sitting up into a headwind feels like hitting a wall because drag depends on your speed through the air, not over the ground. A 15 km/h headwind at 25 km/h feels like riding at 40 km/h in still air. If you go 10% faster, by roughly how much does your drag power rise? 1.1³ ≈ 1.33 : about a third more power, for a tenth more speed.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag, position & drafting
chunks.text: ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Climbing & watts per kilo
chunks.text: Uphill, the air hardly matters. Your weight does. On a gradient, gravity pulls back with m g sin θ , where tan θ = gradient ÷ 100. Climbing is slow, so drag is small and most of your power lifts you and the bike. That's why climbers talk about watts per kilo and height gained per hour . Worked example · 200 W steady, smooth road, hoods position Gradient Rider + bike Speed Share of power lifting you Height gained per hour 5% 85 kg ≈ 14.7 km/h ≈ 85% ≈ 734 m 8% 85 kg ≈ 10.0 km/h ≈ 92% ≈ 796 m 8% 75 kg ≈ 11.2 km/h ≈ 92% ≈ 894 m 8%, 85 kg: gravity = 85 × 9.81 × sin(arctan 0.08) ≈ 66 N. At 2.77 m/s that's ≈ 184 W of the 200 W. Height per hour = v sin θ × 3,600 ≈ 796 m.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Climbing & watts per kilo
chunks.text: Pacing a climb Steady beats surges: because drag barely matters uphill, extra watts go almost entirely into climbing, but a surge you can't sustain costs you later. Gear down early to keep a comfortable cadence (Ch 4). Descents: the height you gain becomes speed on the way down. Brake before bends, not in them (Ch 5). A 70 kg rider holds 210 W. What's their power-to-weight ratio? 210 ÷ 70 = 3.0 W/kg (using rider mass; the lab uses rider + bike). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gears & cadence
chunks.text: Gears don't make power. They trade force for pedalling speed. The gear ratio is chainring teeth ÷ cog teeth : how many times the rear wheel turns per pedal revolution. Multiply by the wheel's circumference and you get how far one pedal stroke moves you. Then speed = distance per stroke × cadence . Worked example · distance per pedal turn and speed at 90 rpm Bike and gear Ratio Per pedal turn Speed at 90 rpm Road, 50 × 11 (top gear) 4.55 ≈ 9.5 m ≈ 51 km/h Road, 34 × 28 (climbing gear) 1.21 ≈ 2.6 m ≈ 14 km/h MTB, 32 × 10 3.20 ≈ 7.4 m ≈ 40 km/h MTB, 32 × 50 (lowest) 0.64 ≈ 1.5 m ≈ 8 km/h Road wheel circumference taken as 2.1 m; 29-inch MTB wheel as 2.3 m.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gears & cadence
chunks.text: 50 ÷ 11 × 2.1 ≈ 9.55 m; × 90 per minute × 60 ÷ 1,000 ≈ 51.5 km/h. Real circumferences vary with tyre size. Why cadence matters For a given power, a higher cadence means less force on each pedal stroke ( P = torque × pedalling speed ). Spinning a lower gear is gentler on your knees and lets you respond to changes in gradient. Shift before the climb gets steep, while you can still ease the pressure on the pedals. At 80 rpm in a gear that moves you 5 m per pedal turn, how fast are you going? 5 × 80 = 400 m per minute = 24 km/h . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cornering & braking
chunks.text: Two thin contact patches handle every turn and every stop. Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance: d = v t react + v² ÷ (2a) . Under braking, weight transfers to the front wheel, so the front brake does most of the work, until the rear lifts. A rough limit: maximum deceleration ≈ g × (horizontal distance from your centre of mass to the front contact patch ÷ its height). Worked example · stopping at 0.5 g after a 1-second reaction Speed Reaction distance Braking distance Total 20 km/h ≈ 5.6 m ≈ 3.1 m ≈ 8.7 m 30 km/h ≈ 8.3 m ≈ 7.1 m ≈ 15.4 m 40 km/h ≈ 11.1 m ≈ 12.6 m ≈ 23.7 m 30 km/h = 8.33 m/s; braking = 8.33² ÷ (2 × 0.5 × 9.81) ≈ 7.1 m.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cornering & braking
chunks.text: Tip-over limit example: centre of mass 1.0 m high and 0.6 m behind the front contact patch gives about 0.6 g. On gravel or a wet road, grip can be far lower. Cornering To follow a bend of radius r at speed v you lean at tan φ = v² ÷ (g r) : at 10 m/s on a 20 m bend, about 27°; at 8 m/s on a 10 m bend, about 33°. Braking and cornering share the same tyre grip, so brake in a straight line before the bend and release as you lean. Safety On the road Wear a helmet, use front and rear lights after dark, ride with the traffic and be predictable. Check brakes and tyres before every ride. Doubling your speed multiplies braking distance by how much? d ∝ v², so by 4 . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Trails, tyres & suspension
chunks.text: Off-road, the ground fights back. Tyres and suspension decide how much. On dirt, tyres sink and knobs squirm, so rolling resistance rises steeply. Low pressures let the tyre wrap around rocks and roots for grip; suspension and bent legs spread out impacts so the wheels stay on the ground. The roughness-resistance idea from Chapter 1 is at its strongest off-road: every root and rock you bounce over lifts you and the bike, and that energy is lost as vibration in your body unless the tyre or suspension absorbs it first. That's the physics behind wide, lower-pressure MTB tyres and suspension forks. A rigid, over-inflated bike can be slower on rough ground as well as harsher.

chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Trails, tyres & suspension
chunks.text: (Suspension that bobs every time you pedal wastes some power too, which is why many forks and shocks have a firmer setting for climbing.) chunks.title: Cycling & Mountain Biking · Physics of Power, Drag & Grip · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Trails, tyres & suspension
chunks.text: Landing on a downslope (a proper landing ramp) turns much of that into forward speed instead. Safety Learn trail skills properly Walk features before riding them, start small, wear a helmet (and gloves and pads for technical trails), and don't ride remote trails alone. A course such as NIM's mountain terrain biking course is a good place to start. How much faster do you land from a 2 m drop than from a 0.5 m drop? v ∝ √h, so √4 = 2 times faster (about 6.3 m/s against 3.1 m/s), with four times the energy. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The ride ladder

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Get fit
chunks.text: In every adventure sport your body is part of the physics. Here is the everyday fitness, routine, food and sleep that schools expect from a beginner, when to check with a doctor first, and a two-minute self-check. Take the self-check → 6-week starter routine 150 minutes of brisk activity a week (WHO) WHO's adult minimum; 150–300 minutes if moderate. 2+ strength days a week WHO and ICMR-NIN both ask for at least 2. 6–8 h sleep (ICMR-NIN) ICMR-NIN's guidance for healthy sleep. 12 self-check questions, each sourced About two minutes; answers stay in this tab.

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Your body is part of the physics. The forces the sport pages work out land on you, and section 1 shows the three that matter most. Schools teach the skills from zero. They expect the basics you bring, and some write them down; section 3 lists what they ask. Some answers mean a doctor first. That is common and often not a barrier. The self-check flags them, and it is general guidance, not medical advice. Take the self-check → 01 · Your body in the physics

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Engine, shock absorber, life support
chunks.text: Every sport page on Kinetic works out the forces. Three of them land on you. ENGINE

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: You make the power
chunks.text: Lifting yourself is work: mass × g × height. A 70 kg climber gaining 1,000 m does about 687 kJ of lifting work; muscles turn only about a fifth of food energy into that, so it costs roughly 820 kcal. From our mountaineering page (illustrative). SHOCK ABSORBER

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Your legs set the force
chunks.text: Drop from 0.5 m and you land at about 3.1 m/s. Stopping in 5 cm with stiff legs, the ground pushes back with about 11× your weight on average. Bend your knees to stop over 25 cm and it falls to about 3×. Average force = weight × (1 + drop ÷ stopping distance). Illustrative. LIFE SUPPORT

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heart and lungs keep up
chunks.text: At 5,029 m on the HMI basic-course route, air pressure is about 53.8 kPa, so the oxygen pressure in each breath is about 53% of sea level. Underwater, your lungs handle changing pressure instead. Standard atmosphere, from our mountaineering and scuba pages. A stronger engine leaves more in reserve, trained legs absorb more, and a fitter heart and lungs have more margin. That margin is what the next five sections build.

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The numbers behind these three cards
chunks.text: Physics in five minutes works through them step by step: the basics every sport shares, with the sport pages holding the specifics. Read Physics in five minutes → 02 · The baseline

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The baseline, and a 6-week start with no gym
chunks.text: WHO's adult target: 150–300 minutes of moderate activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days. WHO 2020 Fit India protocol ICMR-NIN gives the same shape for Indian adults: 30–60 minutes of moderate activity on at least 5 days, and strength work on at least 2. ICMR-NIN 2024 How hard is moderate? You can talk but not sing. If you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath, that's vigorous. CDC 6 WEEKS

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: A sample week
chunks.text: Mon Brisk walk Tue Strength + balance Wed Brisk walk Thu Rest or gentle yoga Fri Brisk walk or stairs Sat Strength + balance Sun Rest or an easy long walk Weeks Each walk Brisk walking a week Strength 1–2 20 min 60 2 days 3–4 25–30 min 75–90 2 days 5–6 30 min, on 5 days 150 2 days From week 5, walk on the strength days too. Progression rule. Add 5–10 minutes to each session every 1–2 weeks over the first 4–6 weeks. After that, add days or intensity as you tolerate it, and step back if you don't. Dept of Health HK Strength, no equipment Squats, lunges, push-ups (on the knees or against a wall to start), plank, partial curl-ups, stairs. Stop a set when your form starts to slip.

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: A sample week
chunks.text: Fit India protocol ICMR-NIN 2024 Balance and breath Vrikshasana on each leg, walking backwards, yoga asanas and pranayama. Fit India protocol ICMR-NIN 2024 Rest is part of it. Shortness of breath, pain, nausea, vomiting or headache are signs your body needs rest. ICMR-NIN 2024 Check yourself at week 0 and week 6 with the Fit India tests: 2 km walk or run, push-ups, 30-second partial curl-ups, sit-and-reach and tree pose. Fit India protocol 03 · By sport

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Eat, drink and sleep for the training
chunks.text: General guidance for healthy adults from India's dietary guidelines. ICMR-NIN 2024 Protein from food. Cereals and pulses together (about 3 parts to 1), with milk, eggs or meat if you eat them. ICMR-NIN advises against protein supplements; most athletes can get enough protein from food. Plenty of vegetables , at least 400 g a day, and no more than 5 g of added salt. Water. About eight glasses (around 2 litres) a day for a healthy adult, more in heat and with hard activity. Buttermilk, tender coconut water or lemon water help in hot weather; soft drinks don't replace water. Heat.

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Eat, drink and sleep for the training
chunks.text: Drink water even if you're not thirsty, train in the cooler morning or evening, and avoid strenuous activity outdoors in the afternoon. MoHFW heat advisory Sleep 6–8 hours.

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Safety No alcohol before diving or flying
chunks.text: Alcohol slows reaction time and judgement and adds to dehydration, a risk factor for decompression sickness. DAN: "alcohol and diving are not compatible." DAN Indian rules say the same for flying: Mizoram's aero-sports rules turn away anyone who has had alcohol in the 8 hours before an operation, Mizoram Aero Sports Rules 2021 and Gujarat's guidelines bar anyone under the influence from aero and water sports. Gujarat Tourism adventure guidelines For flying after diving, see the scuba page. 05 · Doctor first

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: When to see a doctor before you start
chunks.text: If you're healthy with no symptoms, you can usually begin light-to-moderate exercise without medical clearance and build up gradually. ACSM 2015 Check with a doctor first if any of these apply: Chest pain or pressure, breathlessness at rest or with light effort, fainting, dizziness, or palpitations. ACSM 2015 A heart, lung, kidney or blood-pressure condition, asthma or diabetes. ICMR-NIN 2024 ACSM 2015 Seizures, blackouts or a head injury. Diver Medical Questionnaire BHPA Surgery, a fracture or a hospital stay in the past year. Diver Medical Questionnaire Ministry of Tourism guidelines Pregnancy, or trying to conceive (and no diving).

chunks.title: Get fit: exercise, routine and food before your first adventure sport · Kinetic by Curiosta

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: One breath. Pressure, oxygen and calm do the rest.
chunks.text: Freediving is physics you can feel: water pressure squeezing the air in your body, oxygen and carbon dioxide racing each other, and buoyancy that flips as you go deeper. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Depth & Breath Lab, then find courses in India and abroad. And never freedive alone. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First breath-hold AIDA4 · 38 m ½ How much your lungs' oxygen pressure drops in the last 10 m up. That's why blackouts happen near the surface, not the bottom. 8 min How late the urge to breathe can come if you hyperventilate first. Oxygen can run low by ≈ 3.3 min. Never freedive alone.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: One breath. Pressure, oxygen and calm do the rest.
chunks.text: 3× How much faster hard kicking burns oxygen than lying still. Calm and streamlined buys you time. −50% How much the air in your ears shrinks in the first 10 m. Equalise early and often near the surface; never force it.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Your body helps. With your face in the water, the dive reflex quietly switches you to saving oxygen. The urge to breathe is a CO₂ alarm. It is not an oxygen gauge, so never use it as one. A buddy watches every dive, even in the pool. They meet you on the way up and stay within reach. Ask before you book a first course → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a depth, your lung volume, your weighting, your wetsuit and how much oxygen is left in your lungs, then see the pressure, how far your lungs are squeezed, your buoyancy and what happens to oxygen on the way up
chunks.text: A simple model: sea water adds 1 bar per 10 m; gas volume follows Boyle's law (P × V constant); residual volume fixed at 1.5 L; the body without air is 2.2 kg heavier than the water it displaces; a 3 mm suit holds gas worth 3 L of buoyancy at the surface and a 5 mm suit 5 L, compressing like the lungs. Learning values only (illustrative): real bodies, suits and lungs vary.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a depth, your lung volume, your weighting, your wetsuit and how much oxygen is left in your lungs, then see the pressure, how far your lungs are squeezed, your buoyancy and what happens to oxygen on the way up
chunks.text: Depth 20 m Lung volume at the surface 6.0 L Lead weight 2 kg Wetsuit None 3 mm 5 mm Oxygen left in your lungs 10% Total pressure 3.0 bar Ch 4 · 1 bar per 10 m, plus the air Lung volume here 2.0 L Ch 4 · 33% of surface volume Lungs reach 1.5 L at 30 m Ch 4 · residual volume depth Lung O₂: here → at the surface 30.4 → 10.1 kPa Ch 3 · why blackouts happen on the way up Net buoyancy here −1.1 kg (sinks) Ch 6 · + floats, − sinks Neutral depth 12 m Ch 6 · below it, you freefall Bar = lung volume as a share of the surface volume. Try 30 m, then take the weight off, then lower the oxygen. Real limits come from training with an instructor and a buddy, never from a calculator (Ch 3). CH 1

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The dive reflex
chunks.text: Hold your breath with your face in water and your body quietly switches to saving oxygen. All mammals, humans included, share a diving response . When you hold your breath, and more strongly with a cold, wet face, the vagus nerve slows the heart (bradycardia) and the sympathetic nerves narrow blood vessels in the limbs, skin and gut (peripheral vasoconstriction). Oxygen-rich blood is kept for the heart and brain. A 2021 physiology review reports heart rates as low as 20–30 beats a minute in deep dives, and describes the spleen contracting to push extra red blood cells into circulation.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The dive reflex
chunks.text: Worked example · an oxygen budget in the lungs (illustrative) Item Number How Lung volume after a full breath 6 L illustrative adult Oxygen you can use, from 21% down to 10% 0.66 L 6 × (0.21 − 0.10) Lasts at 0.25 L/min (resting) ≈ 2.6 min 0.66 ÷ 0.25 Lasts at 0.20 L/min (reflex saving 20%) ≈ 3.3 min 0.66 ÷ 0.20 Lasts at 0.75 L/min (kicking hard) ≈ 0.9 min 0.66 ÷ 0.75 Blood and muscle hold more oxygen than this, so real breath-holds can be longer. The lesson stands: relaxing and moving efficiently stretch the budget; effort burns it. Where the rest of the oxygen is The lungs aren't your only tank.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The dive reflex
chunks.text: Haemoglobin in your blood carries most of the body's oxygen, and muscle has its own store (myoglobin). The diving response decides who gets it: by narrowing vessels in the limbs it leaves working muscles to run on their own store and on anaerobic energy, which is why a hard swim up leaves lactate behind. Worked example · oxygen carried by the blood (illustrative) The 2021 review models fully saturated blood with 15 g of haemoglobin per decilitre, each gram carrying 1.36 mL of oxygen: 15 × 1.36 ≈ 20 mL per 100 mL of blood . An adult with about 5 L of blood (illustrative) therefore carries roughly 1 L of oxygen , more than the lungs' usable 0.66 L above.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The dive reflex
chunks.text: The review's model adds about 5% more oxygenated haemoglobin from the spleen during the dive: 0.75 g/dL × 50 dL × 1.36 ≈ 0.05 L . Small, but it arrives when you need it most. You can't use all of it, though: the brain fails long before the blood is empty (Ch 3). 🫧 Feel the number Kicking hard can use oxygen about three times as fast as lying still. That's why freedivers train to be calm and streamlined. With 0.66 L of usable lung oxygen at 0.33 L/min, how long does it last? 0.66 ÷ 0.33 = 2 min . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Oxygen, CO₂ & the urge to breathe
chunks.text: The urge to breathe is a CO₂ alarm, not an oxygen gauge. During a breath-hold, oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises . CO₂ is a powerful stimulus to breathe; low oxygen is a much weaker one. Divers Alert Network (DAN) defines hyperventilation as any breathing that drops your CO₂, such as fast or deep breathing or long exhalations. It doesn't add useful oxygen, but it delays the alarm, so you can run low on oxygen before you feel the need to breathe. DAN's advice: breathe normally until the final breath, and never hyperventilate.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Oxygen, CO₂ & the urge to breathe
chunks.text: Worked example · why a delayed alarm is dangerous (illustrative numbers) Start CO₂ at start Urge to breathe (at 6.7 kPa, rising 0.4 kPa/min) Oxygen runs low (from Ch 1) Normal breathing 5.3 kPa ≈ 3.5 min ≈ 3.3 min After hyperventilating 3.5 kPa ≈ 8 min ≈ 3.3 min (6.7 − 5.3) ÷ 0.4 = 3.5 min; (6.7 − 3.5) ÷ 0.4 = 8 min. The numbers are made up to show the idea: after hyperventilating, the alarm can come long after the oxygen has run low, with no warning in between. Contractions: the alarm getting louder Partway through a long hold, most people feel the diaphragm start to jerk on its own.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Oxygen, CO₂ & the urge to breathe
chunks.text: The 2021 review calls these involuntary breathing movements : they mark the body's "break-point", and they get stronger as CO₂ climbs, oxygen falls and blood pressure rises. They are a signal from your chemistry, not a performance target. How long you hold after they start is exactly the kind of limit you only explore in training, with an instructor and a buddy watching. If CO₂ starts at 4.5 kPa and rises 0.4 kPa a minute, when does it reach 6.7 kPa? (6.7 − 4.5) ÷ 0.4 = 5.5 min , later than the oxygen budget in Ch 1. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hypoxia & blackout
chunks.text: The danger isn't at the bottom. It's in the last few metres, and at the surface. What pushes oxygen into your blood is its partial pressure : the oxygen fraction × the total pressure. At depth, the squeezed lungs raise it; on the way up it falls with the pressure, while you keep using oxygen. Too little reaching the brain ( hypoxia ) can cause a sudden loss of consciousness: a blackout . A DAN article says 99 percent of blackouts happen at the surface or within 16 feet (about 5 m) of it, and that most problems happen in the last third of the ascent.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hypoxia & blackout
chunks.text: Worked example · 10% oxygen left in the lungs on a dive to 30 m (from our Depth & Breath Lab) Depth Total pressure Lung oxygen partial pressure 30 m 4 bar 0.40 bar (40.5 kPa) 20 m 3 bar 0.30 bar (30.4 kPa) 10 m 2 bar 0.20 bar (20.3 kPa) Surface 1 bar 0.10 bar (10.1 kPa) Same gas, same oxygen: only the pressure changes. From 10 m to the surface the partial pressure halves, which is why the end of the ascent is the riskiest part. A margin of a few millimetres of mercury Before a breath-hold, the oxygen pressure in your arteries is around 97 mmHg (13 kPa; the figure the 2021 review starts its model from).

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hypoxia & blackout
chunks.text: The review cites a study of competitive divers in which those who surfaced with about 20 mmHg (2.7 kPa) of oxygen in their exhaled air lost motor control, while those at about 23 mmHg (3.1 kPa) did not. That's a gap of roughly 3 mmHg between "fine" and "can't hold your own head up", which is why no one, however experienced, can feel their way safely to the edge. Now add Boyle: lung gas holding 5.4 kPa of oxygen at 10 m holds only 2.7 kPa at the surface.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hypoxia & blackout
chunks.text: Surfacing: the dive isn't over yet In competition, AIDA only accepts a dive if the diver shows control on surfacing: take off the mask or goggles and nose clip, give the OK sign and say "I am OK", in that order, keeping the airway out of the water throughout. Recreational freedivers use the same idea every time. Divers also take deliberate recovery breaths on surfacing to help restore blood flow and oxygen to the brain, because the risk doesn't end when your face clears the water: remember DAN's figure that almost all blackouts happen at or near the surface. Your buddy stays within arm's reach and watches your face, not the view.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hypoxia & blackout
chunks.text: Safety Never freedive alone DAN's two most repeated rules: never breath-hold dive alone, and don't hyperventilate. That includes the pool: DAN's advice is a capable buddy closely watching you throughout any pool or open-water freedive at any depth . A trained buddy watches every dive, meets you on the way up (for deeper dives, DAN describes buddies meeting the diver at a third of their depth), stays within reach for your recovery breaths at the surface, and knows how to bring you back. One DAN author advises staying out of the water for at least 24 hours after a blackout or loss of motor control.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hypoxia & blackout
chunks.text: With 8% oxygen in the lungs at 20 m (3 bar), what's the partial pressure there and at the surface? 0.08 × 3 = 0.24 bar at 20 m; 0.08 × 1 = 0.08 bar at the surface. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Boyle's law & lung squeeze
chunks.text: Every 10 m of sea adds another atmosphere. Your lungs feel every one of them. Sea water adds about 1 bar of pressure for every 10 m, on top of 1 bar of air. Boyle's law says a gas's pressure × volume stays constant at a fixed temperature, so the air in your lungs, sinuses, ears and mask shrinks as you go down: V = V 0 ÷ P . When the lungs reach the volume left after a full exhale ( residual volume ), simple physics would predict trouble. The 2021 review puts that depth around 40–50 m after a full breath, and describes a blood shift into the chest that limits the effect; going too deep too fast can still injure the lungs ( lung squeeze ).

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Boyle's law & lung squeeze
chunks.text: Worked example · 6 L of air in the lungs at the surface (from our Depth & Breath Lab) Depth Pressure Lung volume Share of surface volume 0 m 1 bar 6.0 L 100% 10 m 2 bar 3.0 L 50% 20 m 3 bar 2.0 L 33% 30 m 4 bar 1.5 L 25% 40 m 5 bar 1.2 L 20% 6 L × 1 bar = V × 4 bar → V = 1.5 L at 30 m. With an illustrative residual volume of 1.5 L, this diver's lungs reach it at 30 m; a bigger breath (8 L) moves that to about 43 m. Exhale dives, lung packing and the blood shift The residual-volume depth depends on how much air you start with.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Boyle's law & lung squeeze
chunks.text: Dive after a relaxed exhale (an "FRC" dive, at functional residual capacity) with, say, 3 L in your lungs and the same 1.5 L residual volume, and you reach it at 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2 bar = 10 m . That's why AIDA leaves FRC dives to its AIDA4 course. Going the other way, many deep divers "pack" extra air with mouth-and-throat gulps on the last breath: the review reports gains of 11–26% (up to 3 L). Packing a 6 L breath by 20% to 7.2 L moves the residual-volume depth from 30 m to (7.2 ÷ 1.5 − 1) × 10 = 38 m , but the review warns that too much packing raises the risk of lung injury and of fainting before the dive even starts. The body also fights back.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Boyle's law & lung squeeze
chunks.text: As the lungs shrink, blood moves into the chest and takes up some of the space: one classic study estimated about 850 mL shifted into the chest on a 40 m dive. It doesn't make the lungs invincible. Modelling suggests the lowest parts of the lungs can start to close from about 18 m, and the review describes lung squeeze showing up soon after surfacing as coughing, coughing up blood, chest tightness or breathlessness. Any of those means stop diving and get medical help. Nitrogen still counts on one breath Each breath-hold dive loads a little nitrogen at depth, as on scuba.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Boyle's law & lung squeeze
chunks.text: Decompression sickness, known in breath-hold diving as taravana , can happen to freedivers, especially with repeated dives and short surface intervals (spearfishing, safety diving, underwater scooters) or extreme depths, and the review notes nitrogen narcosis is not unusual beyond about 70–90 m. On a mixed trip, DIVEIndia's advice is to freedive first and scuba after, not the other way round. Your mask is an air space too: breathe a little air into it through your nose on the way down, or it squeezes your face. Unlike scuba divers, freedivers don't breathe compressed air at depth; our Scuba page covers what changes when you do. A 7 L breath at 25 m (3.5 bar): what volume? 7 ÷ 3.5 = 2 L .

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Boyle's law & lung squeeze
chunks.text: ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Equalisation
chunks.text: The first 10 m are the hardest on your ears. Your middle ears and sinuses are air spaces with stiff walls. As you descend, you have to push air into them to match the water pressure, or the eardrum bends painfully. In the Valsalva method you pinch your nose and push with your chest muscles; it gets harder head-down and as the lungs compress. In the Frenzel method you close the airway to the lungs and use the tongue and throat as a piston on the air in your mouth and nose, so a small amount of air does the job. AIDA teaches Frenzel in its AIDA3 course, and deeper techniques such as mouthfill (storing air in the mouth for the deep part of the dive) in AIDA4.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Equalisation
chunks.text: Worked example · how much an air space shrinks over each 10 m Depth change Pressure change Volume change 0 → 10 m 1 → 2 bar −50% 10 → 20 m 2 → 3 bar −33% 20 → 30 m 3 → 4 bar −25% 30 → 40 m 4 → 5 bar −20% Volume ratio = P before ÷ P after : 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67, a 33% drop. Equalise early and often near the surface; never force it. Why freedivers use small masks Keeping an air space at its size takes extra gas as you go down: volume × (P − 1) in surface litres. A 200 mL scuba-style mask held at full size to 30 m (4 bar) needs 0.2 × 3 = 0.6 L of surface air, 10% of a 6 L breath. A 100 mL low-volume freediving mask needs half that.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Equalisation
chunks.text: The ears need far less, but every millilitre comes from lungs that are shrinking too. Worked example · the mouthfill shrinks as well Frenzel works while the lungs can still push air up into the mouth. Deeper, divers take a mouthfill : a pocket of air in the mouth, "charged" from the lungs before they get too small, and then used for every equalisation below. Charge 0.5 L at 30 m (4 bar) and by 50 m (6 bar) it has shrunk to 0.5 × 4 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.33 L , before you've spent any of it on your ears. That is why mouthfill is an AIDA4-level skill, taught with a coach and a line. By how much does an air space shrink from 40 m to 50 m? 5 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.83, a 17% drop. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, freefall & the disciplines
chunks.text: Swim hard for the first few metres, then let the sea pull you down. Near the surface, air in your lungs and wetsuit makes you float. As both compress, you displace less water; at the neutral depth buoyancy equals weight, and below it you sink without kicking: freefall . The 2021 review says this usually happens within the first 20 m or so, depending on body, suit, weights, lung volume and water. A DAN article warns against overweighting and advises weighting so that a blacked-out diver would end up at the surface.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, freefall & the disciplines
chunks.text: Worked example · 6 L lungs, 3 mm suit, 2 kg of lead (from our Depth & Breath Lab, illustrative) Depth Lungs + suit gas Net buoyancy Surface 9.0 L +5.0 kg (floats) 10 m 4.5 L +0.4 kg 12 m 4.1 L ≈ 0 (neutral) 20 m 3.0 L −1.1 kg (sinks) 30 m 2.3 L −1.9 kg (sinks) Net = 1.025 × gas volume ÷ P − 2 kg lead − 2.2 kg body. At 20 m: 1.025 × 9 ÷ 3 − 4.2 ≈ −1.1 kg. How fast is freefall? Below the neutral depth you sink until water drag balances your net weight. Drag rises with the square of speed ( ½ ρ C d A v² ), so speed settles at v = √(2W ÷ (ρ C d A)) .

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, freefall & the disciplines
chunks.text: With an illustrative streamlined C d A of 0.036 m², the diver above sinks at about 0.76 m/s at 20 m (1.1 kg heavy) and 1.0 m/s at 30 m (1.9 kg heavy), close to the 1 m/s the 2021 review uses in its model dive. The same numbers bite on the way up: you start the ascent at your heaviest, so every kick has to beat that weight plus drag. Good streamlining (head neutral, arms tidy) lowers C d A and saves oxygen both ways; our Swimming page works through drag in more detail.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, freefall & the disciplines
chunks.text: The disciplines AIDA's competition disciplines: STA (static apnea: a breath-hold at the surface, the only one timed); DYN , DYNB and DNF (dynamic: horizontal distance with a monofin or fins, with bifins, or with no fins); and depth: CWT (constant weight with fins or monofin), CWTB (with bifins), CNF (no fins) and FIM (free immersion: pulling down and up the rope). AIDA also lists variable weight (VWT) and no limits (NLT), and says it stopped sanctioning NLT attempts in 2015 because of the extreme risks. Same diver, 4 kg of lead instead of 2: about where's the neutral depth? P = 1.025 × 9 ÷ (4 + 2.2) ≈ 1.49 bar → about 5 m . More lead means sinking sooner, and a harder swim up.

chunks.text: Four agencies dominate recreational freediving: AIDA, PADI, SSI and Molchanovs. Their levels line up roughly as below; the requirements are the ones each agency publishes. Crossovers between agencies need an evaluation by an instructor.

chunks.title: Freediving · Physics of Breath-Hold, Pressure & Buoyancy · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Try it → first certification → advanced → master → competition & instructor
chunks.text: Step 1 · Try it An introduction, no certification needed to start Intro courses AIDA AIDA1 Introduction to Freediving 18+ (16+ with parental consent); swim 100 m non-stop At least 1 day (6 h), maximum depth 10 m SSI Try Freediving · Basic Freediver Basic Freediver certifies you to freedive with a buddy in a pool or confined water to 5 m Science you're using The dive reflex Ch 1 and Ch 2 Step 2 · First certification Freedive with a buddy in open water AIDA2 · Freediver · Wave 1 AIDA AIDA2 Freediver At least 3 days; chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance on a moving base. Four legs, a rhythm, and you on top, following it.
chunks.text: Riding is physics you can feel: a centre of mass over a base that walks, trots and turns, a body that has to soak up the bounce, and a jump that follows a parabola. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Gait & Jump Lab, then see the riding ladder and where to take your first lesson. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First lesson First show 6× How much a 3 cm helmet liner softens a head-first fall. Your head rides about 2.4 m up: always wear a helmet. ≈ 350° How much of the world a horse sees, with blind spots. Approach where it can see you, and speak. 1.16 g How hard a bouncy trot can drop the saddle away. A stiff rider leaves the saddle; soft joints follow it.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance on a moving base. Four legs, a rhythm, and you on top, following it.
chunks.text: 500 kg A horse weighs about seven riders. You can't out-muscle it: riding is signalling, not force.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: You start on a schooled horse. First lessons are with a coach, often on a lead rein or lunge. Each gait has its own beat. Walk is four beats, trot two, canter three: listen, and move with it. Ask who supervises. A listing isn't a safety guarantee: ask about helmets, beginner-suited horses and supervision. Ask before you book a first lesson → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of horse riding?
chunks.text: 15 questions on balance over a moving base, gaits and footfall patterns, shock absorption and posture, the physics of jumping, aids and horse senses, and falls, helmets and body protectors: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Gait & Jump Lab to see each gait's footfall pattern and how speed and angle shape a jump. Interactive · Gait & Jump Lab

chunks.text: Footfall orders follow a 2007 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology (right lead shown for canter and gallop); the spacing of the dots is a sketch, not a measurement. The jump treats the horse's centre of mass as a projectile with no air drag, starting 1.25 m above the ground at take-off, and assumes the lowest part of the horse's tucked-up body passes 0.6 m below its centre of mass. Learning values only (illustrative): real horses adjust their stride, angle and tuck at every fence. Gait Walk Trot Canter (right lead) Gallop (right lead) One stride, left to right: a dot is a hoof landing; the shaded stretch is a moment with no feet on the ground.

chunks.text: EFI show-jumping courses are ridden at 325–375 m/min, about 5.4–6.3 m/s (Ch 4). CH 1

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Your centre of mass over a moving base
chunks.text: Standing on the ground, your base keeps still. On a horse, it walks, trots and turns underneath you. You stay balanced while your centre of mass sits above your base of support . In the saddle that base is your seat bones, thighs and stirrups, and it moves with every step. The German national federation's handbook (reprinted by the US Dressage Federation) puts the rider's aim like this: follow the horse's movement smoothly, keeping your centre of gravity in harmony with the horse's. For the basic seat it asks for the upper body upright above the seat bones and an imaginary vertical line from shoulder to heel. When the horse speeds up, slows down or turns, your base accelerates.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Your centre of mass over a moving base
chunks.text: To stay balanced without gripping, you have to lean so that gravity and the push from the saddle add up along your body. Speeding up at a rate a needs a lean forward of tan φ = a ÷ g ; turning at speed v on a circle of radius r needs a lean into the turn of tan φ = v² ÷ (r g) , the same physics as a cyclist in a bend. Worked example · how far to lean in a turn (illustrative speeds) Speed Circle radius Lean into the turn 3 m/s (a trot) 10 m 5.2° 5 m/s (a canter) 20 m 7.3° 5 m/s (a canter) 10 m 14.3° 7 m/s (a fast canter) 20 m 14.0° 5 m/s on a 10 m radius: 5² ÷ (10 × 9.81) ≈ 0.255, and tan⁻¹ 0.255 ≈ 14.3°. Halving the radius doubles the lean's tangent; doubling the speed quadruples it.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Your centre of mass over a moving base
chunks.text: The horse leans too, which is why a rider who stays upright while the horse tips into the turn ends up off-centre. 🐎 Feel the number A dressage arena is 20 m wide (the EFI describes a 20 × 60 m arena), so a circle filling its width has a radius of 10 m. Canter that circle at 5 m/s and the right lean is about 14°. The horse accelerates forward at 2 m/s². About how far forward must you lean to stay balanced? tan φ = 2 ÷ 9.81 ≈ 0.20, so φ ≈ 11.5° . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gaits & footfall patterns
chunks.text: Listen to the hoofbeats: four, two, three, four. A 2007 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology measured the footfalls of ridden horses with sensors on all four legs. Its footfall table (LH = left hind, LF = left fore, and so on): Walk: four beats. LH, LF, RH, RF at roughly even intervals, with two to four feet on the ground and no moment in the air. Trot: two beats. Diagonal pairs land together, LH with RF, then RH with LF; between them there can be a moment with no feet down. Canter: three beats. On the right lead: LH, then RH and LF together (or nearly), then RF, then a moment in the air. The last foreleg down before that moment (here RF) is the leading leg . Gallop: four beats.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gaits & footfall patterns
chunks.text: The diagonal pair splits: LH, RH, LF, RF on the right lead, then a moment in the air. In that study (eight Icelandic horses ridden in an arena), walks were measured from 0.6 to 3.2 m/s, trots from 1.8 to 6.7 m/s, canters from 4.0 to 8.9 m/s and gallops from 4.7 to 8.8 m/s. The canter and gallop speeds overlapped: what defines a gait is its footfall pattern, not its speed. Speed is stride length times stride frequency, v = L × f .

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gaits & footfall patterns
chunks.text: Worked example · stride length and hoofbeats (illustrative speeds and stride rates) Gait Speed Strides per second Stride length Hoofbeats per second Walk 1.5 m/s 0.9 1.67 m 3.6 Trot 3.5 m/s 1.4 2.50 m 2.8 Canter 6.0 m/s 1.7 3.53 m 5.1 Stride length = speed ÷ strides per second: 3.5 ÷ 1.4 = 2.50 m. Hoofbeats you hear = beats per stride × strides per second: trot 2 × 1.4 = 2.8 per second. The Gait & Jump Lab draws each pattern. Why a horse changes gait: energy If speed is just stride length × frequency, why switch from trot to canter at all?

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gaits & footfall patterns
chunks.text: A classic experiment by Donald Hoyt and Richard Taylor ( Nature, 1981 ) trained small horses to walk, trot and gallop on a treadmill across a wide range of speeds, including speeds they wouldn't normally choose in that gait, and measured their oxygen use. Within each gait, the energy to cover a metre had a minimum at one particular speed and rose on either side. The speeds the horses picked naturally sat close to those minimums, and the switch to the next gait happened where it became the cheaper way to go. A horse pushed to trot very fast is spending more energy per metre than if it cantered.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gaits & footfall patterns
chunks.text: Worked example · what that means for you in the saddle What you feel What the energetics says A trot that keeps speeding up and gets choppy before the horse breaks into canter It's near the top of its trot range, where trotting costs more per metre than cantering would A horse that "falls" back to trot from a slow canter Very slow canter is expensive too; collected canter takes training and strength A relaxed, rhythmical working gait Usually near the horse's own most economical speed for that gait The study's exact speeds were for its own small horses on a treadmill, so we don't quote them as targets.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gaits & footfall patterns
chunks.text: Bigger horses, riders' weight and footing all shift the numbers; the shape of the curve, a cheapest speed within each gait, is the lesson. You hear "da-da-dum … da-da-dum" with a pause after each group. Which gait is it? Three beats and a moment in the air: the canter . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Shock absorption, posture & following the motion
chunks.text: The saddle rises and falls under you. Your joints decide whether you go with it or bounce. Each time a pair of legs pushes off, the horse's body is lifted and then falls back. In trot each diagonal pair does this, so the back rises and falls twice per stride. Model that motion as a smooth up-and-down wave of amplitude A and frequency f: the saddle's biggest downward acceleration is a = A (2π f)² . If that is more than g, the saddle drops away faster than gravity can pull a stiff rider after it, so the rider lifts off and lands again: the bounce.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Shock absorption, posture & following the motion
chunks.text: Worked example · how hard the saddle drops away (illustrative amplitudes and frequencies) Up-and-down amplitude Bounces per second Peak acceleration Compared with g ±2 cm 1.8 2.6 m/s² 0.26 g: easy to sit ±3 cm 2.4 6.8 m/s² 0.70 g ±5 cm 2.4 11.4 m/s² 1.16 g: a stiff rider leaves the saddle ±5 cm 2.8 15.5 m/s² 1.58 g 0.05 × (2π × 2.4)² ≈ 11.4 m/s² ÷ 9.81 ≈ 1.16 g. Doubling the frequency quadruples the acceleration. Riders deal with it in three ways.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Shock absorption, posture & following the motion
chunks.text: First, springs : the handbook's light seat asks for the hip, knee and ankle to work like springs, with a supple ankle letting the heel sink below the toe, and a back that swings with the horse's back, so the rider's centre of mass moves less than the saddle does. Second, rising trot : the rider stands up on one beat and sits on the next, meeting only every other bounce. Third, fewer contact points to brace on : the BHS Stage 1 riding test includes walk and trot without stirrups and trot and canter in a light seat, both of which train balance rather than grip. A collapsed hip or a hollow back, faults the handbook names, makes the rider stiff where they need to give.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Shock absorption, posture & following the motion
chunks.text: Why does a rider who grips hard with the knees bounce more, not less? Gripping locks the joints that act as springs, so the rider's body has to follow the saddle as one rigid lump: when the saddle drops faster than g, the whole rider lifts off . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The physics of jumping: take-off, arc & landing
chunks.text: Once the last hind foot leaves the ground, the arc is fixed. In the air, the only big outside force on horse and rider is gravity, so the horse's centre of mass follows a parabola set entirely at take-off. Legs can tuck and the neck can stretch, but nothing done in the air changes that arc. Leaving the ground at speed v and angle θ, the centre of mass rises (v sin θ)² ÷ 2g , stays airborne for 2 v sin θ ÷ g (landing at take-off height) and travels v² sin 2θ ÷ g . For the top of the arc to be over the fence, the horse has to take off half that distance before it.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The physics of jumping: take-off, arc & landing
chunks.text: Worked example · one horse's flight at different take-offs (from our Gait & Jump Lab, illustrative) Take-off Rise Time in the air Flight Take-off distance 5 m/s at 30° 0.32 m 0.51 s 2.21 m 1.10 m 6 m/s at 30° 0.46 m 0.61 s 3.18 m 1.59 m 6 m/s at 35° 0.60 m 0.70 s 3.45 m 1.72 m 7 m/s at 30° 0.62 m 0.71 s 4.33 m 2.16 m 6 m/s at 30°: v sin θ = 3.0 m/s, rise = 3.0² ÷ 19.62 ≈ 0.46 m, time = 6.0 ÷ 9.81 ≈ 0.61 s, flight = 36 × sin 60° ÷ 9.81 ≈ 3.18 m. A steeper take-off buys height but shortens the flight, so the horse must take off closer to the fence. 6 m/s is 360 m/min, inside the 325–375 m/min the EFI sets for its show-jumping grades.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The physics of jumping: take-off, arc & landing
chunks.text: Landing: where the big forces are The arc is set at take-off, but the forces come at landing, and they go through the forelegs. Meershoek and colleagues ( Equine Veterinary Journal, 2001 ) put force plates under the landing side of a 1 m vertical fence and filmed six experienced jumping horses (599 kg on average), each ridden by its usual rider (74 kg on average). The first foreleg to land is the trailing leg, then the leading leg. Each reached a peak vertical force of about 1.5 times the horse's body weight , and the trailing leg's flexor tendons were loaded harder. Worked example · landing a 1 m fence (Meershoek et al.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The physics of jumping: take-off, arc & landing
chunks.text: 2001, averages) Measure Trailing foreleg (lands first) Leading foreleg Peak vertical force ≈ 1.5 × body weight ≈ 8.8 kN ≈ 1.5 × body weight ≈ 8.8 kN Time on the ground 171 ms 218 ms Peak fetlock flexor moment 2.44 N·m per kg 1.93 N·m per kg Main job Pushes on; hardly brakes Brakes for the first 60% of stance, then pushes 599 kg × 9.81 × 1.5 ≈ 8,800 N, the weight of about 900 kg resting on one leg for a fraction of a second. The study found the peak coffin- and fetlock-joint moments were 82% and 45% higher than published values for trot. That's one reason coaches limit the number of jumps in a session and care about the footing on the landing side. The rider is a projectile too.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The physics of jumping: take-off, arc & landing
chunks.text: The handbook's forward (jumping) seat (upper body in front of the vertical, elastic hip and knee joints, deep heel and knee, quiet hands) keeps the rider's centre of mass over the horse's as the horse's body rotates up and then down over the fence. If your centre of mass gets behind or ahead of the horse's, your two parabolas no longer match, and the difference has to be made up through your seat, legs and hands, usually with a jolt. Fence heights climb steadily: the BHS Stage 2 riding test asks for a course of fences up to 75 cm, the EFI's Preliminary show-jumping grade is 0.90–1.05 m, and its Grand Prix 1.35–1.50 m.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The physics of jumping: take-off, arc & landing
chunks.text: A horse takes off at 6 m/s and 30° and its centre of mass starts 1.25 m up. How high does the centre of mass get? 1.25 + 0.46 ≈ 1.71 m . If the tucked legs hang 0.6 m below it, the horse clears a 1.0 m rail by about 11 cm, and hits a 1.2 m one. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rider–horse system: aids, communication & horse senses
chunks.text: You can't out-muscle half a tonne. Riding is signalling, not steering by force. Momentum is mass times velocity, p = m v . A 500 kg horse carrying a 70 kg rider (illustrative masses) has about 850 kg·m/s of momentum at 1.5 m/s and about 3,400 kg·m/s at 6 m/s. Stopping from that canter in 3 s takes an average force of 3,420 ÷ 3 ≈ 1,140 N, roughly the weight of a 116 kg mass, and it is the horse's legs that supply it. The rider's job is to ask. Riders ask with aids : signals through the seat, the legs and the hands on the reins. The handbook calls a correct seat the basic prerequisite for applying all of them, because a rider who is off balance sends signals by accident.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rider–horse system: aids, communication & horse senses
chunks.text: Equitation science explains why light aids work. The International Society for Equitation Science's training principles say pressure from the bit, leg, spur or whip must be removed at the onset of the correct response , and that light signals should come before a pressure-release sequence so the horse learns to answer the light signal. The release, not the pull, is what teaches.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rider–horse system: aids, communication & horse senses
chunks.text: Worked example · what the horse senses (sources in this page's sources.md) Sense What it can do What it means for you Vision Panoramic view of up to about 350°; 55–80° seen with both eyes when the head is raised (UC Davis) Small blind spots directly below the nose, in front of the forehead and directly behind: speak and approach where the horse can see you Hearing Each ear swivels about 180°, moved by 10 muscles (Extension Horses) Ears turn towards a sound the horse is focusing on: a clue to what it has noticed Touch Skin is the main channel between rider and horse; most sensitive around the eyes, nostrils and mouth (Frontiers review, 2020) Light, consistent leg and rein contact; a busy hand is noise 500 kg + 70 kg = 570 kg; 570 × 6 = 3,420 kg·m/s; 3,420 ÷ 3 s = 1,140 N; 1,140 ÷ 9.81 ≈ 116 kg.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The rider–horse system: aids, communication & horse senses
chunks.text: That's why no rider stops a bolting horse by strength alone. Your horse stops when you squeeze the reins. When should the squeeze end? As soon as the horse starts to respond. Releasing the pressure at that moment is what tells the horse it was the right answer. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls & safety: helmets and body protectors
chunks.text: In the saddle, your head is higher than most doorways. Falling from there is a real impact. Sitting on a horse about 1.6 m tall at the withers, a rider's head is roughly 2.4 m above the ground (illustrative). Dropping from that height, the head reaches v = √(2 g h) ≈ 6.9 m/s, about 25 km/h, straight down, before adding any of the horse's forward speed: in a 6 m/s canter the total is √(6.9² + 6²) ≈ 9.1 m/s.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls & safety: helmets and body protectors
chunks.text: Worked example · stopping a head moving at 6.9 m/s (average deceleration, illustrative) Stopping distance Average deceleration In g 0.5 cm (hard ground, no helmet) 4,761 m/s² 485 g 1 cm 2,381 m/s² 243 g 2 cm 1,190 m/s² 121 g 3 cm (a crushable helmet liner) 794 m/s² 81 g a = v² ÷ (2d): 6.9² ÷ (2 × 0.03) ≈ 794 m/s². Six times the stopping distance means one-sixth of the average force. Real impacts are messier (peaks, rotation, angles), which is why helmets are tested to standards rather than designed on a napkin. Helmets.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls & safety: helmets and body protectors
chunks.text: The EFI's Technical Guidelines make a properly fastened helmet with a three-point retention harness compulsory for anyone jumping a horse, and protective headgear that meets international testing standards mandatory while riding on the show grounds. British Eventing lists the helmet standards it accepts (such as PAS 015 and VG1), recommends replacing a helmet every 3–5 years, and says any helmet involved in a fall where the rider's head hits the ground should be replaced at once, because internal damage isn't always visible.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls & safety: helmets and body protectors
chunks.text: Worked example · how riding helmets are tested (Virginia Tech Helmet Lab summary of the standards) Standard Flat-anvil drop Impact speed Peak acceleration allowed VG1 1.8 m 5.9 m/s 250 g PAS 015 1.8 m 5.9 m/s 250 g (and under 225 g averaged over 3 impacts) ASTM F1163 1.8 m 5.9 m/s 300 g Snell 2.0 m 6.26 m/s 300 g PAS 015 and ASTM also drop the helmet at 5.4 m/s onto a kerb-shaped "hazard" anvil (limits 200 g and 300 g). Compare our 6.9 m/s head drop above: energy goes with speed squared, so (6.9 ÷ 5.9)² ≈ 1.37, about 37% more energy than the standard flat-anvil test, before any forward speed.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls & safety: helmets and body protectors
chunks.text: Passing a standard is a minimum, not a guarantee; the same lab now publishes independent star ratings for riding helmets. Source table: Virginia Tech Helmet Lab, "Equestrian Standards Helmet Impact Criteria" (as of Dec 2022). Body protectors are designed to absorb the energy of a fall, a kick or being stepped on, protecting the chest, ribs and abdomen. British Eventing makes them mandatory for cross-country and requires the BETA 2018 Level 3 or EN 13158:2018 Level 3 standard, the highest of three levels; a good fit covers the chest, ribs and spine and finishes above the saddle when you sit.

chunks.title: Horse riding · Physics of Balance, Gaits, Jumping & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls & safety: helmets and body protectors
chunks.text: Stay off unfamiliar horses, ride with a coach until you're independent, and listen when the coach says a horse, a gait or a fence is too much for today. Safety Protect your head In the saddle your head is about 2.4 m up, and a fall can bring it down at about 25 km/h. A helmet’s crushable liner makes that stop far gentler. Replace any helmet after a fall where your head hits the ground, even if it looks fine, and ride with a coach until you’re independent. Your head hits the ground in a fall but your helmet looks fine. What should you do with it? Replace it. British Eventing advises replacing any helmet after a fall where the head hits the ground, because the damage inside may not show.

chunks.text: In India the EFI runs national competitions and is the country's member of the FEI, the world governing body. Riding schools set their own teaching syllabus; several follow the British Horse Society's system. We checked each on an official source.

chunks.text: World governing body FEI · Fédération Équestre Internationale Governs international Jumping, Dressage and Para Dressage, Eventing, Driving and Para Driving, Endurance and Vaulting; its members are national federations such as the EFI. It describes its mission as celebrating the bond between horse and human, with athlete welfare and ethical partnership with the horse. inside.fei.org Rider-education framework FEI Solidarity · Rider's Education Programme A curriculum from beginner to early competition that national federations can apply to adopt, with two national certificates: a Rider's Diploma and a Rider's Licence. chunks.text: No Indian school or governing body found as of Oct 2026. Under the ice the coldest water is at the top, your regulator can freeze open and the only exit is a hole you can't see. Learn the physics that shapes every ice dive, and how the world underwater federation's standard handles it. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Open water Under ice 4 °C Where fresh water is densest, so 0 °C water sits under the ice. You dive in the coldest water, right below the roof. ≈ 23× How much better water conducts heat away than air. Cold water drains body heat fast. 4.4 m Miss from a 5° compass error, 50 m from the hole. You can't pop up to look: follow the line home.
