chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Grip & Corner Lab to see how the corner, the tyres and the wings change the limit. Interactive · Grip & Corner Lab

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a corner radius, your tyre grip, a straight-line speed, wings and the weight of kart or car plus driver, then see your limit speed through the corner, the g you'd pull, how far and how long it takes to stop, and how much the wings press you down
chunks.text: A simple model: a flat corner taken at the grip limit, with the tyres giving μ times the load on them (Ch 1, Ch 2); downforce ½ ρ C L A v² adds to that load (Ch 6), with air at 1.2 kg/m³. Braking is in a straight line at constant grip, ignoring downforce and reaction time (Ch 5). Learning values only (illustrative): real tyres, tracks and cars are far more complicated, and the limit is found gradually with an instructor, never with a calculator.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a corner radius, your tyre grip, a straight-line speed, wings and the weight of kart or car plus driver, then see your limit speed through the corner, the g you'd pull, how far and how long it takes to stop, and how much the wings press you down
chunks.text: Corner radius 30 m Tyre grip μ 1.2 Speed before braking 100 km/h Wings: downforce area C L A 0 (no wings) Kart or car + driver 150 kg Limit speed through the corner 68 km/h Ch 2 · v = √(μ g r) Sideways g at the limit 1.20 g Ch 2 · v² ÷ (g r) Time through a 90° bend 2.51 s Ch 4 · (π r ÷ 2) ÷ v Braking distance 32.8 m Ch 5 · d = v² ÷ (2 μ g) Braking time 2.36 s Ch 5 · t = v ÷ (μ g) Downforce at that speed none (no wings) Ch 6 · ½ ρ C L A v² ÷ m g Bar = sideways g at the limit, out of 3 g. Try a 120 m corner, then change the weight with no wings (nothing changes: Ch 2). Then set 700 kg, wings of 3 m², a 100 m corner and 200 km/h, and watch downforce lift the limit (Ch 6). CH 1

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tyre grip, slip angle & the friction circle
chunks.text: Four patches of rubber, each about the size of a hand or a postcard, do all the work. Everything a kart or car does (accelerate, brake, turn) is a force from the track on the tyres. A simple model says a tyre can give at most F = μ N , where N is the load pressing it down and μ is the grip coefficient. Racing tyres on dry tarmac can give μ above 1, so they can hold more than the car's weight in sideways force (we use μ = 1.2 as an illustrative value throughout this page). That grip is a budget shared between braking or accelerating and cornering. Draw the forward and sideways forces as arrows: their combination has to stay inside a circle of radius μ N, the friction circle .

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tyre grip, slip angle & the friction circle
chunks.text: Brake at 80% of the limit and only about 60% is left for turning, because √(1 − 0.8²) = 0.6 . Worked example · sharing one tyre's grip (friction circle) Grip used for braking Grip left for cornering 0% 100% 50% 87% 80% 60% 100% 0% √(1 − 0.5²) ≈ 0.87. Grip left falls slowly at first, then very quickly: that's why the last bit of braking into a corner has to be released so smoothly. How does a tyre make a sideways force at all? When you steer, the wheel points slightly inside the direction it is actually travelling. The difference is the slip angle , usually a few degrees. The rubber in the contact patch twists, and that twist pushes the kart sideways.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tyre grip, slip angle & the friction circle
chunks.text: More slip angle gives more force up to a peak; beyond it the tyre slides and the force drops away. That drop is why the limit arrives so suddenly. You're using 50% of the grip for braking. How much is left for turning? √(1 − 0.5²) ≈ 87% : far more than the 50% you might guess. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cornering force: m v² ÷ r
chunks.text: A corner is a constant sideways push towards its centre, and only the tyres can give it. Following a curve of radius r at speed v needs a centripetal force F = m v² ÷ r . On a flat track the tyres provide it, up to μ m g. Setting the two equal gives the limit speed: v = √(μ g r) . The mass cancels, so in this simple model a heavy car and a light kart on the same tyres have the same limit (real tyres lose a little grip per kilo at high loads, so weight still costs a bit). The sideways acceleration at the limit is v² ÷ r = μ g : 1.2 g for μ = 1.2.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cornering force: m v² ÷ r
chunks.text: Worked example · limit speed through different corners (no downforce, from our Grip & Corner Lab) Corner radius Dry, μ = 1.2 Less grip, μ = 0.8 10 m 39 km/h 32 km/h 30 m 68 km/h 55 km/h 60 m 96 km/h 78 km/h 120 m 135 km/h 110 km/h For 30 m: √(1.2 × 9.81 × 30) ≈ 18.8 m/s × 3.6 ≈ 68 km/h. Four times the radius only doubles the speed, because v grows with √r. 🏎️ Feel the number For a 150 kg kart and driver at 68 km/h on a 30 m radius, the tyres push sideways with about 150 × 18.8² ÷ 30 ≈ 1,780 N: more than the whole weight of kart and driver, on every corner. With μ = 1.2, what's the limit speed through a 20 m radius corner? √(1.2 × 9.81 × 20) ≈ 15.3 m/s, about 55 km/h .

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cornering force: m v² ÷ r
chunks.text: ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Weight transfer
chunks.text: Brake, and the nose dips; turn, and the outside tyres take the load. The tyres push on the ground, but the mass of the car sits higher up, at its centre of mass. When you brake at deceleration a, that height creates a turning effect that moves load from the rear tyres to the front ones: ΔF = m a h ÷ L , where h is the height of the centre of mass and L the wheelbase. Accelerating moves load to the rear, and cornering moves it to the outside tyres (with the track width in place of L).

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Weight transfer
chunks.text: Worked example · a 1,000 kg car, centre of mass 0.5 m high, wheelbase 2.5 m (illustrative) Braking at Load moved to the front Like moving… 0.5 g ≈ 980 N 100 kg 1.0 g ≈ 1,960 N 200 kg 1.2 g ≈ 2,350 N 240 kg 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.5 ÷ 2.5 ≈ 1,960 N at 1 g. A lower centre of mass, or a longer wheelbase, means less transfer. Weight transfer is why technique matters. Loaded front tyres grip better, so the car turns in eagerly just as you come off the brakes; lift off the throttle suddenly mid-corner and the rear goes light and can slide.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Weight transfer
chunks.text: Karts are an extreme case: they have no differential (the rear axle is solid), so the chassis is designed to flex and lift the inside rear wheel a little in corners, letting the kart turn. And because grip is shared (Ch 1), drivers do most of their braking in a straight line, then trade brake for steering as they turn in. Why moving load costs grip If μ were fixed, moving load from one tyre to another would change nothing: the total μ N would stay the same. Real tyres are load-sensitive . Pile more load on a tyre and its grip grows, but less than in proportion, so its μ falls a little. Move load across an axle and the tyre that gains it grips less than the other one loses.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Weight transfer
chunks.text: Worked example · one axle carrying 4,000 N, tyre μ falling from 1.3 at 1,000 N to 1.1 at 3,000 N (illustrative) Inside tyre load Outside tyre load Axle's total sideways grip Change 2,000 N (μ 1.2) 2,000 N (μ 1.2) 4,800 N — 1,500 N (μ 1.25) 2,500 N (μ 1.15) 4,750 N −1% 1,000 N (μ 1.3) 3,000 N (μ 1.1) 4,600 N −4% 0 N (wheel lifted) 4,000 N (μ 1.0) 4,000 N −17% 1,000 × 1.3 + 3,000 × 1.1 = 4,600 N. The straight-line μ figures are a teaching model; real tyre curves come from testing. A small transfer costs almost nothing, a big one costs a lot. That's why racing cars are built low and wide, and why sudden, jerky inputs that slam load across the car cost grip.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Weight transfer
chunks.text: The kart's solid rear axle Through a corner the outside rear wheel travels a longer arc than the inside one, but on a kart both are bolted to one axle and must turn at the same rate. Something has to give: one tyre scrubs, and the scrubbing tyres push the kart straight on. The extra distance for the outside wheel is track width ÷ radius as a fraction of the inside path. Lifting the inside rear wheel, through chassis flex and the weight transfer above, removes the fight. You give up that wheel's grip to stop it pushing the kart straight on.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Weight transfer
chunks.text: Worked example · rear track 1.1 m (illustrative), how much further the outside rear wheel rolls Corner radius (kart centre) Outside wheel's extra distance 5 m (hairpin) ≈ 25% 10 m ≈ 12% 20 m ≈ 6% 40 m ≈ 3% At 10 m: (10 + 0.55) ÷ (10 − 0.55) ≈ 1.116, so about 12% further. Every 90° corner adds about 1.1 × π ÷ 2 ≈ 1.7 m to the outside wheel's path whatever the radius. In a tight hairpin that's a quarter more distance, so tight corners are where an unlifted solid axle hurts most. Same car, braking at 0.5 g. How much load moves forwards? 1,000 × 0.5 × 9.81 × 0.5 ÷ 2.5 ≈ 980 N , about 100 kg. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The racing line & the apex
chunks.text: The fastest way round a corner is the one with the biggest radius you can fit on the track. Because the limit speed is √(μ g r) (Ch 2), drivers use the whole width of the track to make the arc as large as possible: outside on the way in, the apex (the point nearest the inside) in the middle, and outside again on the way out. For a 90° bend with inside radius a on a track of width w, the biggest arc that fits has a radius of about a + 3.4 w .

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The racing line & the apex
chunks.text: Worked example · a 90° bend, 8 m-wide track, 5 m inside radius, μ = 1.2 (illustrative) Line Radius Limit speed Hugging the inside 5 m 28 km/h Down the middle 9 m 37 km/h Outside–inside–outside ≈ 32 m 70 km/h 5 + 3.41 × 8 ≈ 32.3 m; √(1.2 × 9.81 × 32.3) ≈ 19.5 m/s ≈ 70 km/h. The wide arc is slightly longer, but you cover it much faster. The perfect geometric arc isn't always the fastest lap, though. A corner that leads onto a long straight is often taken with a late apex : you turn in a little later and do most of the turning early, so the car is straightened up sooner and you can accelerate earlier.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The racing line & the apex
chunks.text: The extra exit speed is carried all the way down the straight, which is worth more than a slightly slower entry. Why does hugging the inside of a bend feel short but lap slowly? Its radius is the smallest, so the grip limit √(μ g r) is the lowest: 28 km/h instead of 70 km/h in our example. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Braking distance & g-forces on the driver
chunks.text: Twice the speed needs four times the room to stop. At the grip limit the tyres can slow you at about μ g, so stopping from speed v takes a distance d = v² ÷ (2 μ g) and a time t = v ÷ (μ g) . Distance grows with the square of speed. On top of that comes the distance you travel before you even press the pedal, which is why track marshals wave flags well before a hazard. Worked example · braking distance at the limit, no downforce, no reaction time (from our Lab) From Dry, μ = 1.2 Less grip, μ = 0.8 Time at μ = 1.2 60 km/h 11.8 m 17.7 m 1.42 s 100 km/h 32.8 m 49.2 m 2.36 s 150 km/h 73.7 m 110.6 m 3.54 s 200 km/h 131.1 m 196.6 m 4.72 s 100 km/h = 27.8 m/s; 27.8² ÷ (2 × 1.2 × 9.81) ≈ 32.8 m.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Braking distance & g-forces on the driver
chunks.text: Lose a third of your grip and the distance grows by half. The distance before the brakes The table assumes you're already braking. Before that, you travel at full speed for your reaction time: d = v × t . Roughly a second is a common rule of thumb for a prepared driver; surprise makes it longer. Worked example · distance covered before braking starts, plus braking at μ = 1.2 Speed Reaction 1.0 s Reaction 1.5 s Braking (from the table) Total with 1.5 s 60 km/h 16.7 m 25.0 m 11.8 m ≈ 37 m 100 km/h 27.8 m 41.7 m 32.8 m ≈ 75 m 150 km/h 41.7 m 62.5 m 73.7 m ≈ 136 m At 60 km/h a slow reaction alone uses twice the braking distance. On a track, marshals' flags and run-off areas buy that distance.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Braking distance & g-forces on the driver
chunks.text: On a public road there's a crossing, a bus or a child in it, which is why speed belongs only on a closed track. Every change of speed or direction is felt by the driver too. At 1.2 g sideways, a head and helmet of roughly 6 kg (a rough figure) need about 7 kg-force from the neck, on every corner of every lap; braking pushes the body forwards into the belts and seat. That's why racers train their necks and core, why the seat is fitted tightly, and why karting and racing schools insist on a proper helmet, gloves and closed shoes. Heat matters too: a closed helmet and race suit in an Indian summer make drinking water part of the plan.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Braking distance & g-forces on the driver
chunks.text: Safety Speed belongs on a closed track At 60 km/h, a slow 1.5 s reaction covers twice the braking distance before you even press the pedal. Listen to the briefing, wear the gear the track requires and obey the flags: they buy you that distance. How far do you need to stop from 150 km/h at μ = 1.2? 41.7² ÷ (2 × 1.2 × 9.81) ≈ 73.7 m , more than twice the distance from 100 km/h. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Downforce & tyre temperature
chunks.text: Wings are upside-down aircraft wings: they push the car into the track. A wing that makes lift on an aircraft makes downforce when it's turned upside down: F = ½ ρ C L A v² , where ρ is the air density and C L A sums up the size and shape of the wings and floor. Downforce adds to the load on the tyres without adding mass, so the friction limit μ N rises while the force needed to turn, m v² ÷ r, doesn't. It grows with v², so it matters most in fast corners. Karts make very little; winged single-seaters make a lot.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Downforce & tyre temperature
chunks.text: Worked example · an illustrative winged car: 700 kg with driver, C L A = 3 m² Speed Downforce As a share of its weight 100 km/h ≈ 1.4 kN 0.20 × 150 km/h ≈ 3.1 kN 0.46 × 200 km/h ≈ 5.6 kN 0.81 × 250 km/h ≈ 8.7 kN 1.26 × ½ × 1.2 × 3 × 55.6² ≈ 5,560 N at 200 km/h. In a 100 m corner with μ = 1.2 the limit rises from 124 km/h without wings to about 149 km/h with them (1.74 g), as our Lab shows. Grip also depends on temperature . Rubber is viscoelastic: as it rolls, it flexes and recovers a little out of step, turning some energy into heat (hysteresis), and that same property helps it key into the track's surface.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Downforce & tyre temperature
chunks.text: Too cold and the rubber is hard and slides early; inside its working range it grips best; overheated, it goes greasy and wears fast. That's why drivers warm up on the first lap, why a session starts gently, and why grip changes as a track rubbers in or cools down. Power and top speed: the cube law On a straight the engine fights air drag and rolling resistance. Drag force grows with v², so the power to push through air grows with v³: P = ½ ρ C d A v³ + C rr m g v . Double the power and you don't get double the speed, only about a quarter more.

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Downforce & tyre temperature
chunks.text: Worked example · a 150 kg kart and driver, C d A 0.6 m², Crr 0.02, 85% of engine power reaching the road (all illustrative) Engine power Theoretical top speed on a long, flat straight 7 bhp ≈ 79 km/h 9 bhp ≈ 87 km/h 14 bhp ≈ 101 km/h 28 bhp ≈ 129 km/h 7 bhp × 745.7 W × 0.85 ≈ 4,440 W, and that balances drag plus rolling at about 21.9 m/s ≈ 79 km/h. Going from 7 to 9 bhp is 29% more power for about 10% more top speed. Real rental karts rarely reach these figures: short straights, gearing and speed limiters keep them slower. They show the shape of the curve, not a track's real numbers. The illustrative car makes 1.4 kN at 100 km/h. What does it make at 200 km/h?

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Downforce & tyre temperature
chunks.text: Twice the speed, four times the force: about 5.6 kN . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · Licences & levels

chunks.title: Karting & Motorsport · Physics of Grip, Corners, Braking & Downforce · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Arrive & drive → karting academy & first licence → national championships → cars → FIA international grades
chunks.text: Recreational karting needs no licence. To race, you need a competition licence from your country's motorsport authority: in India that's FMSCI, whose licence portal lists One Event, Club Sport, National and International licences. International grades follow the FIA's Appendix L. The licence names and rules below come from FMSCI, the FIA and championship regulations; the order of the steps is our suggestion.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Go high, slowly. Thin air, cold and gravity set the rules.
chunks.text: Mountains are physics you breathe: air pressure halving on the way up, temperature falling with every kilometre, every kilo in your pack lifted by your legs, and snow slopes balanced between holding and sliding. Take the challenge, learn the science with an Altitude Lab, then find India's mountaineering institutes and their course ladder. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First trek Advanced course · 5,500 m+ ≈ 50% Of sea-level oxygen in each breath at about 5,400 m. Walking uphill there feels like running at home. 500 m Most to raise your sleeping height per day above 3,000 m. Fitness doesn't protect you from altitude illness. Time does.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Admit to symptoms early. Never go up to sleep higher with any altitude-illness symptoms, however mild. If symptoms worsen, go down. AMS usually improves quickly after descending 300 m or more. It gets colder as you climb. Every 1,000 m up is about 6.5 °C colder, before the wind. Ask before you book a first trek → 01 · The challenge

chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of the mountains?
chunks.text: 15 questions on thin air and oxygen, acclimatisation and altitude illness, cold and wind chill, the energy cost of climbing, slips on snow and self-arrest, and avalanche slopes: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Altitude Lab to see how height, wind and your pack change the mountain. Interactive · Altitude Lab

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick an altitude, the temperature at sea level, the wind and your pack weight, then see the air pressure, the oxygen in every breath, how cold it feels and the energy it takes to climb 1,000 m
chunks.text: A simple model: the International Standard Atmosphere for pressure; oxygen is 20.95% of the air at every height; temperature falls 6.5 °C per 1,000 m; the US National Weather Service wind chill index (defined only at or below 10 °C, with wind of at least 5 km/h); a 70 kg climber whose muscles turn 20% of food energy into lifting work. Learning values only (illustrative): real weather, bodies and mountains vary.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick an altitude, the temperature at sea level, the wind and your pack weight, then see the air pressure, the oxygen in every breath, how cold it feels and the energy it takes to climb 1,000 m
chunks.text: Altitude 5,000 m Temperature at sea level 25 °C Wind speed 30 km/h Pack weight 15 kg Air pressure 54.0 kPa Ch 1 · 101.3 kPa at sea level Oxygen partial pressure 11.3 kPa Ch 1 · 21.2 kPa at sea level Oxygen per breath vs sea level 53% Ch 2 · why you acclimatise slowly Air temperature −7.5 °C Ch 3 · −6.5 °C per 1,000 m Feels like (wind chill) −16 °C Ch 3 · heat loss from bare skin Energy to climb 1,000 m 996 kcal Ch 4 · body + pack, 20% efficient Bar = oxygen in each breath compared with sea level. Try 3,000 m, then 8,000 m, then take the wind to 0. Real limits come from training at an institute and acclimatising slowly, never from a calculator (Ch 2). CH 1

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thin air: pressure & oxygen
chunks.text: The air up high is still 21% oxygen. There's just less of it in every breath. Air pressure is the weight of the air above you, so it falls as you climb. The share of oxygen stays the same, 20.95%, but its partial pressure , the push that moves oxygen into your blood, falls in step with the total: PO₂ = 0.2095 × P . The International Standard Atmosphere gives a good average for the pressure: P = 101.325 × (1 − 2.256 × 10⁻⁵ × h) 5.256 kPa , with h in metres. The CDC's travel health guide says that at about 3,050 m the oxygen pressure you breathe in is only 69% of the sea-level value, and that arriving there quickly can lower the oxygen saturation of your blood to 88–91%.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thin air: pressure & oxygen
chunks.text: Worked example · the route of HMI Darjeeling's Basic Mountaineering Course (standard atmosphere, from our Altitude Lab) Place Altitude Air pressure Oxygen partial pressure vs sea level Sea level 0 m 101.3 kPa 21.2 kPa 100% Yuksum 1,850 m 81.0 kPa 17.0 kPa 80% Tshoka ≈ 3,050 m (10,000 ft) 69.7 kPa 14.6 kPa 69% Dzongri ≈ 4,030 m (13,220 ft) 61.4 kPa 12.9 kPa 61% Chaurikhang base camp ≈ 4,450 m (14,600 ft) 58.1 kPa 12.2 kPa 57% Mt Renok (height-gain climb) ≈ 5,030 m (16,500 ft) 53.8 kPa 11.3 kPa 53% At 4,450 m: (1 − 2.256 × 10⁻⁵ × 4450) 5.256 ≈ 0.57, so 0.57 × 101.3 ≈ 58.1 kPa, and 0.2095 × 58.1 ≈ 12.2 kPa. Real pressure also shifts with weather and season.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thin air: pressure & oxygen
chunks.text: Our Running page shows what thin air does to your pace. Real Himalayan air is a little kinder than the standard atmosphere The standard atmosphere is a mid-latitude average. Near the tropics, especially in summer, the air column is warmer and the pressure falls off more slowly with height. Physiologist John West showed in 1996 that a model atmosphere for these latitudes predicts measured high-altitude pressures to within about 1%: P (mmHg) = e 6.63268 − 0.1112 h − 0.00149 h² , with h in kilometres ( J Appl Physiol, 1996 ). He warns it shouldn't be used above about 45° latitude; all of the Indian Himalaya lies far south of that.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thin air: pressure & oxygen
chunks.text: Worked example · standard atmosphere vs West's low-latitude model Place Altitude Standard atmosphere West model Difference Tshoka 3,050 m 69.7 kPa 71.1 kPa +2% Chaurikhang base camp 4,450 m 58.1 kPa 59.9 kPa +3% Everest base camp ≈ 5,364 m 51.4 kPa 53.4 kPa +4% South Col, Everest 7,986 m 35.7 kPa 37.9 kPa (284 mmHg) +6% Everest summit 8,849 m 31.4 kPa 33.7 kPa (253 mmHg) +7% Measured checks ( West, J Appl Physiol 1999 ): the summit barometer read 253 mmHg in October 1981 and within about 1 mmHg of that in May 1997; a barometer left on the South Col in 1998 averaged 284 mmHg in May, rising to 287 mmHg by August. 1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thin air: pressure & oxygen
chunks.text: The difference is small at trekking heights and matters most near 8,000 m, where every few percent of oxygen counts. Our Altitude Lab keeps the standard atmosphere, so it's slightly pessimistic up high. 🏔️ Feel the number At HMI's base camp, every breath holds a little more than half the oxygen of a breath in Mumbai or Chennai. Walking uphill there feels like running at home. About what share of sea-level oxygen is in each breath at 5,400 m (Everest base camp)? (1 − 2.256 × 10⁻⁵ × 5400) 5.256 ≈ 0.51 : about half. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: Fitness doesn't protect you. Time does. Your body adjusts to thin air ( acclimatises ) mainly by breathing more. The CDC says the crucial first phase takes about 3–5 days after each ascent, and that training and fitness don't change your risk. Go too high too fast and you can get acute mountain sickness (AMS) : a headache like a hangover, with poor appetite, dizziness, tiredness or nausea, usually 2–12 hours after arriving higher. Two rarer forms can kill: HACE (fluid on the brain: confusion, stumbling, drowsiness) and HAPE (fluid in the lungs: breathlessness at rest, cough, falling performance). For both, descent is the key treatment.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: The ascent rules the CDC quotes from the Wilderness Medical Society: don't go from low altitude to sleep above 2,750 m in one day; once above 3,000 m, raise your sleeping altitude by no more than 500 m a day; and add an extra night for every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude you gain. Climbing higher in the day and sleeping lower ("climb high, sleep low") is how courses like HMI's use acclimatisation walks.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: Worked example · planning nights from 3,000 m to 5,000 m with the 500 m rule Night Sleep at Gain Note 1 3,000 m n/a arrive 2 3,500 m +500 m 3 4,000 m +500 m 1,000 m gained 4 4,000 m 0 extra night 5 4,500 m +500 m 6 5,000 m +500 m 2,000 m gained 7 5,000 m 0 extra night 2,000 m ÷ 500 m = 4 days of climbing, plus 2 extra nights. The CDC notes these rules can still be too fast for some people and too slow for others. What the 2024 guidelines say, and how AMS is scored The Wilderness Medical Society updated its guidelines in 2024 ( WMS summary ).

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: The ascent advice is the same idea, phrased slightly differently: above 3,000 m, raise your sleeping altitude by no more than 500 m a day, and take a rest day (no higher sleep) every 3–4 days . Sleeping one night at an intermediate altitude also lowers the risk. It found no benefit from "forcing" fluids, coca products or short puffs from oxygen canisters. For HAPE it advises descending at least 1,000 m, or until symptoms resolve, with as little exertion as possible.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: Doctors and expedition leaders often use the Lake Louise AMS score (2018 version, used by the WMS): four symptoms, each scored 0 (none) to 3 (severe): headache, stomach upset (poor appetite, nausea, vomiting), fatigue or weakness, and dizziness or light-headedness. A total of 3–5 with a headache is mild AMS; 6–12 is moderate to severe. Worked example · scoring two trekkers on the evening they reach 4,000 m Headache Stomach Fatigue Dizziness Total Reading Trekker A 1 1 1 0 3 Mild AMS: don't go higher Trekker B 2 2 2 1 7 Moderate–severe: rest, get medical advice; descend if worse The score helps a group talk about symptoms honestly; it doesn't diagnose HACE.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: Stumbling (failing a heel-to-toe walk) or confusion is a sign of HACE whatever the score: that person goes down. Medicines for altitude are a decision for a doctor, not for this page. Safety The three rules that prevent deaths From the CDC: know the early symptoms and admit to them; never go up to sleep higher with any symptoms of altitude illness, however mild; and go down if symptoms get worse despite rest or treatment. AMS usually improves quickly after descending 300 m or more. Discuss any altitude medicine with a doctor before you go. You sleep at 3,000 m tonight. Using the 500 m rule, which is the earliest night you can sleep at 4,000 m?

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Acclimatisation & altitude illness
chunks.text: Night 2 at 3,500 m, night 3 at 4,000 m , then an extra night there. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cold, wind chill & frostbite
chunks.text: Every 1,000 m up is about 6.5 °C colder. Then the wind arrives. Rising air expands and cools, so the standard atmosphere drops 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m . Wind then strips heat from bare skin faster. The US National Weather Service (NWS) wind chill index turns air temperature and wind into how cold it feels on your face; in metric: WC = 13.12 + 0.6215T − 11.37V 0.16 + 0.3965T·V 0.16 , with T in °C and V in km/h. The NWS says the index is defined only at or below 10 °C (50 °F) with wind above about 5 km/h (3 mph), that bright sun can make it feel 10–18 °F (about 6–10 °C) warmer, and that frostbite needs the actual air temperature to be below freezing.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cold, wind chill & frostbite
chunks.text: Worked example · 25 °C at sea level, at 5,000 m (illustrative, from our Altitude Lab) Wind Air temperature Feels like Calm −7.5 °C −7.5 °C (no wind chill) 10 km/h −7.5 °C −12 °C 30 km/h −7.5 °C −16 °C 50 km/h −7.5 °C −18 °C 25 − 6.5 × 5 = −7.5 °C. At 30 km/h, V 0.16 ≈ 1.72, so WC ≈ 13.12 − 4.66 − 19.59 − 5.12 ≈ −16 °C. The first few km/h of wind make the biggest difference. Layers trap still air, which insulates; wind and wet clothing destroy that. That's why institute kit lists, such as NIM's, ask for heavy woollen socks, two kinds of gloves, a woollen cap, thermal innerwear and dark goggles, and why HMI's course includes classes on mountain clothing and its materials.

chunks.heading: Cold, wind chill & frostbite
chunks.text: Air at 0 °C with a 30 km/h wind: what's the wind chill? 13.12 + 0 − 11.37 × 1.72 + 0 ≈ −6.5 °C . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Load, height & energy
chunks.text: Every kilo in your pack is a kilo you lift up the mountain. Lifting a mass m through a height h takes work W = m g h . Your muscles turn only part of the food energy they burn into that work; our examples use an illustrative 20% , so the energy you burn is about five times the work. Thin air also caps how hard you can work: the CDC notes that maximal exercise performance at high altitude is always lower than at sea level, even after acclimatising.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Load, height & energy
chunks.text: Worked example · a 70 kg climber gaining 1,000 m (from our Altitude Lab, illustrative) Pack Total mass Lifting work Energy burned (20%) 0 kg 70 kg 687 kJ 821 kcal 10 kg 80 kg 785 kJ 938 kcal 15 kg 85 kg 834 kJ 996 kcal 25 kg 95 kg 932 kJ 1,114 kcal 85 × 9.81 × 1000 ≈ 834 kJ; ÷ 0.20 ≈ 4,169 kJ; ÷ 4.184 ≈ 996 kcal. This is only the lifting: walking, keeping warm and the descent cost more. Walking costs too, and the ground matters Lifting work is only part of the bill.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Load, height & energy
chunks.text: Army researchers Pandolf, Givoni and Goldman fitted an equation to measurements of soldiers walking with loads ( J Appl Physiol, 1977 ): M = 1.5W + 2.0(W + L)(L/W)² + η(W + L)(1.5V² + 0.35VG) , in watts, with body mass W and load L in kg, speed V in m/s, grade G in % and a terrain factor η measured by Soule and Goldman ( 1972 ): 1.1 for a dirt road, 1.5 for heavy brush, 2.5 for 15 cm of soft snow, 3.3 for 25 cm.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Load, height & energy
chunks.text: Worked example · 70 kg trekker, 15 kg pack, 0.8 m/s up a 15% trail (432 m of height an hour) Ground (η) Metabolic rate To gain 1,000 m (2 h 19 min) Share that's lifting Dirt road (1.1) 595 W ≈ 1,190 kcal 17% Heavy brush, rough trail (1.5) 771 W ≈ 1,540 kcal 13% Soft snow, 15 cm (2.5) 1,209 W ≈ 2,410 kcal 8% Soft snow, 25 cm (3.3) 1,560 W ≈ 3,110 kcal 6% Standing terms: 1.5 × 70 + 2 × 85 × (15/70)² ≈ 113 W. Walking term: 85 × (1.5 × 0.8² + 0.35 × 0.8 × 15) ≈ 439 W, × η. Lifting power is 85 × 9.81 × 0.12 ≈ 100 W. On a good trail the equation's answer is close to our 20% rule of thumb above; in deep snow the same climb costs two to three times as much, which is why nobody keeps 0.8 m/s in it.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Load, height & energy
chunks.text: Later studies found the equation under -predicts for heavy loads and fast paces, and it doesn't account for altitude, so treat these as minimums. That's why the institutes ask for fitness before you arrive. NIM recommends a month of walking at least 5 km with a 15 kg pack, 30 minutes of cardio a day, and being able to do 20 push-ups and 5 pull-ups, and it tests trainees on a 10 km walk with a load before they go into the mountains (10 kg in its 2026 programme, 15 kg in its 2027 programme). ABVIMAS suggests at least two months of cardio and strength training. A 60 kg climber with a 10 kg pack gains 500 m. About how much energy at 20% efficiency?

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Slips on snow & self-arrest
chunks.text: On hard snow, a slip becomes a slide in seconds. On a slope at angle θ, gravity pulls you down the slope with g sin θ and friction holds you back with μ g cos θ , where μ is the friction coefficient. On hard, icy snow μ is small, so once you slide you keep accelerating: a = g (sin θ − μ cos θ) , and after sliding a distance d your speed is v = √(2 a d) . That's why mountaineers learn self-arrest : rolling onto the ice axe and driving its pick into the snow immediately, before the speed builds. HMI's Basic Mountaineering Course includes self-arrest, glacier travel, fixed ropes and crevasse rescue at its base camp.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Slips on snow & self-arrest
chunks.text: Worked example · sliding on a 30° slope of hard snow, μ = 0.1 (illustrative) Distance slid Speed (m/s) Speed (km/h) 5 m 6.4 23 10 m 9.0 32 20 m 12.7 46 50 m 20.1 72 a = 9.81 × (sin 30° − 0.1 × cos 30°) = 9.81 × (0.5 − 0.087) ≈ 4.06 m/s². After 20 m: √(2 × 4.06 × 20) ≈ 12.7 m/s. Soft snow (μ = 0.3) cuts that to about 9.7 m/s, which still hurts on rocks. Ropes on a mountain work on the same physics as on a crag: stretch absorbs a fall's energy, and the angle between anchor points multiplies the load. Our Rock Climbing page works through fall factors and anchor angles. On a 20° slope with μ = 0.1, what's the acceleration, and the speed after 20 m?

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Snow slopes & avalanches
chunks.text: The most dangerous slopes are steep enough to slide, but not so steep that snow can't build up. Snow falls in layers. A slab avalanche starts when a weak layer under a stiffer slab can no longer hold it. The slab's weight pulls along the slope with a shear stress on the weak layer of about τ = ρ g d sin θ (ρ the snow density, d the slab thickness measured at right angles to the slope), so steeper slopes load the weak layer harder. Avalanche.org says most slab avalanches start where the steepest part of the slope is between 30° and 50°, citing a Swiss dataset of over 1,000 avalanches in which 96% released on 30–50° slopes and most on 34–45°.

chunks.title: Trekking & Mountaineering · Physics of Altitude, Cold & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Snow slopes & avalanches
chunks.text: Avalanches can then run out onto much gentler ground below. Worked example · a 0.5 m slab of snow at 200 kg/m³ (illustrative) Slope angle sin θ Shear stress on the weak layer 20° 0.34 336 Pa 30° 0.50 490 Pa 38° 0.62 604 Pa 45° 0.71 694 Pa 200 × 9.81 × 0.5 ≈ 981 Pa; × sin 30° ≈ 490 Pa. A weak layer that holds 550 Pa would survive at 30° and fail at 38°. Real snow strength varies hugely, which is why avalanche forecasting is a skill, not a sum. Safety This page doesn't teach avalanche safety Avalanche terrain needs training, a transceiver, probe and shovel you know how to use, a current local forecast and an experienced leader.

chunks.heading: Snow slopes & avalanches
chunks.text: HMI's Basic Course includes classes on mountain hazards and avalanches; our Skiing & Snowboarding page covers avalanches from a skier's side. Same slab on a 35° slope (sin 35° ≈ 0.57): what's the shear stress? 981 × 0.57 ≈ 563 Pa . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The mountaineering ladder

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Flying without an engine is applied physics.
chunks.text: A paraglider is a fabric wing that is always gliding downhill through the air. Every climb you see is the air itself going up faster. Learn lift, glide, thermals and stalls with real numbers, and the sky starts to make sense. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science landing cloud base 8.5 km How far a beginner wing carries you from 1,000 m up. No engine, still air. Wind shortens or stretches it. 7 km/h Your ground speed into a 30 km/h headwind on a 37 km/h wing. Wind stronger than your wing and you go backwards. That's why schools set low wind limits. +13% The extra speed a wing needs to fly in thin air at 2,400 m. A harder launch run and faster landings.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Flying without an engine is applied physics.
chunks.text: 2 g A steep 60° turn makes you feel twice your weight. You also sink almost 3× faster: turns cost height.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Wind sets the day. A 30 km/h headwind slows a 37 km/h wing to walking pace. Your weight is part of the flight. Each wing is certified for a weight range; flying inside it matters. “Not today” is a safety call. Most accidents trace back to a decision made on the ground. Ask before you book a tandem → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Do you know what's holding you up?
chunks.text: 15 questions on what's really going on up there: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Six chapters, from launch to landing
chunks.text: Each chapter takes one idea and follows it into the sky, with worked numbers you can check on a calculator. Our reference wing is an illustrative beginner (EN-A-style) glider: about 21 m² of projected area, trim speed 37 km/h and glide ratio 8.5 at 95–100 kg all-up. Real wings vary; your instructor and the wing's manual are the authority. Interactive · Glide Lab

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Set the height and the wind, and watch your glide change
chunks.text: An illustrative model of the reference wing: trim speed 37 km/h at 95 kg all-up at sea level, scaled with √(weight) and with air density. Constant sink, no rising or sinking air. For learning only; it is not a flight planner.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Set the height and the wind, and watch your glide change
chunks.text: Real gliders sink faster at higher speeds (the "polar curve") and the air is never perfectly still, so treat every number here as a teaching example. Never fly over unlandable terrain on the strength of a calculation. CH 1

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & the wing
chunks.text: A bag of nylon becomes a wing the moment air fills it. A paraglider wing is two skins of ripstop fabric joined by ribs into dozens of cells. Openings at the leading edge let air in, and that ram-air pressure inflates the cells into an aerofoil: a curved shape, thicker at the front, that turns the oncoming air slightly downward. By Newton's third law, pushing air down pushes the wing up. The same effect also shows up as lower pressure over the top surface than under the bottom (Bernoulli's principle). They are two descriptions of one flow.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & the wing
chunks.text: The lift equation Every wing, from a paraglider to a jet, obeys L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × C L : air density ρ, airspeed v, wing area S, and a lift coefficient C L set mostly by the angle of attack (the angle between the wing and the oncoming air). The pilot changes C L with the brakes and the speed bar. Worked example · what the reference wing needs at trim Pilot + gear + wing ≈ 100 kg, so weight ≈ 100 × 9.81 = 981 N.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & the wing
chunks.text: At trim, 37 km/h = 10.3 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³): Step Calculation Result Dynamic pressure q ½ × 1.225 × 10.3² ≈ 65 Pa Lift needed ≈ weight (lines are close to vertical) 981 N Lift coefficient needed 981 ÷ (65 × 21 m²) C L ≈ 0.72 A C L around 0.7 is an ordinary, comfortable value for a wing at a moderate angle of attack. Pull brake and C L rises while speed falls; push the speed bar and the reverse happens. Lift stays roughly equal to weight either way. ✋ Feel the number 65 Pa is tiny: about 6.6 kg-force spread over a square metre, the weight of a large bag of rice laid on a dining table.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & the wing
chunks.text: Spread over 21 m² it holds up a whole person, which is why a paraglider is so big, light and slow. Speed squared: small changes, big effects Because v is squared, 20% more airspeed means 1.2² = 1.44× the lift at the same angle of attack, and 20% less means only 0.64×. Drag follows the same law. This is why gusts feel so strong, and why a wing that loses airspeed close to the ground loses its lift quickly. Drag: the cost of making lift Drag is the force pulling backwards along the flight path. Part is parasitic (lines, pilot, harness, fabric), part is induced (the unavoidable cost of making lift with a finite wing, including the swirling wingtip vortices).

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & the wing
chunks.text: In steady glide the pilot's weight is balanced by lift (up) and drag (back), and the glider descends at exactly the angle where they balance. For the reference wing, drag = weight ÷ glide ratio = 981 ÷ 8.5 ≈ 115 N. The polar, briefly Plot sink rate against airspeed and you get the wing's polar curve . At low speed, sink is high (you are near the stall). As you speed up, sink falls to a minimum (best for staying up in weak lift), then rises again as parasitic drag grows with v². The shallowest line from the origin to the polar touches at best glide (best L/D). Those two speeds are different: min-sink is slower than best-glide. That is why Chapter 2 spends time on "speed to fly".

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & the wing
chunks.text: Speed bar and angle of attack The speed bar (speed system) shortens the front risers, lowers the angle of attack, and lets the wing fly faster along its polar. Lift still equals weight, but at a lower C L and higher v. Pushing bar in still air trades some glide for speed; into a headwind or through sinking air, that trade often improves glide over the ground (see Ch 2). A pilot flies at 30 km/h instead of 37 km/h at the same weight. Roughly what lift coefficient is needed now? Lift must still equal weight, so C L scales with 1/v²: 0.72 × (37/30)² ≈ 1.1 . That's a much higher angle of attack, closer to the stall (Chapter 5). Slow flight is not "safer" by default. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Glide ratio, sink & wind
chunks.text: Height is your fuel tank, and glide ratio is your mileage. The glide ratio (L/D) is how many metres you travel forward for each metre of height lost in still air. It equals lift ÷ drag. Beginner wings are typically quoted somewhere around 8 to 9; high-performance competition wings go well above 10. The sink rate is how fast you descend: airspeed ÷ glide ratio.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Glide ratio, sink & wind
chunks.text: Worked example · a 1,000 m flight (roughly Billing take-off to Bir landing) Condition Ground speed Glide over ground Distance in ~14 min Still air 37 km/h 8.5 : 1 8.5 km 15 km/h headwind 22 km/h ≈ 5.1 : 1 ≈ 5.1 km 15 km/h tailwind 52 km/h ≈ 11.9 : 1 ≈ 11.9 km Sink rate = 10.3 m/s ÷ 8.5 ≈ 1.2 m/s, so 1,000 m lasts ≈ 830 s ≈ 14 min whatever the wind. Wind only changes where you land. (The Billing–Bir height difference of about 1,000 m comes from secondary sources; see sources.md.) The polar curve and the speed bar Every wing has a "polar": a graph of sink rate against airspeed.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Glide ratio, sink & wind
chunks.text: Minimum sink comes at a slow speed (best for staying up in weak lift); best glide comes at a slightly faster speed (best for going far in still air). Into a headwind or through sinking air, pilots speed up with the speed bar to get through the bad air faster. They give up a little glide through the air to gain glide over the ground. Worked example · speed-to-fly (illustrative numbers) Suppose the reference wing at trim (37 km/h) sinks 1.2 m/s (L/D 8.5). On half bar at 45 km/h it might sink about 1.6 m/s (L/D ≈ 7.8) — worse through the air.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Glide ratio, sink & wind
chunks.text: Into a 15 km/h headwind: Choice Ground speed Sink Glide over ground Trim 22 km/h 1.2 m/s ≈ 5.1 : 1 Half bar (illustrative) 30 km/h 1.6 m/s ≈ 5.2 : 1 The bar helps you punch the headwind even though air L/D fell. Real polars are measured in certification and published by manufacturers; these numbers are teaching examples only. 🧭 Feel the number A 30 km/h headwind against a 37 km/h wing leaves you crawling forward at 7 km/h, slower than a brisk walk. Wind stronger than your trim speed means you go backwards over the ground. That is why every school sets conservative wind limits for students. You're 300 m above a landing field 2 km upwind. Wind is 15 km/h.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Glide ratio, sink & wind
chunks.text: Can you make it with the reference wing? Ground glide into a 15 km/h headwind ≈ 5.1 : 1, so 300 m buys about 300 × 5.1 ≈ 1.5 km . Not enough, so pick a landing option downwind or nearer. This is the reasoning behind "always have a landable field within glide". ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals & ridge lift
chunks.text: You never climb by yourself. You find air that climbs faster than you sink. If your wing sinks at 1.2 m/s and you're inside air rising at 3 m/s, your vario reads +1.8 m/s. All soaring comes down to this subtraction. The two main lift sources are thermals (heat) and ridge lift (wind on a slope). Thermals: buoyancy you can ride Sunlight heats the ground unevenly: dry fields, rock and villages warm faster than forest or water. Air touching a warm patch gets warmer and less dense than the air around it, so it rises (Archimedes again, as with a hot-air balloon). Bubbles or columns break away and climb, often marked by circling birds or, higher up, by a cumulus cloud.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals & ridge lift
chunks.text: Rising air expands and cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate : about 9.8 °C per 1,000 m. Its dew point falls more slowly, roughly 2 °C per 1,000 m. When temperature meets dew point, water vapour condenses and a cloud forms. That gives pilots a rule of thumb: Worked example · predicting cloud base Cloud base above ground ≈ 125 m × (temperature − dew point). On a day of 30 °C with dew point 14 °C: 125 × 16 = ≈ 2,000 m above the ground . With dew point 22 °C (humid, post-monsoon), only 125 × 8 = 1,000 m. A humid day means low, often weak thermals. Cloud streets On a windy, unstable day, thermals can line up downwind into long rows marked by streets of cumulus.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals & ridge lift
chunks.text: Fly along the sunny side of a street and you stay in lift for kilometres; cross the blue gap between streets and you sink. The physics is the same buoyancy as a single thermal, organised by the wind into a roll pattern in the boundary layer. Wave lift (mountain lee waves) When a stable layer of air flows over a mountain range, it can oscillate downwind in standing waves, sometimes marked by lens-shaped (lenticular) clouds. The rising side of each wave can be smooth and strong — the same phenomenon sailplane pilots ride to great height.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals & ridge lift
chunks.text: Paragliders occasionally use the lower, gentler parts of wave, but rotor under the wave and strong winds aloft make it an advanced, site-specific skill, not a beginner tool. Ridge (dynamic) lift When wind blows onto a slope, the air has to go up. The upward component near the face is roughly wind speed × sin(slope angle). Wind onto the face Slope Upward air near the face Net climb for a 1.2 m/s-sink wing 10 km/h (2.8 m/s) 30° ≈ 1.4 m/s ≈ +0.2 m/s (barely soarable) 18 km/h (5 m/s) 30° ≈ 2.5 m/s ≈ +1.3 m/s 18 km/h (5 m/s) 15° ≈ 1.3 m/s ≈ +0.1 m/s Simplified: real lift is strongest just in front of and slightly above the ridge line, and fades with height.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals & ridge lift
chunks.text: Kamshet's evening sea-breeze soaring on the Western Ghats ridges is a classic example (Nirvana Adventures describes "lift bands" as the breeze creeps up the Ghats). Safety Behind the ridge is rotor On the downwind (lee) side the air spills over and tumbles into turbulent, sinking eddies called rotor. Being caught there low is one of the classic accident scenarios. Rule: if you can't stay upwind of the ridge, go out in front and land, never behind. Your vario reads +0.5 m/s in a thermal and your wing sinks at 1.2 m/s at that speed. How fast is the air itself rising? Air speed upward = your climb + your sink = 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7 m/s . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wing loading & altitude
chunks.text: Same wing, different pilot, different mountain: different speeds. Wing loading is all-up weight divided by wing area. Every certified wing size comes with a weight range in its manual, and flying inside it matters. From the lift equation, if weight goes up, speed must rise as √(weight) to keep the same angle of attack. Worked example · bottom vs top of a weight range Suppose a wing is certified for 85–105 kg. √(105/85) ≈ 1.11, so the heavy pilot flies about 11% faster , and sinks 11% faster too. To a first approximation the glide ratio doesn't change: a heavier glider goes down the same slope, just quicker.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wing loading & altitude
chunks.text: Heavier loading feels more solid in turbulence; lighter loading climbs better in weak lift. Thin air at mountain sites Air density falls with altitude. In the standard atmosphere it is about 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level and about 0.97 kg/m³ at 2,400 m. To make the same lift, true airspeed rises by √(1.225/0.97) ≈ 1.13. Altitude (ISA) Air density True airspeed at "trim" Effect 0 m 1.225 kg/m³ 37 km/h Reference 1,000 m ≈ 1.11 kg/m³ ≈ 39 km/h +5% 2,400 m (Billing take-off, approx.) ≈ 0.97 kg/m³ ≈ 41.7 km/h +13%: faster launches and landings Hot days make it worse: warm air is less dense, so "density altitude" can be higher than the real altitude.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wing loading & altitude
chunks.text: You need a longer, stronger run to launch, and you land faster. 🏃 Feel the number Kinetic energy grows with speed squared. Landing at 41.7 instead of 37 km/h carries (41.7/37)² ≈ 27% more energy into your legs if you don't flare well. A 70 kg pilot borrows a wing rated 85–105 kg. With 15 kg of gear, are they in range? All-up weight = 70 + 15 = 85 kg : right at the bottom of the range. The wing will be slow and more easily deformed by turbulence. Instructors size wings by all-up weight, not body weight. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: A wing has two ways to stop working: too much angle, or too little. Too much angle of attack: the stall Lift coefficient rises with angle of attack, but only up to a critical angle. Beyond it the airflow can no longer follow the curved top surface, separates, and lift collapses. On a paraglider this usually comes from too much brake for too long. The wing slows, falls back behind the pilot, and recovery needs exactly the right, trained response. A stall happens at a critical angle , not at a fixed speed you can read. Too little angle of attack: collapses A paraglider holds its shape only by internal air pressure.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: If turbulence suddenly reduces the angle of attack (for example a strong gust from above, or flying fast into sinking air), part of the leading edge can fold under: an asymmetric or frontal collapse. Modern wings are tested to reopen by themselves. Under EN 926-2 (and the related DHV LTF classes), beginner wings are class A (most passive); B, C and D demand progressively more skill — see the governing-bodies section. Collapse recovery physics (what schools drill) An asymmetric collapse reduces lift on one side, so the wing yaws and rolls toward the collapsed side and can enter a dive.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: Trained response: weight-shift and brake toward the open side to stop the turn, keep the open side flying (not stalled), and let the collapsed side reinflate — then damp the surge as the wing dives forward and reinflates. A frontal (symmetric) collapse usually reinflates if you keep hands up; deep brake on a collapsed wing risks a stall. These are instructor-taught manoeuvres; the quiz and chapters are not a substitute for SIV. Turning costs height: load factor In a banked turn the lift must hold you up and pull you round the circle, so the wing has to make more lift than your weight. Load factor n = 1 ÷ cos(bank).

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: Bank Load factor Stall speed × Sink rate × (same C L ) 30° 1.15 g 1.07 ≈ 1.24 45° 1.41 g 1.19 ≈ 1.68 60° 2.0 g 1.41 ≈ 2.83 Stall speed scales with √n, and sink at the same lift coefficient scales with n 1.5 . A spiral dive, used deliberately to lose height fast, can reach several g and heavy sink rates. That's why it's taught under supervision and why pilots must know how to exit it. Spiral dive versus spin A spiral is a steep, banked, high-speed descending turn with the wing still flying (high load factor, high airspeed, high sink). Exit by gradually reducing inside brake and weight-shift, then damping the surge.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: A spin (stall-spin) is different: one side of the wing is stalled and the glider autorotates with low airspeed and the wing back. Recovery needs a different, trained input (weight-shift and outside brake, then damp). Confusing the two is dangerous — another reason SIV exists. The safety layers SIV (Simulation d'Incident en Vol) courses teach collapses, stalls and recoveries over water with an instructor on the radio and a rescue boat below. Pilots also carry an emergency (reserve) parachute .

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: Deploying it is a last resort when the wing is unrecoverable or you are too low to fix it: look, clear, pull the reserve handle, and then try to keep the main wing from interfering (schools teach specific techniques). Descent under a reserve is still fast — typically several metres per second — so you need height. APPI's rules require a certified reserve on high flights from APPI 2 onward. Himachal Pradesh's 2025 amendment to its Aero Sports Rules requires tandem pilots to complete a safety (SIV) course; already-registered tandem pilots were given until 31 August 2026 (news reports; see sources.md).

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, collapses & turns
chunks.text: Why does a pilot who pulls a lot of brake to "slow down for safety" in turbulence risk making things worse? More brake = higher angle of attack, closer to the stall, while the gusts keep changing the angle. Instructors teach active flying : small, quick brake inputs to keep the wing overhead and pressurised, not a big constant pull. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & micro-meteorology
chunks.text: The sky is a fluid, and you're flying a leaf in it. Wind gradient near the ground Friction slows the lowest layers of air, so wind is usually weaker near the ground than at take-off height. On final approach you descend into slower-moving air and your headwind component drops. Keep a little extra speed near the ground and don't hang on deep brake until the flare. Venturi, rotor and gusts Wind squeezed through a gap or over a pass speeds up (continuity: same flow through a smaller area). Obstacles (trees, buildings, ridges) leave turbulent rotor downwind. A forecast "average" wind of 12 km/h with gusts to 30 km/h is a very different day from a steady 12.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & micro-meteorology
chunks.text: Storms: cumulonimbus A cumulus that keeps growing vertically can become a thunderstorm. Its updraft can be strong enough to carry a paraglider into the cloud ("cloud suck"), and its downdraft hits the ground as a gust front that spreads outward. When towers start building, pilots land early. India's flying seasons are monsoon-shaped Kamshet (Western Ghats) Oct–May (Temple Pilots); Nov–mid-June (Nirvana Adventures). East winds in winter, west sea-breeze in summer. Monsoon suspends flying for about four months. Bir Billing (Dhauladhar) Billing Paul Adventure runs courses all year except 15 Jul–15 Sep. International competitions have been held here in late Oct–Nov (PWCA, 2023 and 2024).

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & micro-meteorology
chunks.text: Panchgani (Sahyadri) The 2026 Paragliding World Cup page describes February as the best month: mild temperatures, strong thermals and sea-breeze convergence lines. Nandi Hills (near Bengaluru) Local club flying (Xtacee Paragliding Club). No published month-by-month calendar on the club site — confirm wind and cloud with the operator; Karnataka's monsoon typically interrupts hill flying in mid-year. Manali / Solang · Yelagiri ABVIMAS lists aero sports among its activities at Manali/Solang, but its paragliding course list was still "coming soon" when checked. Yelagiri has historical training mentions; no current school site was verified this pass.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & micro-meteorology
chunks.text: Ask locally and check state rules before you go. Safety Know your limits, then halve them Most accidents in free flight trace back to a decision on the ground: flying in conditions beyond the pilot's skill. Talk to your instructor and local pilots, check the forecast, and remember that not flying is always an option. Tandem passengers: in Himachal Pradesh, operators and tandem pilots must be registered with the state tourism department. Ask to see the registration. A forecast says ground temperature 26 °C, dew point 22 °C, light winds. What kind of thermal day do you expect? Spread 4 °C → cloud base ≈ 125 × 4 = 500 m .

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & micro-meteorology
chunks.text: Low base, humid air, weak or short thermals: a training or short local-flying day, not a cross-country day. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · Pilot ratings & skill levels

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first ground handling to senior pilot
chunks.text: The world's common yardstick is the FAI/CIVL IPPI card , which maps national and school ratings onto five "SafePro Para" stages. Schools then teach to a system such as APPI or a national federation's (BHPA in the UK, USHPA in the US). Figures below come from each body's published standards (checked 3 Oct 2026). Where we couldn't read the official text, we say so. Step 0 · Try it Tandem flight (not a rating) Passenger with a tandem pilot What it is You fly as a passenger The pilot does everything; some schools let you hold the controls in calm air No training credit or licence Schools set their own age and weight limits (e.g.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first ground handling to senior pilot
chunks.text: Temple Pilots: children above 6, body weight up to 95 kg, case by case above) India Registration matters Himachal Pradesh's Aero Sports Rules 2022 require operators and pilots to register with the state tourism department 2025 amendment: tandem pilots must complete a safety (SIV) course FAI / APPI / BHPA — Passengers need no rating. Tandem pilots need advanced ratings: APPI 5 opens the APPI tandem course, and SafePro Para lists a separate non-commercial tandem stage.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first ground handling to senior pilot
chunks.text: Step 1 · Ground & first hops Ground handling and low flights IPPI stage 1 · Ground Skimming (yellow) FAI SafePro Para Stage 1 · Ground Skimming "Not flying higher than you would care to fall" At least 2 practice days Student status: always under instructor supervision APPI APPI 1 Discover Minimum 3-day course, at least 1 day of ground handling First solo flight if weather allows (not required for the rating) Instructor supervision by radio; certified reserve on high flights BHPA · USHPA Elementary Pilot (EP) · P1 Beginner BHPA EP is a "progress award" from your school marking the introductory stage USHPA P1 details: official page did not load for us Step 2 · Supervised high flights Take-off to landing, on the radio IPPI stage 2 · Altitude Gliding (orange) FAI SafePro Para Stage 2 · Altitude Gliding Height and space to manoeuvre, no soaring At least 4 practice days and 10 flights APPI APPI 2 Explore (≈ IPPI 2) Minimum 10 days of course in total At least 10 high flights under instructor supervision Still flies only under supervision with radio contact BHPA · USHPA Club Pilot (Novice) · P2 Novice BHPA Club Pilot: end of formal instruction; fly within BHPA clubs with coaches USHPA P2 details not verified Step 3 · Independent at your site Active flying IPPI stage 3 · Active Flying (green) FAI SafePro Para Stage 3 · Active Flying Keep the wing flying in turbulent air; chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first ground handling to senior pilot
chunks.text: Requirements not verified from the official page. How it works in India National air sports sit under MoCA guidelines; schools still use mixed systems. The Aero Club of India (ACI) is India's National Air Sports Control (NAC-India), recognised by the Ministry of Civil Aviation under the National Air Sports Guidelines 2023, and it issues FAI sporting licences. A Lok Sabha reply (27 Jul 2026) confirms the 2022 National Air Sports Policy was superseded by those 2023 guidelines, and that the sports ministry has not recognised any national sports federation for paragliding.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first ground handling to senior pilot
chunks.text: We found no air-sports body named "HAPAI"; the pilots' association with a published national rating ladder is the Paragliding Association of India (PAI) . PAI National Rating System (NPRS) — published on PAI's site — lists paragliding levels P1 Introduction, P2 Student Pilot, P3 Novice, P4 Intermediate, P5 Advanced, then P7 Tandem Pilot through P10 Examiner, and says the skill levels follow the FAI SafePro Para system. Ask whether a school's "P1–P4" means PAI NPRS, APPI, or a local certificate. Schools use different systems. Temple Pilots and Nirvana Adventures (Kamshet) run APPI courses and are on APPI’s school listings; both also appear on ACI’s accredited-schools pages.

chunks.text: PG Gurukul (Bir) is ACI-accredited, and says it follows BHPA-style training under a BHPA-certified instructor and issues ACI licences carrying an IPPI rating. Billing Paul Adventure (APPI-listed as Paul International Paragliding School) offers both local Pilot Levels and APPI 1–3. Skylark School of Paragliding and Antigravity (Bir) publish local P1–P3/P4 courses without naming a certifying body. Before you book, ask: which system, which IPPI stage (if any), and who signs it? Each school card in Where to fly shows what we could verify. 04 · Governing bodies

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Globally, the FAI's hang gliding and paragliding commission (CIVL) writes the proficiency standards and sanctions championships. National federations and school systems train to them. In India, air sports sit under the civil aviation ministry's guidelines, with state tourism departments regulating operators where it matters most (Himachal Pradesh). Every body below was checked on its official website unless noted.

chunks.title: Paragliding: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: World federation FAI: World Air Sports Federation · CIVL CIVL is FAI's Hang Gliding and Paragliding Commission. It publishes the SafePro Para proficiency standards behind the IPPI card and sanctions world and continental championships. fai.org › CIVL Training system APPI Association of Paragliding Pilots and Instructors: an international school and instructor system with five pilot levels mapped to IPPI. APPI states its ratings give no legal right to fly in a country unless the local authority recognises them. flyappi.org › education system National federation BHPA (UK) British Hang Gliding and Paragliding Association.

Wing certification EN 926-2 · DHV LTF classes A–D European standard EN 926-2 (current amendment A1:2022) and the German DHV LTF scheme classify wings by flight-test behaviour, not pilots.

chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: Class A is maximum passive safety (suitable including in training); B is still forgiving; C needs active, regular pilots familiar with recoveries; D is demanding with potentially violent reactions. The overall class is the hardest single manoeuvre rating. These classes say nothing about glide performance. dhv.de › classification Competition PWCA: Paragliding World Cup Association Organises the Paragliding World Cup series and its regional tours, including events at Bir (2023 Pre-World Cup, 2024 Asian Tour) and Panchgani (Feb 2026). pwca.org

chunks.heading: India
chunks.text: National air sports control Aero Club of India (NAC-India) India's designated National Air Sports Control, recognised by the Ministry of Civil Aviation under the National Air Sports Guidelines 2023. Handles ACI membership and FAI sporting licences, and says it works only through its official website. Under the 2023 guidelines it also accredits schools: its site named six accredited paragliding schools on 5 Oct 2026 (PG Gurukul, Orange Life, Temple Pilots, Paragliding Bawas, Nirvana Adventures, Indus Paragliding). aeroclubofindia.com · accredited schools Pilots' association Paragliding Association of India (PAI) Registered in Goa on 26 May 2010 under the Societies Registration Act.

chunks.text: Publishes a National Rating System (NPRS) for PG and PPG with levels mapped toward FAI SafePro, plus membership, school affiliation and group accident insurance. Has helped organise FAI/CIVL-framework competitions in India (including CAT-2 events). paraglidingassociationofindia.org Central government Ministry of Civil Aviation · National Air Sports Guidelines 2023 The 2023 guidelines replaced the National Air Sports Policy 2022 as the framework for air sports, including paragliding (confirmed in a Lok Sabha reply of 27 Jul 2026).

chunks.heading: The competitive path
chunks.text: 1 Tandem flights and pilot courses Schools; Aero Club of India is the national air-sports body 2 Open competitions in India Organisers under the FAI sporting code 3 Paragliding World Cup and FAI Category 1 championships PWCA and FAI Entry Competitions set their own pilot-rating requirements. International India hosts a Paragliding World Cup at Panchgani. First year General guidance, not a source. Months 1–3: learn the basics with a school or club on this page. Months 3–6: join a club affiliated to the state association. Months 6–9: enter a club, district or open event. Months 9–12: ask your club about registering with the national federation and state trials.

Why it matters: an accredited school is checked against a standard for instructors, equipment and safety; a school’s own claim isn’t checked. ✓ APPI-listed or ✓ ACI-accredited means we found the school named on that body’s own official list: APPI’s worldwide school map or the Aero Club of India’s accredited-schools pages. Checked 5 Oct 2026. ① Tandem (no rating) ② Learn: P1–P2 ③ Pilot: P3 & soaring ④ SIV, XC & competitions You're here if… You want to feel free flight before committing to a course. Temple Pilots states a minimum age of 16, and needs a doctor's certificate and adventure insurance. Read Ch 1 and Ch 5 . Ask before you book Which system (APPI, BHPA-style, local P-levels)? chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Inflate. Throttle up. Let thrust replace the hill.
chunks.text: A paramotor is a paraglider with an engine and propeller on your back, so you can take off from a flat field. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Thrust Lab, then find paramotor courses in India, the rating systems schools use and the rules you need to know. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Paraglider PPG3 ≈ 1.05 km Engine-off glide from 300 m into a 15 km/h headwind. Why pilots always stay within glide of a field. ≈ 4 m Take-off run into a 20 km/h headwind, vs 26 m in calm. Taking off downwind does the opposite. 45 N·m The twist a full-power engine puts on the pilot. Strongest at take-off and climb, close to the ground.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta

chunks.text: You learn to paraglide first. Paramotoring builds on the same wing skills; ask which rating you need before the course. No licence is required in India. So ask how the school certifies your level, and keep a logbook. Plan the way home before you leave. Go out upwind and come home downwind, so the slow leg isn't last.
