chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of paramotoring?
chunks.text: 15 questions on thrust and drag, the PPG wing, thrust line and torque, forward and reverse launches, fuel, endurance and weight-shift, and wind, weather and the rules: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Thrust Lab to see how mass, wing, thrust and wind change the flight. Interactive · Thrust Lab

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set the all-up mass, the wing's glide ratio, airspeed, engine thrust and the wind, then see the drag, the power you need, your climb, your groundspeed and how far you could glide with the engine off
chunks.text: A simple steady-flight model: drag = weight ÷ (L/D), power = drag × airspeed, climb = (thrust − drag) × airspeed ÷ weight, engine-off glide from 300 m into the wind = 300 m × L/D × (airspeed − headwind) ÷ airspeed. Wing loading uses a 22 m² wing. Learning values only (illustrative): real wings, motors and propellers vary.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set the all-up mass, the wing's glide ratio, airspeed, engine thrust and the wind, then see the drag, the power you need, your climb, your groundspeed and how far you could glide with the engine off
chunks.text: All-up mass 110 kg Wing glide ratio (L/D) 5 : 1 6 : 1 7 : 1 Airspeed 36 km/h Thrust 400 N Wind 15 km/h Drag in level flight 180 N Ch 1 · weight ÷ L/D Power to hold height 1.80 kW Ch 1 · drag × airspeed Climb rate 2.0 m/s Ch 1 · spare thrust Groundspeed into / with the wind 21 / 51 km/h Ch 6 · airspeed ∓ wind Engine-off glide from 300 m into wind 1.05 km Ch 6 · keep a field in reach Wing loading (22 m²) 5.0 kg/m² Ch 2 · trim speed Bar = thrust used just to hold height (drag ÷ thrust); the rest is spare for climbing. Try 200 kg (a tandem) or a 25 km/h wind. Fly only after training at a school (Ch 6). CH 1

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust vs drag
chunks.text: A paraglider with a fan on your back: thrust replaces the hill. A paraglider "spends" height to keep moving (our Paragliding page covers glide in detail). A paramotor , or powered paraglider (PPG), adds a propeller on the pilot's back. In level flight four forces balance: lift = weight and thrust = drag . Since lift ÷ drag is the glide ratio, drag = weight ÷ (L/D) . Any thrust beyond that makes you climb. Worked example · 110 kg all-up, 36 km/h (10 m/s), 400 N thrust (from our Thrust Lab, illustrative) Wing L/D Drag Power to hold height Climb rate 5 : 1 ≈ 216 N ≈ 2.16 kW ≈ 1.7 m/s 6 : 1 ≈ 180 N ≈ 1.80 kW ≈ 2.0 m/s 7 : 1 ≈ 154 N ≈ 1.54 kW ≈ 2.3 m/s Weight = 110 × 9.81 = 1,079 N; ÷ 6 ≈ 180 N.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust vs drag
chunks.text: Climb = (400 − 180) × 10 ÷ 1,079 ≈ 2.0 m/s. Propellers aren't perfectly efficient, so the engine must make more than this power. Why thrust falls as you speed up A static thrust figure (propeller pushing hard while you stand still) is not what you get in flight. In the simple momentum picture, the propeller accelerates a disk of air; as your airspeed rises, the same power adds less extra speed to that stream, so available thrust drops . Climb is hardest just after lift-off, when you still want full thrust and the wing is slow — then improves a little as you accelerate, then falls again as drag rises with speed.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust vs drag
chunks.text: Density altitude (hot, high, humid) cuts both propeller thrust and wing lift, so the same field can feel short on a hot afternoon. Order of magnitude · disk loading (illustrative 1.25 m propeller) What Number Meaning Propeller disk area ≈ 1.23 m² π (0.625)² 400 N static thrust on that disk ≈ 325 N/m² About 3% of atmospheric pressure — a firm breeze through the cage Ideal power for that thrust at zero speed (momentum theory) ≈ 2.3 kW √(T³ ÷ (2 ρ A)); real engines need more because props are not ideal ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³. The Thrust Lab's 400 N is an all-up push you dial in; real static thrust depends on prop, reduction drive and density.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust vs drag
chunks.text: Use the lab to feel how climb collapses when mass rises or L/D falls — not as an engine-dyno sheet. 🪂 Feel the number Holding a paramotor level takes about 1.8 kW in our example: roughly the power of an electric kettle, delivered as a gentle 18 kg push. Full climb power is several times that, and much of it goes into spinning air rather than into your altitude. A 150 kg tandem on a 6 : 1 wing: what drag in level flight? 150 × 9.81 ÷ 6 ≈ 245 N . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The PPG wing
chunks.text: The same kind of fabric wing, loaded heavier and flown faster. A PPG wing is a ram-air fabric wing like a paraglider: air enters openings at the front and inflates the cells. With an engine, fuel and frame on your back, the wing carries more weight per square metre. Wing loading (kg per m²) sets how fast the wing flies at trim: in steady flight, lift must equal weight, so speed rises with the square root of the load, v ∝ √(loading) . Worked example · a 22 m² wing (illustrative) All-up mass Wing loading Trim speed (scaled from 36 km/h at 110 kg) 110 kg 5.0 kg/m² 36 km/h 125 kg ≈ 5.7 kg/m² ≈ 38.4 km/h 36 × √(125 ÷ 110) ≈ 38.4 km/h.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The PPG wing
chunks.text: Every wing has a certified weight range; flying outside it changes how the wing behaves. Certified wings The Safety Guidelines for Paramotoring and powered parachutes (Version E5) say wings should be EN, LTF, DHV or DGAC certified and recommended for powered flying, with annual airworthiness checks and records kept. Trimmers, speedbar and reflex Many PPG wings add trimmers (risers you lengthen or shorten in flight to change the angle of attack) and a speedbar (a foot stirrup that pulls the A-risers forward). Released trimmers and a speedbar let you fly faster for cruise or into wind; pulled-in trimmers slow you for launch and landing.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The PPG wing
chunks.text: Some PPG wings are reflex : the aerofoil is shaped so that at speed the nose wants to pitch up if the wing is unloaded, which helps resist collapses in rough air — at the cost of different stall and recovery behaviour than a classic free-flight wing. The USPPA's PPG2 syllabus expects pilots to explain speedbar and trimmers, their use, risks and limitations, including for reflex wings. Learn each wing from its manual and from an instructor who knows that model. Your all-up mass rises by a quarter. Roughly how much faster does the wing trim? √1.25 ≈ 1.12, so about 12% faster . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust line & torque
chunks.text: Spin a propeller one way and it tries to spin you the other. Newton's third law works on rotation too: the engine turns the propeller, so the propeller pushes back on the engine, and on you, with an equal and opposite torque . Torque = power ÷ angular speed, so a slow-turning propeller at high power gives the biggest twist. It tends to roll and turn the pilot against the propeller's direction; frames often build in offsets and pilots learn to correct for it. Where the push acts matters too: if the thrust line sits above or below the hang points, adding power pitches you forward or back.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust line & torque
chunks.text: Worked example · reaction torque (illustrative motor) Power Propeller speed Torque on the pilot 15 kW (full power) 3,200 rpm ≈ 45 N·m 5 kW (cruise) 2,200 rpm ≈ 22 N·m 3,200 rpm = 335 rad/s; 15,000 ÷ 335 ≈ 45 N·m: like a 4.5 kg mass hanging on a 1 m lever. Torque is strongest at full power, which is during take-off and climb, close to the ground. Thrust line and pitch Reaction torque tries to roll you. A separate effect is pitch : if the thrust line does not pass through the hang points (where the wing holds you), adding power creates a couple.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust line & torque
chunks.text: Thrust above the hang points pitches the pilot back (harder to push the wing overhead on launch; a climb attitude that can stall if you also hold brakes); thrust below pitches you forward. Frames, hang-point adjustments and harness geometry are designed to keep that couple manageable — which is why copying a friend's settings onto a different motor can surprise you.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust line & torque
chunks.text: Worked example · pitch couple from a thrust-line offset (illustrative) Offset of thrust above hang points Thrust Pitch couple Like… 5 cm 400 N 20 N·m About 2 kg on a 1 m lever, pitching you back 10 cm 400 N 40 N·m Nearly the same size as the 45 N·m roll torque above 10 cm 200 N (cruise) 20 N·m Half the thrust, half the couple Couple = thrust × offset. Real hang-point charts matter more than this toy model; the point is that a few centimetres at full power are not trivial when you are running with a wing overhead.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Thrust line & torque
chunks.text: The USPPA's PPG2 rating (a US reference) requires pilots to understand torque effects and to train on a simulator, a frame hung from a hang point so you can feel the controls on the ground. It also asks them to explain how centre of gravity and wing connection location on the harness affect the machine. Same 15 kW but the propeller turns at 2,400 rpm. More or less torque? More: 15,000 ÷ (2,400 × 2π ÷ 60) ≈ 60 N·m . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Forward & reverse launch
chunks.text: The wing needs airspeed, not groundspeed. Wind gives you some for free. To lift off, the wing must reach its flying airspeed . Facing into the wind, groundspeed = airspeed − headwind , so a headwind means a shorter, slower take-off run. In calm air you run and use thrust to build the speed: a forward launch , facing the way you'll fly. In more wind, pilots often use a reverse launch : face the wing to inflate and check it, then turn round and go. Worked example · wing flies at 32 km/h, acceleration 1.5 m/s² (illustrative) Headwind Groundspeed at lift-off Take-off run 0 km/h 32 km/h ≈ 26 m 10 km/h 22 km/h ≈ 12 m 20 km/h 12 km/h ≈ 4 m Run distance = v² ÷ (2a): (32 ÷ 3.6)² ÷ 3 ≈ 26 m.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Forward & reverse launch
chunks.text: Halving the groundspeed needed cuts the run to about a quarter. Taking off downwind does the opposite. The USPPA's PPG1 (student) rating, for example, asks for two forward and two reverse inflations, 30 seconds of kiting the wing overhead, and two unassisted flights, in winds of no more than 8 mph (about 13 km/h). The wing flies at 32 km/h and there's a 12 km/h headwind. What groundspeed at lift-off? 32 − 12 = 20 km/h . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Fuel, endurance & weight-shift
chunks.text: Plan the trip home before you leave, and steer with your hips. Endurance is usable fuel ÷ burn rate, and range depends on the wind. Into a headwind your groundspeed drops; downwind it rises. The point of no return is how far you can go out and still get back on the fuel you have.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Fuel, endurance & weight-shift
chunks.text: Worked example · 36 km/h airspeed, 15 km/h wind, 2 h of usable fuel after a reserve (illustrative) Item Number How Groundspeed into wind 21 km/h 36 − 15 Groundspeed downwind 51 km/h 36 + 15 Furthest you can go upwind and return ≈ 30 km R ÷ 21 + R ÷ 51 = 2 h 12 L of petrol ≈ 8.9 kg about 0.74 kg per litre: 8% of a 110 kg all-up mass Go out upwind and come home downwind: if you go out downwind, the slow, fuel-hungry leg comes last. Weight-shift and brakes You steer by pulling a brake toggle (which pulls down one side of the trailing edge) and by shifting your weight in the harness.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Fuel, endurance & weight-shift
chunks.text: A banked turn needs more lift: the load factor is n = 1 ÷ cos(bank) , so 30° of bank needs 1.15 g, 45° needs 1.41 g and 60° needs 2 g. The USPPA's PPG2 novice rating limits flying to no more than 30° of bank. A 45° banked turn: what load factor? 1 ÷ cos 45° ≈ 1.41 g . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, weather & the rules
chunks.text: Fly smooth air, always within glide of a field, and with the right permissions. A paramotor flies at only roughly 30–45 km/h (illustrative), so wind matters a lot: a 25 km/h headwind can leave you barely moving over the ground. Engines can stop, so always fly with a landing area within gliding distance. Into the wind, your glide over the ground shrinks. Worked example · engine-off glide from 300 m, 6 : 1 wing, 36 km/h airspeed (from our Thrust Lab) Wind Glide over the ground Distance from 300 m Still air 6 : 1 1.8 km 15 km/h headwind 3.5 : 1 ≈ 1.05 km 15 km/h tailwind 8.5 : 1 ≈ 2.55 km 300 × 6 × (36 − 15) ÷ 36 = 1,050 m.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, weather & the rules
chunks.text: What the safety guideline says Smooth air: motorised flying needs smooth, laminar wind, so early morning and evening are generally suitable for training. Tandem: not in more than 18 km/h of wind; no aerobatic manoeuvres below 600 ft; always fly with a landing zone within glide in case of engine failure. Engines: instruments for cylinder-head temperature and RPM. Permissions: an NOC through the district collector's office (with police clearance), Airports Authority of India clearance and a NOTAM giving the radius and height ceiling, then daily permission from local ATC. Safety The rules in India NASG 2023 superseded the 2022 air-sports policy (confirmed in a July 2026 Lok Sabha reply).

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, weather & the rules
chunks.text: Press reports of Civil Aviation answers the same year describe ASFI as the NASG framework body, and list DGCA's safety/licensing remit for gliders, microlights, LSA, gyroplanes, balloons and powered hang gliders — not powered paragliders. The Version E5 safety guideline says PPG and powered parachutes are not regulated in India, so officially no licence is required, but pilots should keep a logbook and schools should certify level; it recommends BHPA, USPPA, APPI PPG or similar. ACI's organogram names a Microlight & Paramotor commissioner; that is not the same as a verified national PPG licence.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind, weather & the rules
chunks.text: Check the current position with the school, state tourism and airspace authorities before you fly. From 300 m on a 6 : 1 wing at 36 km/h, with a 20 km/h headwind, how far can you glide over the ground? 300 × 6 × (36 − 20) ÷ 36 = 800 m . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The paramotor ladder

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Learn to paraglide → paramotor course → PPG1 student → PPG2 novice → PPG3 experienced → tandem & instructor
chunks.text: India has no DGCA-issued national paramotor licence that we could verify. Schools set their own courses and, as the Version E5 safety guideline recommends, often base them on BHPA, USPPA or APPI PPG. ACI’s organogram names a Microlight & Paramotor commissioner; that is not the same as a public, verified national PPG licence scheme. We use the USPPA ratings below as a published reference: they are voluntary US ratings, not Indian law.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Paramotor competitions come under the FAI; rating systems come from national associations abroad; in India, air sports sit under the Ministry of Civil Aviation's NASG 2023, with state safety guidelines for operators. We checked each on an official source.

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: World federation FAI Microlight and Paramotor Commission (CIMA) The FAI commission for microlights and paramotors: world championships, records and competition rules. (Paragliding without an engine is under CIVL.) fai.org Rating system (reference) United States Powered Paragliding Association (USPPA) Publishes voluntary PPG1–PPG3 pilot ratings and tandem instructor requirements, based on the US FAA's Part 103 rules and advisory circular 103-7. Its public school directory is US-centred; we found no Indian school named there (checked 5 Oct 2026).

chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: usppa.org National association (UK) British Hang Gliding & Paragliding Association (BHPA) Runs a Powered Paragliding pathway (wing first, then motor, air law and navigation). BHPA Power qualifications are for solo flight only — no dual/passenger power qualification. Registered schools are listed on BHPA's site (UK-focused). bhpa.co.uk

chunks.title: Paramotoring · Physics of Thrust, Torque & Powered Paragliding · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: India
chunks.text: Ministry Ministry of Civil Aviation · NASG 2023 A July 2026 Lok Sabha reply (Youth Affairs) confirms NASG 2023 superseded the National Air Sports Policy 2022. Separate Civil Aviation answers reported in the press (Aug 2026) describe NASG as the framework through ASFI. Read the primary documents; press summaries can blur which ministry answered what. sansad.in (AU1311) Regulator Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) As reported from the ministry's 2026 answers, DGCA continues to regulate safety and licensing for gliders, microlights, light sport aircraft, gyroplanes, balloons and powered hang gliders under the Aircraft Rules; powered paragliders were not on that list.

chunks.heading: India
chunks.text: Confirm the current CAR position before you rely on it. dgca.gov.in Safety guideline Safety Guidelines for Paramotoring & powered parachutes (Version E5) A Maharashtra-focused guideline; the same text appears in Maharashtra Tourism's air-activity safety guidelines. States PPG/PPC are not regulated so officially no licence is required, recommends BHPA/USPPA/APPI PPG-style training, logbooks and school-issued levels. safetyguidelines.co.in National aero club Aero Club of India · Microlight & Paramotor seat ACI's published organogram includes a Commissioner for Microlight & Paramotor (and an ACI membership category for microlights & paramotors).

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How much of the basics do you already have?
chunks.text: 12 questions, two for each chapter. No trick wording and no exam pressure: you get a score, an explanation for every answer and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. It is a self-check, not a certification. 02 · The basics

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six ideas, from weight to turning
chunks.text: Each chapter takes one idea in two sentences, works one example with every step shown, shows how a handful of sports bend it, and says what your body does about it. These are general physics refreshers using standard constants (g = 9.81 m/s², sea-level pressure 101.325 kPa). Not medical or training advice. CH 1

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Forces & weight
chunks.text: A kilogram is how much; a newton is how hard. A force is a push or a pull, counted in newtons (N); one newton is the weight of about 102 g, because 1 ÷ 9.81 = 0.102 kg. Your weight is gravity's pull on your mass, W = m × g , with g = 9.81 m/s², and a "g" in a sport page just means a force counted in multiples of your own weight. Worked example · a 70 kg person Step Working Result 1. Weight 70 kg × 9.81 m/s² ≈ 686.7 N, call it 687 N 2. That force in g 687 N ÷ 687 N 1 g, by definition Worked example · a banked turn (100 kg pilot and wing, from the paragliding page) Weight = 100 × 9.81 = 981 N.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Forces & weight
chunks.text: In a steady bank only the upward part of the lift, lift × cos(bank), holds you up, so lift = weight ÷ cos(bank) and the load factor is 1 ÷ cos(bank). Bank cos(bank) Load factor 1 ÷ cos Lift needed (981 N ÷ cos) 30° 0.866 1.15 g ≈ 1,133 N 45° 0.707 1.41 g ≈ 1,387 N 60° 0.500 2.00 g 1,962 N The 1.15, 1.41 and 2.0 g are on the paragliding page (Ch 5); the newton column is the same division carried out. How each sport bends it Same idea, different specifics. Each line is a figure from that sport's own page; follow the chip for the whole chapter. Paragliding · Ch 5 A 60° bank is 2 g, so the wing must carry twice your weight.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Forces & weight
chunks.text: Bungee & zipline · Ch 3 A 70 kg jumper on a 20 m cord of 100 N/m feels a peak of about 3.6 × body weight. Rock climbing · Ch 3 A fall factor of 0.35 loads the rope with about 4.2 kN for a 70 kg climber. Ice skating · Ch 2 At 4 m/s on a 5 m radius the blade takes about 1.05 × body weight. 🦵 What your body does about it Your skeleton and muscles carry that weight all day, and sport multiplies it. Strong legs, hips and trunk are what hold a 2 g turn or a landing together, which is why the starter routine on Get fit is mostly leg and core work (WHO and ICMR-NIN guidance are cited there). A 60 kg person carries a 10 kg pack. What is the total weight in newtons?

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Forces & weight
chunks.text: Mass = 70 kg, so weight = 70 × 9.81 = ≈ 687 N . Gear counts: it is the all-up mass that gravity pulls on. At 45° of bank, what load factor does a wing carry, and what does 100 kg weigh at that moment? 1 ÷ cos 45° = 1 ÷ 0.707 = 1.41 g , so the wing carries about 1.41 × 981 = 1,387 N, which feels like 141 kg. Sources: NIST: standard acceleration of gravity · Newton's second law ↑ Back to the self-check CH 2

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy & work
chunks.text: Climbing is lifting yourself, and lifting is paid in joules. Work is force × distance and energy is the ability to do work, both counted in joules (J), with 1 kcal = 4,184 J. Lifting a mass m through a height h takes W = m × g × h , and dropping through the same height gives it back as speed, ½ m v² = m g h . Worked example · a 70 kg climber gains 1,000 m (from the mountaineering page) Step Working Result 1. Lifting work 70 kg × 9.81 m/s² × 1,000 m 686,700 J ≈ 687 kJ 2. Food energy at 20% efficiency (illustrative) 687 kJ ÷ 0.20 ≈ 3,435 kJ 3.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy & work
chunks.text: In kilocalories 3,435,000 J ÷ 4,184 J/kcal ≈ 821 kcal Carrying a 15 kg pack makes it 85 kg: 85 × 9.81 × 1,000 = 833,850 J ≈ 834 kJ, then ÷ 0.20 = 4,169 kJ, then ÷ 4,184 = ≈ 996 kcal. The 20% is an illustrative figure used on the mountaineering page; the exact value varies from person to person. How each sport bends it Same idea, different specifics. Each line is a figure from that sport's own page; follow the chip for the whole chapter. Mountaineering · Ch 4 A 70 kg climber gaining 1,000 m does about 687 kJ of lifting work, roughly 821 kcal of food. Archery · Ch 1 A 40 lb bow stores about 43.5 J; about 32.6 J reaches a 20 g arrow, leaving at about 57 m/s.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy & work
chunks.text: Big-wave surfing · Ch 2 Wave energy grows with height squared: a 15 m face carries about 25 × the energy of a 3 m one. Rock climbing · Ch 6 Lifting a 70 kg climber 20 m is about 13.7 kJ of mechanical work, about 3.3 kcal. Skydiving · Ch 3 At 53.6 m/s a 90 kg jumper carries about 129 kJ of kinetic energy. 🍚 What your body does about it Your body is the engine, and muscles turn only a fraction of the food energy they burn into lifting (the 20% above). Long days need real fuel, fluids and sleep; the numbers and sources are in Food & sleep on Get fit. A 60 kg hiker with a 10 kg pack climbs 500 m. How much lifting work is that? 70 × 9.81 × 500 = 343,350 J ≈ 343 kJ .

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy & work
chunks.text: At the same illustrative 20%, that is 343 ÷ 0.20 ÷ 4.184 ≈ 410 kcal of food. A 20 g (0.020 kg) arrow leaves the bow at 57.1 m/s. What is its kinetic energy? ½ × 0.020 × 57.1² = 0.010 × 3,260 ≈ 32.6 J , which matches the archery page's figure. Sources: NIST SP 811: guide for the use of the SI · work ↑ Back to the self-check CH 3

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pressure & buoyancy
chunks.text: Water piles up on you; thin air thins out each breath. Pressure is force per area, counted in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²; 1 bar ≈ 100,000 Pa). In water it grows with depth, in air it falls with height, a gas squeezes in step ( Boyle's law: P × V = constant ), and anything submerged is pushed up by the weight of the water it displaces. Worked example · 10 m of seawater, and a 6 L balloon going down Step Working Result 1. Mass of water above 1 m² 10 m³ × 1,025 kg/m³ 10,250 kg 2. Its weight, spread over 1 m² 10,250 kg × 9.81 m/s² ≈ 100,550 Pa ≈ 1 bar The scuba page rounds this to 100,500 Pa (about 1 bar); fresh water is about 10.2 m per bar, because 100,000 ÷ (1,000 × 9.81) ≈ 10.2.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pressure & buoyancy
chunks.text: Depth Absolute pressure Volume = 6 L × 1 bar ÷ pressure Change 0 m 1 bar 6.0 L n/a 10 m 2 bar 3.0 L −50% 20 m 3 bar 2.0 L −33% 30 m 4 bar 1.5 L −25% 40 m 5 bar 1.2 L −20% Absolute pressure = 1 bar of air + 1 bar for every 10 m. This is the table on the scuba and freediving pages. The shallows change the most. Interactive · Pressure lab

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Take a 6 L breath down
chunks.text: Pressure = 1 bar + 1 bar per 10 m (more exactly ρ × g × depth), volume = 6 L ÷ pressure. Warm-up for the scuba and freediving pages; not a dive planner. Depth 10 m Water Sea water Fresh water Absolute pressure 2.01 bar 1 bar of air + the water above Volume of the 6 L breath 2.99 L Boyle: P × V stays constant Compared with the surface 50% of the surface volume Falls fastest near the top Treats the surface as 1 bar, as the scuba page does. Learning aid only. Worked example · lift in the water, then thin air Step Working Result 1. Foam lift (kayak page) 7 L = 0.007 m³; 0.007 × 1,000 kg/m³ × 9.81 ≈ 68.7 N ≈ 69 N, about 7 kg of lift 2.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Take a 6 L breath down
chunks.text: Sea vs fresh water, 100 L diver (scuba page) 100 L × 1.025 kg/L versus 100 L × 1.000 kg/L 102.5 kg versus 100 kg: 2.5 kg more lift in the sea 3. Air pressure at 5,029 m (standard atmosphere) 101.325 × (1 − 2.25577×10⁻⁵ × 5,029) 5.25588 ≈ 53.8 kPa 4. Oxygen pressure there 0.2095 × 53.8 kPa, against 0.2095 × 101.325 = 21.2 kPa at sea level ≈ 11.3 kPa 5. As a share of sea level 11.3 ÷ 21.2 ≈ 53% Steps 3 to 5 are the mountaineering page's standard-atmosphere working for Mt Renok (about 5,030 m), the same figures that appear on Get fit. How each sport bends it Same idea, different specifics. Each line is a figure from that sport's own page; follow the chip for the whole chapter.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Take a 6 L breath down
chunks.text: Scuba · Ch 1 Pressure rises about 1 bar per 10 m of seawater, so a breath of 6 L is 3 L at 10 m. Freediving · Ch 4 A 6 L lungful shrinks to 1.5 L at 30 m. Mountaineering · Ch 1 At 5,029 m the air pressure is about 53.8 kPa and the oxygen about 53% of its sea-level value. Surfing · Ch 3 An 80 L board floats about 82 kg of weight in the sea. Kayaking & rafting · Ch 3 7 L of foam gives about 69 N (about 7 kg) of lift. 👂 What your body does about it Air spaces in your body (ears, sinuses, lungs) feel pressure first, so equalise early and often; the scuba ears chapter shows why.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Take a 6 L breath down
chunks.text: At altitude the body copes mainly by breathing more, and the mountaineering page (citing CDC) says the first phase takes about 3 to 5 days and that being fit does not change your risk. A 4 L pocket of air at the surface is taken to 20 m. What volume is it there? At 20 m the pressure is 1 + 2 = 3 bar, so V = 4 × 1 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.33 L . What is the absolute pressure at 30 m in seawater, and what has happened to the gas in your lungs? 1 bar of air + 3 bar of water = 4 bar , so a breath takes a quarter of the surface volume (6 L → 1.5 L).

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drag & friction
chunks.text: Go twice as fast and the air or water pushes back four times as hard. Drag is the fluid's push against your motion, D = ½ × ρ × CdA × v² : it grows with the square of speed, and the power to beat it (drag × speed) with the cube. Sliding friction is simpler, F = μ × m × g on level ground, so on a very slippery surface (small μ) there is almost nothing to push against. Worked example · a skydiver's top speed (90 kg, belly-down, from the skydiving page) Terminal speed is where drag equals weight: ½ ρ CdA v² = m g, so v = √(2 m g ÷ (ρ CdA)). Air density ρ = 1.1 kg/m³, CdA = 0.56 m². Step Working Result 1. Weight 90 × 9.81 882.9 N 2. 2 × weight 2 × 882.9 1,765.8 N 3. ρ × CdA 1.1 × 0.56 0.616 4.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drag & friction
chunks.text: Divide 1,765.8 ÷ 0.616 ≈ 2,866.6 5. Square root √2,866.6 ≈ 53.5 m/s 6. In km/h 53.5 × 3.6 ≈ 193 km/h The skydiving page shows 53.6 m/s from the same inputs; the 0.1 difference is rounding. Head-down, CdA is 0.31 m² and the page gets about 257 km/h. Worked example · doubling a swimmer's speed (CdA 0.06 m², water 1,000 kg/m³, from the swimming page) Speed Drag ½ × 1,000 × 0.06 × v² Power = drag × speed 1.0 m/s 30 N 30 W 2.0 m/s 120 N 240 W Double the speed: drag × 4 (2² = 4), power × 8 (2³ = 8). Worked example · how slippery is snow and ice? Step Working Result 1. Skater on ice, 70 kg, μ ≈ 0.005 0.005 × 70 × 9.81 ≈ 3.4 N 2.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drag & friction
chunks.text: Skier on cold groomed snow, 75 kg, 15° slope, μ ≈ 0.05 0.05 × 75 × 9.81 × cos 15° ≈ 36 N 3. Gravity along that slope 75 × 9.81 × sin 15° ≈ 190 N, so friction is only a fifth Steps 1 and 2 are from the ice-skating and skiing pages; step 3 is the same sum for the along-slope part. The μ values are illustrative. How each sport bends it Same idea, different specifics. Each line is a figure from that sport's own page; follow the chip for the whole chapter. Skydiving · Ch 1 Belly-down a 90 kg jumper tops out near 193 km/h; head-down, about 257 km/h. Cycling & MTB · Ch 2 At 200 W, sitting upright (CdA 0.60 m²) gives about 27.9 km/h; hands on the hoods (0.32 m²) about 33.9 km/h.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drag & friction
chunks.text: Swimming · Ch 1 Doubling speed from 1.0 to 2.0 m/s takes drag from 30 to 120 N and power from 30 to 240 W. Paragliding · Ch 1 20% more airspeed gives 1.2² = 1.44 × the lift, and drag follows the same square law. Ski & snowboard · Ch 2 On cold groomed snow (μ about 0.05) friction is about 36 N for a 75 kg skier on a 15° slope. Ice skating · Ch 3 Steel on ice has μ of about 0.005, roughly 3.4 N for a 70 kg skater. 🚴 What your body does about it You are the adjustable part. Changing your position changes CdA, and the sport pages show how much: the same 200 W gives about 27.9 km/h sitting upright and about 33.9 km/h on the hoods ( cycling page ).

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drag & friction
chunks.text: Holding a low, steady position is a trained skill, so build it in lessons rather than on the day. In air, you double your speed. By what factor do drag and the power to beat it change? Drag × 2² = × 4 ; power × 2³ = × 8 . How much friction acts on an 80 kg skater on level ice with μ ≈ 0.005? 0.005 × 80 × 9.81 = ≈ 3.9 N , about the weight of 400 g. Sources: NASA Glenn: the drag equation · friction ↑ Back to the self-check CH 5

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Impacts & landing
chunks.text: It is not the fall that hurts; it is how quickly you stop. A fall from height h reaches the ground at v = √(2 × g × h) whatever you land on. What you control is the stopping distance d : the average force is weight × (1 + h ÷ d) , so doubling d halves the extra load. Worked example · a 0.5 m drop, stiff legs against bent knees (from Get fit) Step Working Result 1. Speed at the ground √(2 × 9.81 × 0.5) = √9.81 ≈ 3.13 m/s ≈ 11.3 km/h 2. Stop time, steady slowdown: t = 2d ÷ v stiff, 5 cm: 2 × 0.05 ÷ 3.13; bent, 25 cm: 2 × 0.25 ÷ 3.13 ≈ 0.032 s against ≈ 0.160 s 3. Average force ÷ weight: 1 + h ÷ d 1 + 0.5 ÷ 0.05; 1 + 0.5 ÷ 0.25 11 × against 3 × 4.

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Impacts & landing
chunks.text: For a 70 kg person (weight 687 N) 11 × 687; 3 × 687 ≈ 7,550 N against ≈ 2,060 N Steps 1 and 3 are on Get fit; steps 2 and 4 are the same numbers carried one step further. The "1 +" is your own weight, which the ground must also hold up. Interactive · Landing lab

chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Change the drop and the stopping distance
chunks.text: Constant-force model: v = √(2 g h), t = 2 d ÷ v, average force = weight × (1 + h ÷ d). It shows why the stopping distance matters. It is not a measure of any real injury threshold, and nobody should practise stiff-legged landings. Drop height 0.50 m Stopping distance 5 cm Your mass 70 kg Speed at the ground 3.13 m/s (11.3 km/h) √(2 g h) Time to stop 32 ms 2 d ÷ v Average force 11.0 × weight weight × (1 + h ÷ d) That force for your mass 7,554 N mass × 9.81 × the factor Slowdown alone 10.0 g h ÷ d, before adding your weight Bar: force ÷ weight on a 1 to 41 scale (capped). Learning aid only. How each sport bends it Same idea, different specifics.

chunks.text: Each line is a figure from that sport's own page; follow the chip for the whole chapter. Rock climbing · Ch 5 Dropping 3 m and stopping over 0.3 m is about 10 g of slowdown; over 0.6 m, about 5 g. Skydiving · Ch 3 Slowing from 53.6 to 5 m/s over 3 s loads the harness near 2.65 g; over 1 s, about 6 g. Paragliding · Ch 4 Landing at 41.7 instead of 37 km/h carries about 27% more energy into your legs. 🦿 What your body does about it Your legs are the shock absorber. Bending the knees turns a 5 cm stop into a 25 cm one, and on Get fit that is the difference between about 11 × and about 3 × your weight ( Your body in the physics ). Strong, practised legs make that automatic.

Same 0.5 m drop, but you stop over 10 cm. What is the average force in multiples of your weight? 1 + 0.5 ÷ 0.10 = 6 × , between the 11 × (5 cm) and 3 × (25 cm) cases. chunks.title: Physics in five minutes: the common foundation of every sport · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance & turning
chunks.text: To go round a bend, something has to push you towards the middle. Turning needs a sideways push towards the centre of the curve, F = m × v² ÷ r , which grows with the square of speed and as the turn gets tighter. You lean so that this push passes through your centre of mass, tan(lean) = v² ÷ (r × g) , and the ground can supply at most μ × m × g. Worked example · a horse at a canter (5 m/s) on a 10 m circle, then the grip limit Step Working Result 1. v² 5 × 5 25 2. r × g 10 × 9.81 98.1 3. tan(lean) 25 ÷ 98.1 = 0.255 lean ≈ 14.3° 4.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & glide
chunks.text: One equation holds up every wing, from a hang glider to a microlight. Height is the fuel tank of anything without an engine. A wing turns the oncoming air slightly downward; by Newton's third law the air pushes the wing up. The size of that push is L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × C L : air density ρ, true airspeed v, wing area S and a lift coefficient C L set mostly by the angle of attack. Making lift always costs some drag : parasitic drag (the pilot, struts, wires and skin friction) grows with speed, while induced drag (the unavoidable cost of making lift, seen in wingtip vortices) shrinks with speed. Their sum is smallest at one particular speed, which is where a wing glides best.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & glide
chunks.text: Worked example · a 450 kg microlight cruising at 25 m/s (90 km/h) with a 15 m² wing, at sea level Weight = 450 × 9.81 ≈ 4,415 N . In level flight lift equals weight, so C L = 2 × 4,415 ÷ (1.225 × 25² × 15) ≈ 0.77 , a comfortable value for a light-aircraft wing. Slow down to 20 m/s and C L must rise to about 1.2: the wing flies at a higher angle of attack, closer to the stall ( Ch 6 ). Glide ratio: metres forward per metre down Without an engine, an aircraft is always sliding down through the air it's in. The glide ratio equals lift ÷ drag (L/D).

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & glide
chunks.text: Typical round numbers, which vary a lot between models: Aircraft Typical glide ratio Still-air glide from 1,000 m Paraglider (see our paragliding page ) ≈ 8–10 ≈ 8–10 km Hang glider (flexible or rigid wing) ≈ 10–16 ≈ 10–16 km Training sailplane ≈ 25–35 ≈ 25–35 km High-performance sailplane ≈ 45–60 ≈ 45–60 km Microlight, engine off ≈ 7–12 ≈ 7–12 km Long, slender wings (high aspect ratio) cut induced drag, which is why sailplanes have such long wings. A headwind shortens the glide over the ground; sinking air can shorten it far more.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & glide
chunks.text: Aspect ratio: why sailplane wings are so long Induced drag coefficient scales roughly as C Di ≈ C L ² ÷ (π × AR × e) , where aspect ratio AR = span² ÷ area and e is an efficiency factor near 0.8–0.9 for a clean wing. Doubling AR roughly halves induced drag at the same C L . That is why a training sailplane with a long slender wing can glide 30:1 while a stubby microlight wing might manage ~10:1 with the engine off — and why folding a hang-glider's tips (or flying a small PPG wing) costs glide.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & glide
chunks.text: Order of magnitude · same C L = 0.8, e = 0.85 Wing Illustrative AR C Di ≈ C L ²/(π AR e) Relative induced drag PPG / short microlight wing ≈ 5 ≈ 0.048 baseline Hang glider ≈ 8 ≈ 0.030 ≈ 0.63× Training sailplane ≈ 20 ≈ 0.012 ≈ 0.25× Illustrative geometry only — real wings add fuselage, wires and tip devices. The point is the AR lever: span is expensive on the ground and priceless in the air. ✋ Feel the number A glide ratio of 40 is a slope of 1.4°, gentler than almost any road. From the height of a tall building (100 m), a good sailplane could glide 4 km in still air. A sailplane glides at 90 km/h (25 m/s) with L/D 40. How fast is it sinking?

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Lift, drag & glide
chunks.text: Sink rate = speed ÷ glide ratio = 25 ÷ 40 ≈ 0.6 m/s . Any air rising faster than that, and the glider climbs ( Ch 2 ). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals, ridges & soaring
chunks.text: A glider never stops sinking through the air. Soaring is the art of finding air that rises faster. Your climb rate over the ground is simply air's vertical speed − your sink rate . Soaring pilots use three main sources of rising air: Thermals: the sun heats the ground unevenly; air over a warm patch (a dry field, a town, a rocky slope) becomes less dense and rises in bubbles or columns. Typical climbs are around 1–3 m/s, stronger on hot, dry days, and the tops are often marked by fluffy cumulus clouds ( Ch 5 ). Gliders circle tightly to stay inside the core. Ridge (slope) lift: wind blowing onto a hillside is forced upward.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals, ridges & soaring
chunks.text: As long as the wind is steady and roughly perpendicular to the ridge, a glider or hang glider can fly back and forth along it. The lee side has sinking air and turbulence. Wave lift: strong wind over a mountain range can set up standing waves in the air downwind, sometimes marked by smooth, lens-shaped clouds. Wave can carry sailplanes far higher than thermals, which is how many gliding altitude records are set.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals, ridges & soaring
chunks.text: Worked example · climb in a thermal, then glide Step Calculation Result Thermal rises at 2.5 m/s; glider sinks 0.8 m/s while circling 2.5 − 0.8 climb 1.7 m/s Time to gain 1,000 m 1,000 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 590 s ≈ 10 min Glide those 1,000 m at L/D 40 in still air 1,000 × 40 ≈ 40 km Same height for a hang glider at L/D 12 1,000 × 12 ≈ 12 km String climbs and glides together and you have cross-country soaring: India's Hadapsar Gliding Centre in Pune, for example, is reported to hold records for distances over 500 km and heights over 20,000 ft. The sinking air you don't see What goes up must come down: around every thermal there is sinking air, often 1–2 m/s or more.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Thermals, ridges & soaring
chunks.text: A glider crossing it loses height much faster than its still-air sink rate. That's why pilots speed up through sink (to spend less time in it) and slow down in lift — the same idea as the classic "speed-to-fly" rules of thumb: in strong expected lift ahead, fly faster between thermals; in weak days, preserve height. ✋ Feel the number 1.7 m/s up is a calm lift ride: about a floor of a building every two seconds, with no engine anywhere. A hang glider sinks at 1.1 m/s while circling. The thermal is rising at 1.0 m/s. What happens? 1.0 − 1.1 = −0.1 m/s : it still sinks slowly, just more slowly than in still air. Weak thermals that keep a sailplane up may not keep a less efficient wing up.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Hot air: buoyancy you can calculate
chunks.text: A hot-air balloon has no wing and no engine pushing it up. It floats because hot air is lighter than cold air. Archimedes' principle: anything immersed in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Air is a fluid. At constant pressure its density falls as temperature rises: ρ = P ÷ (R × T) , with R = 287 J/(kg·K) for dry air and T in kelvin (°C + 273.15). The envelope is open at the bottom, so the pressure inside is essentially the same as outside; only the temperature differs. The gross lift is V × (ρ outside − ρ inside ) .

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Hot air: buoyancy you can calculate
chunks.text: Equipment (envelope, basket, burners, fuel) is an assumed 0.14 kg per m³ for illustration; people at 80 kg each, pilot included. Real balloons carry safety margins, and commercial operators use much bigger envelopes for more passengers. How a balloon is flown Up: the pilot fires the propane burner to heat the air; each extra °C inside adds about 7 kg of lift to our example balloon. Down: let the air cool, or open a vent at the top to release hot air. Sideways: no direct control. A balloon moves with the wind, so pilots steer by changing height to find winds blowing in different directions, and plan landing areas downwind.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Hot air: buoyancy you can calculate
chunks.text: ✋ Feel the number The 0.28 kg/m³ difference between 15 °C and 100 °C air is about the mass of a full glass of water (≈ 280 g) for every cubic metre. It takes 2,800 cubic metres to lift a small family. Why do hot-air balloon flights in India (and most places) mostly happen around sunrise? Two reasons from the physics: the air is coolest, so the same envelope temperature gives more lift (the table above), and winds near the ground are usually lightest and steadiest before the sun starts thermals ( Ch 5 ). Late afternoon, as heating dies down, is the other window. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Powered vs unpowered flight
chunks.text: An engine doesn't hold you up. The wing does that. The engine pays for the drag, and for the climb. In steady level flight four forces balance: lift = weight and thrust = drag . A glider has no thrust, so gravity provides it: the glider tilts slightly nose-down and "spends" height to keep moving. A powered aircraft (microlight, light sport aircraft, paramotor, motor glider) replaces that with a propeller. Since drag = weight ÷ (L/D), the power needed is P = drag × speed , and any extra power becomes climb: climb rate = extra power ÷ weight .

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Powered vs unpowered flight
chunks.text: Worked example · three ways to fly, side by side (illustrative numbers) Sailplane Microlight Paramotor All-up mass 400 kg 450 kg 110 kg (pilot, motor, wing) Speed · L/D 25 m/s · 40 25 m/s · 10 10 m/s · 6 Drag = weight ÷ L/D ≈ 98 N ≈ 441 N ≈ 180 N Power to fly level = drag × speed ≈ 2.5 kW, paid by height (0.6 m/s sink) ≈ 11 kW ≈ 1.8 kW Extra power to climb needs rising air ( Ch 2 ) +11 kW for 2.5 m/s +1.6 kW for 1.5 m/s Propellers are not perfectly efficient (often roughly 60–80%), so the engine has to deliver more than these figures, plus a margin for take-off and hot, high days ( Ch 5 ).

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Powered vs unpowered flight
chunks.text: The paramotor's L/D is lower than a free-flying paraglider's because the motor, cage and higher speed add drag. Our Paramotoring Thrust Lab lets you dial mass, L/D, thrust and wind to see climb and engine-off glide — the same force balance as this table, with a fabric wing on your back. What the engine changes, and what it doesn't Changes: you can take off from flat ground, climb without rising air, and fly when there's no lift. A paramotor needs only a field (see our Paramotoring page ); a microlight needs a runway or strip.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Powered vs unpowered flight
chunks.text: Doesn't change: the wing still stalls at the same angle of attack ( Ch 6 ), turbulence and wind still matter, and an engine failure turns you into a glider, so pilots always keep a landing option within gliding range. Balloons: the burner isn't thrust at all; it's a heater for buoyancy ( Ch 3 ). ✋ Feel the number About 11 kW is roughly what a typical 150 cc motorbike engine puts out, enough to hold a two-seat microlight in the air at 90 km/h. The microlight's engine and propeller deliver 20 kW of useful thrust power at 25 m/s. Roughly how fast can it climb? Spare power = 20 − 11 = 9 kW. Climb = 9,000 ÷ 4,415 N ≈ 2 m/s (about 400 ft per minute), less on a hot day. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & density altitude
chunks.text: Light aircraft, gliders and balloons are guests of the weather. Reading it is the first skill, not the last. Hot, high and thin: density altitude Wings, propellers and engines all work less well in thin air. Air density depends on both elevation and temperature, so a hot day at a high airfield can feel like flying from a much higher one.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & density altitude
chunks.text: Worked example · air density compared with a standard sea-level day (1.225 kg/m³) Conditions Density % of standard True airspeed needed for the same lift Sea level, 15 °C 1.225 100% × 1.00 430 m, 15 °C 1.164 95% × 1.03 430 m, 35 °C 1.088 89% × 1.06 430 m, 45 °C (north Indian summer) 1.054 86% × 1.08 1,500 m, 30 °C 0.972 79% × 1.12 Speed factor = √(1.225 ÷ density). Engines also make less power in thin air, so take-off runs get longer and climbs weaker on hot afternoons. Clouds, thermals and storms Cloud base: rising air cools as it expands; when it reaches its dew point, cloud forms. A common rule of thumb is about 125 m of height per °C of spread between temperature and dew point.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & density altitude
chunks.text: Cumulonimbus (thunderstorms): powerful up- and downdrafts, gust fronts that spread out from the storm, hail and lightning. They're a hard no-go for every aircraft on this page. Monsoon: low cloud, heavy rain and embedded storms. Balloon operators in India typically fly in the drier months; SkyWaltz, for example, lists a season from 1 September to 30 April. Wind: balloons need light winds to launch and land; gliders and hang gliders need the right wind for ridge lift but can be overpowered by strong, gusty wind. Air flowing over hills, trees and buildings leaves turbulence (rotor) on the downwind side.

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Weather & density altitude
chunks.text: Safety The pilot's call is final Cancellations for weather are a sign of a good operator, not a bad one. If a pilot or instructor says the conditions aren't right, they're reading physics you can't see yet. It's 34 °C with a dew point of 22 °C. Roughly where's the cloud base? Spread 12 °C × 125 m ≈ 1,500 m above the ground. A bigger spread means a higher base and usually deeper thermals. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Recreational flying: gliders, microlights, hang gliders, paramotors & balloons, the physics explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Stalls, turns & control
chunks.text: A wing stalls at an angle, not a speed. Turning, or adding weight, moves the speed at which you reach that angle. Raise the angle of attack and C L rises, until the airflow can no longer follow the top of the wing. It separates, lift drops sharply and drag jumps: a stall . From the lift equation, the speed at which you reach that maximum C L is V stall = √(2 × n × W ÷ (ρ × S × C L,max )) , where n is the load factor (g). In a level turn n = 1 ÷ cos(bank).

chunks.heading: Stalls, turns & control
chunks.text: Three ways to control an aircraft Control type Aircraft How you steer Three-axis Sailplanes, fixed-wing microlights, light sport aircraft Ailerons (roll), elevator (pitch) and rudder (yaw) via stick and pedals Weight-shift Hang gliders, microlight "trikes", powered hang gliders Push and pull a control bar to move your weight relative to the wing Brakes and weight Paramotors, paragliders, powered parachutes Brake toggles pull down the trailing edge; plus weight shift and throttle Buoyancy only Hot-air balloons Burner and vent for up and down; the wind decides direction Safety Low, slow and turning Most stall accidents in light aircraft happen close to the ground: a steep turn at low speed after take-off or before landing.

chunks.heading: Stalls, turns & control
chunks.text: Instructors drill keeping speed up and banks shallow when you're low. Why does a hang glider pilot push the bar out (nose up) to slow down, and what's the risk? Moving weight back raises the nose and the angle of attack, so the wing slows. Push too far and you reach C L,max : the wing stalls. Recovery means lowering the angle of attack again, which needs height. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The licence ladder

chunks.text: In India, flying an aircraft as pilot generally needs a licence from the DGCA (Directorate General of Civil Aviation). chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Grip, gravity and the physics of a good catch.
chunks.text: Bouldering, sport and trad climbing all come down to the same physics: friction on your feet, torque on your arms and a rope that stretches when you fall. Take the challenge, learn the science, then find a gym, a boulder field or a crag at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Gym Crag ≈ 8 kN Peak rope force in a 4 m fall on just 2.5 m of rope. Not how far you fall: how much rope can stretch. ≈ 10 g Average stop from a 3 m boulder fall onto a pad giving 30 cm. Bend your knees: 60 cm of give halves it. ≈ 17.5 kg Arm pull needed with your hips sagging 30 cm off the wall. Hips in halves it: use your legs, save your arms.

chunks.text: Your belay gets checked. Belaying is learned hands-on, and gyms check it before you belay there. An easy grade isn't a safety rating. chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set up a lead fall and see what the rope, you and the top bolt feel
chunks.text: An idealised model: the rope is a perfect spring (stiffness EA ≈ 24 kN, chosen so an 80 kg mass in the standard factor-1.77 test gives ≈ 9 kN, inside the 12 kN limit), the belay is fixed, and nothing else absorbs energy. Real falls are softer, thanks to rope slip, a moving belayer and your body. For learning only; it is not a guide to how far you can safely fall.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction, rubber & rock
chunks.text: Climbing shoes don't stick by magic. They press, and the rock pushes back. Friction is the sideways force that stops your shoe or fingers sliding. In the simple model every physics class uses, the most friction you can get is F ≤ μ × N : the friction coefficient μ (how grippy the two surfaces are together) times the normal force N (how hard you press into the rock). On a slab tilted at angle α, gravity tries to slide you down the slope with a force mg sin α while pressing you in with mg cos α. You only stay put if μ ≥ tan α .

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction, rubber & rock
chunks.text: Worked example · friction needed to stand on a smooth slab, all weight on one foot Slab angle (from horizontal) tan α = μ needed What it feels like 30° 0.58 Walkable in good rubber 40° 0.84 Committing; trust your feet 45° 1.00 Needs very good rubber and technique 60° 1.73 Beyond pure friction: you need edges, holds or hands tan 30° = 0.577, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = 1.732. Real rubber on rough rock behaves better than this simple model on steep ground, because soft rubber also deforms around tiny crystals. That's why sticky rubber can beat "μ ≤ 1". What helps grip Weight over your feet: leaning into a slab feels safer but reduces the push into the rock, so your feet skate. Hips out, heels down.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction, rubber & rock
chunks.text: Chalk: magnesium carbonate dries sweat from your fingers. Brush excess chalk off holds; caked chalk gets slippery. Conditions: cool, dry air beats heat and humidity. Climbers at Badami start very early, even in January, because direct sun makes rock and rubber greasy. Rock type: Hampi's granite and Badami's sandstone feel completely different: rough crystals versus a finer, sometimes softer surface. Wet sandstone can be weakened, so let it dry after rain. Does chalk really help? What a measurement found Climbers swear by chalk, but one early lab study (Li and colleagues, 2001) found chalk lowered fingertip friction on sandstone, granite and slate.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction, rubber & rock
chunks.text: That test pressed a fingertip onto a small sliding block, with forces far below a hanging climber's. A more climbing-like test, by Amca, Vigouroux, Aritan and Berton ( Sports Biomechanics, 2012 ), had eleven experienced climbers hang from real limestone and sandstone holds on a hang board that slowly tilted until their hands slipped; the tilt at the moment of slip gives the friction coefficient. Chalk raised it by 18.7% on limestone and 21.6% on sandstone , and sandstone was about 16–18% grippier than limestone. They found no clear link with the day's humidity or temperature.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction, rubber & rock
chunks.text: Worked example · what +19% and +22% mean on a sloping hold (illustrative starting μ) Hold μ (illustrative) Steepest slope you can hold by friction alone Limestone, no chalk 0.60 arctan 0.60 ≈ 31° Limestone, chalk (+18.7%) 0.71 ≈ 35° Sandstone, no chalk (+15.6% vs limestone) 0.69 ≈ 35° Sandstone, chalk (+21.6%) 0.84 ≈ 40° Only the percentages come from the study; the starting μ of 0.60 is our round number to show the effect. 0.60 × 1.187 = 0.712; 0.60 × 1.156 = 0.694; 0.694 × 1.216 = 0.843. A few degrees of slope is often the difference between a sloper you can hang and one you slide off.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction, rubber & rock
chunks.text: Both studies agree on one thing: a thick, caked layer of chalk on the hold acts like loose grit, so brush holds and use a thin coat. ✋ Feel the number Stand on a sloping roof-like surface in sports shoes and slowly lean back: the point where you start to slide tells you the angle where your shoes' μ equals tan α. Your shoes give μ ≈ 0.84 on a smooth slab. What's the steepest angle you can stand on with no holds? α = arctan 0.84 ≈ 40° . Steeper than that, and you need an edge or a hold. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Body position & torque
chunks.text: Good climbers aren't just strong. They put their weight where the wall can hold it. On a vertical wall, your weight acts at your centre of mass, roughly at your hips. If your hips are a distance d out from the wall, gravity creates a torque (turning effect) of m g × d that tries to topple you backwards around your feet. Your hands, roughly a height h above your feet, must pull in with a force that cancels it: F arms ≈ m g × d ÷ h .

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Body position & torque
chunks.text: Worked example · 70 kg climber (weight 686.7 N), hands 1.2 m above the feet Hips out from the wall Arm pull needed As "kilograms" 0.30 m (sagging back) 686.7 × 0.30 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 172 N ≈ 17.5 kg 0.15 m (hips in) ≈ 86 N ≈ 8.8 kg Steep overhang, feet cut loose ≈ 687 N (your whole weight) ≈ 70 kg A simplified static model: it ignores friction at your feet and assumes you pull straight in. It still shows why moving your hips 15 cm closer to the wall halves the work your arms do. Moves that use the physics Straight arms: hanging from straight arms lets bones and ligaments take the load while muscles partly recover. Legs push, arms steer: leg muscles are far bigger than forearm muscles.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Body position & torque
chunks.text: Stand up on your feet; don't pull up on your arms. Drop-knee and flagging: turning a hip into the wall or pushing a leg out sideways moves your centre of mass under the hold, so you don't "barn-door" (swing open like a door). Overhangs: keep tension through your core and toes so your feet stay on. If they cut loose, your arms suddenly carry your whole weight. ✋ Feel the number Hold a 2 kg bag at arm's length, then close to your chest. Same weight, different torque. Your hips on a wall work the same way. A 60 kg climber keeps their hips 0.2 m out, hands 1.0 m above their feet. What arm pull do they need? 60 × 9.81 × 0.2 ÷ 1.0 ≈ 118 N , about 12 kg-force. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ropes, falls & fall factor
chunks.text: It's not how far you fall. It's how much rope is there to stretch. A falling climber has kinetic energy that the rope must absorb by stretching. A dynamic climbing rope is designed to stretch, so it stops you over a longer distance with a lower peak force. The key number is the fall factor : f = fall distance ÷ rope length paid out . A 3.5 m fall on 10 m of rope (f = 0.35) is far gentler than a 3.5 m fall on 2.5 m of rope near the belay (f = 1.4), because there's four times less rope to stretch. Treating the rope as an ideal spring of stiffness EA gives the peak force F = m g (1 + √(1 + 2 f EA ÷ m g)) .

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ropes, falls & fall factor
chunks.text: Notice that the length of the fall on its own isn't in the formula: only the fall factor is. Worked example · 70 kg climber, ideal dynamic rope (EA ≈ 24 kN, our Fall Lab's model) Fall Rope out Fall factor Peak force (model) 1 m 10 m 0.10 ≈ 2.6 kN 3.5 m 10 m 0.35 ≈ 4.2 kN 3.5 m 5 m 0.70 ≈ 5.5 kN 4 m 2.5 m 1.60 ≈ 8.0 kN Example: f = 0.35, mg = 686.7 N. 2 × 0.35 × 24,000 ÷ 686.7 ≈ 24.5; √25.5 ≈ 5.05; F ≈ 686.7 × 6.05 ≈ 4,150 N. The same model with 80 kg at f = 1.77 gives ≈ 9.0 kN.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ropes, falls & fall factor
chunks.text: The standard drop test The UIAA's rope standard (UIAA 101, which requires the European norm EN 892) drops a test mass, 80 kg for single and twin ropes and 55 kg for half ropes, in a severe factor-1.77 fall onto a fixed metal edge. A single rope must hold the first drop with a peak force of no more than 12 kN (8 kN for a half rope, 12 kN for a twin pair), survive at least 5 drops (12 for twins), and stretch no more than 40% during the fall. Rope maker Petzl points out that real falls are usually softer than the test, because the belayer moves, the rope slips through the device and your harness and body flex.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ropes, falls & fall factor
chunks.text: Safety Static ropes are not climbing ropes Low-stretch "static" ropes are for abseiling, hauling and rescue. Lead-fall on one and the peak force can be several times higher: switch the Fall Lab to "static" to see it. Belaying is a skill you learn hands-on from an instructor, and every gym will check it before you belay there. You're 2 m above your last bolt with 12 m of rope out and no slack. What's your fall distance and fall factor? You fall 2 m to the bolt and 2 m below it: 4 m (plus rope stretch). f = 4 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33 . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Anchors & protection
chunks.text: Two good bolts can be worse than one if the angle between them is wrong. When a sling or rope shares a load F between two anchor points, each leg carries F ÷ (2 cos(θ/2)) , where θ is the angle between the legs. Narrow angles share the load nicely. Wide angles multiply it. Worked example · load on each anchor leg Angle between legs Each leg carries With a 6 kN load 0° 0.50 × F 3.0 kN 60° 0.58 × F 3.5 kN 90° 0.71 × F 4.2 kN 120° 1.00 × F 6.0 kN 150° 1.93 × F 11.6 kN At 120°: cos 60° = 0.5, so each leg takes F ÷ (2 × 0.5) = F. At 150°: cos 75° ≈ 0.259, so each leg takes ≈ 1.93 F.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Anchors & protection
chunks.text: Why the top bolt sees more than you In a lead fall, the rope runs from you, up through the top quickdraw, and back down to the belayer. The bolt holds both strands: your side and the belayer's side (a bit less, because of friction over the carabiner). That's why it can see well over your own peak force; the Fall Lab uses an illustrative 1.6 ×. Where does 1.6 come from? A physics group at the University of Alabama (R. Schad and colleagues, "Safety Analysis of Sport Climbing Falls" ) fitted accelerometers to a real lead climber and belayer on an outdoor route and took repeated falls of 1.3 to 3.2 m with a GriGri.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Anchors & protection
chunks.text: The rope pulled on the climber 1.7 to 1.9 times harder than on the belayer, in every fall: the bend over the carabiner acts as a brake. The bolt holds both strands, so it sees the climber's force × (1 + 1 ÷ 1.7…1.9). Worked example · top-bolt load for a 4.2 kN pull on the climber (the f = 0.35 fall from Ch 3) Climber side ÷ belayer side Belayer side Bolt = sum Bolt ÷ climber 1.0 (a frictionless pulley) 4.2 kN 8.4 kN 2.0 × 1.7 (measured, low end) 2.5 kN 6.7 kN 1.59 × 1.9 (measured, high end) 2.2 kN 6.4 kN 1.53 × "8 : 5 : 3" rule of thumb (bolt : climber : belayer) 2.5 kN 6.7 kN 1.6 × 4.2 ÷ 1.7 = 2.47 kN; 4.2 + 2.47 = 6.67 kN.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Anchors & protection
chunks.text: If you model the bend as rope friction round a 180° turn (T climber = T belayer × e μπ ), a ratio of 1.8 means an effective μ ≈ ln 1.8 ÷ π ≈ 0.19. In the Alabama falls themselves, the climber felt up to about 4 × body weight and the bolt never saw more than 4.5 kN. The same study found two things every new leader should know. The climber fell about 1.8 times the "nominal" distance, because the rope stretched about 12% and the belayer was lifted up to about 1 m, and that was with no slack and a locking belay device.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Anchors & protection
chunks.text: And belayer weight matters: a belayer much lighter than the climber gets pulled up hard (the authors put the limit for catching at all near 55% of the climber's mass), while a much heavier one gives a harsher, more static catch. That's why gyms teach weight-matched belaying, ground anchors and a soft catch, in person. Sport versus trad Sport climbing: you clip pre-placed bolts. At Badami, local climbers report that some bottom bolts have been stolen or chopped, so a stick clip (a pole for clipping the first bolt from the ground) is recommended. Trad climbing: you place removable protection, such as nuts wedged into constrictions and spring-loaded cams.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Anchors & protection
chunks.text: A cam turns your pull into outward pressure on the crack walls; friction holds it. It needs solid rock and the right crack shape. Strength markings: certified carabiners and slings are marked with their rated strength in kN. Even so, rock quality is often the weak link. Safety Learn this in person Building anchors and placing trad gear are life-critical skills. This chapter explains the physics; it doesn't teach the technique. Learn from qualified instructors on real rock, and have your placements checked. A sling joins two bolts at a 90° angle and holds 4 kN. What does each bolt take? 4 ÷ (2 × cos 45°) = 4 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 2.8 kN each. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Bouldering falls & landings
chunks.text: No rope means every fall ends on the ground. The pad's job is to make that ending longer. Bouldering means short, hard climbs close to the ground, protected by crash pads and spotters instead of a rope. Falling from height h, you hit the ground at v = √(2 g h) . To stop, you need an average deceleration of a = v² ÷ (2 d) , where d is your stopping distance: the pad's compression plus how much your knees bend.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Bouldering falls & landings
chunks.text: Worked example · landing from different heights Fall height Impact speed Stopping over 0.3 m Stopping over 0.6 m 1 m 4.4 m/s ≈ 3.3 g ≈ 1.7 g 2 m 6.3 m/s ≈ 6.7 g ≈ 3.3 g 3 m 7.7 m/s ≈ 10 g ≈ 5 g 4 m 8.9 m/s ≈ 13 g ≈ 6.7 g 3 m: v = √(2 × 9.81 × 3) ≈ 7.67 m/s; a = 7.67² ÷ (2 × 0.3) ≈ 98 m/s² ≈ 10 g. A neat shortcut: a ÷ g = h ÷ d. Doubling the stopping distance halves the deceleration. Landing well Feet first, knees soft, then roll back onto your bottom and back. Don't put your arms out straight to catch yourself: wrists break. Pads cover the landing, not the rock: place them where you'll actually fall, and close gaps between pads. Hampi's boulders often have uneven, rocky landings.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Bouldering falls & landings
chunks.text: Spotters steer, they don't catch: hands up near your hips and back, guiding you onto the pad and protecting your head. Down-climb or jump on purpose: a controlled drop beats a surprise fall. ✋ Feel the number Jumping off a 1 m wall and landing stiff-legged feels jarring; landing with bent knees feels fine. Same speed, longer stopping distance. Your pad and knee-bend give 0.5 m of stopping distance. From what height would you see 6 g? a ÷ g = h ÷ d, so h = 6 × 0.5 = 3 m . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy, grip & pump
chunks.text: Your legs could carry you up the wall all day. Your forearms are the bottleneck. Lifting your body up a route takes mechanical work W = m g h . Your body burns several times more than that, because muscles are inefficient and much of climbing is gripping and holding still, which costs energy without lifting you at all. Worked example · lifting a 70 kg climber Climb Height Work = m g h In kcal Gym boulder problem 4 m ≈ 2.7 kJ ≈ 0.7 kcal Badami single pitch 20 m ≈ 13.7 kJ ≈ 3.3 kcal A 200 m multi-pitch 200 m ≈ 137 kJ ≈ 33 kcal 70 × 9.81 × 20 = 13,734 J; ÷ 4,184 J per kcal ≈ 3.3 kcal.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy, grip & pump
chunks.text: Badami's bolted routes are mostly single pitches of roughly 9–23 m, according to the Bangalore Climbing Initiatives guide. The pump Squeezing a hold hard and continuously compresses the blood vessels inside your forearm muscles. Less oxygen gets in and waste products build up; the muscles swell and your grip fades. The fixes are mostly technique: climb smoothly, rest on big holds with straight arms, shake out each arm in turn, and grip only as hard as you need. Fingers need time In a crimp (fingertip on a small edge, middle joint bent to about 90°), the flexor tendons try to bowstring away from the bone and press on the A2 "pulley", a band of tissue that holds them in.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy, grip & pump
chunks.text: Andreas Schweizer measured this directly in climbers' fingers ( Journal of Biomechanics, 2001 ): the edge of the A2 pulley carried about 3 times the force at the fingertip. Extrapolating his data, 118 N at one fingertip would put about 373 N on the pulley, close to the roughly 400 N breaking strength reported for A2 pulleys in earlier cadaver tests.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy, grip & pump
chunks.text: Worked example · A2 pulley load ≈ 3 × fingertip force (crimp grip) Situation (illustrative) Force at one fingertip Pulley load ≈ 3 × 70 kg climber, feet on, about 25% of body weight shared by 8 fingers ≈ 21 N ≈ 64 N Steep wall, half body weight on 4 fingers of one hand ≈ 86 N ≈ 258 N Schweizer's extrapolated point 118 N ≈ 373 N (his figure) 70 × 9.81 = 687 N. 687 × 0.25 ÷ 8 ≈ 21 N; 687 × 0.5 ÷ 4 ≈ 86 N. Real fingers don't share load equally (the middle and ring fingers often take more), so a single finger can be worse off. Schweizer found the open-hand ("slope") grip bowstrings much less. This is why a sudden foot slip while crimping is the classic pulley injury.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy, grip & pump
chunks.text: Tendons and the finger "pulleys" that hold them adapt much more slowly than muscles. Sharp pain in a finger during a hard crimp is a reason to stop. Warm up on easy climbs, build up volume gradually, and get finger injuries checked by a professional. ✋ Feel the number Climbing a 20 m route lifts you the height of a six- or seven-storey building, but the mechanical work is only about 3 kcal. The tiredness you feel is grip, not height. A 55 kg climber does five laps of a 15 m route. How much lifting work is that? 55 × 9.81 × 15 × 5 ≈ 40 kJ (about 9.7 kcal). ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The climbing ladder

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gym → boulders → top rope → lead → trad & mountains → competition
chunks.text: Rock climbing has no single licence. Instead, gyms run their own inductions and belay checks, institutes run graded courses, and competitions follow World Climbing (IFSC) rules through the Indian Mountaineering Foundation. The steps below are a typical path, with the real requirement we found at each step. They aren't official grades.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Climbing has two kinds of rule-makers: sport federations that run competitions, and safety bodies that set equipment standards. We checked each on its own official website.

chunks.title: Rock Climbing · Physics of Grip, Falls & Ropes · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: Competition World Climbing (IFSC) The International Federation of Sport Climbing, now branded World Climbing, governs competition climbing worldwide: Boulder, Lead, Speed and Para Climbing. Its member list names the Indian Mountaineering Foundation as India's federation. ifsc-climbing.org Safety standards UIAA The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation sets safety standards for climbing equipment and awards the UIAA Safety Label. Its rope standard, UIAA 101, sets the 12 kN single-rope drop-test limit used in Ch 3. theuiaa.org

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: From your first 5K to Khardung La, it's all physiology.
chunks.text: Every stride is a small collision with the ground, every kilometre a bill paid in oxygen, and every race at altitude a negotiation with thin air. Learn running economy, ground forces, VO₂ max, fuel, altitude and heat with real numbers, then pick your race. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science easy jog race pace ≈ 650 W Heat your body makes running at 10 km/h: a room heater. Most of the energy you burn becomes heat. ≈ 1 kg/h Sweat you must evaporate at an easy 10 km/h. Sweat that drips off cools you very little; humidity hurts. ≈ 2,000 kcal The carbohydrate your body stores, less than a marathon burns. That's the wall at around 30 km. Practise fuelling.
