chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Run-walk is fine. Build time on your feet gradually over weeks, mostly at an easy, conversational pace. Heat illness is an emergency. Confusion, stopping sweating or collapse: stop, get into shade, cool down fast, call medics. Downhill bites later. Your thighs brake every downhill step; that causes the deep soreness after hilly races. Ask before you book a first race → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Do you know what your body is doing at race pace?
chunks.text: 15 questions on the science of running, from the footstrike to the high passes: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Six chapters, from the first stride to the highest pass
chunks.text: Each chapter takes one idea and follows it onto the road, with worked numbers you can check on a calculator. Our reference runner weighs 70 kg and has a VO₂ max of 45 mL/kg/min. Energy and oxygen costs are textbook round values for adults; real ones vary between people, shoes, surfaces and conditions. This page is for adults; it is not medical advice. Interactive · Pace & Altitude Lab

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pick a race, a pace and an altitude, and see what your body has to deliver
chunks.text: An illustrative model: energy ≈ 1 kcal per kg per km, oxygen cost ≈ 200 mL per kg per km, cadence 170 steps/min, peak foot force ≈ 2.5 × body weight, and a rule-of-thumb VO₂ max loss of about 7% per 1,000 m above 1,000 m. Standard-atmosphere air pressure. For learning only; it is not a training, medical or acclimatisation tool.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pick a race, a pace and an altitude, and see what your body has to deliver
chunks.text: Pace 6:00 /km Body mass 70 kg Your VO₂ max at sea level (mL/kg/min) 45 Race 5K 10K Half Marathon Altitude Sea level (Mumbai) Leh · 3,505 m Khardung La · 5,370 m Finish time 2:06:35 pace × distance Energy used 1,477 kcal Ch 1 · ≈ 1 kcal/kg/km Steps ≈ 21,500 Ch 2 · 170 per minute Peak force per footstrike 1,717 N Ch 2 · ≈ 2.5 × body weight Oxygen this pace needs 33.3 Ch 3 · mL/kg/min Your VO₂ max here 45.0 Ch 5 · altitude rule of thumb Share of your ceiling 74% Ch 3 · need ÷ ceiling Air pressure vs sea level 100.0% Ch 5 · O₂ partial pressure 21.2 kPa Sweat to evaporate 0.96 kg/h Ch 6 · if every drop evaporates Bar = share of your aerobic ceiling (0–110%).

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pick a race, a pace and an altitude, and see what your body has to deliver
chunks.text: Real numbers vary a lot between people: altitude effects in particular differ by individual and improve with acclimatisation. Treat every number as a teaching example, and follow your race's acclimatisation rules and medical advice, not this lab. CH 1

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: A kilometre costs about the same whether you jog it or race it. Racing just pays faster. A long-standing rule of thumb from exercise physiology: running on the flat costs about 1 kcal per kilogram of body mass per kilometre (≈ 4.2 kJ/kg/km), and the figure changes surprisingly little with speed. In oxygen terms, that's about 200 mL of oxygen per kg per km ; each litre of oxygen you use releases about 5 kcal from food, so the two rules agree. Individual runners vary by roughly ±10–20%: that spread is running economy .

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: Worked example · energy for our 70 kg reference runner Race Distance Energy (≈ 1 kcal/kg/km) Oxygen used 5K 5 km ≈ 350 kcal ≈ 70 L 10K 10 km ≈ 700 kcal ≈ 140 L Half marathon 21.1 km ≈ 1,480 kcal ≈ 295 L Marathon 42.2 km ≈ 2,950 kcal ≈ 590 L Oxygen = 200 mL × 70 kg × distance. For the marathon: 0.2 × 70 × 42.2 ≈ 590 litres of oxygen, about 2,800 litres of air's worth of oxygen at sea level, all drawn in through your lungs. What changes your economy Training: years of running, plus strength and plyometric work, generally improve economy. Technique and springiness: tendons such as the Achilles store and return elastic energy each stride ( Ch 2 ).

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: Shoes: lighter shoes cost less to swing, and studies of some modern foam-and-plate racing shoes report a few per cent better economy for many runners. The size of the effect varies by person. Hills, wind and surface: uphill costs extra; trails and sand cost more than smooth roads; a headwind adds air drag, which is small for most runners at everyday paces but grows with speed squared.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: "Super shoes": what was measured, and what it's worth In a lab study at the University of Colorado ( Hoogkamer et al., Sports Medicine, 2018 ; funded by Nike, which made the prototype), 18 high-calibre runners ran on a treadmill at 14, 16 and 18 km/h in a prototype shoe with a soft, springy foam and a stiff carbon plate, and in two established racing shoes of matched weight. The prototype cut the energy cost of running by about 4% on average, for every one of the 18 runners, at all three speeds. Later studies of similar shoes found the benefit varies more from runner to runner. A 4% saving in energy doesn't make you exactly 4% faster.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: The same group worked out how economy turns into speed ( Kipp et al., Frontiers in Physiology, 2019 ): below about 3 m/s (slower than about 5:33/km) your speed gains slightly more than the economy gain; faster than that, less; and at world-class marathon pace (5.5 m/s) only about two-thirds as much, because air resistance grows quickly with speed.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: Worked example · what a 4% economy gain might be worth in a marathon (rough) Marathon time Average speed Speed gain (from Kipp et al.) New time (approx.) 2:04 5.7 m/s ≈ 2.6% (about ⅔ of 4%) ≈ 2:00:50 3:30 3.3 m/s a little under 4% ≈ 3:22–3:23 4:30 2.6 m/s about 4%, slightly more ≈ 4:19–4:20 The paper's own example: at 2:04 pace, a 3% economy gain gives 1.97% more speed, or about 2:01:36. Scaling that to 4%: 124 min ÷ 1.026 ≈ 120.8 min. The other rows use the paper's rule of thumb (gain ≈ economy gain near 3 m/s), so treat them as rough. And it only helps if the shoe actually gives you a 4% saving.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: To stop shoes running away with the sport, World Athletics' Athletic Shoe Regulations (in force from 1 January 2026) cap the sole at 40 mm for road races and 20 mm for track and field events; mountain and trail races allow any thickness. The rule applies at World Athletics, area and label competitions, where results count for records. Most city-race runners can wear what they like, but check your race's rules if you're chasing a qualifying time. ✋ Feel the number A 70 kg runner's 10K costs about 700 kcal, roughly what's in three or four plates of rice. A marathon costs more than most people eat in a day. A 55 kg runner and an 85 kg runner both finish a marathon.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Running economy & energy cost
chunks.text: Roughly how much energy did each use? 55 × 42.2 ≈ 2,320 kcal ; 85 × 42.2 ≈ 3,590 kcal . Energy scales with the mass you carry. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ground forces, cadence & stride
chunks.text: Running is a series of short collisions. The shorter the contact, the harder the hit. Walking always keeps one foot on the ground. Running has a flight phase , when both feet are off it. Over a whole stride you don't accelerate up or down on average, so the ground's average push must equal your weight (Newton's second law). But the ground only gets to push while your foot is down, so during contact the force has to be much larger.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ground forces, cadence & stride
chunks.text: Worked example · cadence 170 steps/min, so each step takes 60 ÷ 170 ≈ 0.353 s Ground contact time Average force during contact Peak force (half-sine shape) For 70 kg (687 N) 0.30 s (easy jog) ≈ 1.18 × BW ≈ 1.85 × BW ≈ 1,270 N 0.25 s ≈ 1.41 × BW ≈ 2.22 × BW ≈ 1,530 N 0.20 s (faster running) ≈ 1.76 × BW ≈ 2.77 × BW ≈ 1,900 N Average during contact = body weight × step time ÷ contact time. A force curve shaped like half a sine wave peaks at π/2 ≈ 1.57 times its average. This simple model lands right in the 2–3 × body weight range measured in running studies (walking is about 1.2 ×).

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ground forces, cadence & stride
chunks.text: Springs in your legs When your foot lands, tendons (especially the Achilles) and the arch of the foot stretch and store elastic energy, then release much of it as you push off, like a bouncing ball. That's a big part of why running is cheaper than its forces suggest. Fatigue, very stiff or very soft surfaces, and long downhills change how well this works. What makes sprinters faster? Force, not fast legs Harvard researchers ran 33 people of very different sprinting ability on a treadmill fitted with a force plate ( Weyand et al., J Appl Physiol, 2000 ). Their top speeds ranged from 6.2 to 11.1 m/s.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ground forces, cadence & stride
chunks.text: The fastest runners didn't swing their legs through the air any faster; swing time didn't differ. Instead they pushed harder on the ground: the average force during contact was 1.26 times greater for an 11.1 m/s runner than a 6.2 m/s one. Running downhill on a 6° slope, the same people reached 9.96 m/s with an average contact force of 2.30 × body weight; uphill (9°), 7.10 m/s with 1.76 × body weight. That fits the model above: if swing time stays the same, the only way to take longer steps at the same rate is to spend less time on the ground and push harder while you're there. It's why sprint coaches talk about force and stiffness, not "quick feet".

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ground forces, cadence & stride
chunks.text: Cadence and step length Speed = cadence × step length. At 5:00/km (200 m per minute) and 170 steps per minute, each step is about 1.18 m: about 36,000 steps in a marathon. Many coaches suggest a slightly quicker cadence for runners who overstride (landing with the foot far ahead of the body), and studies find that modest cadence increases reduce loading at the knee and hip. There's no single "correct" footstrike: changing how you land mostly shifts load between the knee and hip and the calf and Achilles, so change gradually. Downhill bites later Running downhill makes the thigh muscles brake each step while lengthening (eccentric contractions).

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ground forces, cadence & stride
chunks.text: That's what causes the deep soreness after hilly races, including long mountain descents such as the drop from Khardung La. Train on descents before a hilly race. You speed up to 4:30/km keeping 170 steps per minute. What's your new step length? 4:30/km = 1,000 m ÷ 4.5 min ≈ 222 m/min. Step length = 222 ÷ 170 ≈ 1.31 m . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: VO₂ max, thresholds & pacing
chunks.text: Your aerobic ceiling sets the limit. Economy and pacing decide how close you live to it. VO₂ max is the most oxygen your body can take up and use per minute, usually in mL per kg per minute. It depends on how much blood your heart pumps and how well your muscles extract oxygen. Many untrained adults are in the 30s to 40s; elite endurance runners can exceed 70. Training raises it, especially in the first months; age gradually lowers it. The oxygen a pace needs is simply economy × speed .

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: VO₂ max, thresholds & pacing
chunks.text: With 200 mL/kg/km: Worked example · oxygen needed vs a VO₂ max of 45 (sea level) Pace Speed Oxygen needed Share of VO₂ max 45 7:00 /km 8.6 km/h ≈ 28.6 mL/kg/min ≈ 63% 6:00 /km 10 km/h ≈ 33.3 ≈ 74% 5:00 /km 12 km/h 40.0 ≈ 89% 4:00 /km 15 km/h 50.0 ≈ 111%: not sustainable Thresholds: how close can you run to the ceiling? As effort rises, there's a point where lactate starts building up in the blood faster than your body can clear it. Above this lactate threshold , fatigue accumulates quickly. Trained runners can hold a higher share of their VO₂ max before they reach it, so they can race longer at a higher percentage.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: VO₂ max, thresholds & pacing
chunks.text: Very roughly, short races are run near the top of the range and marathons well below it. Pacing Because oxygen cost rises with speed and anything above threshold accumulates fatigue, an even pace (or a slightly faster second half) is usually the most economical way to race. Starting too fast borrows from later and spends carbohydrate quickly ( Ch 4 ). Heat and altitude lower the pace you can hold at the same effort ( Ch 5 , Ch 6 ). A runner with a VO₂ max of 52 races at 5:00/km. What share of their ceiling is that? Need = 200 × (1 ÷ 5) = 40 mL/kg/min. 40 ÷ 52 ≈ 77% . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Energy systems & the wall
chunks.text: Three engines, one tank that runs low, and a wall at around 30 km. Muscles run on ATP, and they only hold a few seconds' worth, so three systems keep refilling it: The three energy systems (approximate time scales) System Fuel Dominates Running example Phosphocreatine Stored creatine phosphate first ~10 s A sprint to the finish line Anaerobic glycolysis Glycogen/glucose, without oxygen ~10 s to ~2 min A 400 m or 800 m race Aerobic metabolism Carbohydrate and fat, with oxygen beyond ~2 min Everything from 5K to ultras The systems overlap; none switches off. But a 5K is already mostly aerobic, and a marathon is overwhelmingly so.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Energy systems & the wall
chunks.text: Why the wall arrives A well-fed runner stores very roughly 400–500 g of glycogen in muscle and about 100 g in the liver: around 2,000 kcal. A 70 kg runner's marathon costs about 2,950 kcal ( Ch 1 ), and at race pace a large share of it comes from carbohydrate. Fat stores are enormous, but fat releases energy more slowly and needs more oxygen per kcal. When glycogen runs low, often around 30–35 km, the pace you can hold drops sharply: the wall . Two levers delay it: start with full stores (carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before), and take carbohydrate during the race.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Energy systems & the wall
chunks.text: Sports-nutrition guidance commonly suggests about 30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour for long races, and up to about 90 g per hour for some athletes using mixed sugars. Practise race-day fuelling in training: guts adapt too. You start with 2,000 kcal of glycogen and burn carbohydrate at 600 kcal/h at marathon pace. Without eating, roughly when do you run low? 2,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 3.3 hours . For a 4-hour marathoner, that's around the 33–35 km mark: right where the wall is reported. 45 g of carbohydrate an hour (≈ 180 kcal) pushes it well past the finish. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Altitude: thin air, acclimatisation & AMS
chunks.text: The air is still 21% oxygen. There's just less air. What drives oxygen into your blood is its partial pressure : about 21% of the total air pressure. Total pressure falls with height, so every breath carries fewer oxygen molecules, even though the percentage hasn't changed. Worked example · International Standard Atmosphere Place Altitude Air pressure vs sea level Oxygen partial pressure Mumbai sea level 101.3 kPa 100% 21.2 kPa (for comparison) 2,000 m 79.5 kPa ≈ 78% 16.7 kPa Leh ≈ 3,505 m (11,500 ft) 65.7 kPa ≈ 65% 13.8 kPa Khardung La top ≈ 5,370 m (17,618 ft) 51.4 kPa ≈ 51% 10.8 kPa The Ladakh Marathon organisers describe it simply: oxygen drops to about 50% at Khardung La top.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Altitude: thin air, acclimatisation & AMS
chunks.text: Real pressure also varies with weather and season by a few per cent. What your body does about it Within hours you breathe faster and deeper, and your heart rate rises at any given effort. Over days, your kidneys rebalance your blood chemistry so you can keep breathing harder. Over weeks, your body makes more red blood cells. That's acclimatisation , and it takes time whatever your fitness: the Ladakh organisers stress it is "not determined by individual fitness levels". Even acclimatised, your aerobic ceiling is lower up high: as a rough rule of thumb, VO₂ max falls by several per cent per 1,000 m above about 1,000 m (the Lab uses 7%), so the same pace feels much harder.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Altitude: thin air, acclimatisation & AMS
chunks.text: The Ladakh Marathon's own rules (13th edition, 2026) Race Arrive in Leh at least Notes from the organisers 5 km Run for Fun, 11.2 km Run 7 days before Even the shortest race is "an altogether different experience" at 11,500 ft Half marathon, marathon 10 days before Bib collection in person on 5–6 Sep 2026 Khardung La Challenge (72 km), Silk Route Ultra (122 km) 15 days before (mandatory) Bib collection 29–30 Aug 2026; medical check of vitals at the start; supplementary oxygen not permitted The organisers also advise complete rest on day 1, going slow, staying hydrated, avoiding alcohol for the first few days, monitoring your oxygen saturation, and visiting SNM Hospital in Leh if you feel any signs of altitude sickness.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Altitude: thin air, acclimatisation & AMS
chunks.text: Their page mentions that many people take Diamox (acetazolamide); it's a prescription medicine, so discuss it with your doctor. Altitude sickness Acute mountain sickness (AMS) usually begins within hours to a day of arriving high: headache with nausea, fatigue, dizziness or poor sleep. Mild AMS often settles with rest and no further ascent. Two rarer conditions are emergencies: HAPE (fluid in the lungs: breathlessness at rest, cough, falling exercise tolerance) and HACE (swelling of the brain: confusion, unsteadiness, drowsiness). Both need immediate descent and medical care.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Altitude: thin air, acclimatisation & AMS
chunks.text: Flying straight into Leh puts you at 3,500 m in an hour, with no gradual climb, which is exactly why the organisers ask for 7–15 days on the ground first. Using the Lab's rule of thumb, what's the VO₂ max at Leh of a runner who has 50 at sea level? And what share of it does a 6:00/km pace need? 50 × (1 − 0.07 × 2.505) ≈ 41.2 . 6:00/km needs ≈ 33.3, so ≈ 81% , against 67% at sea level. Same pace, much harder. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Heat, sweat & hydration
chunks.text: Most of the energy you burn becomes heat. Sweat only helps when it evaporates. Muscles turn only around a fifth to a quarter of their energy into movement; the rest becomes heat. Our 70 kg runner at 10 km/h burns about 700 kcal per hour ≈ 810 W, so roughly 650 W of heat : like a small room heater inside you. Your body sheds it mainly by evaporating sweat, which takes about 2.4 MJ per kilogram. Worked example · sweat needed if all of it evaporates (80% of energy as heat) Runner Speed Heat produced Sweat to evaporate 55 kg 10 km/h ≈ 510 W ≈ 0.76 kg/h 70 kg 10 km/h ≈ 650 W ≈ 0.96 kg/h 70 kg 12 km/h ≈ 780 W ≈ 1.16 kg/h 85 kg 12 km/h ≈ 950 W ≈ 1.40 kg/h Heavier and faster runners make more heat.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Heat, sweat & hydration
chunks.text: Sweat that drips off cools you very little, so real sweat losses in humid heat are often higher than these numbers. Humidity is the real enemy Evaporation needs dry air to carry vapour away. On a humid coastal morning, you sweat just as hard but cool less, so your core temperature and heart rate climb at the same pace. Indian city races start early in the cooler months for this reason: the Vedanta Delhi Half Marathon is in October and the Tata Mumbai Marathon in January. Heat adaptation (training gradually in warm conditions over a week or two) increases sweat rate and lowers heart rate in the heat.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Heat, sweat & hydration
chunks.text: Hydration: neither too little nor too much Losing a lot of body water raises heart rate and body temperature. But drinking far more than you sweat, especially plain water over many hours, can dilute blood sodium ( hyponatraemia ), which is dangerous too. Weigh yourself before and after long training runs to learn your own sweat rate, and drink to a plan. At high altitude the air is cold and very dry, so you lose extra water just by breathing hard; the Ladakh organisers make hydration packs mandatory for ultra runners. Safety Heat illness is an emergency Confusion, stopping sweating, collapse or a very high body temperature during a run can mean heat stroke.

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Heat, sweat & hydration
chunks.text: Stop, get into shade, cool the person rapidly, and call the race medical team or emergency services. You weigh 70.0 kg before an hour's run and 68.9 kg after, having drunk 0.4 L. What was your sweat loss? Mass lost 1.1 kg + 0.4 kg drunk = about 1.5 L of sweat per hour , higher than the "all evaporates" estimate, as expected when some sweat drips off. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The race ladder

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: 5K → 10K → half → full → ultra → high altitude
chunks.text: Running has no licence or grading. The real "certificates" are timing certificates from your previous races, and India's big events increasingly ask for them. Below, each step shows the real entry rules we found on the organisers' own pages, so you can see what the next rung asks of you. Courses themselves get certified too: see "What makes a course official" below the ladder.

chunks.heading: What makes a course (and a time) official
chunks.text: Course measurement AIMS–World Athletics measurement AIMS and World Athletics accept only the calibrated bicycle method for measuring road races, by accredited Grade A or B measurers. For world records, a course may drop no more than 1 m per km and the start and finish may be no more than 50% of the distance apart. The Ladakh Marathon says it is AIMS-certified. aims-worldrunning.org › measurement Race labels World Athletics Label road races World Athletics grants labels to road races meeting its standards. The TCS World 10K Bengaluru describes itself as a World Athletics Gold Label Road Race.

Times must come from a course certified by USATF, AIMS or a national governing body, and meeting the standard doesn't guarantee entry (the 2027 cut-off was 5 min 17 s faster than standard). baa.org › qualify 04 · Governing bodies

chunks.title: Running, road to high altitude: the science, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: World Athletics governs athletics worldwide, including road running, and works with AIMS on course measurement. Trail running has its own points system through ITRA. In India, the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) is the national body. Every body below was checked on its official website.

chunks.heading: Harness the wind. A sail is a wing standing on its end.
chunks.text: Sailing is physics you can steer: a sail that works like a wing, a wind that changes as you speed up, a fin underwater that stops you sliding sideways, and your own weight holding the boat upright. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Wind & Sail Lab, then find courses and clubs in India and abroad. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First sail Racing Skills · Nationals 2.25× Sail force when a 12 kn breeze gusts to 18 kn. Ease the sail when a gust hits. 62 kg Crew weight needed to keep a dinghy level, close to the wind. Lean out or ease the sail, or the boat tips. ≈ 6.5× How much harder a keel rights a boat than a hiking crew. In a dinghy, your body is the ballast.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Capsizing is normal. Dinghy courses teach capsize recovery early, so you practise it before you need it. If you capsize, stay with the boat. Don't count on an air pocket underneath; follow the drill you practised. Wear a buoyancy aid every time. Ask whether a safety boat is on the water during lessons. Ask before you book a first sail → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set the true wind, your course, your boat speed and your sail area, then see the wind you actually feel, how hard the sail pulls, how much of that pull drives you forward and how much tips you over
chunks.text: A simple model: apparent wind is the true wind plus the headwind from your own speed; the sail works like a wing with a lift coefficient of 1.0 and no drag, pulling at right angles to the apparent wind; the heeling force acts 2.5 m above the centreboard, and the crew sits 1 m out from the centreline. Learning values only (illustrative): real sails, boats and crews vary. Courses from close-hauled (40°) to a beam reach (90°).

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How a sail makes lift
chunks.text: Upwind, a sail isn't pushed. It's a wing standing on its end. A curved sail set at a small angle to the wind turns the airflow . To bend the air around it, the sail needs lower pressure on its curved, downwind (leeward) side and higher pressure on its windward side; that pressure difference is the sail's force, called lift even though it acts sideways and forward. The air on the two sides doesn't have to "meet up" at the back: the sail simply turns the flow, like a wing. The force grows with the air's density ρ, the sail area A, the square of the wind speed V and a lift coefficient C L that depends on the sail's shape and angle: F = ½ ρ V² A C L .

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How a sail makes lift
chunks.text: India's Yachting Association teaches "how sails work" in its Racing Skills course. Worked example · a 7 m² sail, C L = 1.0, air at 1.225 kg/m³ (from our Wind & Sail Lab, illustrative) Wind In m/s ½ρV² (pressure) Force on 7 m² 6 kn 3.09 5.8 Pa 41 N 12 kn 6.17 23.3 Pa 163 N 18 kn 9.26 52.5 Pa 368 N 1 knot = 0.514 m/s. At 12 kn: ½ × 1.225 × 6.17² ≈ 23.3 Pa; × 7 m² ≈ 163 N. Double the wind and the force goes up four times; triple it and the force is nine times bigger. ⛵ Feel the number 163 N is roughly the weight of a 17 kg bag. In a gust from 12 to 18 kn, it becomes the weight of a 37 kg bag, which is why sailors ease the sheet when a gust hits.

chunks.heading: How a sail makes lift
chunks.text: Same 7 m² sail: what's the force at 12 kn on a 10 m² sail instead? 23.3 Pa × 10 m² ≈ 233 N . Force grows in step with area. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Apparent wind
chunks.text: The wind you feel on a moving boat isn't the wind on the shore. When you move, you feel a headwind from your own speed. On board, it adds to the true wind (the wind a moored boat feels) to make the apparent wind , and that's the wind your sails actually use. It's a vector sum: AWS = √(TWS² + BS² + 2·TWS·BS·cos TWA) , where TWS is the true wind speed, BS the boat speed and TWA the angle between your course and the true wind. Speeding up always swings the apparent wind forward , so you trim your sails in as you accelerate. Sailing upwind, the apparent wind is stronger than the true wind; sailing downwind, it's weaker.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Apparent wind
chunks.text: Worked example · 12 kn of true wind from the side (a beam reach, 90°), from our Wind & Sail Lab Boat speed Apparent wind speed Apparent wind angle 0 kn 12.0 kn 90° 3 kn 12.4 kn 76° 5 kn 13.0 kn 67° 8 kn 14.4 kn 56° At 90°, cos TWA = 0, so AWS = √(12² + 5²) = 13.0 kn, and the angle is cos⁻¹(5 ÷ 13) ≈ 67°. The faster the boat, the further forward the wind. True wind 8 kn at 90°, boat speed 6 kn: apparent wind speed? √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 kn , at cos⁻¹(6 ÷ 10) ≈ 53°. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Points of sail, tacking & gybing
chunks.text: You can't sail straight into the wind, so you zigzag. The sail force acts at right angles to the apparent wind, so only part of it drives you forward: drive = F × sin(apparent angle) . Point too close to the wind and the drive vanishes; the sails flap and the boat stops in the no-go zone (stuck there, you're "in irons"). Our examples use 45° either side of the wind, a typical figure for a dinghy. Bearing away, you pass through close-hauled , close reach , beam reach (wind at 90°), broad reach and the run (wind from behind). To get upwind you beat , zigzagging and turning the bow through the wind (a tack ).

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Points of sail, tacking & gybing
chunks.text: Downwind, turning the stern through the wind is a gybe : the boom swings across fast, so the crew must duck and the helm must control it. YAI's Basic Skills 2 course covers tacking and gybing on a triangle course. Worked example · reaching a mark 1 km straight upwind (illustrative boat speeds) Angle to the true wind Distance sailed Boat speed Speed made good upwind 40° 1.31 km 3.6 kn 2.76 kn 45° 1.41 km 4.0 kn 2.83 kn 50° 1.56 km 4.3 kn 2.76 kn 60° 2.00 km 4.8 kn 2.40 kn Distance = 1 km ÷ cos(angle); speed made good (VMG) = boat speed × cos(angle). Pointing higher shortens the path but slows the boat; sailing lower is faster but longer. Here, 45° wins.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Points of sail, tacking & gybing
chunks.text: When two boats meet on opposite tacks while racing, the Racing Rules of Sailing (Rule 10) say the boat on port tack (wind over its left side) keeps clear of the boat on starboard tack. YAI teaches Rule 10 and its neighbours in its Racing Skills course. How far do you sail to reach a mark 2 km upwind, tacking at 45°? 2 ÷ cos 45° = 2 × 1.41 ≈ 2.83 km . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Centreboard, keel & sideways slip
chunks.text: The sail pulls sideways. A fin underwater says no. Close-hauled, more of the sail's force pushes sideways than forward. Without something to resist it, the boat would just slide downwind. A dinghy's centreboard (or daggerboard) and a yacht's keel are underwater wings: the boat slips sideways a little ( leeway ), so water meets the board at a small angle, and the board makes lift that opposes the sail's sideways pull. Water is about 840 times denser than air (1025 vs 1.225 kg/m³), so a board much smaller than the sail can balance it, but only once the boat is moving: like the sail's, the board's force grows with the square of the speed.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Centreboard, keel & sideways slip
chunks.text: Downwind there's little sideways force, so dinghy sailors raise the board part of the way to cut drag. Worked example · a 0.25 m² board with a lift coefficient of 0.3 (illustrative) Boat speed In m/s ½ρV² in sea water Sideways force the board can make 1 kn 0.51 136 Pa 10 N 3 kn 1.54 1,220 Pa 92 N 5 kn 2.57 3,391 Pa 254 N Force = ½ × 1025 × V² × 0.25 m² × 0.3. Compare the air: 13 kn of apparent wind gives only 27 Pa, about 124 times less than water at 5 kn. At 1 kn the board can't hold the sail's pull (74 N on our beam reach, more close-hauled), so a boat that has stalled slides sideways until it builds speed again. What sideways force can the same board make at 2 kn (1.03 m/s)?

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Centreboard, keel & sideways slip
chunks.text: ½ × 1025 × 1.03² ≈ 543 Pa; × 0.25 × 0.3 ≈ 41 N . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heeling, hiking & capsize
chunks.text: The sail pushes high up, the board pushes low down: the boat wants to tip. The sail's sideways force acts high on the mast, and the board's opposing force acts low in the water. Together they make a heeling moment : force × the height between them. In a dinghy, the crew's weight is the main thing that pushes back (the righting moment ), so you sit on the windward side and lean out ( hike ), or stand out on a wire ( trapeze ), which YAI teaches in Basic Skills 3. When a gust hits, you can also ease the sheet to spill wind. If the heeling moment wins, you capsize.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heeling, hiking & capsize
chunks.text: Worked example · a 7 m² sail, heeling force 2.5 m above the board, crew 1 m out (from our Wind & Sail Lab, illustrative) Situation Heeling force Heeling moment Crew weight to balance 12 kn wind, beam reach, 5 kn 74 N 185 N·m 19 kg 12 kn wind, close-hauled (45°), 5 kn 244 N 610 N·m 62 kg 18 kn wind, close-hauled (45°), 5 kn 439 N 1,098 N·m 112 kg Weight = moment ÷ (9.81 × lever). 244 N × 2.5 m = 610 N·m; ÷ (9.81 × 1 m) ≈ 62 kg. In 18 kn, one sailor sitting 1 m out isn't enough: hike further out, trapeze, ease the sheet, or stay ashore.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heeling, hiking & capsize
chunks.text: Why a dinghy rights (or doesn't) without a keel A yacht's lead keel puts the centre of mass deep under the water, so heel lifts that weight and creates a strong righting moment even with nobody on board. A dinghy is different: almost all the righting comes from crew weight on the windward side (and a little from the hull's form as it heels and immerses more beam). That is why hiking and trapezing matter so much on a Laser, 420 or Optimist, and why an empty dinghy blown over stays over until someone climbs on the centreboard.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heeling, hiking & capsize
chunks.text: Worked example · same heeling moment, keel vs dinghy (illustrative) Boat How it rights Rough righting available at 20° heel Keelboat, 1,000 kg bulb 1.5 m below waterline Ballast pendulum ≈ 1,000 × 9.81 × 1.5 × sin 20° ≈ 5.0 kN·m Dinghy, 70 kg crew hiking 1.2 m out Crew on the rail ≈ 70 × 9.81 × 1.2 × cos 20° ≈ 0.77 kN·m The keelboat's ballast alone dwarfs one hiker; a dinghy needs the crew outboard, or a trapeze, or an eased sheet. Numbers are teaching models, not a particular class.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heeling, hiking & capsize
chunks.text: Safety Learn capsize recovery before you need it Capsizing is a normal part of dinghy sailing, and courses teach it early: RYA Level 2 includes capsize recovery, and YAI's syllabus moves from actions on capsize to man-overboard drills, a fully inverted ("turtle") boat and what to do if a crew member is trapped underneath. Under a turtled hull an air pocket can linger, but you cannot count on it — get out, stay with the boat, and follow the drill you practised. YAI's syllabus starts with clothing and safety equipment, including a buoyancy aid, and teaches you to find and read weather forecasts. Wear a buoyancy aid every time.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heeling, hiking & capsize
chunks.text: With a heeling moment of 610 N·m, how much crew weight balances it sitting 1.5 m out? 610 ÷ (9.81 × 1.5) ≈ 41 kg . A longer lever needs less weight, which is why a trapeze works. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & the boats
chunks.text: A heavy hull gets trapped in its own wave. A light one climbs out. A boat pushing through the water makes a bow wave. Deep-water waves travel at v = √(gλ ÷ 2π) , so a wave as long as the boat's waterline moves at about 1.25 × √L m/s , or 2.43 × √L knots (the old rule: 1.34 × √(length in feet)). At this hull speed the boat sits in a trough between its own bow and stern waves, and going faster means climbing the bow wave. A heavy displacement hull rarely can. A light dinghy with enough power can lift onto the water's surface and skim on it: planing . Racing dinghies and skiffs are built light for exactly this.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & the boats
chunks.text: Worked example · hull speed for different waterline lengths Waterline length Wave speed (m/s) Hull speed 3 m 2.16 4.2 kn 4 m 2.50 4.9 kn 5 m 2.79 5.4 kn 6 m 3.06 6.0 kn √(9.81 × 4 ÷ 6.283) ≈ 2.50 m/s ≈ 4.9 kn. Doubling the length raises hull speed by only √2 ≈ 1.41 times. Froude number: when a dinghy starts to climb its wave Naval architects track Fr = v ÷ √(g L) . Around Fr ≈ 0.4 the bow wave is about as long as the waterline — hull speed. A light dinghy that can reach Fr ≈ 0.5–0.7 begins to climb onto that wave and plane; a heavy keelboat usually cannot.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & the boats
chunks.text: (The same Fr idea shows up for swimmers on our swimming page .) Worked example · 4 m waterline dinghy (hull speed ≈ 4.9 kn from the table above) Boat speed Fr = v ÷ √(gL) What it feels like 3.0 kn (1.54 m/s) ≈ 0.25 Displacement: pushing a bow wave ahead 4.9 kn (2.50 m/s) ≈ 0.40 Hull speed: sitting between bow and stern wave 7.0 kn (3.60 m/s) ≈ 0.57 Climbing out: planing if the boat is light enough 10 kn (5.14 m/s) ≈ 0.82 Fully planing skiff / sportsboat territory √(9.81 × 4) ≈ 6.26 m/s. Fr = 2.50 ÷ 6.26 ≈ 0.40 at hull speed; Fr = 3.60 ÷ 6.26 ≈ 0.57 at 7 kn. Flat sections, light weight and enough sail power (or a kite / foil) decide whether you get there.

chunks.title: Sailing · Physics of Lift, Apparent Wind & Heeling · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & the boats
chunks.text: The Olympic boats At the LA28 Olympics, World Sailing's programme has ten sailing events. Six are boats at the Port of Los Angeles: the ILCA 7 (men) and ILCA 6 (women) one-person dinghies, the mixed 470 dinghy, the mixed Nacra 17 catamaran, and the 49er and 49erFX skiffs. The other four are boards at Long Beach (iQFOiL windsurfing and Formula Kite); see our Windsurfing and Kitesurfing pages. What's the hull speed of a 9 m waterline? 2.43 × √9 = 2.43 × 3 ≈ 7.3 kn . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The sailing ladder

chunks.text: In India, the Yachting Association of India (YAI) runs a Small Boat Sailing Scheme of five modules, taught at YAI training centres and clubs. Many centres abroad teach the UK's RYA National Sailing Scheme. The two ladders line up roughly as below; the content is what each body publishes.

chunks.text: World Sailing governs the sport worldwide and writes the racing rules; national bodies run training and championships. In India that's the Yachting Association of India, with state associations and academies below it. We checked each on an official source.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Breathing underwater is applied physics.
chunks.text: Every rule your instructor gives you comes from a law of nature: Boyle, Archimedes, Henry, Beer–Lambert. Learn the why, with real numbers, and diving gets safer, calmer and a lot more fun. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science 0 m 40 m 2× The water pressure on you at just 10 m down. So the air in your ears and mask shrinks by half. ≈ 1.2 m The depth at which a blocked ear can lock shut. Equalise early and often, before it hurts. 12 L What a held 6 L breath from 10 m becomes at the surface. Lungs can't double. Never hold your breath as you rise. 4× How much faster you use air at 30 m than at the surface. A 90-minute tank up top lasts about 22 min there.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Buoyancy feels twitchy. A try dive stays within 12 m, where gas volumes change fastest. Your lungs steer you. A deep breath adds about 2 kg of lift. Breathe slowly and continuously; never hold it. Answer the medical questionnaire honestly. A “yes” means you need a doctor’s clearance first. Ask before you book a try dive → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Would your physics keep you safe at 30 m?
chunks.text: 15 questions on what's really going on down there: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Six chapters, from the surface to 40 m
chunks.text: Each chapter takes one physical law and follows it underwater, with worked numbers you can check on a calculator. We round seawater to "1 bar per 10 m". The precise figure is about 1 bar per 10.06 m, and the difference doesn't matter for anything here. Interactive · Depth Lab

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag yourself down and watch the physics change
chunks.text: All six chapters on one slider. The assumptions: seawater, surface air consumption 20 L/min, a 12-litre cylinder used from 200 to 50 bar (1,800 L usable), and clear "pure-water" light absorption.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag yourself down and watch the physics change
chunks.text: 0 m Absolute pressure 1.0 bar Ch 1 · 1 bar air + 1 bar / 10 m Air use (SAC 20) 20 L/min Ch 3 · surface-equivalent litres Usable air lasts 90 min Ch 3 · 1,800 L ÷ consumption No-stop limit (air) > 3 h Ch 4 · first dive, table values* Nitrogen pressure 0.79 bar Ch 4 · narcosis: unlikely Oxygen pressure · air 0.21 bar Ch 4 · 21% × pressure Oxygen pressure · EAN32 0.32 bar within limit 6 L surface balloon 6.00 L Ch 1 · Boyle: P×V constant balloon to scale (volume) Ch 6 · Share of surface sunlight left at this depth (straight down, pure water): Red 700 nm 100% Orange 600 nm 100% Green 550 nm 100% Blue 450 nm 100% *No-stop limits are the published first-dive values of the widely used PADI Recreational Dive Planner (air), shown here for illustration only.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag yourself down and watch the physics change
chunks.text: Always dive by your own computer or planner and your training. Real coastal water (Goa, Tarkarli, Pondicherry) absorbs and scatters more than pure water, so colours fade even faster. CH 1

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pressure & Boyle's law
chunks.text: The ocean is heavy, and the air you carry gets squeezed. At sea level you're already under one "atmosphere" of air: about 1.013 bar, which we'll call 1 bar. Water is roughly 850 times denser than air, so it piles on pressure fast. A column of seawater 10 m tall over one square metre holds 10 m³ × 1,025 kg/m³ = 10,250 kg. Its weight (× 9.81 m/s²) spread over that square metre is about 100,500 pascals. That's ≈ 1 bar. So: every 10 m of seawater adds one more atmosphere. Your gauge shows depth, but your body responds to absolute pressure, which is air plus water. Fresh water is about 2.5% lighter, so it takes roughly 100,000 ÷ (1,000 × 9.81) ≈ 10.2 m of a pool, lake or quarry to add one bar.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pressure & Boyle's law
chunks.text: Close enough to ignore for depth, but the same density gap matters a lot for weighting (Chapter 2). Boyle's law: squeeze the gas, shrink the gas For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, P₁ × V₁ = P₂ × V₂ . Double the pressure and the volume halves. Your body is mostly liquid, and liquids barely compress. The gas spaces are what feel it: lungs, middle ears, sinuses, mask, BCD, the bubbles in your wetsuit. Worked example · a 6-litre balloon going down Depth Absolute pressure Balloon volume Change from previous row 0 m 1 bar 6.0 L n/a 10 m 2 bar 3.0 L −50% (pressure doubled) 20 m 3 bar 2.0 L −33% 30 m 4 bar 1.5 L −25% 40 m 5 bar 1.2 L −20% Look at the last column.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pressure & Boyle's law
chunks.text: Pressure doubles in the first 10 m, but going from 30 m to 40 m adds only 25% more. The shallows are where gas volumes change fastest . That's why buoyancy is twitchiest near the surface, why your ears need the most attention in the first few metres, and why the last 5 m of an ascent (1.5 → 1 bar, a 50% expansion) deserve the most care. One family of gas laws Boyle is one face of a single rule for a fixed amount of gas: P × V ÷ T = constant , with T in kelvin (°C + 273). Hold temperature still and you get Boyle. Hold volume still (a steel cylinder) and pressure tracks temperature: that's Gay-Lussac's law, and it's why a tank reads lower once it cools in the sea (Chapter 3).

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pressure & Boyle's law
chunks.text: Two more laws handle mixtures and liquids, and Archimedes handles lift: Law In one line Where you meet it Boyle P × V stays constant (temperature fixed) Lungs, ears, mask, BCD, wetsuit ( Ch 1 , Ch 5 ) Charles / Gay-Lussac V ∝ T at fixed pressure; P ∝ T at fixed volume Hot fills that cool in the water ( Ch 3 ) Dalton Each gas's partial pressure = its fraction × total pressure Oxygen limits, nitrox, narcosis ( Ch 4 ) Henry Gas dissolved in a liquid ∝ its partial pressure Nitrogen loading and no-stop limits ( Ch 4 ) Archimedes Lift = weight of the water you displace Weighting, trim, hovering ( Ch 2 ) ✋ Feel the number At 10 m, every square centimetre of your skin carries about 2 kg-force (2 bar ≈ 2.04 kgf/cm²).

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pressure & Boyle's law
chunks.text: Your palm, about 100 cm², has roughly 200 kg-force pressing on it. You don't feel it because it pushes equally from every side through tissue that doesn't compress. Only air pockets notice. The one rule that's pure physics: never hold your breath Your regulator gives you air at whatever pressure surrounds you. Fill your lungs with 6 L at 10 m (2 bar), then swim up holding that breath. By the surface (1 bar) that same gas wants to take up 12 L . Lungs can't double in size. Small air sacs tear, and air can be forced into the chest cavity or bloodstream (pulmonary barotrauma, arterial gas embolism).

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Pressure & Boyle's law
chunks.text: Diving-medicine literature describes these injuries after breath-hold ascents of only a metre or two, so this isn't just a deep-dive risk. The fix is simple: breathe slowly and continuously, all the time , and on an emergency ascent keep exhaling ("ahhh"). You're at 5 m with 4 L of air in your BCD and you rise to the surface without venting. How much does it want to expand to? 5 m = 1.5 bar. 4 L × 1.5 ÷ 1 = 6 L , so 2 L more air, which means about 2 kg more lift (Chapter 2). That runaway lift is why you vent on every ascent. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: Archimedes is your co-pilot: you float by the litre. Archimedes' principle: anything in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. Displace more water than you weigh and you float. Displace less and you sink. Match exactly and you hover. That's "neutral buoyancy", the skill that separates calm divers from flailing ones. Every litre you displace in seawater (density ≈ 1.025 kg/L) gives you about 1.025 kg of lift . In fresh water it's 1.000 kg. Your fine controls are all gas volumes: BCD air, wetsuit bubbles and your lungs.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: Worked example · lake to sea A diver plus gear displacing about 100 L gets 100 kg of lift in fresh water and 100 × 1.025 = 102.5 kg in the sea: about 2.5 kg extra . So if you trained in a pool or lake, expect to add roughly 2 to 3 kg of lead for the ocean. A quick rule of thumb is about 2.5% of your total weight with gear. Always confirm with a buoyancy check at the surface. The shrinking wetsuit Neoprene is a foam full of tiny gas cells, and Boyle's law applies to them too. Say a full suit gives you about 4 kg of lift at the surface (it varies a lot with thickness and size). If it behaved like pure gas it would give ~2 kg at 10 m and ~1 kg at 30 m.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: Real neoprene doesn't quite compress that fully, but the trend is real: you get heavier as you go down . You make up for it with small puffs into the BCD on descent, then vent that air as it expands on ascent. Why hovering is a balancing act Neutral buoyancy is an unstable balance, like a pencil standing on its tip. Drift up half a metre and every gas space expands a little, so you gain lift and drift up faster. Sink a little and they compress, so you sink faster. Nothing pulls you back to where you were; you have to do it.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: That's why good divers make small, early corrections (a breath, a short puff, a short vent) rather than big late ones, and why the feedback is fiercest in the shallows where Boyle's percentages are largest. Worked example · the runaway from 10 m You're neutral at 10 m (2 bar) with 2 L of air in your BCD. Rise to 5 m (1.5 bar) without venting and it becomes 2 × 2 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 2.7 L : about 0.7 kg of extra lift. Keep going to the surface and it's 2 × 2 ÷ 1 = 4 L , 2 kg more than you started with, plus whatever your wetsuit re-expands. Each metre up makes the next one faster, so dump air as you rise, not after.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: You get lighter as you breathe Worked example · the weight of air A 12 L cylinder at 200 bar holds about 12 × 200 = 2,400 L of surface air. Air weighs ~1.2 g per litre, so that's about 2.9 kg of gas . Breathe it down to 50 bar and you've exhaled roughly 2.2 kg. You're now ~2 kg more buoyant than at the start. Your weights must still hold you at a 5 m safety stop with a near-empty tank. That's how a proper weight check is done. 🫁 Feel the number Your lungs are the finest buoyancy control you own. A deep breath can add 2 L or more of volume, which is ~2 kg of lift . Experienced divers hover over coral by breathing a little deeper or a little shallower, without touching the BCD.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: Trim: the physics of looking effortless Water is about 850× denser than air, so drag dominates everything. Drag grows with your frontal area and with the square of your speed, which means the power you need grows with the cube of speed. Swim twice as fast and you need roughly 8× the power. A diver swimming at a 45° angle pushes a much bigger cross-section through the water than one lying flat. "Trim" (horizontal, streamlined, gear tucked in) cuts drag, and that cuts effort and air use (Chapter 3). Slow and flat wins. Halfway through a dive you're slowly sinking even though you're kicking. What's the physics-first fix?

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy, weighting & trim
chunks.text: Stop kicking and add a short puff to your BCD, because your wetsuit has compressed with depth. Then fine-tune with your breathing. Kicking to stay up wastes air and stirs up sand. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Why your tank shrinks at depth
chunks.text: Same lungs, same breaths, but each one costs more at depth. Your regulator delivers air at the surrounding pressure, or you couldn't inhale. So a lungful at 30 m (4 bar) holds four times as many air molecules as a lungful on the beach, and it drains the cylinder four times as fast. Divers measure breathing as SAC (surface air consumption): litres per minute at surface pressure. A relaxed recreational diver might be around 15–25 L/min. Cold, stress, currents and poor trim push it up, sometimes a lot. We'll use 20 L/min. Worked example · how long does a 12 L tank last? 12 L cylinder filled to 200 bar = 2,400 surface litres. We keep 50 bar (600 L) as a reserve, so 1,800 L is usable .

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Why your tank shrinks at depth
chunks.text: Consumption at depth = SAC × absolute pressure. Depth Pressure Air used per minute Time on 1,800 L 0 m 1 bar 20 L 90 min 10 m 2 bar 40 L 45 min 20 m 3 bar 60 L 30 min 30 m 4 bar 80 L 22.5 min 40 m 5 bar 100 L 18 min These are simplified: they ignore descent and ascent time, and real gas at 200 bar packs slightly less than the ideal-gas figure. The shape is what matters: the same tank lasts a quarter as long at 30 m as at the surface. Hot fills and cool water: Gay-Lussac at work Compressing air heats it, and cylinders often sit in the sun. A steel or aluminium cylinder hardly changes volume, so its pressure follows its temperature in kelvin.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Why your tank shrinks at depth
chunks.text: Worked example · the "missing" 8 bar A tank reads 200 bar while still warm at 40 °C (313 K). Jump into 28 °C water (301 K) and, once it cools, it reads 200 × 301 ÷ 313 ≈ 192 bar . No air leaked: the same molecules are simply moving more slowly. The reverse is why full cylinders shouldn't bake on a deck: 200 bar at 28 °C becomes 200 × 323 ÷ 301 ≈ 215 bar at 50 °C. Plan your dive on the pressure you read in the water. Why keep a reserve? Do the ascent maths From 30 m, rising at 9 m/min takes ~3 minutes at an average of about 2.5 bar: 20 × 2.5 × 3 ≈ 150 L . A 3-minute safety stop at 5 m (1.5 bar) costs 20 × 1.5 × 3 = 90 L . That's ~240 L, or 20 bar from a 12 L tank, for a calm diver .

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Why your tank shrinks at depth
chunks.text: Now picture sharing air with an out-of-air buddy who's breathing hard: two people, maybe double the SAC. A 50-bar reserve stops looking conservative. 🎈 Feel the number Air at 30 m is 4× denser, so it's literally heavier to move through your regulator and airways. That's part of why exertion at depth feels harder, and why slow, deep breaths make your gas last longer than quick shallow ones. Your SAC rises from 20 to 30 L/min in a current. How long does 1,800 L now last at 20 m? 30 × 3 bar = 90 L/min, so 1,800 ÷ 90 = 20 minutes instead of 30. Effort costs gas, and depth multiplies the cost. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Your body is a soda bottle, and you decide how fast to open it. Air is about 79% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. Each gas behaves as if it were alone, with a partial pressure = fraction × absolute pressure (Dalton's law). Henry's law says the amount of gas that dissolves in a liquid is proportional to its partial pressure. Your blood and tissues are the liquid. Depth Absolute Nitrogen pp (air) Oxygen pp (air) Oxygen pp (EAN32) 0 m 1 bar 0.79 0.21 0.32 10 m 2 bar 1.58 0.42 0.64 20 m 3 bar 2.37 0.63 0.96 30 m 4 bar 3.16 0.84 1.28 40 m 5 bar 3.95 1.05 1.60 ⚠ Loading up: tissues with half-times At 30 m, you're breathing nitrogen at 3.16 bar while your tissues are still at ~0.79. Nitrogen flows in.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: It doesn't flow in all at once. Decompression models picture the body as a set of "compartments", from fast ones like blood to slow ones like joints and fat, each with a half-time . Common models span half-times from a few minutes to more than ten hours. Worked example · a 20-minute tissue at 30 m Gap to fill: 3.16 − 0.79 = 2.37 bar. After one half-time (20 min) the tissue is halfway: 0.79 + 0.5 × 2.37 ≈ 1.98 bar . After two half-times (40 min) it's three-quarters: ≈ 2.57 bar , more than three times its surface level. Bring that tissue straight to 1 bar and it's heavily supersaturated, like a shaken soda.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Coming up: why slow ascents and safety stops work A modest supersaturation leaves your tissues harmlessly through the lungs. Too much, too fast, and the gas forms bubbles in tissue and blood. That's decompression sickness ("the bends"): joint pain, numbness, fatigue, and in serious cases paralysis. Recreational divers stay within no-decompression limits (NDLs), ascend slowly (agency maximums are 18 m/min, and many computers want ~9–10 m/min), and add a 3-minute safety stop at about 5 m . Depth (air) 12 m 18 m 30 m 40 m First-dive no-stop limit* 147 min 56 min 20 min 9 min *Published values of the PADI Recreational Dive Planner (air), for illustration. Computers and other tables differ.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Note how fast the limit collapses with depth. What "no-decompression" really means The no-stop limit is the longest you can stay at a depth and still ascend straight to the surface at the normal rate, without required stops on the way. Stay longer and your model says some tissues are too loaded for a direct ascent: you now owe decompression stops , which are mandatory and need training, gas and planning that recreational courses don't cover. The 3-minute stop at 5 m is different. It's a safety stop, recommended on every dive, and it buys extra margin. Recreational diving stays inside the no-stop limit, and the Andaman & Nicobar guidelines allow only no-decompression diving (see the ladder ).

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: The second dive: why fast tissues forgive and slow ones remember On the surface you breathe out nitrogen at the same half-time rates you loaded it. Fast compartments clear in an hour or so. Slow ones barely start. That leftover ("residual") nitrogen is why your second dive of the day gets a shorter no-stop limit than the first, and why tables and computers ask for your surface interval.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Worked example · 20 min at 30 m, then an hour on the boat Tissue half-time After 20 min at 30 m After 60 min on the surface Extra nitrogen still there 20 min (fast) 1.98 bar 0.94 bar 12.5% (3 half-times) 120 min (slow) 1.05 bar 0.97 bar 71% (half a half-time) Start: 0.79 bar in every tissue; breathing 3.16 bar of nitrogen at 30 m. The 120-min tissue only loads 11% of the gap in 20 minutes ( 1 − 0.5^(20/120) ), but it also unloads slowly. These are teaching numbers from the same half-time maths as above, not a dive plan. Real models track many compartments with different allowed limits.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Flying after diving A plane cabin is pressurised to roughly 0.75–0.8 bar, lower than sea level, which makes any leftover nitrogen more likely to bubble. Widely used guidance (originally from DAN workshops, and repeated by Indian dive centres) is to wait at least 12 hours after a single no-stop dive and 18 hours after multiple dives or days of diving , and longer after decompression dives. Andaman divers flying out of Port Blair: plan your last dive day around your flight. Nitrogen narcosis: the "martini effect" At high partial pressure, nitrogen acts like a mild anaesthetic: slowed thinking, overconfidence, fixation, giggles or anxiety.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Many divers start to notice it around 30 m , which is one reason the Advanced level stops there. It varies between people and from day to day. Two things make it manageable: it gets stronger the deeper you go, and it fades within moments when you go up a few metres . No hangover. Oxygen: essential, then toxic Breathing oxygen at a high partial pressure can trigger convulsions without warning, which underwater can mean drowning. Recreational training uses 1.4 bar as the working limit (1.6 as an absolute contingency).

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: That sets a maximum operating depth (MOD) for each gas: Worked example · maximum depths at ppO₂ 1.4 bar Air (21%): 1.4 ÷ 0.21 = 6.67 bar, which is ~56 m , far below recreational limits. EAN32: 1.4 ÷ 0.32 = 4.375 bar, which is ~34 m . EAN36: 1.4 ÷ 0.36 = 3.89 bar, which is ~29 m . Why bother with nitrox, then? Less nitrogen. At 30 m on EAN32 your nitrogen pressure is 0.68 × 4 = 2.72 bar, the same as breathing air at only ~24.4 m (the "equivalent air depth"). That means longer no-stop times and shorter surface intervals. DIVEIndia, for example, requires nitrox certification for its Barren Island trips.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Nitrogen, decompression & narcosis
chunks.text: Safety If something feels wrong after a dive Joint pain, tingling, unusual fatigue or breathlessness after diving needs oxygen and medical help, fast. The PADI destination guide lists a hyperbaric chamber at Port Blair for the Andamans. Know where your nearest chamber is before you dive, and consider dive insurance (for example through DAN). You planned a 30 m dive on EAN36. Is that OK? 30 m = 4 bar, and 0.36 × 4 = 1.44 bar , just over the 1.4 working limit. Use EAN32 (1.28 bar at 30 m) or plan shallower (MOD ≈ 29 m). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ears, sinuses & equalising
chunks.text: Why ears hurt at 2 m, and why the deep end is easier. Behind each eardrum is the middle ear , a small pocket of air connected to the back of your throat by the narrow Eustachian tube . As you descend, water pushes the eardrum inward. The air behind it stays at surface pressure until you open the tube and let higher-pressure air in. That's equalising . Worked example · the force on your eardrum at 2 m Pressure difference at 2 m: 0.2 bar = 20,000 Pa. An eardrum's working area is well under a square centimetre (say ~0.7 cm² = 0.00007 m²). Force = 20,000 × 0.00007 ≈ 1.4 newtons , about the weight of a 140 g object balanced on a membrane thinner than paper.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ears, sinuses & equalising
chunks.text: At 2 m you're barely below the surface, and it already hurts. Remember the Boyle table: the change from 0 to 2 m (1 → 1.2 bar) squeezes an air space by about 17%. From 30 to 32 m it's only 5%. The shallows are where equalising matters most. 👂 Feel the number If the pressure difference builds too far, soft tissue around the tube's opening can press it shut, and then no amount of blowing opens it. Diving-medicine texts commonly put this around 90 mmHg ≈ 0.12 bar, about 1.2 m of seawater . Wait until it hurts and you may already be past the point where equalising works.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ears, sinuses & equalising
chunks.text: How to equalise: early, often, gently Start before you leave the surface , then equalise every half-metre to metre in the first few metres, and keep going all the way down. Valsalva : pinch your nose and blow gently against it. Never hard. Toynbee : pinch your nose and swallow. Frenzel : pinch your nose and push air up with your tongue like a piston. It takes a bit of practice but is very gentle. Wiggle your jaw. Descend feet-first, which helps air rise into the tubes. If it hurts, go up a metre and try again. Never push through pain, because a burst eardrum or inner-ear injury can end your diving. Don't dive congested.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ears, sinuses & equalising
chunks.text: Decongestants can wear off mid-dive and trap air on the way up (a "reverse block"). The same physics applies to your sinuses (which equalise on their own through small openings, so congestion blocks them) and your mask : breathe out a little through your nose on descent, or the mask "squeezes" your face. Worked example · the mask and the way up A mask holding about 200 mL of air at the surface would shrink to 200 × 1 ÷ 2 = 100 mL by 10 m if you never breathed into it. The space can't shrink that much, so the low pressure inside pulls on your eyes and face instead.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Ears, sinuses & equalising
chunks.text: On the ascent, Boyle runs backwards: the air in your middle ears and sinuses expands and normally leaks out through the tubes on its own. If it can't (a "reverse block"), stop, go down a metre to ease the pressure, then come up more slowly. Never hold your breath to fix it. Why is equalising easier between 20 and 30 m than between 0 and 10 m? 0 → 10 m doubles the pressure (1 → 2 bar, a 100% change). 20 → 30 m goes from 3 → 4 bar, only 33%. Smaller relative change means smaller volume change, so less air to add per metre. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Light, colour, sound & heat
chunks.text: Water is a filter, a lens, a speaker and a heat sink. Why reds vanish first Water molecules absorb light, and they absorb long wavelengths (red) far more strongly than short ones (blue). Light fades exponentially with distance (the Beer–Lambert law): I = I₀ × e^(−a·d) , where a is the absorption coefficient for that colour. Using laboratory values for pure water: Colour a (per m) 5 m 10 m 20 m 30 m 🔴 Red 700 nm 0.62 4.4% 0.2% ≈0 ≈0 🟠 Orange 600 nm 0.22 33% 11% 1.2% 0.1% 🟢 Green 550 nm 0.057 75% 57% 32% 18% 🔵 Blue 450 nm 0.009 95% 91% 83% 76% Share of surface sunlight left travelling straight down through pure water (coefficients: Pope & Fry, 1997).

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Light, colour, sound & heat
chunks.text: Real seawater also has plankton and sediment, which absorb and scatter more, especially along India's west-coast mainland sites. Worked example · the red snapper at 15 m Sunlight reaching 15 m keeps e^(−0.624 × 15) ≈ 0.009% of its red, essentially none. So the fish has no red light to reflect and looks grey-brown. Then you switch on a torch 1 m away. The light travels 1 m out and 1 m back: e^(−0.624 × 2) ≈ 29% of the red survives. The fish suddenly turns scarlet. That's why underwater photographers use strobes and get close. The mask is a magnifying glass Light bends where it passes from water (refractive index ≈ 1.33) through your flat mask into air.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Light, colour, sound & heat
chunks.text: Objects appear at about three-quarters of their real distance , so they look about a third bigger . That "2-metre" fish was probably 1.5 m, and the reef you're about to touch is further away than it looks. Sound: louder, faster, directionless Sound travels at about 1,500 m/s in seawater versus ~343 m/s in air , roughly 4.4× faster. Your brain locates sounds mostly from the tiny difference in when they reach each ear. Underwater that difference shrinks by the same factor, and sound also travels through your skull bones straight to both inner ears. Result: you hear a boat engine clearly but can't tell where it is.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Light, colour, sound & heat
chunks.text: Treat engine noise as "look up, stay close to the line or reef, and surface carefully" , ideally with a surface marker buoy. Heat: why 28 °C water still chills you Water conducts heat about 25× faster than air (≈0.6 vs ≈0.025 W/m·K) and holds vastly more heat per litre. Your body is at 37 °C, so even the warm 26–30 °C seas of the Andamans and Lakshadweep steadily pull heat out on a long dive or a third dive of the day. A wetsuit works by trapping a thin layer of water that your body warms. Cold also raises your air consumption (Chapter 3). A diver at 25 m says the blood from a small cut looks green. Is something wrong? No.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Light, colour, sound & heat
chunks.text: Blood's red has been absorbed by 25 m of water, so what's left reflecting is mostly green. Shine a torch on it and it's red again. Pure Beer–Lambert. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · Certifications & skill levels

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first breath to pro
chunks.text: Most of the world's recreational divers train with one of a handful of agencies. Their courses map closely onto the international ISO 24801 levels, so a PADI, SSI or CMAS card is accepted at dive centres everywhere, including all the Indian centres listed below. Figures are taken from each agency's published standards (checked 3 Oct 2026).

chunks.heading: The ladder, from first breath to pro
chunks.text: deep & night Max 40 m Commonly mapped to ISO dive-leader level Two Indian twists to know Andaman & Nicobar rules split dive centres into two categories. "Category A" centres follow WRSTC/ISO agency standards (the PADI/SSI/CMAS limits above). "Category B" centres follow National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS) norms instead. For Category B, the A&N guidelines set a 12–60 age band and a 12 m limit for introductory dives . The A&N rules also allow only no-decompression diving , and require an orientation dive if you have fewer than 30 logged dives or haven't dived in 3 months. Ask your centre which category it is. Equivalence is approximate.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Recreational scuba has no single world regulator. Standards come from training agencies, coordinated through the WRSTC and written into ISO standards. Countries and states add their own operating rules on top. In India, training follows agency standards, while state and UT tourism departments register and regulate operators. Every body below was checked on its official website.

chunks.title: Scuba diving: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: World federation CMAS: World Underwater Federation The international federation for underwater sports (finswimming, freediving, underwater hockey and more) and a diver-training system with the One/Two/Three Star ladder. Its training standards are published free on its site. Breath-hold diving has its own page: see Freediving . cmas.org Training agency PADI Professional Association of Diving Instructors. The largest agency, with over 30 million certifications since 1966 (PADI's own figure). Most dive centres in India are PADI. padi.com Training agency SSI: Scuba Schools International Global agency whose Open Water and Divemaster programmes are aligned to ISO 24801-2 and -3.
