chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hold still. Press smooth. Let the physics land the ten.
chunks.text: The 10 m air rifle 10-ring is a half-millimetre dot, and you hit it with angles, breathing and a steady trigger. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Hold & Score Lab, then find supervised ranges, competitions and coaching courses in India at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First lesson International ≈ 7.7 J The energy of a 10 m air-rifle pellet. Enough to injure an eye: treat every gun as loaded. ≈ 57 ms How long a pellet takes to cross the 10 m range. Hold still through the whole shot, not just the trigger. 8 mm How far a trigger jerk moves the hit at 10 m. Press smoothly: the shot isn't over until the pellet leaves.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hold still. Press smooth. Let the physics land the ten.
chunks.text: 0.5 mm The bullseye of a 10 m air-rifle target. You hit it with angles: tiny wobbles cost points.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Guns point downrange, always. You load only on the command, and on STOP, shooting stops immediately. Your body is never perfectly still. Shooters settle into the natural pause after breathing out and take the shot there. Start at a recognised club or range. Ask whether a qualified coach supervises every session. Ask before you book a taster session → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of sport shooting?
chunks.text: 15 questions on pellet flight and gravity, recoil and momentum, angles and the 10-ring, breathing and the hold, trigger control, and range safety: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Hold & Score Lab to see how wobble, speed and gun mass change the shot. Interactive · Hold & Score Lab

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set your aiming wobble, the pellet speed and the gun's mass, then see where a 10 m shot lands and how much the gun recoils
chunks.text: A simple model of a 10 m event: a 0.5 g, 4.5 mm pellet (illustrative mass), no air drag, ISSF target ring sizes. A shot scores the highest ring that any part of the pellet hole touches. Learning values only: this lab is about aim, angles and momentum, not about equipment. Aiming wobble 0.4 mrad Pellet speed 175 m/s Gun mass 5.0 kg Target 10 m air rifle 10 m air pistol Shot lands off centre by 4.0 mm Ch 3 · angle × distance Ring scored 9 Ch 3 · ISSF ring sizes Flight time to the target 57 ms Ch 1 · distance ÷ speed Gravity drop over 10 m 16.0 mm Ch 1 · ½ g t² Pellet energy 7.7 J Ch 6 · why ranges have rules Gun recoil speed 1.75 cm/s Ch 2 · momentum conserved Bar = ring scored, out of 10.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set your aiming wobble, the pellet speed and the gun's mass, then see where a 10 m shot lands and how much the gun recoils
chunks.text: Try a bigger wobble, then switch to the pistol target. Real shooting happens only at a supervised range (Ch 6). CH 1

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pellet flight & gravity
chunks.text: Even over 10 m, the pellet is falling the whole way. Ignoring drag, a pellet crosses the range at constant speed, so its flight time is t = d ÷ v . While it flies, gravity pulls it down by ½ g t² . Sights are set (zeroed) for the target distance, so that drop is built into the aim: you never see it, but it's there. Worked example · 10 m, 0.5 g pellet, no drag (illustrative speeds) Pellet speed Flight time Gravity drop Pellet energy 150 m/s ≈ 67 ms ≈ 21.8 mm ≈ 5.6 J 175 m/s ≈ 57 ms ≈ 16.0 mm ≈ 7.7 J 200 m/s 50 ms ≈ 12.3 mm 10 J 175 m/s: t = 10 ÷ 175 ≈ 0.0571 s; drop = ½ × 9.81 × 0.0571² ≈ 0.016 m. ISSF rules set 10 m air events at 4.5 mm (.177) calibre.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pellet flight & gravity
chunks.text: ⏱️ Feel the number 57 milliseconds is about a third of the time it takes you to blink. Your hold has to stay still for the whole shot, not just the moment the trigger breaks. At 160 m/s, how long does the pellet take to cover 10 m? 10 ÷ 160 ≈ 63 ms . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Recoil & momentum
chunks.text: Push something forward and you get pushed back. A shot is no exception. Before the shot, the gun and pellet have zero total momentum. Afterwards, the pellet carries momentum m v forward, so the gun must carry the same amount backward: M V = m v . A heavier gun gets the same momentum at a lower speed, which is one reason target rifles are heavy (ISSF caps a 10 m air rifle at 5.5 kg with sights). Worked example · 0.5 g pellet at 175 m/s Gun mass Pellet momentum Recoil speed Recoil energy 5.0 kg (rifle) 0.0875 kg·m/s ≈ 1.75 cm/s ≈ 0.77 mJ 1.0 kg (pistol, illustrative) 0.0875 kg·m/s ≈ 8.75 cm/s ≈ 3.8 mJ V = 0.0005 × 175 ÷ 5 = 0.0175 m/s.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Recoil & momentum
chunks.text: The rifle's recoil energy (½ × 5 × 0.0175²) is 10,000 times smaller than the pellet's 7.7 J, the same ratio as the masses. Why recoil still matters at 10 m The pellet is still in the barrel while the gun starts to move, so any movement you add then (a flinch, a grip that changes) goes into the shot. That's why shooters train a position that stays the same through every shot. The same pellet from a 2.5 kg gun: what recoil speed? 0.0875 ÷ 2.5 = 3.5 cm/s . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Angles, wobble & the 10-ring
chunks.text: The rifle 10-ring is a half-millimetre dot. You hit it with angles, not luck. On the ISSF 10 m air rifle target the 10-ring is a white dot just 0.5 mm across, and each ring is 5 mm wider than the last, out to 45.5 mm. The 10 m air pistol 10-ring is 11.5 mm, out to 155.5 mm. A shot scores the higher ring whenever any part of the pellet hole touches it, so with a 4.5 mm pellet the centre only has to be within 2.5 mm of the middle for a rifle 10, and within 8 mm for a pistol 10. An aiming error is an angle. At 10 m, 1 milliradian (mrad) = 10 mm on the target.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Angles, wobble & the 10-ring
chunks.text: Worked example · wobble → miss → score at 10 m (from our Hold & Score Lab) Aiming wobble Off centre Air rifle ring Air pistol ring 0.2 mrad 2 mm 10 10 0.4 mrad 4 mm 9 10 0.7 mrad 7 mm 8 10 1.4 mrad 14 mm 5 9 Rifle 9-ring: 5.5 mm across, radius 2.75 mm + pellet radius 2.25 mm = 5.0 mm, so a 4 mm miss scores 9. Rifle 10: 0.25 + 2.25 = 2.5 mm, so 2.5 mm ÷ 10 m = 0.25 mrad, about 0.014°. Decimal scores With electronic targets, each ring can be split into ten decimal rings (10.0 to 10.9). ISSF uses decimal scoring for 10 m air rifle qualification at its championships; 10 m air pistol is scored in whole rings. Does a steadier hold really score more?

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Angles, wobble & the 10-ring
chunks.text: What a study measured Finnish researchers tested 58 novices, each firing 30 standing shots with an air rifle at 10 m, while a force plate tracked their body sway and an optical system tracked where the barrel pointed ( Mononen et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2007 ). Shooters who swayed less and held the aim steadier did score more on average: the correlations ran from −0.29 to −0.45. But together, side-to-side body sway and side-to-side aim wobble explained only 26% of the difference in scores between shooters. And for any one shooter, a steadier shot wasn't reliably a better one. So a steady hold matters, but it's not the whole story.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Angles, wobble & the 10-ring
chunks.text: The rest comes from what this page covers next: timing the shot (Ch 4) and a clean trigger (Ch 5). The study's authors suggest balance training as one way to improve. A 0.6 mrad wobble at 10 m: how far off centre, and which rifle ring? 6 mm. The 8-ring reaches 5.25 + 2.25 = 7.5 mm, so 8 . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breathing, heartbeat & the hold
chunks.text: Your body is never perfectly still. Shooters learn when it's stillest. Breathing moves your chest, shoulders and the gun with them. Shooters settle into a natural pause after breathing out and take the shot there. Even then the heartbeat sends small pulses through the body, so the sight picture drifts in a small, slow pattern rather than sitting dead still. Training is about making that pattern as small and as calm as possible.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breathing, heartbeat & the hold
chunks.text: Worked example · the time you have Item Number What it means ISSF 10 m air rifle qualification 60 shots in 75 min 75 s per shot on average, including rest Heart at 60 beats per minute 1 beat per second Several beats during a typical aim A pulse that nudges the gun 0.1 mrad (illustrative) 1 mm at 10 m 40% of the 2.5 mm rifle-10 window 75 min × 60 ÷ 60 shots = 75 s. 0.1 mrad × 10 m = 1 mm; 1 ÷ 2.5 = 40%. Breathe, settle, aim: take the shot in the natural pause, not while holding your breath to the point of strain. If the hold isn't settling, don't force it. Lower the gun downrange, breathe and start again; there's time (75 s per shot on average).

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breathing, heartbeat & the hold
chunks.text: Champions shoot between heartbeats Each heartbeat has two phases: systole , when the heart contracts and pushes a pulse of blood out, and diastole , when it relaxes and refills. Helin, Sihvonen and Hänninen recorded the ECG, the trigger-finger muscle and the gun's movement in six Finnish rifle and pistol champions and three beginners ( Br J Sports Med, 1987 ). The champions fired during diastole ; the beginners fired in both phases, and their diastole shots scored better than their systole shots. Worked example · how long is the quiet part of each beat?

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breathing, heartbeat & the hold
chunks.text: (systole held at about 0.3 s, illustrative) Heart rate One beat lasts Diastole (approx.) Share of the beat 60 bpm 1,000 ms ≈ 700 ms ≈ 70% 72 bpm 833 ms ≈ 530 ms ≈ 64% 90 bpm 667 ms ≈ 370 ms ≈ 55% 120 bpm 500 ms ≈ 200 ms ≈ 40% One beat = 60,000 ms ÷ heart rate. Systole changes much less with heart rate than diastole does, so we hold it at about 300 ms (a textbook resting value; it shortens a little at higher rates). 72 bpm: 833 − 300 ≈ 530 ms. When nerves push your heart rate up, the quiet window shrinks fast, which is one reason calm breathing between shots helps. At 72 beats per minute, how many beats in a 5 s aim? 72 ÷ 60 × 5 = 6 beats . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Trigger control & follow-through
chunks.text: The shot isn't over when the trigger breaks. It's over when the pellet has left. Between the trigger breaking and the pellet leaving the barrel there are a few milliseconds when the gun can still move. A smooth press that doesn't disturb the hold keeps the aim where it was; a jerk rotates the gun just when it matters. Follow-through means keeping your position and aim steady through the shot and a moment after it. Worked example · what moves during the shot (illustrative values) What happens Angle Miss at 10 m Air rifle 10 becomes Slow drift 2 mrad/s for 10 ms 0.02 mrad 0.2 mm still 10 Small flinch 0.4 mrad 4 mm 9 Trigger jerk 0.8 mrad 8 mm 7 2 mrad/s × 0.010 s = 0.02 mrad; × 10 m = 0.2 mm.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Trigger control & follow-through
chunks.text: Jerk: 0.8 × 10 = 8 mm; the 7-ring reaches 7.75 + 2.25 = 10 mm. How heavy can a trigger be? The rule book ISSF rules set a minimum trigger pull for some guns, so the trigger can't be set to go off at the lightest touch. It's checked by hanging a test weight from the trigger with the barrel vertical ( ISSF Rule Book, Edition 2025, second print effective 1 July 2026 ): Worked example · ISSF minimum trigger pull as a force Gun Minimum trigger pull As a force 10 m air rifle No minimum n/a 10 m air pistol 500 g ≈ 4.9 N 25 m pistols 1,000 g ≈ 9.8 N 300 m standard rifle 1,500 g ≈ 14.7 N Force = mass × g: 0.5 kg × 9.81 m/s² ≈ 4.9 N.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Trigger control & follow-through
chunks.text: The 10 m air pistol itself may weigh at most 1,500 g, so a 500 g trigger is a third of the gun's weight, pressed by one finger without moving the sights. That's why pistol shooters practise "dry firing" (pressing the trigger with no pellet loaded) for thousands of repetitions. A 0.3 mrad flinch at 10 m: how far off, and what rifle ring? 3 mm. Inside 5.0 mm but outside 2.5 mm, so 9 . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Range safety, rules & the law
chunks.text: On a well-run range, safety comes from rules that leave nothing to chance. Even a 10 m pellet carries several joules (Ch 1), enough to injure an eye. ISSF rules (2026 edition) build safety into every step on the range: Safety flags: bright flags go into every rifle and pistol to show it is unloaded; for air guns the flag runs the full length of the barrel. Muzzle discipline: on the firing point, guns always point in a safe direction, and the action is closed only when pointing downrange. Commands: range officials give LOAD, START, STOP and UNLOAD. Guns are loaded only on the firing point after LOAD or START; on STOP, shooting stops immediately.

chunks.title: Shooting · Physics of Aim, Recoil & Range Safety · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Range safety, rules & the law
chunks.text: Nobody handles guns while anyone is forward of the firing line. Hearing protection is required near the 25 m, 50 m and 300 m firing lines and on shotgun ranges; shotgun athletes must wear shatterproof eye protection. Worked example · energy and the eye Projectile Speed Energy 0.5 g pellet 175 m/s ≈ 7.7 J 20 g arrow (Archery page) 57 m/s ≈ 32.6 J ½ × 0.0005 × 175² ≈ 7.7 J. Small, but concentrated on a 4.5 mm point: treat every gun as loaded. Safety The law in India Firearms licences in India are governed by the Arms Act, 1959 and the Arms Rules, 2016 (Ministry of Home Affairs). The Act refers to target practice by members of rifle clubs or associations recognised by the Central Government.

chunks.heading: Pop, roll, drop in. Physics all the way down.
chunks.text: An ollie is a projectile, a ramp is an energy swap, and a good fall is a long stop. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Ramp & Ollie Lab, then find parks and the competition pathway in India. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First push Park final ≈ 20 g Catching a fall on a stiff arm on concrete. Roll out of it and it drops to about 2 g. ≈ 2.7 g What your legs carry at the bottom of a 1.5 m drop-in. About 160 kg pushing through a 60 kg skater. 5° Of deck tilt turns you on a 1.7 m circle. At speed, small wobbles grow: weight forward, knees bent. ≈ 79% Of a small wheel's push a 10 mm stone turns backwards. Bigger, softer wheels roll over stones more easily.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Learn at a park, not on the road. A beginner area away from traffic is somewhere safe to learn. Leaning back is the classic fall. chunks.text: 15 questions on pushing and rolling, balance and turning, the ollie, ramps and pumping, falling safely, and wheels and scoring: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Ramp & Ollie Lab to see the speed, g-force and airtime behind your tricks. Interactive · Ramp & Ollie Lab

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drop into a ramp and pop an ollie, and see the speed, the g-force and the airtime
chunks.text: An idealised model: no friction or air drag, and you drop from rest. Speed at the bottom comes from energy (v = √(2gh)); the push from the ramp at the bottom of a curve of radius r is your weight × (1 + 2h ÷ r). The ollie section treats the jump as a simple projectile. For learning only; it is not a guide to what you're ready to ride.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drop into a ramp and pop an ollie, and see the speed, the g-force and the airtime
chunks.text: Drop-in height 1.5 m Transition radius 1.8 m Skater mass 60 kg Ollie obstacle height 30 cm Rolling speed 4.0 m/s Speed at the bottom 19.5 km/h Ch 4 · height becomes speed G-force in the transition 2.67 g Ch 4 · 1 + 2h ÷ r Push through your legs 1,570 N Ch 4 · bend your knees Ollie take-off speed (up) 2.43 m/s Ch 3 · √(2gH) Airtime 0.49 s Ch 3 · 2v ÷ g Distance travelled in the air 1.98 m Ch 3 · speed × airtime Bar = g-force in the transition on a 0–5 g scale. Real ramps lose some speed to friction, and real skaters add or lose energy by pumping (Ch 4). Start small, wear a helmet and learn to fall (Ch 5). CH 1

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pushing, rolling & coasting
chunks.text: Every push is a short burst of force. Then rolling resistance slowly takes it back. When you push, your foot shoves the ground backwards and the ground shoves you forwards. Once you're coasting, rolling resistance ( C rr × m g ) slows you at a = C rr × g , so you roll a distance d = v² ÷ (2 C rr g) before stopping (ignoring air drag). Worked example · coasting distance after a push (illustrative C rr ) Speed after pushing Surface C rr Rolls about 4 m/s (14 km/h) Smooth skatepark concrete 0.01 ≈ 82 m 4 m/s Rougher concrete 0.02 ≈ 41 m 3 m/s (11 km/h) Rougher concrete 0.02 ≈ 23 m 4² ÷ (2 × 0.02 × 9.81) ≈ 41 m. Speed squared means a slightly harder push carries you much further.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pushing, rolling & coasting
chunks.text: Air drag and small stones shorten real distances. Pushing well Weight on the front foot, over the front truck, so the board stays under you while the back foot pushes. Short, smooth pushes beat big lunges: you stay balanced and can stop. Learn to stop first: foot-brake (drag the back foot), or step off safely at low speed. To coast twice as far, how much faster do you need to be going? d ∝ v², so √2 ≈ 1.4 times faster. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: Keep your centre of mass over the board, and the board does what you ask. You stay up as long as your centre of mass is above the area between the wheels. Drift outside it and gravity creates a turning moment that tips you off. Bent knees lower your centre of mass and give you room to correct. Whether you ride left foot forward (regular) or right foot forward (goofy) is simply what feels natural. How trucks steer Skateboard trucks are built so that tilting the deck swings the axles: lean toe-side or heel-side and the board carves that way. To hold a curve of radius r at speed v you must lean into it at tan φ = v² ÷ (g r) .

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: Worked example · lean angle for a carve Speed Carve radius Lean angle 4 m/s (14 km/h) 3 m ≈ 29° 5 m/s (18 km/h) 4 m ≈ 33° tan φ = 4² ÷ (9.81 × 3) ≈ 0.54 → φ ≈ 29°. Looser trucks turn more for the same lean, but wobble more at speed. Inside the truck: tilt becomes steering Each truck's hanger swings around a pivot axis (the kingpin direction) that is tilted at an angle λ from the deck. When you tilt the deck by β, the axle yaws by a steering angle δ, with tan δ = tan λ × sin β . This is the steering relation used in skateboard-dynamics research going back to Hubbard (1979); Varszegi and colleagues (2016) write it the same way using the complementary "rake" angle.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: The front and rear trucks steer in opposite directions, so with a wheelbase L between the axles the board follows a curve of radius about R ≈ L ÷ (2 tan δ) . Worked example · wheelbase 0.36 m (illustrative), no bushing squash or wheel slip Deck tilt β 50° pivot axis: steer δ 50°: turn radius 44° pivot axis: steer δ 44°: turn radius 2° ≈ 2.4° ≈ 4.3 m ≈ 1.9° ≈ 5.3 m 5° ≈ 5.9° ≈ 1.7 m ≈ 4.8° ≈ 2.1 m 10° ≈ 11.7° ≈ 0.87 m ≈ 9.5° ≈ 1.1 m 5° tilt, 50° axis: tan δ = tan 50° × sin 5° ≈ 1.19 × 0.087 ≈ 0.104; R ≈ 0.36 ÷ (2 × 0.104) ≈ 1.7 m. A steeper pivot axis turns more for the same tilt.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: The 3 m carve from the table above needs only about 3° of deck tilt by this geometry, while your body leans about 29°. Deck tilt and body lean aren't the same angle. Real boards need a bit more tilt because bushings squash unevenly and wheels slip slightly. Why the same tilt feels twitchy at speed The truck fixes the radius for a given tilt, but the lean you need for that radius grows with v².

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: Hold the deck at 5° (a 1.7 m curve on the 50° trucks above) and see what balance demands: Worked example · lean needed on a 1.7 m curve, tan φ = v² ÷ (g R) Speed Body lean needed What it means 2 m/s (7 km/h) ≈ 13° Easy, relaxed carve 3 m/s (11 km/h) ≈ 28° A committed carve 4 m/s (14 km/h) ≈ 43° Very hard to hold 5 m/s (18 km/h) ≈ 56° Not realistic: you'd be thrown outward So at speed, a few degrees of accidental tilt is a big steering input. That's why fast riders keep the deck almost flat, and why tighter bushings or a lower pivot angle feel more stable downhill. Speed wobble is the same story with a delay in it.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: A 2016 study in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface (Varszegi, Takacs, Stepan and Hogan) modelled the skater's balance corrections with a human reflex delay. The range of correction strengths that keeps the board stable shrinks as speed rises, and standing ahead of the board's centre tolerates longer reflex delays than standing behind it. That matches the classic advice: weight over the front truck, smooth small corrections, and slow down before it starts. ✋ Feel the number Speed wobbles happen when small side-to-side oscillations grow faster than you correct them. Weight forward, knees bent and a lower speed calm them down.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Balance, stance & turning
chunks.text: Over-correcting hard and late, or leaning back, usually makes them worse. At 3 m/s, what lean angle holds a 2 m carve? tan φ = 9 ÷ (9.81 × 2) ≈ 0.46 → φ ≈ 25° . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The ollie
chunks.text: Snap, jump, slide, level. Physics does the rest. Snapping the tail down pivots the board over the back wheels; the ground pushes back on the tail and the board pops up. You jump at the same moment and slide your front foot forward, which drags the nose up and levels the board under you. Once you're in the air you're a projectile: to clear a height H you need an upward speed of v = √(2 g H) , and you'll be airborne for about t = 2v ÷ g .

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The ollie
chunks.text: Worked example · what an ollie needs (rolling at 4 m/s) Obstacle height Take-off speed (up) Airtime Forward distance in the air 10 cm ≈ 1.40 m/s ≈ 0.29 s ≈ 1.1 m 20 cm ≈ 1.98 m/s ≈ 0.40 s ≈ 1.6 m 30 cm ≈ 2.43 m/s ≈ 0.49 s ≈ 2.0 m 50 cm ≈ 3.13 m/s ≈ 0.64 s ≈ 2.6 m 30 cm: √(2 × 9.81 × 0.3) ≈ 2.43 m/s; airtime 2 × 2.43 ÷ 9.81 ≈ 0.49 s; 4 × 0.49 ≈ 1.98 m. Idealised: it assumes you land at take-off height and the board rises with you. Why practice matters more than strength Height needs √h more speed, so twice the height needs only about 1.4 times the pop. Timing (snapping the tail exactly as you jump) matters more than force. Practise standing still on grass or carpet first, then rolling slowly.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The ollie
chunks.text: You pop with 2 m/s upward speed. How high can you clear? H = v² ÷ (2g) = 4 ÷ 19.62 ≈ 0.20 m (20 cm). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ramps, bowls & pumping
chunks.text: A ramp swaps height for speed and back again. The curve pushes back hard. Dropping in from height h, you reach the bottom at v = √(2 g h) (ignoring friction). Following a curve of radius r needs a centripetal force m v² ÷ r , so at the bottom of the transition the ramp pushes on you with m g (1 + 2h ÷ r) : more than your weight.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ramps, bowls & pumping
chunks.text: Worked example · dropping into a 1.8 m-radius transition, 60 kg skater Drop height Speed at the bottom G-force at the bottom Push through your legs 0.5 m ≈ 11.3 km/h ≈ 1.56 g ≈ 916 N 1.0 m ≈ 15.9 km/h ≈ 2.11 g ≈ 1,243 N 1.5 m ≈ 19.5 km/h ≈ 2.67 g ≈ 1,570 N 2.0 m ≈ 22.6 km/h ≈ 3.22 g ≈ 1,897 N 1.5 m: v = √(2 × 9.81 × 1.5) ≈ 5.42 m/s; g-load = 1 + 2 × 1.5 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 2.67; push = 60 × 9.81 × 2.67 ≈ 1,570 N. Friction makes real speeds a little lower. Pumping Crouch as you go into the curve, then stand up through it while the ramp is pushing hardest. You do work against that extra force and gain energy, like pumping a swing. That's how bowl skaters keep going without pushing.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Ramps, bowls & pumping
chunks.text: Safety Drop in small first Commit with your weight over the front truck; leaning back is the classic fall. Start on low ramps with a helmet and pads, and give other skaters their turn. A bigger transition radius (say 3 m) for the same 1.5 m drop: what g-force? 1 + 2 × 1.5 ÷ 3 = 2.0 g : bigger curves are gentler. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falling safely
chunks.text: Everyone falls. The trick is to stop slowly. Average force during a stop depends on how far you take to stop: average deceleration = v² ÷ (2 × stopping distance) . Falling from standing, your body (centre of mass about 1 m up) reaches the ground at about √(2 × 9.81 × 1) ≈ 4.4 m/s . Worked example · stopping from 4.4 m/s How you land Stopping distance Average deceleration Stiff arm on concrete ≈ 5 cm ≈ 20 g Knee pads, slide ≈ 20 cm ≈ 5 g Roll out of it ≈ 50 cm ≈ 2 g For a fall from 1 m, deceleration in g = 1 m ÷ stopping distance: 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 g. Illustrative distances. How to fall Get low when you feel it going: less height, less speed.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falling safely
chunks.text: Roll onto your shoulder or side instead of reaching out with a straight arm. On a ramp, slide down on your knee pads. Helmet always. World Skate's competition rules (used in the RSFI rulebook) require all park skaters, and street skaters under 18, to wear a helmet in practice and competition. Halving your stopping distance does what to the average force? It doubles it. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wheels, bearings & contests
chunks.text: Small wheels spin fast. And in contests, five judges decide. A wheel turns once per circumference: revs per second = v ÷ (π d) . Smaller wheels spin faster for the same speed, and the bearings take it. Worked example · wheel spin at 15 km/h (4.17 m/s) Wheel diameter Turns per km Spin at 15 km/h 52 mm ≈ 6,121 ≈ 1,530 rpm 54 mm ≈ 5,895 ≈ 1,474 rpm 60 mm ≈ 5,305 ≈ 1,326 rpm 54 mm: circumference π × 0.054 ≈ 0.170 m; 4.17 ÷ 0.170 ≈ 24.6 turns per second ≈ 1,474 rpm. Hard or soft wheels? Bigger, softer wheels deform over stones and cracks and meet them at a gentler angle, so they suit rough streets and cruising. Smaller, harder wheels are lighter and slide more predictably on smooth park surfaces.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wheels, bearings & contests
chunks.text: Cracks and pebbles: the geometry of getting stopped When a wheel of radius R meets a step or pebble of height h, the push from the edge acts along the line from the edge to the axle. The higher h is compared with R, the more of that push points backwards, against your motion. That's the moment the board stops and you don't. Worked example · share of the edge's push pointing backwards (rigid wheel, geometry only) Obstacle 52 mm park wheel 60 mm wheel 70 mm cruiser wheel 3 mm crack lip ≈ 47% ≈ 44% ≈ 41% 5 mm pebble ≈ 59% ≈ 55% ≈ 52% 10 mm stone ≈ 79% ≈ 75% ≈ 70% The edge-to-axle line makes an angle θ with the vertical where cos θ = (R − h) ÷ R; the backward share is sin θ.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wheels, bearings & contests
chunks.text: 5 mm on a 52 mm wheel: cos θ = 21 ÷ 26 → θ ≈ 36°, sin θ ≈ 0.59. A softer wheel also squashes around the obstacle, which lowers the effective h further. These are geometry comparisons, not stopping forces. Soft wheels: grip versus roll Wheel hardness is measured on a durometer scale (the "A" number on the wheel); a lower number is softer. On smooth concrete, a harder wheel flexes less and wastes less energy rolling. On rough tarmac, a softer wheel absorbs bumps that would otherwise shake your body, the same "roughness resistance" idea explained on our cycling page . A softer wheel also grips more before it slides, which helps on carves and hurts when you want to slide on purpose.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wheels, bearings & contests
chunks.text: Bearings and what "ABEC" really means Almost every skateboard wheel holds two "608"-size bearings: an 8 mm bore, 22 mm outside diameter and 7 mm width, according to board maker Sector 9. The ABEC number on the box is a precision class from the Annular Bearing Engineers' Committee: it sets dimensions and tolerances, not speed. Bones Bearings, a bearing maker, points out that ABEC ignores side loads, impact resistance, lubrication and shields, which matter more for skating. Its estimate is that 90% of skating happens below about 2,000 rpm, consistent with the roughly 1,500 rpm in the table above. Clean, undamaged bearings matter more than the number.

chunks.title: Skateboarding · Physics of Ollies, Ramps & Falls · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wheels, bearings & contests
chunks.text: How contests are scored The RSFI skateboarding rulebook follows World Skate rules for the two Olympic disciplines, street and park , with no age limits. In park, skaters get at least two runs of 30–50 seconds; five judges score each run from 0 to 100, the highest and lowest scores are dropped and the remaining three averaged. The best run counts. In the Olympic street format, skaters do 2 runs of 45 seconds and 5 single tricks; the best run plus the 2 best tricks make the score. Judges score 70, 74, 76, 80 and 91. What's the run score? Drop 91 and 70: (74 + 76 + 80) ÷ 3 = 76.67 . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The skate ladder

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Eight small wheels, a lot of physics.
chunks.text: Quad or inline, every roll is a contest between your push and three thieves: rolling resistance, air drag and gravity. Learn bearings, wheels, balance, braking and ramps with real numbers, and you'll know exactly why that hill feels faster than it looks. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science rolling stopped ≈ 15 m Gentle braking distance from 20 km/h, vs about 4 m from 10. Learn to stop before you learn to go fast. ≈ 23 km/h Your speed at the bottom of a 2 m slope. Gravity is a free engine. It has no brakes. ≈ 14 km/h Fastest you can take a 5 m turn on a wet road marking. Dust, paint and water cut grip: slow before turns.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Eight small wheels, a lot of physics.
chunks.text: 1.6 m Hitting the ground at 20 km/h is like falling this far. Helmet, wrist guards and pads spread the impact.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Bend your knees. Knees bent and weight forward lower your centre of mass and stop the classic sit-down fall. Start somewhere smooth, flat and traffic-free. Wear full protective gear, ideally with a coach or beginner group. Match speed to stopping space. Only skate as fast as you can stop in the clear space ahead. Ask before you book a first lesson → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Do you know what's really slowing you down?
chunks.text: 15 questions on the physics of rolling: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Six chapters, from first roll to the bottom of the ramp
chunks.text: Each chapter takes one idea and follows it onto the tarmac, with worked numbers you can check on a calculator. Our reference skater weighs 70 kg (686 N) with gear. Rolling-resistance coefficients, drag areas and braking decelerations are illustrative round values; real ones depend on wheels, surface, posture and skill. Why this page doesn't cover skateboarding Skateboarding shares wheels and bearings with roller sports, and the same bodies govern it: World Skate globally, and in India the RSFI, which calls itself "the governing body for skateboarding and roller sports". But the core physics is different.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Six chapters, from first roll to the bottom of the ramp
chunks.text: The board isn't attached to your feet, so tricks like the ollie (popping the tail to make the board leap) and riding with both feet sideways on one deck are a different set of problems from striding on two skates. Its skill ladder and its Olympic events (street and park) are also separate. It deserves its own page, so here we stick to quad (roller) and inline skates. Interactive · Roll Lab

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Change the speed, surface and stance, and see what it costs to go and to stop
chunks.text: An illustrative model: constant rolling resistance, air drag at density 1.2 kg/m³, and a constant braking deceleration you choose. Flat ground, no wind. For learning only; it is not a safety calculator. Speed 20 km/h Skater + gear 70 kg Braking deceleration 2.0 m/s² Reaction time 0.7 s Surface Smooth rink Smooth concrete Rough asphalt Stance Upright Low tuck Rolling resistance 6.9 N Ch 1 · Crr × weight Air drag 8.3 N Ch 4 · ½ρv²·CdA Power to hold speed 84 W Ch 4 · force × speed Coast distance (no push) 103 m Ch 1 & 4 · rolling + drag Braking distance 7.7 m Ch 5 · v² ÷ 2a Total stopping distance 11.6 m Ch 5 · incl.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Change the speed, surface and stance, and see what it costs to go and to stop
chunks.text: reaction 3.9 m Same energy as a drop of 1.57 m Ch 6 · v² ÷ 2g 80 mm wheel speed 1326 rpm Ch 2 · v ÷ circumference Bar = total stopping distance on a 0–40 m scale. Real braking depends on technique, wheel grip, brake-pad wear, slope and surface (wet, sandy or oily ground can halve your grip). Treat every number as a teaching example. CH 1

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: A wheel doesn't roll for free. It squashes, a little, every turn. Skate wheels are made of polyurethane. Where the wheel meets the ground it flattens slightly, then springs back as it rolls on, but not perfectly: some energy is lost as heat (materials scientists call it hysteresis ). Bumps and grit add small impacts. Together they create rolling resistance , a nearly constant force: F = Crr × weight , where Crr is the rolling-resistance coefficient.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: Worked example · the same skater on three surfaces (illustrative Crr) Surface Crr Force (70 kg) Coast from 15 km/h, rolling only Smooth indoor rink ≈ 0.005 ≈ 3.4 N ≈ 177 m Smooth concrete ≈ 0.01 ≈ 6.9 N ≈ 88 m Rough asphalt ≈ 0.02 ≈ 13.7 N ≈ 44 m Coasting distance from rolling resistance alone = v² ÷ (2 × Crr × g). With 15 km/h = 4.17 m/s and Crr 0.01: 17.4 ÷ 0.196 ≈ 88 m. Add air drag (Chapter 4) and the real figure is shorter. Notice the surface matters more than almost any upgrade you could buy. What a real measurement found Measured numbers for inline wheels are rare.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: One careful test, in a 1994 McGill University thesis by Sarah Cartwright, rolled a four-wheel cart carrying 39 kg (about 10 kg per wheel, close to what each wheel of a 70 kg skater carries with both feet down) over marks at 0, 3, 9 and 12 m, timed it, and turned the slowdown into a resistance force. It tested two wheel types (78A and 82A), "precision" and "semi-precision" bearings, and two surfaces. We've converted each mean force into a coefficient (Crr = force ÷ cart weight).

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: Measured · four inline wheels, 39 kg cart, mean of nine runs each (Cartwright 1994) Wheel · surface Precision bearings Semi-precision bearings Crr range Coast from 15 km/h, rolling only 78A · polished concrete (rink floor) 2.38 N 3.71 N ≈ 0.006–0.010 ≈ 142 m → 91 m 78A · asphalt 3.07 N 3.98 N ≈ 0.008–0.010 ≈ 110 m → 85 m 82A · polished concrete 4.17 N 5.08 N ≈ 0.011–0.013 ≈ 81 m → 67 m 82A · asphalt 4.63 N 5.14 N ≈ 0.012–0.013 ≈ 73 m → 66 m 78A, concrete, precision: Crr = 2.38 ÷ (39.05 × 9.81) ≈ 0.0062. The measured range, about 0.006–0.013, sits right where our illustrative 0.005–0.02 table above puts smooth and ordinary surfaces.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: The study found wheel, bearing and surface effects all statistically significant. It was one cart, one brand of bearing and two wheel models, with a lighter load per wheel on one skate than a real skater puts down, so treat it as a careful snapshot, not a law. Bearings: the bit everyone over-thinks Almost all inline and most quad wheels use the same bearing size, the 608 : 8 mm bore, 22 mm outside diameter, 7 mm wide. Each wheel takes two, with a spacer between, so a pair of 4-wheel inline skates or quads carries 16 bearings. The ABEC number (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) printed on many bearings is a scale of manufacturing tolerance : how precisely the parts are made. It is not a speed rating.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: Wheel rpm on skates is modest (Chapter 2), and at those speeds a clean, lightly lubricated bearing loses far less energy than the wheel's own rolling resistance. Dirt, sand and water are what really slow bearings down, and they ruin them. Bearings aren't nothing, though. In the cart test above, the semi-precision set added 0.5 to 1.3 N, between 11% and 56% more total resistance than the precision set, and the skaters used measurably more oxygen with the cheaper bearings (their heart rates didn't differ significantly). Notice what the comparison was: two grades of one maker's bearings, both presumably clean. It doesn't show that a higher ABEC number on the box rolls faster.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Rolling resistance & bearings
chunks.text: Keep bearings clean and dry first; buy a better grade second. ✋ Feel the number 6.9 N is about the weight of a 700 g bag of sugar. It's what you'd feel pulling a skater along smooth concrete at walking pace with a luggage scale. Drag it across rough asphalt and the scale reads twice as much. A 90 kg skater rolls on rough asphalt (Crr 0.02). What's the rolling resistance, and does it change how far they coast from 15 km/h? Force = 0.02 × 90 × 9.81 ≈ 17.7 N . But coast distance = v² ÷ (2 × Crr × g) has no mass in it: still ≈ 44 m on rolling resistance alone. More weight, more force, but more momentum to match. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wheels, size & durometer
chunks.text: Soft or hard, big or small: every wheel is a trade-off. Durometer: how hard the urethane is Wheel hardness is measured on the Shore A durometer scale, printed as a number and the letter A (e.g. 78A, 85A). Lower is softer. Soft wheels (roughly the high 70s A) deform around pebbles and cracks: better grip, a smoother ride, a little more rolling resistance and faster wear. Harder wheels (mid-80s A and up) deform less on smooth floors: faster, more willing to slide, but harsh and skittish on rough tarmac. Outdoor recreational wheels sit at the soft end; rink and slide wheels at the hard end. "Harder is faster" is a smooth-floor rule.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wheels, size & durometer
chunks.text: In the measured cart test ( Ch 1 ), the 82A wheels rolled with more resistance than the 78A wheels on both concrete and asphalt, by about 50–75% with precision bearings. The two wheels were different models, so that result doesn't isolate hardness alone. But it fits the physics of rough ground: a wheel that can't swallow a bump has to lift you over it, and that costs energy (the cycling page's roughness-resistance section explains the same effect on tyres). Its skaters' oxygen use didn't differ significantly between the two wheel types.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wheels, size & durometer
chunks.text: Diameter: big rolls easier, small turns quicker A bigger wheel meets each bump at a gentler angle and spreads its contact patch over a longer, narrower area, so it typically carries speed better. That's why speed and marathon skaters use large wheels (often 100–125 mm). Smaller wheels (around 72–80 mm) sit lower and accelerate and turn more nimbly, favoured for hockey, freestyle slalom and learning. Worked example · how fast do the wheels spin at 20 km/h (5.56 m/s)?

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wheels, size & durometer
chunks.text: Wheel diameter Circumference Revolutions per second rpm 80 mm 0.251 m ≈ 22.1 ≈ 1,326 90 mm 0.283 m ≈ 19.6 ≈ 1,179 100 mm 0.314 m ≈ 17.7 ≈ 1,061 110 mm 0.346 m ≈ 16.1 ≈ 965 125 mm 0.393 m ≈ 14.1 ≈ 849 For comparison, a typical car tyre about 65 cm across turns at roughly 800 rpm at 100 km/h, so a skate wheel at jogging-plus speed spins faster than a car wheel on the highway. Bearings handle that easily, as long as they're clean. Quad vs inline Quad skates put two wheels side by side at the front and back, giving a wider side-to-side base and a short front-to-back one. They're stable standing still and agile for dance and rink skating, and they usually have a toe stop for braking.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Wheels, size & durometer
chunks.text: Inline skates line three to five wheels in a single row: narrow side-to-side (you balance like on a bicycle, steering under yourself) but long front-to-back, which makes them stable at speed and efficient for distance. Most inline skates for learners carry a heel brake . Your 80 mm wheels are at 1,326 rpm. You swap to 100 mm wheels and skate at the same speed. New rpm? rpm scales with 1/diameter: 1,326 × 80 ÷ 100 ≈ 1,061 rpm . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Balance, lean & centre of mass
chunks.text: You're an upside-down pendulum on wheels. Bend your knees. Standing on skates, your body behaves like an inverted pendulum : the centre of mass (roughly at your navel) sits about a metre above a very small support base. If your centre of mass drifts outside that base, gravity starts toppling you, and the further it drifts the faster you go. Balancing on skates means keeping it over the wheels, by moving the wheels back under you (steering) or by shifting your body. Why the "ready position" works Coaches teach a stance with knees bent, hips back, weight over the middle-to-front of the foot and hands forward.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Balance, lean & centre of mass
chunks.text: Three physics gains: the centre of mass is lower, so small tilts take longer to grow; bent legs act as springs, soaking up bumps; and weight forward stops the classic beginner fall, where the wheels roll ahead and you sit down hard behind them. Leaning into turns Just like on ice or a bicycle, a turn needs a force toward the centre, m × v² ÷ r, supplied by wheel grip, so you must lean in: tan θ = v² ÷ (g × r) . Worked example · lean angles on wheels Speed Turn radius Centripetal acceleration Lean from vertical 15 km/h 10 m 1.7 m/s² ≈ 10° 15 km/h 5 m 3.5 m/s² ≈ 19.5° 20 km/h 5 m 6.2 m/s² ≈ 32° Halve the radius and the lean roughly doubles at gentle angles.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Balance, lean & centre of mass
chunks.text: Wheels have far less sideways grip on dusty, wet or painted surfaces than on clean concrete, so a lean that's fine on a dry rink can slide out on a wet road marking. Grip sets the limit The wheels can only push sideways as hard as friction allows: sideways force ≤ μ × weight, where μ is the friction coefficient between urethane and ground. Combine that with the lean equation and the steepest lean you can hold is tan θ = μ , and the fastest you can take a curve of radius r is v = √(μ × g × r) .

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Balance, lean & centre of mass
chunks.text: Worked example · the grip limit on a 5 m-radius turn (illustrative μ) Surface condition (illustrative) μ Maximum lean Fastest speed on r = 5 m Clean, dry concrete, grippy wheels 0.8 ≈ 39° ≈ 22.6 km/h Dusty or painted surface 0.5 ≈ 27° ≈ 17.8 km/h Wet road marking, hard wheels 0.3 ≈ 17° ≈ 13.8 km/h μ = 0.5: v = √(0.5 × 9.81 × 5) ≈ 4.95 m/s ≈ 17.8 km/h. The μ values are teaching examples, not measurements. Compare the lean table above: the 32° lean at 20 km/h on a 5 m turn is already beyond the 27° that a dusty surface allows. That's the mechanism behind the classic slide-out on a painted line. ✋ Feel the number A 32° lean puts your hips (about 1 m up) roughly 0.6 m inside your skates.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Balance, lean & centre of mass
chunks.text: That's a dramatic, committed position, which is why tight turns at speed are an intermediate skill and not a first-day one. You're comfortable leaning 15°. What's the tightest turn you can make at 15 km/h? r = v² ÷ (g × tan θ) = 17.4 ÷ (9.81 × 0.268) ≈ 6.6 m . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The stride, power & drag
chunks.text: Wheels roll forward freely, so you push sideways. A wheel rolls easily along its direction and grips hard sideways. Push straight back and the skate just rolls back. So skaters angle the pushing skate outward and drive it sideways. The ground pushes back perpendicular to the wheels, and the forward share of that push propels you, while the gliding skate carries you on. Good skaters make each push long, low and sideways, then bring the leg back under the body. The cost of going faster Two forces resist you on the flat: rolling resistance (constant, Chapter 1) and air drag, ½ × ρ × v² × CdA , which grows with the square of speed. Power is force × speed.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The stride, power & drag
chunks.text: Worked example · power to cruise, 70 kg, smooth concrete (Crr 0.01), upright CdA ≈ 0.45 m² Speed Air drag Rolling Power needed 10 km/h 2.1 N 6.9 N ≈ 25 W 15 km/h 4.7 N 6.9 N ≈ 48 W 20 km/h 8.3 N 6.9 N ≈ 84 W 25 km/h 13.0 N 6.9 N ≈ 138 W 30 km/h 18.8 N 6.9 N ≈ 213 W 30 km/h, low tuck (CdA 0.30) 12.5 N 6.9 N ≈ 161 W Air drag overtakes rolling resistance at about 18 km/h for this skater. From 10 to 30 km/h, speed triples but power rises more than eight-fold. Tucking low saves about a quarter of the effort at 30 km/h, which is why speed skaters skate bent double with their hands behind their backs. Work per push: where the watts come from Power arrives in pushes.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The stride, power & drag
chunks.text: Each push does an amount of work W, so power = W × pushes per second . In Cartwright's 1994 study, hockey players skating inline at about 20–23 km/h kept a nearly constant stride length of roughly 3.8–4.7 m and went faster mostly by pushing more often, about 79 to 101 strides a minute, the same pattern earlier research found on ice. Classic speed-skating research by van Ingen Schenau's group points the other way for elite racers: better skaters stand out by doing more work per stroke, with a long glide and a sideways, horizontal push-off.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The stride, power & drag
chunks.text: Worked example · work per push for our 70 kg skater (power from the table above) Speed Power At 60 pushes/min: work per push · glide per push At 80 pushes/min: work per push · glide per push 15 km/h 48 W 48 J · 4.2 m 36 J · 3.1 m 20 km/h 84 W 84 J · 5.6 m 63 J · 4.2 m 25 km/h 138 W 138 J · 6.9 m 104 J · 5.2 m 30 km/h 213 W 213 J · 8.3 m 160 J · 6.3 m 20 km/h at 80 pushes a minute (1.33 per second): 84 W ÷ 1.33 ≈ 63 J per push, and 5.56 m/s ÷ 1.33 ≈ 4.2 m of travel per push, close to the stride lengths measured in the 1994 study. Push rates here are illustrative.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The stride, power & drag
chunks.text: ✋ Feel the number 63 J is lifting a 6.4 kg bag of rice one metre off the floor, once every three-quarters of a second, with your legs, for as long as you skate at 20 km/h. Is roller skating the same movement as ice speed skating? A 1987 study by de Boer and colleagues had eight trained marathon skaters go all-out on both. Power, work per stroke, stroke frequency, push-off effectiveness and oxygen uptake were statistically the same. The roller skaters' maximum speed was lower because their wheels had more friction than steel blades on ice, and their upper leg sat about 7.5° more upright while gliding. A 15 km/h headwind hits you while you skate at 15 km/h. What air speed does the drag "see"?

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The stride, power & drag
chunks.text: 30 km/h: drag goes from 4.7 N to ≈ 18.8 N , four times as much, while your ground speed hasn't changed. Headwinds are brutal on skates. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Braking & stopping distance
chunks.text: Learn to stop before you learn to go fast. The maths explains why. Every stop turns your kinetic energy, ½mv², into heat, either in a rubber brake pad or in wheels scrubbing sideways across the ground. The common methods, roughly in the order they're taught: Heel brake (inline) or toe stop (quad): scissor one foot forward and press the pad down. Simple and controllable; the first stop most instructors teach. Plough / A-frame and spin stops : steer the skates to scrub speed or turn it into a circle. T-stop : drag the back skate at right angles behind the front one. Effective, but wears wheels and needs balance. Powerslide and hockey-style stops : advanced.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Braking & stopping distance
chunks.text: The wheels are deliberately slid sideways. Grass stop : roll off onto grass and let the high rolling resistance slow you, with weight back and knees bent. Worked example · stopping distances, braking distance = v² ÷ (2 × deceleration) Speed Gentle 1 m/s² Good 2 m/s² Strong 3.5 m/s² + reaction (0.7 s) Same energy as a drop of 10 km/h 3.9 m 1.9 m 1.1 m +1.9 m 0.39 m 15 km/h 8.7 m 4.3 m 2.5 m +2.9 m 0.88 m 20 km/h 15.4 m 7.7 m 4.4 m +3.9 m 1.57 m 30 km/h 34.7 m 17.4 m 9.9 m +5.8 m 3.54 m Decelerations are illustrative: a beginner's heel brake may manage ~1 m/s²; skilled skaters can do much better on good surfaces.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Braking & stopping distance
chunks.text: The last column is the height you'd have to fall from to hit the ground at the same speed. At 30 km/h, hitting something is like falling from a first-floor window. Safety Rule of thumb Only skate as fast as you can stop in the clear space you can see ahead. On a path with pedestrians, at 20 km/h that's more than 11 metres even with a good brake. At 25 km/h with a 2 m/s² brake and 0.7 s reaction, what's the total stopping distance? v = 6.94 m/s. Reaction 6.94 × 0.7 ≈ 4.9 m; braking 48.2 ÷ 4 ≈ 12.1 m. Total ≈ 17 m . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Hills, ramps & falling
chunks.text: Gravity is a free engine. It has no brakes. Ramps: height becomes speed Rolling down from rest, potential energy (mgh) becomes kinetic energy (½mv²), so v = √(2gh) . Mass cancels: heavy and light skaters reach the same speed, if we ignore friction and air. Worked example · speed at the bottom (no friction) Drop height Speed In km/h 0.5 m 3.1 m/s ≈ 11 km/h 1 m 4.4 m/s ≈ 16 km/h 2 m 6.3 m/s ≈ 23 km/h 3 m 7.7 m/s ≈ 28 km/h Long hills: the terminal speed On a long slope, you speed up until air drag plus rolling resistance balance the downhill pull of gravity.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Hills, ramps & falling
chunks.text: For our 70 kg upright skater (CdA 0.45, Crr 0.01), the speed you'd settle at with no braking is: Slope (gradient) Terminal speed, no braking 3% (3 m drop per 100 m) ≈ 26 km/h 5% ≈ 36 km/h 8% ≈ 48 km/h A 5% slope barely looks like a hill, but left alone it takes you to 36 km/h, faster than most recreational skaters can stop from safely. Heavier skaters go faster still, because drag is a smaller share of their weight. Control speed on hills from the top (slaloming turns, plough or brake), and walk down anything you're unsure of. Falling well From a standing centre-of-mass height of about 1 m, a fall reaches ≈ 4.4 m/s, before adding any forward speed.

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Hills, ramps & falling
chunks.text: Instructors teach falling forward and low onto knee pads, then elbows, then wrist guards, rather than backwards onto the tailbone or head. Protective gear works by sliding and spreading the impact: a longer stopping time means a smaller peak force for the same change in momentum. Helmet, wrist guards, elbow and knee pads are standard requirements in instructor programmes and many clubs. A skate park bowl is 1.5 m deep. Ignoring friction, how fast are you moving at the bottom if you drop in from the top? v = √(2 × 9.81 × 1.5) ≈ 5.4 m/s ≈ 19.5 km/h , and it all turns back into height on the far side. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · Skill levels

chunks.title: Roller & inline skating: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first roll to the national championships
chunks.text: Unlike diving or paragliding, roller and inline skating has no single international learner grading . So we've built a clearly labelled Kinetic milestone ladder , anchored to something real: the skills an instructor must be able to teach under the Inline Certification Program (ICP) Level 1. Alongside it, we show India's actual competitive pathway under the Roller Skating Federation of India (RSFI). Instructor certifications (ICP, Skate IA) are explained below the ladder.

chunks.heading: Instructor certifications: how to recognise a trained coach
chunks.text: Instructor certification ICP: Inline Certification Program Levels 1–3 for inline instructors. Level 1 covers teaching gliding, striding, stopping and turning, and is offered online and in person. Candidates must wear full protective gear and a heel brake, and pass theory (85%), practical teaching (80%) and skating-skills assessments. ICP's own blog reports a Level 1 course for six Indian instructors at a track in Pune in March 2016.

chunks.text: World Skate governs roller sports and skateboarding worldwide. In India, the Roller Skating Federation of India (RSFI) is the national body, working through state associations and district units that affiliate clubs and register skaters. Every body below was checked on its official website.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gravity pulls. Your edges decide where.
chunks.text: Every run is a negotiation between gravity, snow friction, air drag and the grip of your edges. Take the challenge, learn the science, then find a 14-day course at Gulmarg, Solang or Auli at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Nursery Off-piste ≈ 52 km/h Your speed after just 50 m straight down a 15° run. Turns are your brakes, not just steering. ≈ 11.5 m Hitting something at 54 km/h is like falling that far. Double your speed and the impact energy quadruples. 30°–45° The slope angles where most slab avalanches start. Often triggered by the skiers themselves. ≈ 61% Of sea-level air pressure at about 4,000 m up.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Snow reflects the sun. Fresh snow and thin air mean strong UV: wear goggles or dark glasses, and sunscreen. Stay on marked slopes. Leaving controlled slopes needs avalanche training, kit and a qualified local guide. Keep space around you. A helmet, controlled speed and space between you and others are the main defences. Ask before you book a first ski lesson → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: How well do you know the physics of skiing?
chunks.text: 15 questions on slope forces, snow friction, air drag, edges and turns, falls and avalanches, and cold and altitude: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Slope Lab to see how slope, snow and stance change your speed. Interactive · Slope Lab

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a slope, a snow and a stance, and see how fast gravity wants to take you
chunks.text: A simple model: gravity along the slope minus snow friction (μ × the push into the slope) minus air drag (½ρC d Av², with air density at about 3,000 m, close to Gulmarg's Kongdori mid-station). Friction coefficients and drag areas are illustrative. "After 50 m" ignores drag and assumes you don't turn. For learning only; it is not a guide to what you can ski.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a slope, a snow and a stance, and see how fast gravity wants to take you
chunks.text: Slope angle 15° Skier mass (with kit) 75 kg Snow Hard & icy (μ 0.03) Cold groomed (μ 0.05) Wet spring (μ 0.10) Stance Upright Racing tuck Steepness 27% Ch 1 · tan θ × 100 Gravity along the slope 190 N Ch 1 · mg sin θ Snow friction 36 N Ch 2 · μ mg cos θ Acceleration (no drag) 2.07 m/s² Ch 1 · g(sin θ − μ cos θ) Speed after 50 m straight 51.7 km/h Ch 4 · why you turn Top speed (drag balances) 85.8 km/h Ch 3 · gravity = friction + drag Bar = top speed on a 0–140 km/h scale. Real skiers almost never reach these speeds because they turn, which is the point: turns are your brakes (Ch 4). Ski in control, within your ability and the slope's markings. CH 1

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gravity on a slope
chunks.text: The steeper the slope, the bigger the share of your weight that pulls you down it. On a slope at angle θ, your weight mg splits in two: mg sin θ along the slope, pulling you downhill, and mg cos θ into the snow, pressing you onto it. Subtract snow friction (Ch 2) and you get the acceleration: a = g (sin θ − μ cos θ) . Slopes are often quoted as a percentage: gradient = tan θ × 100 .

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gravity on a slope
chunks.text: Worked example · 75 kg skier, cold groomed snow (μ ≈ 0.05), no air drag Slope Gradient Pull down the slope Acceleration Speed after 50 m straight 5° 9% 64 N 0.37 m/s² ≈ 22 km/h 15° 27% 190 N 2.07 m/s² ≈ 52 km/h 25° 47% 311 N 3.70 m/s² ≈ 69 km/h 35° 70% 422 N 5.22 m/s² ≈ 82 km/h 15°: 75 × 9.81 × sin 15° ≈ 190 N; a = 9.81 × (0.259 − 0.05 × 0.966) ≈ 2.07 m/s²; v = √(2 × 2.07 × 50) ≈ 14.4 m/s ≈ 52 km/h. Without drag, mass cancels: heavy and light skiers accelerate alike. Why beginners start on gentle slopes On a 5° nursery slope, speed builds slowly enough to practise the snow plough.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Gravity on a slope
chunks.text: Below about 3° on groomed snow, gravity barely beats friction and you'll hardly move at all: try it in the Slope Lab. ✋ Feel the number A 27% road is very steep for a car. On skis, that 15° slope is a typical intermediate run, and gravity would take you past 50 km/h in 50 m if you never turned. What's the gradient of a 20° slope, and the pull on a 60 kg skier? tan 20° ≈ 0.36, so 36% ; pull = 60 × 9.81 × sin 20° ≈ 201 N . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction & the snow
chunks.text: You're not sliding on ice. You're sliding on a film of water you just made. The friction between a waxed base and snow is low, typically quoted around μ ≈ 0.03–0.1. A big reason is frictional melting : rubbing heats the contact points and makes a microscopic water layer that lubricates the base. Very cold, dry snow melts less and feels slow; wet spring snow can feel sticky because water films create suction. Worked example · friction on a 15° slope, 75 kg skier (illustrative μ) Snow μ Friction force Acceleration Hard and icy 0.03 ≈ 21 N 2.25 m/s² Cold groomed 0.05 ≈ 36 N 2.07 m/s² Wet spring 0.10 ≈ 71 N 1.59 m/s² Friction = μ × mg cos θ = 0.05 × 75 × 9.81 × 0.966 ≈ 36 N.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction & the snow
chunks.text: These μ values are typical classroom figures; real values vary with temperature, snow crystals, wax and speed. Base glide vs edge bite Like an ice blade (see our ice-skating edge chapter ), a ski or snowboard is anisotropic. A waxed base glides with low friction along the snow; a tipped edge digs in and scrapes, raising the effective resistance sharply. That is how a snow plough brakes: you trade glide for sideways scrape. Carving (Ch 4) keeps more of the base sliding while the edge holds a line — less scrape, more speed held.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction & the snow
chunks.text: Order of magnitude · what changes μ (illustrative) Condition Effect on glide Why (teaching picture) Very cold, dry snow Feels slow / grabby Less frictional meltwater under the base Cold groomed, good wax Fast and quiet Thin melt film + smooth track Warm, wet spring snow Can feel sticky Thick water film / suction; wax matters a lot Edges engaged (plough / hard carve) Much more drag Snow is sheared and ploughed sideways Wax "temperature windows" are real shop craft; we do not prescribe brands. Ask the hire shop what they waxed for today's snow. Snow plough to parallel Beginners brake with the snow plough : tails pushed apart, skis tipped onto their inside edges so they scrape snow sideways.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Friction & the snow
chunks.text: IISM Gulmarg's 14-day basic course syllabus builds from walking and sliding to snow plough, snow plough turns, traversing, uphill swings and side stepping, then basic swings; the intermediate and advanced courses move on to side-slip garlands, downhill swings and parallel turns with open and then closed skis, and slalom. ✋ Feel the number A friction coefficient of 0.05 means a 75 kg skier on the flat needs a push of only about 37 N, about the weight of a 4 kg bag, to keep sliding. On wet snow (μ = 0.1), what's the gentlest slope on which you'll start to slide? You slide when tan θ > μ: θ > arctan 0.1 ≈ 5.7° . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag & top speed
chunks.text: Gravity keeps pulling. Eventually the air pushes back just as hard. Air drag is ½ ρ C d A v² : air density × drag area × speed squared. As you speed up, drag grows until gravity along the slope equals friction plus drag. That's your top (terminal) speed: v max = √(2 (mg sin θ − μ mg cos θ) ÷ (ρ C d A)) . Unlike acceleration, top speed does depend on mass: heavier skiers go faster when drag matters. Worked example · 75 kg skier, μ = 0.05, air density 0.91 kg/m³ (≈ 3,000 m) Slope Upright (C d A ≈ 0.6 m²) Racing tuck (C d A ≈ 0.25 m²) 10° ≈ 66 km/h ≈ 102 km/h 15° ≈ 86 km/h ≈ 133 km/h 25° ≈ 115 km/h ≈ 178 km/h 15°, upright: (190.4 − 35.5) N × 2 ÷ (0.909 × 0.6) ≈ 568 → √568 ≈ 23.8 m/s ≈ 86 km/h.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Air drag & top speed
chunks.text: Drag areas are typical illustrative values. Air density from the International Standard Atmosphere. Altitude and drag Gulmarg's gondola climbs from about 2,650 m to 3,980 m, according to IISM. At 3,980 m the standard atmosphere gives about 61% of sea-level pressure, so the air is thinner and drag a little lower. Racers in a tuck exploit drag; recreational skiers control speed with turns instead (Ch 4). If you halve your drag area, by what factor does your top speed rise? v max ∝ 1 ÷ √(C d A), so by √2 ≈ 1.41 . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Edges, turns & speed control
chunks.text: Turns aren't just for changing direction. They're your brakes. To follow a curve of radius r at speed v, something must push you sideways with force m v² ÷ r . On skis or a snowboard, that's the snow pushing back on your tilted edge. To balance, you lean into the turn at angle φ with tan φ = v² ÷ (g r) . Worked example · lean angle for a turn Speed Turn radius Lean angle Sideways force on a 75 kg skier 10 m/s (36 km/h) 15 m ≈ 34° ≈ 500 N 10 m/s 10 m ≈ 46° ≈ 750 N 15 m/s (54 km/h) 20 m ≈ 49° ≈ 844 N tan φ = 10² ÷ (9.81 × 15) ≈ 0.68 → φ ≈ 34°; force = 75 × 100 ÷ 15 = 500 N. Sidecut and the carved radius A ski is narrower at the waist than at tip and tail — the sidecut .

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Edges, turns & speed control
chunks.text: Laid flat, that shape is part of a circle with a printed "sidecut radius" (often 12–18 m on recreational skis). Tip the ski onto its edge by an angle β and the running edge becomes a tighter arc on the snow: roughly R ≈ R sidecut × cos β in a simple geometric model (real skis also bend under your weight, which can tighten the turn further). Higher edge angles → shorter carved turns → more of your path across the fall line → more speed control without a scrape. Worked example · sidecut radius on edge (illustrative R sc = 15 m) Edge angle β Approx.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Edges, turns & speed control
chunks.text: carved radius R sc cos β Lean at 10 m/s for that r (tan φ = v²/gr) 0° (flat) 15 m ≈ 34° 30° ≈ 13 m ≈ 38° 45° ≈ 10.6 m ≈ 44° 60° ≈ 7.5 m ≈ 54° Numbers are a teaching model: snow hardness, ski stiffness and how hard you press change the real radius. The lesson is that edge angle is a speed-control dial, not only a style choice. How turns control speed Across the fall line: the steepest line down the hill is the fall line. Ski across it and the slope along your path is far gentler — less mg sin θ along your track (Ch 1). Skidding vs carving: a skidded turn scrapes snow and converts kinetic energy into heat (high effective μ from Ch 2); a carved turn rides the edge cleanly and keeps more speed.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Edges, turns & speed control
chunks.text: Beginners skid on purpose to stay slow; experts choose when to skid and when to carve. Snowboarding: the same physics on one board, with heel-side and toe-side edges. ABVIMAS (Solang) and IISM (Gulmarg) both run snowboarding courses. You turn at 8 m/s on a 12 m radius. What lean angle do you need? tan φ = 64 ÷ (9.81 × 12) ≈ 0.54 → φ ≈ 29° . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls, collisions & avalanches
chunks.text: Speed is energy, and every stop has to put it somewhere. Kinetic energy is ½ m v² : double your speed and you carry four times the energy into any fall or collision. A helmet, a controlled speed and space between you and others are the main defences. Worked example · energy of a 75 kg skier Speed Kinetic energy Same as falling from 5 m/s (18 km/h) ≈ 0.9 kJ ≈ 1.3 m 10 m/s (36 km/h) ≈ 3.8 kJ ≈ 5.1 m 15 m/s (54 km/h) ≈ 8.4 kJ ≈ 11.5 m ½ × 75 × 15² ≈ 8,440 J; equivalent height = v² ÷ (2g) = 225 ÷ 19.62 ≈ 11.5 m. Slope etiquette is physics too The skier below has priority: they can't see you. Give them room. Stop where you're visible from above, and look uphill before setting off.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Falls, collisions & avalanches
chunks.text: Ski in control, at a speed where you could stop or avoid someone. Avalanches (read carefully — this is not training) Snow builds up in layers. When a weak layer fails under a stiffer slab, the slab can release and slide. Most slab avalanches start on slopes of roughly 30°–45° , often triggered by the victim or their group. Look back at Chapter 1: those are also the angles where gravity already accelerates a 75 kg skier hard on groomers — the same steepness that feels "fun" in a resort can be the danger band off-piste. Gulmarg's high terrain above the gondola is serious avalanche country. Teaching link · slope angle (not a forecast) Approx.

chunks.heading: Falls, collisions & avalanches
chunks.text: slope On a marked run (Ch 1) Off-piste context (general) < ~25° Gentler; easier to keep speed down Slab risk lower but not zero ~30°–45° Steep; speed builds fast if you don't turn Where most fatal slab avalanches release > ~45° Very steep / expert Slabs less common; other hazards dominate Angle alone does not make a slope safe or unsafe. Snowpack, weather, aspect and recent loading matter. We give no local bulletin and no route advice. Safety Off-piste needs training, kit and a guide Never leave marked, controlled slopes without avalanche training, a transceiver, probe and shovel (and the skills to use them), a current avalanche forecast and a qualified local guide.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cold, altitude & sun
chunks.text: India's ski slopes are high. The air is thin, the sun is fierce and the cold is real. Indian ski areas sit high: Auli at around 2,800 m (Uttarakhand Tourism), and Gulmarg from about 2,650 m to 3,980 m at the gondola top (IISM). The International Standard Atmosphere gives the drop in air pressure, and with it the oxygen in every breath. Worked example · air pressure and oxygen vs sea level (standard atmosphere) Place Altitude Pressure vs sea level Oxygen per breath Gulmarg resort ≈ 2,650 m ≈ 72% ≈ 28% less Auli ≈ 2,800 m ≈ 71% ≈ 29% less Gulmarg gondola top ≈ 3,980 m ≈ 61% ≈ 39% less ISA pressure ratio = (1 − 2.256 × 10⁻⁵ × h)^5.256. At 3,980 m: ≈ 0.61.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Cold, altitude & sun
chunks.text: Oxygen stays 20.95% of the air, so its partial pressure falls in proportion. Staying well Altitude: take it easy on day one, drink water, and descend if headache, nausea or breathlessness get worse. Cold: IISM notes Gulmarg can drop to −8 °C in winter. Layers, gloves, a hat under the helmet; watch fingers, toes and faces for frostbite. Sun: fresh snow reflects most sunlight and thin air filters less UV. Goggles or dark glasses prevent snow blindness; sunscreen on face and lips. ✋ Feel the number At Gulmarg's top station, every breath holds about the oxygen of 0.6 of a sea-level breath. That's why climbing back up in ski boots leaves you gasping.

chunks.heading: Race abroad: Vasaloppet
chunks.text: The race Vasaloppet is a 90 km cross-country ski race from Berga by in Sälen to Mora in Dalarna, Sweden, held since 1922. The 103rd Vasaloppet is on Sunday 7 March 2027, with a joint start at 08:00. It is skied in classic technique only, and skating can lead to disqualification. You can enter from the year you turn 17. The winter week The organiser's winter week for 2027 runs from 26 Feb to 7 Mar, with shorter races, night races and a youth race around the main event. Öppet Spår Sunday (28 Feb 2027) is the same 90 km classic course as a leisure event where you ski only against yourself, and the organiser also calls it a seeding event for Vasaloppet.

chunks.title: Skiing & Snowboarding · Physics of Slopes, Edges & Snow · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Race abroad: Vasaloppet
chunks.text: The Öppet Spår races on Monday 1 Mar are skied in free technique. Who it suits General guidance, not a source: skiers who already ski classic technique and can keep moving for most of a day. The organiser gives about 12 hours to finish, and there are seven checkpoints with cut-off times; if you reach one too late you stop and are bussed to Mora. Rescue and medical staff can remove participants from the course, and the organiser says your safety comes before finishing. For the day, it suggests carrying a phone, extra socks, an extra hat, snacks and a headlamp if you may still be out after 17:00. For why cold matters, see Ch 6 .

chunks.text: Skydiving is a balance of forces: gravity against drag in free fall, then lift and drag under a canopy that flies like a wing. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Freefall Lab, then find dropzones in India and abroad, from a first tandem to a licence. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Tandem D licence ≈ 193 km/h Your falling speed, reached about 10 s after you exit. About 54 m every second, held steady by the air. ≈ 2.65 g Average harness load during a normal 3-second canopy opening. Real openings peak a little higher. ≈ 58 km/h Landing speed downwind, vs about 28 km/h into the wind. That's why canopies always land into the wind.
