chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick an exit altitude, an opening altitude, your body position, your mass with gear and the wind, then see your terminal velocity, your freefall time and how far the wind carries you under the canopy
chunks.text: A simple model: drag = ½ ρ CdA v², with air density fixed at 1.1 kg/m³; belly-to-earth CdA 0.56 m² and head-down 0.31 m² (chosen so a 90 kg jumper falls at about 120 and 160 mph, the speeds in USPA's freefall table). Freefall from rest with that drag; canopy descent 5 m/s; air pressure from the standard atmosphere. Learning values only (illustrative).

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick an exit altitude, an opening altitude, your body position, your mass with gear and the wind, then see your terminal velocity, your freefall time and how far the wind carries you under the canopy
chunks.text: Exit altitude 10,000 ft 13,000 ft 15,000 ft Opening altitude 5,000 ft Body position Belly-to-earth Head-down Mass with gear 90 kg Wind under canopy 20 km/h Terminal velocity 193 km/h Ch 1 · drag = weight Time to reach 95% of it 10.0 s Ch 1 · the acceleration phase Freefall time to opening 32 s Ch 1 · including the speed-up Air pressure at exit 68.8% Ch 5 · of sea level Time under canopy 5.1 min Ch 4 · at 5 m/s down Wind drift under canopy 1.69 km Ch 6 · why spotting matters Bar = freefall time out of 75 s. Try head-down from 15,000 ft, then a stronger wind. Your first jumps are tandem or with instructors (Ch 6). CH 1

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall & terminal velocity
chunks.text: You speed up for about ten seconds. Then the air holds you at a steady speed. Leaving the aircraft, gravity accelerates you at 9.81 m/s². As you speed up, air drag ½ ρ CdA v² grows until it equals your weight. Then you stop accelerating: that's terminal velocity , v t = √(2 m g ÷ (ρ CdA)) . CdA is your drag area: spread out belly-down it's big, head-down it's small. Worked example · 90 kg with gear, ρ 1.1 kg/m³ (from our Freefall Lab, illustrative) Position CdA Terminal velocity 95% reached after Belly-to-earth 0.56 m² ≈ 193 km/h (≈ 120 mph) ≈ 10 s, 341 m Head-down 0.31 m² ≈ 257 km/h (≈ 160 mph) ≈ 13 s, 606 m v t = √(2 × 90 × 9.81 ÷ (1.1 × 0.56)) ≈ 53.6 m/s.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall & terminal velocity
chunks.text: Real terminal velocity changes with air density, so jumpers fall a little faster high up. Thinner air, faster fall Because v t ∝ 1 ÷ √ρ , a drop in density raises terminal speed. At about 10,000 ft the standard atmosphere is only ~69% of sea-level pressure (Ch 5); density is lower by a similar fraction, so the same belly position runs a little faster than our sea-level-ish lab value until you get lower. Order of magnitude · same 90 kg belly jumper if density were 0.9× the lab value Relative density ρ / ρ lab Terminal velocity Compared with lab 193 km/h 1.00 (lab) ≈ 193 km/h baseline 0.90 ≈ 203 km/h ≈ +5% 0.75 (roughly high-exit air) ≈ 223 km/h ≈ +15% √(1/0.90) ≈ 1.054; √(1/0.75) ≈ 1.155.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall & terminal velocity
chunks.text: USPA's freefall-time table is still the practical planning tool; density is one reason real times vary. How long is the freefall? USPA's Skydiver's Information Manual gives freefall times at constant speed: at 120 mph, 10,000 ft takes about 57 s and 5,000 ft about 28 s; at 160 mph, 10,000 ft takes about 43 s. It notes that many factors affect terminal velocity. Our lab includes the speed-up after exit, so it gives a little longer: about 32 s from 10,000 ft to an opening at 5,000 ft. 🪂 Feel the number At 193 km/h you drop about 54 m every second: the height of a 15-storey building, each second. At a steady 120 mph (53.6 m/s), how long to fall 1,000 m? 1,000 ÷ 53.6 ≈ 19 s .

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Free fall & terminal velocity

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Body position & fall rate
chunks.text: Your body is the control surface. Arch, and the air does the rest. A stable belly-to-earth arch (hips forward, arms and legs out) puts your centre of mass below your centre of drag, like a shuttlecock, so you settle face-down. Moving arms and legs changes how the air pushes on you: you can turn, move forward and change fall rate. Because v t ∝ √m , heavier jumpers fall faster in the same position, so groups match fall rates with jumpsuits and body position.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Body position & fall rate
chunks.text: Worked example · same belly position (CdA 0.56 m², illustrative) Mass with gear Belly terminal velocity Head-down terminal velocity 70 kg ≈ 170 km/h ≈ 227 km/h 90 kg ≈ 193 km/h ≈ 257 km/h 110 kg ≈ 213 km/h ≈ 285 km/h 193 × √(110 ÷ 90) ≈ 213 km/h. To match a 70 kg friend, the 110 kg jumper needs about 1.57 times the drag area, or the light jumper less. Tracking: falling forward on purpose After a formation breaks off, jumpers track : arms swept back, legs extended, body slightly de-arched so the air pushes you forward as well as up. You trade some vertical drag for horizontal speed, opening horizontal separation before deployment.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Body position & fall rate
chunks.text: The physics is the same drag equation with a tilted body: the relative wind is no longer straight up your chest. USPA's A-licence practical exam asks for a track of at least 100 ft after breakoff — distance that comes from that horizontal component of drag. A jumper's mass doubles. What happens to terminal velocity in the same position? It rises by √2, about 41% . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Deployment & opening forces
chunks.text: From 193 km/h to a gentle glide in a few seconds. At opening altitude you throw a small pilot chute , which pulls out the bag holding the main canopy; the lines stretch, then the canopy inflates. A fabric slider on the lines slows the inflation so the opening is a few seconds long rather than a snap. Spreading the deceleration over time lowers the force: F = m (Δv ÷ Δt + g) . Worked example · 90 kg, from 53.6 m/s to 5 m/s (illustrative) Opening time Average deceleration Average harness load 1 s (too fast) ≈ 5.0 g ≈ 6.0 g (≈ 5.3 kN) 3 s ≈ 1.65 g ≈ 2.65 g (≈ 2.3 kN) 5 s ≈ 1.0 g ≈ 2.0 g (≈ 1.8 kN) (53.6 − 5) ÷ 3 ≈ 16.2 m/s² ≈ 1.65 g; plus 1 g to hold you up against gravity.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Deployment & opening forces
chunks.text: Real openings peak above the average. Where the kinetic energy goes At 53.6 m/s a 90 kg jumper carries about ½ m v² ≈ 129 kJ — roughly the energy of dropping that mass 146 m. The opening does not destroy that energy instantly; the slider and the stretching canopy dump it into heating and moving air over a few seconds. Halving the opening time roughly doubles the average force (same Δv, half Δt), which is why a snivelling, staged inflation is kinder than a hard snatch. Two canopies and a backup Sport rigs carry a main and a reserve canopy. An automatic activation device (AAD) fires the reserve if you're still falling fast at a set low altitude.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Deployment & opening forces
chunks.text: Skyhigh India, for example, describes its tandem system as having a main, a reserve and an AAD. If the opening took 2 s instead of 3 s, what's the average deceleration? (53.6 − 5) ÷ 2 ≈ 24.3 m/s² ≈ 2.5 g (3.5 g harness load). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Canopy flight: glide & flare
chunks.text: A modern canopy is a wing. You land it like a plane: into the wind, then flare. A ram-air canopy flies forward and down: its glide ratio is forward speed ÷ sink rate. Steering toggles pull down the trailing edge on one side to turn. Just before landing you flare : pulling both toggles down swaps forward speed for a moment of extra lift, slowing both your descent and your forward speed so you touch down gently. Landing into the wind cuts your groundspeed.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Canopy flight: glide & flare
chunks.text: Worked example · canopy at 12 m/s forward, 5 m/s down (illustrative student canopy) Item Number How Glide ratio (still air) 2.4 : 1 12 ÷ 5 Airspeed ≈ 43 km/h 12 × 3.6 Groundspeed landing into 15 km/h ≈ 28 km/h 43 − 15 Groundspeed landing downwind ≈ 58 km/h 43 + 15 Wing loading, 90 kg on 21 m² (≈ 226 ft²) ≈ 4.3 kg/m² heavier loading = faster canopy Kinetic energy rises with speed squared: landing downwind at 58 km/h carries (58 ÷ 28)² ≈ 4.3 times the energy of landing into wind. What the flare is doing In steady glide, lift ≈ weight and you sink at a few metres per second.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Canopy flight: glide & flare
chunks.text: A flare raises the wing's angle of attack: lift briefly exceeds weight, sink rate falls toward zero, and forward speed bleeds off as induced drag rises. Start too high and you float then sink hard; start too low and you still have forward speed at touchdown. Heavier wing loading (same canopy, more mass — or a smaller canopy) raises trim speed the same way a PPG wing does ( paramotoring Ch 2 ): landings become less forgiving, which is why student canopies are large and lightly loaded.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Canopy flight: glide & flare
chunks.text: USPA's B licence needs a completed canopy proficiency card (including accuracy landings within 10 m / 33 ft on 10 jumps), and its C licence asks for 25 landings within 2 m of a target: canopy skill is trained, not assumed. A canopy flies 10 m/s forward and sinks 4 m/s. What glide ratio? 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 : 1 . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Altitude, air & oxygen
chunks.text: At 10,000 ft every breath holds less oxygen. Air pressure falls with height. Oxygen is still about 21% of the air, but each breath carries less of it, because the partial pressure of oxygen, which drives it into your blood, falls with total pressure. Thinner air also means less drag, so you fall slightly faster high up. And it's colder: in the standard atmosphere, temperature falls about 6.5 °C per kilometre.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Altitude, air & oxygen
chunks.text: Worked example · standard atmosphere (from our Freefall Lab) Altitude Pressure Share of sea level Oxygen partial pressure Sea level 101.3 kPa 100% 21.2 kPa 5,000 ft 84.3 kPa 83.2% 17.7 kPa 10,000 ft 69.7 kPa 68.8% 14.6 kPa 13,000 ft 61.9 kPa 61.1% 13.0 kPa 15,000 ft 57.2 kPa 56.4% 12.0 kPa p = 101.325 × (1 − 2.256 × 10⁻⁵ h) 5.256 kPa, h in metres; O₂ partial pressure ≈ 0.2095 × p. At 10,000 ft (3,048 m) it's about 20 °C colder than at sea level. Rules on extra oxygen for high jumps vary between countries and dropzones; ask yours. Tandem jumps at Skyhigh India are from 10,000 ft, the company says. At 13,000 ft, what share of sea-level pressure is there? About 61% .

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind drift, spotting & the rules
chunks.text: Jump from the right place in the sky, or the wind lands you somewhere else. Under canopy you drift with the wind for several minutes, so the aircraft drops jumpers upwind of the landing area. Choosing that exit point is called spotting . Winds aloft are often stronger and in a different direction from those on the ground, which is why dropzones check them before every load. Worked example · opening at 5,000 ft (1,524 m), descending at 5 m/s (from our Freefall Lab) Wind Time under canopy Drift with the wind 10 km/h ≈ 5.1 min ≈ 0.85 km 20 km/h ≈ 5.1 min ≈ 1.69 km 30 km/h ≈ 5.1 min ≈ 2.54 km 1,524 ÷ 5 ≈ 305 s ≈ 5.1 min; 20 km/h × 5.1 ÷ 60 h ≈ 1.69 km.

chunks.title: Skydiving · Physics of Free Fall, Terminal Velocity & Canopy Flight · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind drift, spotting & the rules
chunks.text: Steering towards the landing area cancels some of this; spotting does the rest. Safety The rules in India NASG 2023 superseded the 2022 air-sports policy (Lok Sabha AU1311, July 2026). Press reports of a separate Civil Aviation Lok Sabha reply (August 2026) describe ASFI under NASG and name six authorised air-sports operators, three with aerial-work authorisation for aircraft used in skydiving: Global Konnect Aviation Services, Go Forth Adventures and Macsen Aviation. We have not re-fetched the original sansad.in annex for that Civil Aviation answer, so treat the operator list as as reported .

chunks.heading: Wind drift, spotting & the rules
chunks.text: Dropzones also publish their own approvals (USPA affiliation, DGCA certification and so on) — those are school claims unless we link an official directory. Confirm a dropzone's current authorisation before you book, and jump only under qualified instructors. Opening at 4,000 ft (1,219 m) at 5 m/s in a 24 km/h wind: about how far do you drift? 1,219 ÷ 5 ≈ 244 s ≈ 0.068 h; × 24 ≈ 1.6 km . ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The skydiving ladder

chunks.text: Wind speed 20 km/h Kite area 9 m² Altitude 2,000 m Air temperature −10 °C Air pressure 79.6 kPa Ch 2 · NASA model Air density 1.05 kg/m³ Ch 2 · p ÷ (R × T) Wind pressure 16.3 Pa Ch 1 · ½ρv² Wind force scale on the kite 146 N ≈ 15 kg · ½ρv² × area vs sea level at 15 °C 86% Ch 2 · same wind, same kite In a gust 50% stronger 329 N Ch 1 · 1.5² = 2.25 × Kite flying across the wind at 2 × wind speed 5 × Ch 3 · apparent wind Wind chill −18 °C Ch 6 · NWS formula Bar = air density compared with sea level at 15 °C. "Wind force scale" is ½ρv² × kite area: real line pull is some multiple of it that depends on the kite's design and where it flies in the wind window.

chunks.heading: Change the wind, the kite, the altitude and the cold
chunks.text: Wind chill uses the wind speed you set; riding into the wind raises the air speed on your face. CH 1

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind pressure grows with speed squared
chunks.text: Double the wind and the kite pulls about four times as hard. Moving air pushes on a kite with a pressure of q = ½ ρ v² , where ρ is air density and v is wind speed. The force on the kite is that pressure times its area times a coefficient that depends on the kite's shape and how it's flown. Because v is squared, small changes in wind make big changes in pull: a gust 50% stronger pulls 1.5² = 2.25 times as hard.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind pressure grows with speed squared
chunks.text: Worked example · a 9 m² kite at sea level, 15 °C (ρ ≈ 1.23 kg/m³) Wind Wind pressure ½ρv² ½ρv² × 9 m² vs 10 km/h 10 km/h 4.7 Pa ≈ 43 N (≈ 4 kg) 1 × 20 km/h 18.9 Pa ≈ 170 N (≈ 17 kg) 4 × 30 km/h 42.6 Pa ≈ 383 N (≈ 39 kg) 9 × 40 km/h 75.7 Pa ≈ 681 N (≈ 69 kg) 16 × 20 km/h = 5.56 m/s; ½ × 1.227 × 5.56² ≈ 18.9 Pa; × 9 m² ≈ 170 N. This is a force scale, not a measured line pull ( Ch 3 ). What it means on the snow Gusts: pull rises with the square of the gust, so gusty days are much harder than the average wind suggests. Kite size: pull scales with area, which is why riders choose smaller kites for stronger wind.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind pressure grows with speed squared
chunks.text: Learn in light, steady wind: schools pick conditions where beginners can control the kite. The wind rises from 15 to 30 km/h. How much more does the kite pull? (30 ÷ 15)² = 4 times . Physics: dynamic pressure q = ½ρv². ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Altitude thins the air, cold thickens it
chunks.text: At 2,000 m the air is about a fifth thinner than at the coast, so the same wind pulls less. Air density is ρ = p ÷ (R × T) : it falls as pressure drops with altitude and rises as the air gets colder. NASA's Earth Atmosphere Model gives pressure in the lower atmosphere as p = 101.29 × [(T + 273.1) ÷ 288.08]^5.256 kPa, with standard temperature T = 15.04 − 0.00649 × h °C at altitude h metres, and density = p ÷ (0.2869 × (T + 273.1)).

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Altitude thins the air, cold thickens it
chunks.text: Worked example · NASA standard atmosphere Altitude Standard temperature Pressure Density vs sea level 0 m 15.0 °C 101.4 kPa 1.23 kg/m³ 100% 1,000 m 8.6 °C 90.0 kPa 1.11 kg/m³ 91% 2,000 m 2.1 °C 79.6 kPa 1.01 kg/m³ 82% 3,000 m −4.4 °C 70.2 kPa 0.91 kg/m³ 74% Cold helps: at 2,000 m but −10 °C instead of the standard 2.1 °C, density is 79.6 ÷ (0.2869 × 263.1) ≈ 1.05 kg/m³, about 86% of sea level at 15 °C. What it means on the snow Mountain spots: the same kite in the same wind pulls less high up, so riders may need a bigger kite or more wind. Cold days: colder, denser air pulls a little harder for the same wind.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Altitude thins the air, cold thickens it
chunks.text: Real example: Haugastøl, a snowkite base on Norway's Hardangervidda plateau, sits at 1,000 m above sea level. Same wind and kite: about how much less pull at 3,000 m (standard atmosphere) than at sea level? 0.91 ÷ 1.23 ≈ 0.74, so about a quarter less . Sources: NASA Glenn: Earth Atmosphere Model · Haugastøl 1000 MOH ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The wind window & apparent wind
chunks.text: A kite moving across the wind feels far more wind than you do. A kite feels the apparent wind : the true wind combined with the air rushing past because the kite itself is moving. If the kite flies across the wind at speed u, the apparent wind is about √(v² + u²) . In the middle of the wind window (the power zone , downwind of the rider) a moving kite gets a lot of apparent wind and pulls hard; at the edge of the window it slows and parks, and the pull drops. Worked example · true wind 20 km/h Kite's own speed across the wind Apparent wind Wind pressure vs a parked kite 0 (parked) 20 km/h 1 × 20 km/h ≈ 28 km/h 2 × 40 km/h ≈ 45 km/h 5 × √(20² + 40²) ≈ 44.7 km/h; (44.7 ÷ 20)² = 5.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The wind window & apparent wind
chunks.text: That's why diving a kite through the power zone can pull you off your feet. Using the window Edge of the window: the place to park the kite when you stop, launch or land. Power zone: where to avoid sending the kite by mistake. Steering: moving the kite up and down through the window controls how much it pulls. True wind 30 km/h and the kite flies across it at 30 km/h. Roughly how much more wind pressure does it feel than when parked? √(30² + 30²) ≈ 42.4 km/h; (42.4 ÷ 30)² = 2 times . Physics: vector addition of velocities, dynamic pressure. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Depower, quick release & the 5th line
chunks.text: Every kite rig has ways to cut the pull fast, and the rules make you carry them. A kite's pull depends on its angle of attack , the angle at which air meets it. Pushing the bar away tilts the kite so air meets it at a smaller angle, which cuts the force: that's depower . A quick release lets go of the bar from the harness, and a safety leash lets the kite fall onto one line so it "flags out", flapping like a flag with almost no pull.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Depower, quick release & the 5th line
chunks.text: What official sources require or describe Source What it says IKA Snowkite Class Rules A detachable kite leash with a safety release, able to fully flag out the kite; a quick release that disconnects the bar from the harness with one hand movement; front lines with a depowering device IKA Snowkite Class Rules A brightly coloured helmet to EN 1385 or EN 1077 (or equivalent) worn at all times when racing Swiss Kitesurf (school) Bars with a double quick release that can be triggered with a 3.5 kg tug; most winter kites have a 5th line so the kite can be landed and kept on the ground without force A 3.5 kg tug is about 34 N (3.5 × 9.81), far less than the pull of the kite in Ch 1 .

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Depower, quick release & the 5th line
chunks.text: Practise before you need it Know your release: schools drill triggering it until it's automatic. Helmet: Swiss Kitesurf gives every student a harness and helmet; Haugastøl asks students to bring a helmet. Space downwind: keep clear of people, fences and slopes where the kite could drag you. Safety Know your quick release before you launch A tug of about 3.5 kg fires the quick release, far less than the kite’s pull. Schools drill it until it’s automatic. Keep space downwind, clear of people, fences and slopes where the kite could drag you. What does a kite do when it "flags out"? It hangs from one line and flaps like a flag , giving almost no pull.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Slopes & avalanches
chunks.text: A kite can pull you up a slope that's steep enough to slide. Switzerland's avalanche institute SLF says a slab avalanche needs a bonded snow slab over a weak layer, an extra load to trigger it, and a slope of at least 30° . Its long-term figures for fatal avalanches triggered by skiers: 97% happened on slopes steeper than 30°, 82% steeper than 35° and 43% steeper than 40°. Worked example · what 30°, 35° and 40° look like as a gradient Slope angle Rise per 100 m across (tan θ) SLF: share of fatal skier-triggered avalanches on steeper slopes 30° ≈ 58 m 97% 35° ≈ 70 m 82% 40° ≈ 84 m 43% tan 30° ≈ 0.577, so a 30° slope climbs about 58 m for every 100 m you travel across the map.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Slopes & avalanches
chunks.text: Slopes look less steep than they are, so riders measure them. What it means for snowkiters Flat and gentle terrain: frozen lakes and open plateaus are where most people learn. Read the bulletin: in the mountains, check the official avalanche bulletin before riding near slopes. Weather changes: Haugastøl warns that weather and visibility on Hardangervidda can change fast. A slope rises 50 m for every 100 m across. Is it steeper than 30°? tan θ = 0.5, so θ ≈ 26.6°: no , just under 30°. SLF's figures still put 3% of fatal skier-triggered avalanches below 30°. Sources: SLF: avalanche types · SLF: avalanche bulletin interpretation guide (PDF) · Haugastøl ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind chill
chunks.text: The wind that powers your kite also pulls heat from your skin. Moving air carries heat away from skin faster than still air, so exposed skin cools as if the air were colder. The US National Weather Service calculates wind chill as 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75V 0.16 + 0.4275TV 0.16 , with T in °F and V in mph. The metric form is 13.12 + 0.6215T − 11.37V 0.16 + 0.3965TV 0.16 with T in °C and V in km/h. Worked example · NWS wind chill (°C) Air temperature 10 km/h 20 km/h 30 km/h 40 km/h −5 °C −9 −12 −13 −14 −10 °C −15 −18 −20 −21 −20 °C −27 −30 −33 −34 −10 °C at 20 km/h: 20 0.16 ≈ 1.615; 13.12 − 6.22 − 18.36 − 6.40 ≈ −17.9 °C. Riding into the wind adds your own speed to the air on your face.

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wind chill
chunks.text: Staying warm Cover skin: wind chill applies to exposed skin, so face, hands and neck matter most. Warm clothes: Haugastøl asks students to bring warm winter clothes along with a helmet and skis or a snowboard. Plan the walk back: if the wind drops, you'll be walking in the cold. Using the table, what does −20 °C feel like on exposed skin in a 30 km/h wind? About −33 °C . Source: US National Weather Service: wind chill formula (PDF) ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The snowkite path

chunks.title: Snowkiting · Physics of Wind, Altitude & Cold · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Skier or snowboarder → snowkite course → riding on your own → racing
chunks.text: There's no world snowkite licence. Riders build on skiing or snowboarding, take lessons at a kite school, then ride on their own. These are real courses and rules we found, each checked on its own official website; the steps are a typical order, not official grades. Step 1 · Skier or snowboarder Comfortable on skis or a board Bring your own What schools ask Swiss Kitesurf, Haugastøl Both ask students to bring their own skis or snowboard and warm clothes Start here Kinetic pages skiing & snowboarding · kitesurfing Kinetic tip Not an official grade Being steady on your skis or board lets you put all your attention on the kite.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Riding a wave is applied physics.
chunks.text: Every wave you catch is energy that crossed an ocean. Learn how swell forms and refracts, why beach, reef and point breaks differ, how board volume, trim and rails work, and how to handle wipeouts and rips — then find a school on India's coast, from Puri to Covelong, at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science Whitewater Line-up 2.4 m/s A rip can pull you out faster than an Olympic swimmer. Swim sideways, not straight in. 4× The energy in a wave twice as tall. A day that's “just a bit bigger” hits much harder. ≈ 1.3 m How deep the water is where a 1 m wave breaks. Waves break in shallow water. Cover your head when dumped.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Riding a wave is applied physics.
chunks.text: ≈ 82 kg How much a big learner board can hold up in the sea. Leash on: a loose board in whitewater hits hard.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Swim confidently first. A wipeout can hold you under longer than it feels. The tide changes the spot. Friendly at high tide can mean shallow and dangerous at low; ask what's underneath. Ask who's teaching. SFI's guidelines say non-certified instructors should never teach beginners on their own. Ask before you book a first lesson → 01 · The challenge

chunks.heading: Would you know what to do in a rip?
chunks.text: 15 questions on swell, breaking waves, board buoyancy, catching and riding, rip currents and wave energy: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
chunks.text: Each chapter explains one idea in plain language, then works a real example. Try the Wave Lab to follow a swell from a distant storm to the moment it breaks over sand, reef or a point. Interactive · Wave Lab

chunks.heading: Dial in a swell and follow it from a distant storm to the sandbar
chunks.text: Uses textbook linear wave theory: deep-water wavelength and speed from the period, energy travelling at half the crest speed, a rule-of-thumb breaking depth of height ÷ 0.78, and wave power per metre of crest. Real surf depends on the seabed, wind and tide. For learning only; it is not a surf forecast or a safety guide.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Dial in a swell and follow it from a distant storm to the sandbar
chunks.text: Before you paddle out, ask the local school or lifeguards, not this lab. CH 1

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swell: formation & refraction
chunks.text: The wave you ride may have started as a storm days ago and a thousand kilometres away. Wind blowing over the sea transfers energy through friction and pressure on the water surface. Close to the storm you get short, choppy wind swell . Farther away, waves sort themselves by speed into regular groundswell , described by its period T (seconds between crests) and height. Water itself barely travels: it moves in orbital circles as the wave's energy passes through. In deep water (deeper than about half a wavelength), linear wave theory gives L = g T² ÷ 2π ≈ 1.56 T² metres and crest speed c = g T ÷ 2π ≈ 1.56 T m/s. The energy moves at the group speed , half of c.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swell: formation & refraction
chunks.text: Worked example · deep-water swell by period Period Wavelength Crest speed Energy speed Time to travel 1,000 km 6 s (wind swell) ≈ 56 m 9.4 m/s 16.9 km/h ≈ 59 h 8 s ≈ 100 m 12.5 m/s 22.5 km/h ≈ 44 h 12 s (groundswell) ≈ 225 m 18.7 m/s 33.7 km/h ≈ 30 h 16 s ≈ 400 m 25.0 m/s 45.0 km/h ≈ 22 h T = 8 s: L = 9.81 × 64 ÷ 6.283 ≈ 99.9 m; c = 9.81 × 8 ÷ 6.283 ≈ 12.5 m/s; group speed ≈ 6.25 m/s; 1,000,000 m ÷ 6.25 m/s ≈ 160,000 s ≈ 44.5 h. Refraction: why waves bend toward shallow water In shallow water the crest speed falls to about c ≈ √(g d) .

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swell: formation & refraction
chunks.text: The part of a wave front that reaches shallower water first slows down, so the whole front bends (refracts) toward the shallows — the same idea as Snell's law for light. That is why waves wrap around headlands and focus energy onto reefs and points, and why a bay can be calmer than the open coast next to it. Worked example · shallow vs deep crest speed (same period) Water depth Approx. crest speed √(g d) Compared with deep-water 8 s crest (12.5 m/s) 10 m ≈ 9.9 m/s Already slower → front starts to bend 4 m ≈ 6.3 m/s About half the deep-water speed 1.3 m (near a 1 m break) ≈ 3.5 m/s Much slower: energy piles into a taller wave √(9.81 × 4) ≈ 6.3 m/s.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swell: formation & refraction
chunks.text: Refraction is why a point break can peel for a long ride while the same swell dumps on a straight beach nearby. Reading a forecast Period matters as much as height: a 1 m, 12 s swell breaks with far more push than a 1 m, 6 s wind chop. Long-period swell arrives first: because longer waves travel faster, the first sign of a distant storm is a long-period "forerunner". Wind direction: light offshore wind (blowing from land to sea) grooms wave faces; onshore wind makes them crumbly and messy. Swell angle vs coast: if the swell is running nearly parallel to the beach, refraction may still bend some energy in — but expect weaker, more inconsistent surf.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swell: formation & refraction
chunks.text: ✋ Feel the number Count the seconds between waves at the beach: that's the period. Multiply it by itself and by 1.56, and you have roughly how far apart the crests were out at sea. A 10-second swell: how long are the waves in deep water, and how fast does the energy travel? L ≈ 1.56 × 100 = 156 m . Crest speed ≈ 15.6 m/s, so the energy travels at about 7.8 m/s (28 km/h) . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breaks, shoaling & tide
chunks.text: A wave breaks when the sea floor trips it up — and the shape of that floor decides the ride. Once the depth is less than about a twentieth of the wavelength, the wave "feels" the bottom and its speed becomes c ≈ √(g d) , where d is the depth. As it slows, the same energy is squeezed into a shorter, taller wave: shoaling . When the wave gets too tall for the depth, the crest outruns the base and spills or pitches forward. A widely used rule of thumb says this happens when the height is about H ≈ 0.78 d (a McCowan-type estimate; real beaches vary).

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breaks, shoaling & tide
chunks.text: Worked example · where waves break (rule of thumb H ≈ 0.78 d) Wave height Breaking depth ≈ H ÷ 0.78 Wave speed there ≈ √(g d) 0.5 m ≈ 0.64 m ≈ 2.5 m/s 1.0 m ≈ 1.28 m ≈ 3.5 m/s 1.5 m ≈ 1.92 m ≈ 4.3 m/s 2.0 m ≈ 2.56 m ≈ 5.0 m/s 1 m wave: d = 1 ÷ 0.78 ≈ 1.28 m; √(9.81 × 1.28) ≈ 3.5 m/s. Real breaking depth varies with beach slope and wave steepness; treat 0.78 as a classroom approximation. Beach, reef and point breaks Beach breaks break over sandbars that shift with seasons and storms. Gentle slopes make soft, spilling waves (foam slides down the face): ideal for learning.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breaks, shoaling & tide
chunks.text: Most Indian surf schools teach on beach breaks — Puri–Konark, Rushikonda, Mulki and Gokarna Main Beach are examples of this kind of setup. Reef breaks break over rock or coral in nearly the same place each time. They can be more powerful and hollow, and the bottom is hard and shallow. Point breaks peel along a headland or jetty as the wave refracts around it, often giving a long one-direction ride. Covelong (Kovalam, Tamil Nadu) has a point a short paddle from the beginner cove that Bay of Life describes as a nursery for beginners. Plunging (pitching) waves form on steeper bottoms: the crest curls and dumps.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breaks, shoaling & tide
chunks.text: That shallow impact zone is why you fall flat, never dive head-first, and protect your head as you surface. Tide and wind Tide changes depth: a spot that is friendly at mid or high tide can go shallow and close-out at low tide (or the reverse on some reefs). Ask how the local break changes through the tide cycle. Offshore wind holds the face up and makes it cleaner; onshore wind chops the surface and makes waves crumble early. Monsoon on the west coast brings big, messy seas — fine for experienced surfers in the right spots, not for first lessons (and Goa's water-sports policy bars surfboard sports in the monsoon).

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Breaks, shoaling & tide
chunks.text: Safety Know the bottom before you paddle out Ask your instructor what's under the waves: sand, rock or reef, and how the tide changes it. A spot that's friendly at high tide can be shallow and dangerous at low tide. Waves are breaking in water about 2 m deep. Roughly how big are they? H ≈ 0.78 × 2 ≈ 1.6 m , about head-high on many adults. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & board volume
chunks.text: Every litre of board holds up about a kilogram. Beginners need lots of litres. Archimedes' principle: anything in water is pushed up by a buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. In symbols, F b = ρ V g , where ρ is the density of seawater (about 1,025 kg/m³, or 1.025 kg per litre), V is the submerged volume and g ≈ 9.81 m/s². So each litre of board volume can support about 1 kg when pushed fully under. A board that floats you high paddles faster and wobbles less; a tiny performance board sits low and duck-dives easily.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & board volume
chunks.text: Worked example · maximum buoyant support in seawater Board Volume Weight of displaced seawater if fully submerged Performance shortboard ≈ 30 L ≈ 31 kg Fun board / mini-mal ≈ 50 L ≈ 51 kg Big foam learner board ≈ 80 L ≈ 82 kg 80 L × 1.025 kg/L ≈ 82 kg. A 70 kg surfer's body also floats a little in seawater, so the board doesn't carry their whole weight, but the more volume to spare (freeboard), the higher and steadier it sits. The board volumes here are typical examples, not a sizing guide; ask your school. Why learner boards look the way they do Length and width: a long, wide board is stable side-to-side and glides into small waves early.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & board volume
chunks.text: Soft-top: a foam deck and flexible fins hurt far less when you fall on the board or it hits you. Kallialay and Bay of Life, for example, put beginners on soft-tops. Wax and rash vests: wax gives grip on hard decks; a rash vest protects skin from the deck and the sun. Progression: as you improve, schools move you to less volume so you can duck-dive and turn harder — Om Surf School in Vizag describes that soft-board → hard longboard → shortboard path for progressing students. ✋ Feel the number A 1-litre water bottle full of air takes a surprising push to hold under in a pool: about 1 kg-force. Your learner board is like 80 of them.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & board volume
chunks.text: Roughly how much support could a 40 L board give if pushed fully under seawater? 40 × 1.025 ≈ 41 kg . That's why advanced surfers on small boards sit low in the water and duck-dive easily. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Planing, trim & rails
chunks.text: Surfing is falling down a hill that keeps moving towards the beach — then steering with the edge of your board. To catch a wave you need to be moving towards the beach as it lifts the back of your board. Once you're on the sloping face, gravity pulls you down the slope while the wave keeps rebuilding it underneath you. At enough speed the board stops ploughing through water and starts to plane : most of its weight is supported by dynamic pressure on the wetted underside, like a speedboat. Drag drops and you accelerate.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Planing, trim & rails
chunks.text: Worked example · speed from dropping down the face (no friction) Drop down the face v = √(2 g h) In km/h 0.5 m 3.1 m/s ≈ 11 km/h 1.0 m 4.4 m/s ≈ 16 km/h 1.5 m 5.4 m/s ≈ 20 km/h 1.5 m: √(2 × 9.81 × 1.5) ≈ 5.42 m/s × 3.6 ≈ 19.5 km/h. Friction and drag reduce this, but the wave keeps feeding you energy as long as you stay on the steep part of the face. Trim: where you stand on the board Paddle trim: too far back and the nose lifts and drags; too far forward and the nose digs in ("pearling"). Find the spot where the board lies flat on the water. Ride trim: weight forward engages the front of the board and builds speed down the line; weight back releases the nose for turns and stalls.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Planing, trim & rails
chunks.text: Small shifts of a few centimetres change how the board planes. Pop-up: hands under your chest, one smooth move to your feet, knees bent, weight centred. A low centre of mass is more stable. Rail engagement: how you turn The long edges of the board are its rails . Leaning puts the board on a rail so water pushes sideways on the submerged edge and fins; that sideways force curves your path, like a bicycle leaning into a bend. More rail in the water → tighter turn and more spray; flat on the belly → speed and stability. Beginners stay flat on soft foam; progressing surfers learn to roll onto a rail for bottom turns and cutbacks.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Planing, trim & rails
chunks.text: Whitewater first: broken waves (foam) push you towards the beach with no need to match a wave's speed. Most schools start you here. Fins: they resist sideways slip so the board tracks when you lean; without them a flat board skids. ✋ Feel the number A 1 m drop gives you about 16 km/h: a brisk cycling pace, on a board, on water. You drop 0.8 m down a face. Ignoring friction, what speed do you gain? √(2 × 9.81 × 0.8) ≈ 4.0 m/s (about 14 km/h). ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Rips, wipeouts & hold-downs
chunks.text: The calm-looking gap between breaking waves is often the most dangerous water on the beach — and a dumped wave can hold you under longer than it feels. Breaking waves carry water towards the shore. It has to return to sea, and it does so in narrow, fast channels: rip currents . They form in gaps between sandbars and along piers, groynes and rocks. The US National Weather Service says channel rips typically flow at about 1–2 feet per second (0.3–0.6 m/s) and can reach 8 feet per second (about 2.4 m/s), which NOAA notes is faster than an Olympic swimmer.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Rips, wipeouts & hold-downs
chunks.text: Worked example · why you swim sideways, not straight in Situation Your speed through the water Rip speed Result Swim straight at the beach 1.0 m/s 1.5 m/s You go backwards at 0.5 m/s and tire fast Swim parallel across a 30 m-wide rip 1.0 m/s 1.5 m/s Out of the rip in ≈ 30 s, carried ≈ 45 m seaward on the way Typical rip, standing at waist depth — 0.5 m/s Hard to stand against, according to the NWS Crossing time = 30 m ÷ 1.0 m/s = 30 s; seaward drift = 1.5 m/s × 30 s = 45 m. Once you're out of the channel, the breaking waves on either side help push you back in. Wipeouts and hold-downs When a wave dumps you, whitewater is a tumbling mix of water and air.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Rips, wipeouts & hold-downs
chunks.text: You are pushed around by turbulent flow, not held by a solid "hand". Hydrostatic pressure rises by about 10 kPa per metre of depth (≈ 1 atmosphere per 10 m), but learner hold-downs are usually shallow and short. The danger is panic and swimming the wrong way while you are still in the foam.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Rips, wipeouts & hold-downs
chunks.text: Worked example · a rough hold-down clock What happens Order of magnitude What to do Typical beginner dump in waist-to-chest whitewater A few seconds of tumbling Relax, cover your head, wait for the foam to pass, then surface Two waves in a set (period ~8–12 s) You may surface between them or take a second dunk One breath at the surface is enough if you stay calm Board on a leash yanking you Sudden tug toward the wave or beach Keep the leash; it is also your float once the set passes Illustrative only — not a dive table. Big reef hold-downs are a different sport and need coaching.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Rips, wipeouts & hold-downs
chunks.text: On a learner beach, the physics lesson is: don't fight the first seconds of foam; protect your head; breathe when you can see air. Spotting and escaping rips Look for: a darker, calmer-looking gap in the line of breaking waves, foam or sediment drifting seaward, or water flowing out along rocks and piers. If caught: don't fight it. Stay calm and float, keep hold of your board, signal for help, and paddle or swim parallel to the shore until you're free. Swimming matters: Kovalam Surf Club asks for basic swimming skills; Kallialay Surf School asks group-lesson students to swim at least 50 m confidently without touching the ground.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Rips, wipeouts & hold-downs
chunks.text: Safety Monsoon seas on the west coast During the monsoon, much of India's west coast gets big, rough, unpredictable surf with strong currents. Learn in the calmer months, follow local warnings and lifeguards, and never surf alone in conditions you don't know. Surf-Forecast also flags dangerous rips at Puri Beach on the Odisha coast — ask your school where the channels sit that day. A rip is 20 m wide and flows at 1 m/s. You swim across it at 0.8 m/s. How far out are you carried? Crossing takes 20 ÷ 0.8 = 25 s; drift = 1 × 25 = 25 m seaward. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wave energy & impact
chunks.text: Twice the height, four times the energy. That's why "just a bit bigger" can be a lot more. In linear wave theory, the energy in each square metre of sea is E = ⅛ ρ g H² , and the power carried per metre of wave crest is P = ρ g² H² T ÷ 64π (ρ ≈ 1,025 kg/m³ for seawater). Energy grows with height squared; power also grows with period. That is why a slightly bigger, longer-period day hits so much harder in a wipeout. Worked example · wave power per metre of crest Height Period Energy per m² of sea Power per m of crest 0.5 m 6 s ≈ 0.31 kJ ≈ 0.7 kW 1 m 8 s ≈ 1.26 kJ ≈ 3.9 kW 2 m 12 s ≈ 5.0 kJ ≈ 23.5 kW 1 m, 8 s: P = 1025 × 9.81² × 1 × 8 ÷ (64π) ≈ 3,920 W/m.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wave energy & impact
chunks.text: E = 1025 × 9.81 × 1 ÷ 8 ≈ 1,257 J per m². Staying safe with all that energy Leash on, board under control: a loose board pushed by whitewater can hit you or someone else hard. Keep it between you and the wave, never between you and other people. Wipeouts: relax, protect your head with your arms as you surface, and wait for the turbulence to pass ( Ch 5 ). Etiquette is safety: one surfer per wave (the one closest to the breaking part has priority), don't drop in, and paddle around the line-up, not through it. Sun and heat: India's water is warm, but the sun is strong: rash vest, reef-safe sunscreen and water.

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Wave energy & impact
chunks.text: ✋ Feel the number A modest 1 m, 8-second swell delivers about 4 kW per metre of beach, like a row of electric kettles every metre along the shore, all day long. The swell grows from 1 m to 1.5 m at the same period. How much more power? 1.5² = 2.25, so about 2.25 times (≈ 8.8 kW/m at 8 s). ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The surf ladder

chunks.title: Surfing · Physics of Waves, Boards & Rips · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Whitewater → green waves → independent → competition → instructor → international
chunks.text: Surfing has no licence. Schools run their own levels, the Surfing Federation of India (SFI) accredits schools and runs national contests, and the International Surfing Association (ISA) certifies instructors and coaches. The steps below are a typical path with the real requirement we found at each one. They aren't official grades.

chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Surfing's rules come from a world federation recognised by the Olympic movement, a professional tour, and India's national federation and its state associations. We checked each on its own official website.

chunks.heading: Global
chunks.text: World federation International Surfing Association (ISA) Surfing's world governing authority, as recognised by the International Olympic Committee. Runs the World Surfing Games and other world championships, and the Coaching and Instructing Program (Surf Level 1 Instructor, Level 2 Coach, judging), with an ISA/ILS water-safety course for instructors. isasurf.org Professional tour World Surf League (WSL) Runs the professional Championship Tour, Challenger Series, Qualifying Series and Junior Tour. Accredits surf and SUP schools and runs national contests and ISA courses. surfingfederationofindia.org State associations SFI state associations SFI lists state associations including the Tamil Nadu Surfing Association (founded 2023), the Karnataka Surfing Association and Surfing Kerala (both founded 2025), with others under review. surfingfederationofindia.org/accreditation Compete

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Water is 800 times denser than air. Swim smarter, not harder.
chunks.text: Every length is a deal with the water: it holds you up, it holds you back, and it's the only thing you can push against. Learn drag, buoyancy, propulsion and breathing with real numbers, then take them to the sea, where currents, sighting and heat join in. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science pool open sea ≈ 4.5 kg The lift your lungs add between empty and full. Full lungs float you; breathed out, most people sink. ≈ 25× How much better water carries heat away from you than air. Cool water chills fast; on long warm swims you overheat. 33 min To swim 1 km against a mild 0.5 m/s current, not 17. In the sea the water itself moves: plan around tides.

chunks.text: 8× The power you need to swim twice as fast. The water's push rises 4×, so effort climbs steeply.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: What you're getting into
chunks.text: Sinking isn't failure. You're almost exactly as dense as water; good coaches teach floating and breathing before strokes. The sea has no black line. Try your first sea swim in a lifeguarded zone, with instructors. A panicking swimmer can push a rescuer under. Unless trained, raise the alarm, then reach or throw something that floats. Ask before you book a swimming lesson → 01 · The challenge

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Do you know what the water is doing to you?
chunks.text: 15 questions on the physics of swimming, from the pool to the open sea: a quick check of what will be happening to you, before you go. No trick wording and no exam pressure. You'll get your score, a verdict, an explanation for every answer, and a link to the chapter for anything you missed. 02 · The science

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Six chapters, from the first float to the open sea
chunks.text: Each chapter takes one idea and follows it into the water, with worked numbers you can check on a calculator. Our reference swimmer weighs 70 kg and displaces about 72 litres with full lungs. Drag areas, body volumes and efficiencies are illustrative round values; real ones vary a lot between people and strokes. Interactive · Swim Lab

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Set your speed, the current and the water, and see what it costs
chunks.text: An illustrative model: drag = ½ × water density × 0.06 m² × speed², a typical order of magnitude for adult front crawl. Reference swimmer 70 kg, 72 L with full lungs and 67.5 L after a full breath out. For learning only; it is not a planning or safety tool.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Set your speed, the current and the water, and see what it costs
chunks.text: Real drag depends on your shape, stroke and skill, and measured values differ between research methods. Real currents vary with tide, wind and place. Treat every number as a teaching example, and get local advice from lifeguards or the event's safety team before any open-water swim. CH 1

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: The water doesn't just slow you down. It charges by the square of your speed. Three kinds of drag act on a swimmer at the surface. Form (pressure) drag comes from the shape you push through the water: a head lifted high or hips dropped low present a bigger, blunter shape. Skin-friction drag is the water dragging along your skin and costume, small at swimming speeds but not zero. Wave drag is the energy you spend making waves; it rises steeply as you swim faster. Together they follow roughly D = ½ × ρ × CdA × v² , where ρ is water density and CdA lumps your shape and size into one "drag area".

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: Worked example · our reference swimmer in a pool (CdA 0.06 m², illustrative) Speed 100 m in Drag Useful power (drag × speed) 0.8 m/s 2:05 ≈ 19 N ≈ 15 W 1.0 m/s 1:40 30 N 30 W 1.5 m/s 1:07 ≈ 68 N ≈ 101 W 2.0 m/s 0:50 120 N 240 W Doubling speed from 1.0 to 2.0 m/s: drag ×4 (v²), power ×8 (v³). "Useful power" is only the work that goes into moving forward. Your muscles burn many times more, because much of the effort just stirs water (Chapter 3) and the body turns only a small fraction of food energy into mechanical work (Chapter 4). Measured drag on real swimmers varies widely, and different research methods give different values, so treat 0.06 m² as a teaching number.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: Why streamlining beats strength Because drag scales with CdA, a small change in shape is worth as much as a big change in effort. A long, flat, narrow body (head in line with the spine, hips high, legs kicking inside the body's "shadow") lowers CdA. A 10% lower drag area gives 10% less drag at any speed. Getting the same gain from fitness alone would take 10% more power. Reynolds number: why friction is the small one Engineers judge a flow by its Reynolds number , Re = v × L ÷ ν : speed times length, divided by the water's kinematic viscosity ν (about 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s at 20 °C, 0.8 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s at 30 °C). For a 2 m swimmer at 1 m/s, Re ≈ 1.0 × 2 ÷ 0.000001 ≈ 2 million .

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: At numbers like that, viscosity only matters in a thin layer next to the skin. The flow can't follow the body's curves, so it breaks away behind the head, shoulders and hips and leaves a turbulent, low-pressure wake. That's why form drag and wave drag are the big terms, and why shape matters far more than a slippery costume. Waves, and why racers go underwater At the surface, part of your effort becomes the bow wave in front of your head and the trough behind. In towing tests with a mannequin (Vennell, Pease & Wilson, 2006), total drag at the surface was up to 2.4 times the drag fully submerged, and wave drag made up as much as 50–60% of the total at 1.7 m/s.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: It fell below 5% once the mannequin was deeper than 0.5 m at 1 m/s , or 0.7 m at 2 m/s . That's why racers glide and dolphin-kick after starts and turns. World Aquatics rules allow you to be fully submerged for no more than 15 metres after the start and each turn in freestyle, backstroke and butterfly; by then your head must have broken the surface.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: Worked example · your "hull speed" (Froude number Fr = v ÷ √(g × L), body 2.34 m fingertip to toe, as in the towing study) Speed Froude number Depth needed to dodge most wave drag (study) 0.9 m/s ≈ 0.2 1.8 chest depths (≈ 0.45 m) 1.7 m/s ≈ 0.36 at the surface, wave drag was up to 60% of the total here 2.0 m/s ≈ 0.42 2.8 chest depths (≈ 0.7 m) √(9.81 × 2.34) ≈ 4.8 m/s, so Fr = speed ÷ 4.8. Boats share the same physics: as Fr nears about 0.4, the bow wave becomes about as long as the hull and the boat is effectively climbing its own wave. Naval architects call this "hull speed". A swimmer at the surface is a short, blunt hull, which is one reason fast surface swimming costs so much.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Drag: form, friction & waves
chunks.text: ✋ Feel the number 30 N is about the weight of a 3 kg bag of rice. Swimming at an easy 1 m/s, the water pushes back on you that hard the whole time. Sprint at 2 m/s and it's like holding up a 12 kg suitcase. At 1.2 m/s, what are the drag and the useful power for our reference swimmer? Drag = ½ × 1,000 × 0.06 × 1.2² = 43.2 N . Power = 43.2 × 1.2 ≈ 52 W . A 20% speed-up cost 44% more drag and 73% more power. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & body position
chunks.text: You're almost exactly as dense as water. Your lungs decide which side of the line you're on. Archimedes: the water pushes up on you with a force equal to the weight of the water you displace. Fat is less dense than water and lean tissue and bone are denser, so people differ, but most adults end up very close to the density of water. The big variable is the air in your lungs: a full breath adds several litres of volume for a few grams of mass.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & body position
chunks.text: Worked example · our 70 kg reference swimmer, lying still (illustrative volumes) Lungs Volume Upthrust in a pool (1.000 kg/L) Net Upthrust in the sea (1.025 kg/L) Net Full breath 72 L 72.0 kg +2.0 kg (floats) 73.8 kg +3.8 kg Fully breathed out 67.5 L 67.5 kg −2.5 kg (sinks) 69.2 kg −0.8 kg The 4.5 L swing between full and empty lungs is a typical adult order of magnitude (it varies with size and fitness). Notice the sea adds about 1.8 kg of upthrust: most people feel noticeably more buoyant in salt water. Why the legs sink Upthrust acts at the centre of buoyancy , around your air-filled chest. Your weight acts at the centre of mass , nearer your hips.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & body position
chunks.text: These two points are a few centimetres apart, so even when the forces balance, they twist you: chest up, legs down. With 687 N of weight and an offset of, say, 2 cm, that's a turning effect of about 14 N·m, enough to swing still legs towards the bottom. Swimmers fight this with body position, not strength: head neutral (eyes down, not forward), a slight press of the chest into the water, a long reach in front (moving mass towards the head), and a small, steady kick. Lifting the head to look forward drops the hips and raises form drag ( Ch 1 ). Scuba divers fine-tune exactly this balance with their lungs and weights (see buoyancy on the scuba page ).

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Buoyancy & body position
chunks.text: For adult learners If you're a "sinker", that's physics, not failure. Learn to float with full lungs first, then practise breathing out slowly underwater (bubbles through the nose) so that each breath in is quick. Good coaches teach balance in the water before they teach strokes. A 60 kg swimmer displaces 61.5 L with full lungs. What's their net upthrust in a pool, and in the sea? Pool: 61.5 − 60 = +1.5 kg . Sea: 61.5 × 1.025 ≈ 63.0 kg, so +3.0 kg . Salt water doubles their spare buoyancy. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Propulsion: lift vs drag, stated honestly
chunks.text: The only thing you can push against is the water. How exactly you do it is still being researched. Start with what's certain: Newton's third law . To move forward, you have to accelerate water backwards. The thrust you get equals the mass of water you move each second multiplied by how much you speed it up: thrust = ṁ × Δv . The two theories Drag-based propulsion treats the hand and forearm as a paddle pushing water straight back. Lift-based propulsion treats the hand as a small hydrofoil: angled and moved partly sideways (sculling), it generates a force at right angles to its motion, like a wing.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Propulsion: lift vs drag, stated honestly
chunks.text: In the 1970s, the lift idea became very popular and coaches taught a pronounced S-shaped pull to "use" it. Later research, with better measurement and flow visualisation, found the picture more mixed. In much of the front-crawl pull, pushing water backwards (drag) does a large share of the work, while lift contributes to varying degrees depending on hand angle, stroke phase and swimmer. Both simple models also assume steady flow, but a real stroke is unsteady : the hand accelerates, sheds vortices and drags water with it. The honest summary: both mechanisms contribute, the exact split varies, and it's still an active research topic .

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Propulsion: lift vs drag, stated honestly
chunks.text: Coaching has moved towards a straighter, deeper pull with the forearm held near vertical early in the stroke, so a big surface pushes water backwards. Worked example · 30 N of thrust (Chapter 1's drag at 1 m/s), made three ways Water moved each second Pushed back by Thrust Energy wasted in the moving water (½ṁΔv²) 60 kg/s 0.5 m/s 30 N 7.5 W 30 kg/s 1.0 m/s 30 N 15 W 15 kg/s 2.0 m/s 30 N 30 W Same thrust, very different waste. Moving a lot of water a little is more efficient than moving a little water a lot. That's the same reason ships use big, slow propellers, and why a good "catch" (getting the hand and forearm set early) matters more than a fast, slipping pull.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Propulsion: lift vs drag, stated honestly
chunks.text: Froude efficiency: how much of your stroke actually pushes you The table above gives the Froude (propelling) efficiency : useful power ÷ (useful power + power wasted in the water). The three rows work out at 30 ÷ 37.5 = 80% , 30 ÷ 45 = 67% and 30 ÷ 60 = 50% . Real swimmers sit near the bottom row: a study that modelled the front-crawl arm stroke as a paddle wheel and included the legs found a Froude efficiency of about 0.5 at 1.0–1.4 m/s (Zamparo et al., 2005). Over that range the power to overcome drag plus the power given to the water rose from 50 to 100 W, and moving the limbs themselves cost another 10–30 W.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Propulsion: lift vs drag, stated honestly
chunks.text: Fins cut the energy cost by 10–15% in the same study, for the reason in the table: a big, slow blade moves a lot of water a little. That's why divers wear them (see the freediving and scuba pages). Arms, legs and the rest of you In front crawl over distance, the arms provide most of the propulsion. For many distance swimmers the legs mainly keep the body level and balanced ( Ch 2 ), adding less thrust while costing a lot of energy, since leg muscles are big. Sprinters kick hard; open-water swimmers usually kick lightly. You need 43 N of thrust at 1.2 m/s. If you push 40 kg of water back each second, how fast must it leave your hand?

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Propulsion: lift vs drag, stated honestly
chunks.text: Δv = thrust ÷ ṁ = 43 ÷ 40 ≈ 1.1 m/s backwards, relative to the water around you. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Breathing & energy
chunks.text: Air comes in tiny, timed sips, and every kilometre costs more than you'd think. Breathing in front crawl You breathe by rotating your head to the side, into the trough your head's bow wave makes beside your face, so your mouth clears the water without lifting your head. Breathe out steadily underwater so that the brief moment of turning is only for breathing in. Breathing every three strokes alternates sides and keeps the stroke symmetrical; every two strokes gives more air at higher effort. In open water, breathing to both sides lets you breathe away from waves and see more.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Breathing & energy
chunks.text: Why breath-holding games are dangerous Your urge to breathe is driven mostly by rising carbon dioxide , not falling oxygen. Over-breathing (hyperventilating) before a long underwater swim washes out CO₂ but adds very little oxygen. The warning then comes too late: oxygen can fall low enough to cause a blackout underwater, without any feeling of distress first. Never hyperventilate, never do breath-hold challenges, and never swim underwater alone. Our freediving page explains blackout physiology in detail, and why even trained freedivers always have a buddy watching.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Breathing & energy
chunks.text: The energy cost of a kilometre Measured energy costs for front crawl: 0.6–0.8 kJ per metre at 1.0–1.4 m/s in one study, where metabolic power rose from 600 to 1,200 W across that speed range (Zamparo et al., 2005). In elite long-distance swimmers it rose from 0.69 to 1.27 kJ per metre as speed went from 1.29 to 1.50 m/s. After a hard 2 km swim it was about 20% higher at the same speed, which the authors linked to a drop in propelling efficiency (stroke rate went up). Earlier studies put front-crawl efficiency at only a few per cent to about ten per cent; counting all the mechanical work, including moving the limbs and the water you throw backwards, the same group got about 20% .

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Breathing & energy
chunks.text: For a 70 kg runner the cost is about 0.3 kJ per metre, so swimming costs roughly 2–4 times as much per kilometre, and beginners far more. Worked example · energy for a good swimmer (≈ 0.8 kJ/m, illustrative) Swim Time at 1.1 m/s Energy used In food terms 1 km ≈ 15 min ≈ 800 kJ ≈ 190 kcal 5 km ≈ 76 min ≈ 4,000 kJ ≈ 960 kcal 10 km ≈ 2 h 32 min ≈ 8,000 kJ ≈ 1,900 kcal 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. Beyond about 90 minutes, your stored carbohydrate starts running low, which is why long sea swims include feeding and hydration stops (Goa's swimathon uses anchored boats; the Coastal Odyssey has support boats for nutrition and hydration). A beginner's cost is closer to 1.5 kJ/m.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Breathing & energy
chunks.text: How much energy does their 2 km swim take? 2,000 × 1.5 = 3,000 kJ ≈ 720 kcal , almost as much as a good swimmer spends on 4 km. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Open water: currents & sighting
chunks.text: In the sea, the water itself is moving, and there's no black line to follow. Currents are just vector addition Your speed over the ground is your swimming speed plus the water's speed, with directions. With the current, they add; against it, they subtract. Across it, you have to aim upstream to hold a straight line, at an angle where sin(angle) = current ÷ your speed .

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Open water: currents & sighting
chunks.text: Worked example · 1 km at a swimming speed of 1.0 m/s Current Speed over the ground Time for 1 km None 1.00 m/s ≈ 16.7 min 0.5 m/s with you 1.50 m/s ≈ 11.1 min 0.5 m/s against you 0.50 m/s ≈ 33.3 min 0.5 m/s across, aiming 30° upstream 0.87 m/s ≈ 19.2 min 0.5 m/s across, not aiming 1.00 m/s forward ≈ 16.7 min, but 500 m off to the side Tides change currents through the day, so organisers time sea races and publish tide information (Goa's race rules link a tide chart). Try it yourself in the Swim Lab above.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Open water: currents & sighting
chunks.text: Worked example · real Indian races as vector sums Race Winning time Average speed over the ground What it tells you SFI National Open Water Championships, 10 km open men (Thanirbhavi Beach, Mangaluru, 9 Jan 2026) 2:26:13 10,000 ÷ 8,773 s ≈ 1.14 m/s A national-level sea pace, tide and chop included Murshidabad 81 km river race, Bhagirathi (31 Aug 2025) 10:35:37 81,000 ÷ 38,137 s ≈ 2.12 m/s Faster than any swimmer can go through still water: if he swam at a strong 1.3 m/s, the river was carrying him at about 0.8 m/s The 1.3 m/s is our assumption, for illustration; only the distance and time are measured.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Open water: currents & sighting
chunks.text: Rip currents A rip is a narrow channel of water flowing out to sea from the beach, often faster than a swimmer. The US National Weather Service says rips have been measured at up to 8 feet per second (about 2.4 m/s ), faster than an Olympic swimmer sprints 50 m, although most of the time they are much slower. Swim straight for the beach at 1 m/s against a 2.4 m/s rip and you still go out to sea at 1.4 m/s. Swimming parallel to the shore takes you out of the channel sideways instead of fighting it. Fighting one head-on exhausts you. Stay calm, float to save energy, raise an arm to signal for help, and swim parallel to the shore to get out of the channel before heading in.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Open water: currents & sighting
chunks.text: Best of all, swim only in the zone the lifeguards mark with flags. Sighting: swimming straight without a line Every few strokes, lift your eyes just above the water to spot the next buoy or a big landmark behind it, then turn your head to breathe as normal. Small errors add up fast: drifting 10° off line over 1 km puts you 1,000 × sin 10° ≈ 174 m off course. Goa's swimathon places sighting buoys every 150–200 m and asks swimmers to keep them on their left. Breathing to both sides helps you correct a stroke that pulls you one way. Mass starts and drafting Open-water races start in a crowd. Organisers ask swimmers to "self-seed": slower swimmers start towards the back, so nobody is swum over.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Open water: currents & sighting
chunks.text: Swimming just behind or beside another swimmer (drafting) means less effort for the same speed, because they've already set the water moving. It's allowed in most open-water races, but stay clear of other swimmers' feet. Triathlon swims start and draft the same way (see the triathlon swim chapter ). You swim at 1.2 m/s across a 0.6 m/s current. What angle do you aim upstream, and what's your speed over the ground? sin(angle) = 0.6 ÷ 1.2 = 0.5, so 30° . Ground speed = √(1.2² − 0.6²) ≈ 1.04 m/s . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Cold, heat & staying safe
chunks.text: Water moves heat 25 times better than air. In India, that usually means you overheat, not freeze. Why water chills you so fast Water's thermal conductivity (about 0.6 W/m·K) is roughly 25 times that of air, and a litre of water soaks up far more heat than a litre of air. Air at 20 °C feels pleasant; water at 20 °C can chill a slim swimmer within an hour. Sudden immersion in cold water also triggers cold shock . The RNLI (the UK's lifeboat charity) treats water at 15 °C and below as cold: the skin's sudden cooling causes an involuntary gasp, breathing rate can rise as much as tenfold, and heart rate and blood pressure jump.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Cold, heat & staying safe
chunks.text: Its advice, "Float to Live": the initial effects pass in less than a minute, so float on your back and wait before trying to swim. Enter cold water slowly. The rules, from the World Aquatics competition regulations Situation Rule Open-water race temperature Minimum 16.0 °C, maximum 31.0 °C, measured 2 hours before the start at a depth of 40 cm Water below 18 °C Wetsuits compulsory Water 18 °C and above Wetsuits not permitted (the Chief Referee may make them mandatory up to 20 °C if conditions are hazardous) Warm seas: the Indian problem is heat Swimming hard, your muscles produce several hundred watts of heat (most of the food energy in Ch 4 ends up as heat).

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Cold, heat & staying safe
chunks.text: In cool water that heat drains away easily. In warm water there's little temperature difference to carry it off. Goa's swimathon expects water at around 26–28 °C and bans wetsuits, warning that they would make swimmers "dehydrate and overheat rapidly". Hydrate before the start, use the feed stations, and respect the sun on long swims. Triathletes face the same problem for hours longer (see heat on the triathlon page ). Jellyfish, kit and good habits Jellyfish: Goa's organisers warn they're always possible, and suggest full-length suits or jammers and a barrier of coconut oil or petroleum jelly on exposed skin. Be seen: a bright cap (events issue one, and it's mandatory).

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Cold, heat & staying safe
chunks.text: Tow floats help visibility, but Goa allows them only in its 5 km and 10 km races, because lines tangle in crowded short races. Medical: Mumbai's Sunk Rock race asks every swimmer for a doctor-attested medical certificate; Goa asks swimmers over 60 for one for its longer races. Never alone: swim with lifeguards, a club or an organised event. Don't swim within 12 hours of drinking alcohol (a Goa race rule, and good advice anywhere). Safety Rescues need training A panicking swimmer can push a would-be rescuer underwater. If someone is in trouble, raise the alarm and reach or throw something that floats rather than swimming out, unless you're trained.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: Cold, heat & staying safe
chunks.text: Lifesaving courses (see Skill levels) teach how to rescue without becoming a second casualty. The water is 17.5 °C on race morning. Under World Aquatics rules, do you wear a wetsuit? Yes: below 18 °C, wetsuits are compulsory . At 18 °C and above they're not allowed, unless the Chief Referee declares them mandatory for safety (up to 20 °C). ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · Skill levels

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first float to marathon swims
chunks.text: India has no single national learn-to-swim grading for adults. So we've built a clearly labelled Kinetic ladder , anchored to real things: the Swim England Learn to Swim stages as a reference syllabus, Indian events' own entry requirements for each open-water distance, and the Swimming Federation of India (SFI) competitive pathway. Lifesaving awards, a separate track, are explained below the ladder.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic
chunks.heading: The ladder, from first float to marathon swims
chunks.text: Step 1 · Water confidence Float, breathe, self-rescue Reference: Swim England Stages 1–7 What you learn Learn to Swim Stages 1–7 Swim England's Learn to Swim Programme teaches children and adults; it recommends completing Stages 1–7 as a minimum English schools' benchmark: swim at least 25 m unaided, confidently and safely, and perform safe self-rescue Physics you're using Buoyancy and balance Floating and body position: Ch 2 Breathing out underwater: Ch 4 In India Survival swimming RLSS(I)'s Swim N Survive: aimed mainly at children, but "people of all ages should be able to meet this minimum standard" Step 2 · Stroke & stamina Continuous swimming, good technique Reference: Swim England Stages 8–10 · Kinetic milestone What you learn Kinetic milestone (not an official grade) Swim 400 m or more of front crawl without stopping, breathing to both sides Streamlined push-offs; a relaxed, low head position Physics you're using Drag and propulsion Streamlining: Ch 1 Catch and pull: Ch 3 In India Pool coaching Coached sessions at a local pool or club.

chunks.title: Swimming, pool to open water: the physics, explained | Kinetic

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swim. Bike. Run. Fuel the physics all the way to the finish.
chunks.text: A triathlon is three sports back to back, and the longer the race, the more it's decided by drag, pacing and how much carbohydrate you can keep putting in. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Race-Day Lab, then find real races in India and around the world, from a first sprint to IRONMAN. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First sprint Kona ≈ 77% Of the energy you burn becomes heat, not motion. Drink to your sweat rate: far more is risky too. 33% Extra power to ride just 10% faster on the flat. Going a little harder costs a lot more than it gives. ≈ 4.3 kg Extra float a wetsuit gives, mostly at hips and legs. Right where new swimmers tend to sink.

chunks.heading: Six chapters. Every number worked out.
