chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a distance, your bike power, your position and how many grams of carbohydrate you eat per hour, then see your bike split and your fuel balance
chunks.text: A simple flat-road model: rider + bike 80 kg, rolling resistance 0.004, air density 1.2 kg/m³, 97% drivetrain efficiency, no wind. Energy assumes your muscles turn about 23% of food energy into pedal power, and that about 60% of that energy comes from carbohydrate at 4 kcal per gram. Learning values only (illustrative), not a race plan.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pick a distance, your bike power, your position and how many grams of carbohydrate you eat per hour, then see your bike split and your fuel balance
chunks.text: Distance Sprint Standard 70.3 Full Bike power 180 W Position Upright Hoods Aero bars Carbs eaten 60 g/h Bike speed 32.9 km/h Ch 4 · drag + rolling = power Bike split 2:44 Ch 2 · distance ÷ speed Share of power fighting air 84% Ch 4 · why aero matters Energy burned on the bike 1,845 kcal Ch 1 · power ÷ efficiency Carbohydrate burned 101 g/h Ch 1 · the glycogen clock Gap the body must cover 41 g/h Ch 1 · eaten vs burned Extra power to pass in 25 s +27 W Ch 4 · the 12 m draft zone Bar = share of the carbohydrate you burn that you're replacing by eating. Try aero bars, then the full distance. Guidance for long events is up to 90 g/h (Ch 1); practise any fuelling plan in training first. CH 1

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy systems & fuelling
chunks.text: Your legs can go all day. Your carbohydrate stores can't. Long triathlons are aerobic: muscles burn a mix of fat and carbohydrate with oxygen. Fat stores are huge, but the harder you go, the more of your energy comes from carbohydrate, and the body only stores a few hundred grams of it as glycogen in muscle and liver (an illustrative ballpark: about 500 g, roughly 2,000 kcal, for a trained athlete). Run low and your pace drops sharply: what endurance athletes call "hitting the wall". Your muscles are only about a quarter efficient (we use 23%, illustrative): to put 180 W into the pedals your body burns about 180 ÷ 0.23 ≈ 780 W of food energy.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy systems & fuelling
chunks.text: Worked example · 180 W on the bike (illustrative values) Item Number How Food energy burned ≈ 673 kcal/h 180 ÷ 0.23 × 3,600 s ÷ 4,184 J/kcal From carbohydrate (60%) ≈ 101 g/h 673 × 0.6 ÷ 4 kcal/g Eating 60 g/h ≈ 41 g/h short covered by glycogen 500 g of glycogen at 41 g/h ≈ 12 h but the run burns more per hour than the bike The ratio of fat to carbohydrate changes with intensity and training, so the 60% is a teaching number, not your number.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy systems & fuelling
chunks.text: What the guidelines say The joint position statement on nutrition and athletic performance from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the American College of Sports Medicine (2016) suggests 30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour during endurance exercise of 1–2.5 h, and up to 90 g/h for ultra-endurance exercise over 2.5–3 h, using glucose-fructose mixtures ("multiple transportable carbohydrates") that the gut can absorb faster. For events longer than 90 minutes it describes carbohydrate loading of 10–12 g per kg of body mass per day for the 36–48 hours before.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Energy systems & fuelling
chunks.text: 🍌 Feel the number 90 g of carbohydrate an hour is roughly what three energy gels or a few bananas give you (illustrative), every hour, for many hours, while racing. Guts can be trained: practise race fuelling in long training sessions, never for the first time on race day. At 200 W with the same assumptions, roughly how many grams of carbohydrate do you burn per hour? 200 ÷ 0.23 × 3,600 ÷ 4,184 ≈ 748 kcal/h; × 0.6 ÷ 4 ≈ 112 g/h . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pacing & power
chunks.text: Going a little harder costs a lot more than it gives. On a flat road most of your power goes into pushing air, and air drag power grows with the cube of speed: P air = ½ ρ CdA v³ . Ride 10% faster and you need about 33% more power for the air part. That's why steady, even pacing beats surges: every surge burns extra carbohydrate (Ch 1) for a small time gain, and you still have to run afterwards.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pacing & power
chunks.text: Worked example · 90 km in the hoods, CdA 0.32 m² (from our Race-Day Lab) Power Speed 90 km split Carbohydrate burned 150 W ≈ 30.7 km/h ≈ 2:56 ≈ 84 g/h 180 W ≈ 32.9 km/h ≈ 2:44 ≈ 101 g/h 200 W ≈ 34.2 km/h ≈ 2:38 ≈ 112 g/h From 150 W to 200 W is 33% more power for about 11% more speed: you save about 18 minutes but burn about a third more carbohydrate every hour. Pacing a whole race Swim: start controlled; a wild first 200 m spikes your heart rate for little gain. Bike: ride steady power, ease off on descents and don't spike up climbs; a power meter or heart rate helps. Run: the race often starts here. Many coaches suggest running the first kilometres slightly slower than feels right.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Pacing & power
chunks.text: If air drag were all of the power, how much more power would 20% more speed need? 1.2³ ≈ 1.73, so about 73% more . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swim drag & wetsuit buoyancy
chunks.text: Water is 800 times denser than air. Position beats power. Drag in water follows the same law as in air, F = ½ ρ C d A v² , but with ρ ≈ 1,000 kg/m³ instead of 1.2. Legs that sink add frontal area and drag, so a high, flat body line matters more than raw strength. Our Swimming page covers drag, buoyancy and open-water skills in detail. A wetsuit is closed-cell foam, full of tiny gas bubbles. It lifts the hips and legs, which cuts drag, and keeps you warm. That's why rules limit when you may wear one.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swim drag & wetsuit buoyancy
chunks.text: Worked example · wetsuit lift (illustrative values) Item Number How Neoprene volume ≈ 5.4 L 1.8 m² of suit × 3 mm average thickness Water it displaces ≈ 5.4 kg 1 L of water ≈ 1 kg Suit's own mass ≈ 1.1 kg foam about 0.2 kg per litre Net extra lift ≈ 4.3 kg 5.4 − 1.1, mostly at hips and legs How much does a wetsuit really help? A measurement Dutch researchers measured the drag on 12 swimmers (eight men, four women) doing front crawl over a row of instrumented push-off pads, with and without a triathlon wetsuit ( Toussaint et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1989 ). At 1.25 m/s , a typical triathlon swim speed, the wetsuit cut drag by 14% , from 48.7 N to 41.8 N; at 1.50 m/s by 12%.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swim drag & wetsuit buoyancy
chunks.text: Most of that came from extra buoyancy (the lift in the table above), but the suit helped the lighter women as much as the heavier men, so a smoother surface probably helps too. Worked example · same effort, 14% less drag (simple model: drag ∝ v², power = drag × speed) Swim No wetsuit, 1.25 m/s Wetsuit, same power Time saved Sprint, 750 m 10:00 ≈ 9:30 ≈ 30 s Olympic, 1.5 km 20:00 ≈ 19:00 ≈ 1 min 70.3, 1.9 km 25:20 ≈ 24:04 ≈ 1 min 15 s Full, 3.8 km 50:40 ≈ 48:09 ≈ 2 min 30 s Power to beat drag = F × v = 48.7 × 1.25 ≈ 61 W without the suit, 41.8 × 1.25 ≈ 52 W with it.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swim drag & wetsuit buoyancy
chunks.text: If drag grows with v², power grows with v³, so at the same 61 W the wetsuit swimmer goes (48.7 ÷ 41.8) 1/3 ≈ 1.052 times faster: about 1.32 m/s. Real swimmers also change their stroke in a suit, so treat this as a rough guide; it shows why rules decide who may wear one. Wetsuit rules (IRONMAN 2026 Competition Rules) Age-group athletes may wear wetsuits in water up to and including 24.5 °C . From 24.5 °C to 28.8 °C, IRONMAN may at some events allow a separate non-competitive wetsuit wave, whose athletes aren't eligible for awards or world championship slots. Wetsuits are prohibited above 28.8 °C ; for professionals the limit is 21.9 °C. Thickness may not exceed 5 mm.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Swim drag & wetsuit buoyancy
chunks.text: World Triathlon events set their own temperature limits in the World Triathlon Competition Rules; check the athlete guide for your race. 🌊 Feel the number Doubling your swim speed needs four times the drag force and eight times the power. A small gain in body position is worth a lot of fitness. Water at 26 °C, an age-group athlete, IRONMAN rules: can you race for an age-group award in a wetsuit? No. 26 °C is above 24.5 °C; at most, the race may offer a non-competitive wetsuit wave without awards or slots. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drafting rules & bike aerodynamics
chunks.text: Your body is most of the drag. CdA is the number that matters. CdA (drag coefficient × frontal area, in m²) sums up how "slippery" you and your bike are. Folding down onto aero bars shrinks your frontal area and smooths the airflow. Our Cycling & MTB page works through rolling resistance, climbing and power in more detail. Worked example · 180 W, 80 kg, flat road (from our Race-Day Lab) Position (illustrative CdA) Speed 90 km 180 km Upright, 0.40 m² ≈ 30.6 km/h ≈ 2:56 ≈ 5:53 Hoods, 0.32 m² ≈ 32.9 km/h ≈ 2:44 ≈ 5:29 Aero bars, 0.25 m² ≈ 35.5 km/h ≈ 2:32 ≈ 5:04 Same power, same legs: the aero position saves about 49 minutes over 180 km compared with sitting up.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drafting rules & bike aerodynamics
chunks.text: Hold it only as long as you can stay comfortable and in control. Why drafting is banned in most age-group racing Riding close behind another rider puts you in their slipstream and can cut your drag a lot, so non-drafting races keep riders apart. World Triathlon's updated competition rules unified the draft zone to 12 m , with 25 s to pass; IRONMAN's 2026 rules use 12 m (about six bike lengths of clear space) and 25 s for age-group athletes, and 20 m for professionals. Once you enter the zone you must keep moving through it; if you're passed, you must drop back out of the passer's zone. How big is the slipstream?

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drafting rules & bike aerodynamics
chunks.text: A computer-simulation answer Blocken and colleagues (TU Eindhoven, KU Leuven and ETH Zürich) simulated the airflow around two riders, checked against wind-tunnel tests, with the riders 1 cm to 1 m apart ( Computers & Fluids, 2013 ). In the time-trial position (the one triathletes use), the rider behind had 13.8% less drag at 1 cm, still 11.7% less at 1 m. Upright, the saving was up to 27%. Surprisingly, the rider in front gained too, up to 2.6%, because the follower fills the low-pressure pocket behind them.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drafting rules & bike aerodynamics
chunks.text: Worked example · air-drag power at 40 km/h in the time-trial position (study's drag areas, air 1.2 kg/m³) Rider Drag area C d A Power against air Saving Riding alone 0.135 m² ≈ 111 W n/a Following at 1 m 0.119 m² ≈ 98 W ≈ 13 W Following at 1 cm 0.116 m² ≈ 95 W ≈ 16 W Leading, follower at 1 cm 0.131 m² ≈ 108 W ≈ 3 W P = ½ ρ C d A v³ = 0.5 × 1.2 × 0.135 × 11.11³ ≈ 111 W. Rolling resistance (not shown) is unchanged by drafting. The study's rider was a single person in a tight position, so your own numbers will differ; the study didn't test gaps beyond 1 m. The 12 m draft zone keeps age-groupers far outside the gaps it measured.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Drafting rules & bike aerodynamics
chunks.text: 🚴 Feel the number To clear 12 m in 25 s you need to ride at least 12 ÷ 25 = 0.48 m/s (about 1.7 km/h) faster than the rider ahead. At 33 km/h in the hoods that takes roughly 27 W more for those 25 seconds. A pass takes you 30 s through someone's 12 m draft zone. What's wrong? The limit is 25 s : that would be a drafting violation and a time penalty. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Running economy on tired legs
chunks.text: The run is a different sport when you start it after the bike. Running costs energy roughly in proportion to your body mass and distance. A common rule of thumb (illustrative) is about 1 kcal per kg per km , nearly whatever your pace. Off the bike, legs feel heavy and stiff for the first kilometres, and tired muscles can make each stride slightly less economical. Our Running page covers pace, cadence and heat in more detail.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Running economy on tired legs
chunks.text: Worked example · a 70 kg athlete (illustrative values) Run Energy (1 kcal/kg/km) If 5% less economical Sprint, 5 km ≈ 350 kcal ≈ 368 kcal Standard, 10 km ≈ 700 kcal ≈ 735 kcal 70.3, 21.1 km ≈ 1,477 kcal ≈ 1,551 kcal Full, 42.2 km ≈ 2,954 kcal ≈ 3,102 kcal A full-distance marathon alone can burn more energy than your glycogen holds (Ch 1), which is why fuelling on the bike matters for the run. Brick sessions (a run straight after a ride) train the switch from cycling to running. Short, quick steps off the bike, then settle into your normal stride. Walk the aid stations if that's what lets you drink and eat properly. A 60 kg athlete runs the 10 km of a standard triathlon.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Running economy on tired legs
chunks.text: About how much energy? 60 × 10 × 1 ≈ 600 kcal . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heat, hydration & transitions
chunks.text: Only about a quarter of your energy moves you. The rest is heat. If 23% of the energy you burn becomes motion (Ch 1), about 77% becomes heat. Your body sheds it mainly by sweating: evaporating sweat carries heat away, and in humid air it evaporates less. The 2016 position statement gives sweat rates of 0.3–2.4 L per hour , depending on intensity, fitness, heat acclimatisation and weather, and suggests drinking enough to keep the total body-fluid deficit under 2% of body mass , because bigger deficits can impair thinking and performance, especially in heat.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heat, hydration & transitions
chunks.text: Worked example · heat and sweat (illustrative values) Item Number How Heat made at 180 W ≈ 600 W 780 W burned × 0.77 2% of a 70 kg athlete 1.4 kg ≈ 1.4 L of fluid Sweating 1.2 L/h, drinking 0.8 L/h 0.4 L/h net loss reaches 1.4 L in 3.5 h Drinking far more than you sweat is risky too. Find your own sweat rate by weighing yourself before and after training sessions. Transitions: the fourth discipline T1 (swim to bike) and T2 (bike to run) count in your race time. IRONMAN's 2026 rules: mount and dismount only at the marked lines; no stopping in the flow zones; keep your kit in your bag or spot; don't touch other athletes' kit.

chunks.title: Triathlon & Ironman · Physics of Fuel, Drag & Pacing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Heat, hydration & transitions
chunks.text: Your helmet must be fastened from the moment you take your bike off the rack until you rack it again. Safety Race safely Get a medical check before you train for a long-distance race, build up gradually, practise open-water swimming with others and with water-safety cover, and know the race's cut-off times and medical support. In heat, slow down early rather than late. T1 takes 4 min and T2 takes 3 min. You cut both to 2 min. How much time do you save? (4 + 3) − (2 + 2) = 3 minutes , with no extra fitness. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The triathlon ladder

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tilt the rig. Trust the wind. Let the physics plane you out.
chunks.text: A windsurf sail is a wing you hold in your hands, and you steer by moving it. Take the challenge, learn the science with a Sail Lab, then find windsurfing schools in Tamil Nadu, Goa, Karnataka and Mumbai, national championships and instructor courses at your level. Take the 15-question challenge → Skip to the science First lesson iQFOiL 2.25× Sail force when the wind rises from 12 to 18 kn. A small rise in wind means much more pull. ≈ 30% Of your weight a sail pulls in 15 kn as you lift it. Uphaul with your legs, not your back. ≈ 41 N The fin's sideways grip at a slow 5 kn. Too little to hold you: slow boards slide downwind. 5.7 kn Your real progress upwind sailing at 8 kn, 45° off the wind.

chunks.heading: Set the true wind, your board speed, your heading and the sail size, then see the apparent wind, the sail's pull, your upwind progress and the lift a foil would give
chunks.text: A simple model: sail force = ½ ρ v² A C L with air density 1.225 kg/m³ and C L 1.0; foil lift = ½ ρ water v² A C L for a 0.1 m² front wing in seawater (1,025 kg/m³) with C L 0.4, compared with an 85 kg rider and board. Learning values only (illustrative), not equipment advice.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Set the true wind, your board speed, your heading and the sail size, then see the apparent wind, the sail's pull, your upwind progress and the lift a foil would give
chunks.text: True wind 15 kn Board speed 10 kn Sail size 6.0 m² Heading off the wind 45° upwind 90° beam reach 135° broad reach Apparent wind 18.0 kn Ch 1 · vector sum Apparent wind angle 56° Ch 1 · from your nose Sail force 316 N Ch 2 · ½ ρ v² A C L Progress upwind (VMG) 0.0 kn Ch 5 · speed × cos θ Foil lift at this speed 543 N Ch 4 · water is 800× denser Foil lift ÷ rider + board weight 65% Ch 4 · 100% = flying Bar = foil lift ÷ the weight of an 85 kg rider and board. Try 13 kn of board speed, then switch to 45° upwind. Learn on the water with a qualified instructor (Ch 6). CH 1

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Apparent wind & the wind window
chunks.text: Your sail never feels the true wind once you move. When you sail, your own motion makes a headwind. The sail feels the vector sum of that and the true wind: the apparent wind . Sailing upwind it's stronger than the true wind; sailing downwind it's weaker. In every direction, the faster you go, the further forward it swings, so you sheet the sail in as you speed up.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Apparent wind & the wind window
chunks.text: Worked example · true wind 15 kn, board speed 10 kn (from our Sail Lab) Heading off the wind Apparent wind Angle from your nose Sail force (6 m²) 45° (upwind) ≈ 23.2 kn ≈ 27° ≈ 522 N 90° (beam reach) ≈ 18.0 kn ≈ 56° ≈ 316 N 135° (broad reach) ≈ 10.6 kn ≈ 93° ≈ 110 N Beam reach: √(15² + 10²) ≈ 18.0 kn, at arctan(15 ÷ 10) ≈ 56° from the nose. 1 kn = 1.852 km/h. 🏄 Feel the number Same wind, same speed: heading upwind your sail feels more than twice the wind it feels on a broad reach, and almost five times the force. Speed pulls the wind forward. Stay on a broad reach (135° off the true wind) and let the board accelerate.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Apparent wind & the wind window
chunks.text: The apparent wind swings round towards the nose, which is why a planing windsurfer sheets in hard even when heading downwind. Worked example · broad reach, true wind 15 kn, board speeding up (Sail Lab model) Board speed Apparent wind Angle from your nose 0 kn (standing still) 15.0 kn 135° 5 kn ≈ 12.0 kn ≈ 118° 10 kn ≈ 10.6 kn ≈ 93° 20 kn (planing) ≈ 14.2 kn ≈ 48° At 20 kn: x = 15 cos 135° + 20 ≈ 9.4, y = 15 sin 135° ≈ 10.6, so √(9.4² + 10.6²) ≈ 14.2 kn at arctan(10.6 ÷ 9.4) ≈ 48°. The wind window: where you can sail. Picture a clock face with the true wind blowing from 12 o'clock. You can't sail straight at it: there's a no-go zone of very roughly 45° on either side.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Apparent wind & the wind window
chunks.text: Every other heading is a point of sail : close-hauled just outside the no-go zone, then beam reach (wind on your side), broad reach and finally a run (wind from behind). Close-hauled and beam reaches are driven mainly by lift from the sail as a wing (Ch 2). On a run, the wind mostly just pushes on the sail, and you can never go faster downwind than the wind itself. That's why fast windsurfers reach across the wind rather than run straight before it. True wind 12 kn on the beam, board speed 9 kn. What apparent wind? √(12² + 9²) = 15 kn . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 2

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The sail as a wing & the harness
chunks.text: A sail is a vertical wing. You are the mast's anchor. A windsurf sail is an aerofoil . Battens and the curve of the mast give it a built-in camber, like an aircraft wing standing on its end. Air flowing round the curved sail speeds up on the curved downwind (leeward) side and slows on the windward side, so pressure is lower to leeward. That pressure difference makes a force, F = ½ ρ v² A C L , roughly at right angles to the apparent wind. Part of it drives you forward; part pushes you sideways, which the fin (and a daggerboard, on some boards) resists (Ch 3).

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The sail as a wing & the harness
chunks.text: Worked example · sail size and wind (C L 1.0, illustrative) Sail 12 kn apparent 18 kn apparent 4.5 m² ≈ 105 N ≈ 236 N 6.0 m² ≈ 140 N ≈ 315 N 7.5 m² ≈ 175 N ≈ 394 N 9.0 m² ≈ 210 N ≈ 473 N 18 kn = 9.26 m/s: 0.5 × 1.225 × 9.26² × 6 ≈ 315 N. Going from 12 to 18 kn multiplies the force by (18 ÷ 12)² = 2.25. Spread over 6 m², 315 N is a pressure difference of only about 53 Pa, around 1/2000 of atmospheric pressure, yet it can pull a person across the water. That v² is why sailors carry several sails: a big sail for light wind, a small one when it's strong. Angle of attack, sheeting and stall.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The sail as a wing & the harness
chunks.text: Pulling in with your back hand (sheeting in) increases the sail's angle to the apparent wind, its angle of attack . Up to a point, more angle means more lift. Too much, and the airflow can no longer follow the leeward curve: it breaks away, lift collapses and drag soars. That's a stall . Too little angle and the front of the sail flaps (luffs) and the force fades. Good sailors keep the sail just short of stalling, and re-trim as the apparent wind shifts with every change of speed (Ch 1). The harness and harness lines. You hold the rig up and lean against its pull.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The sail as a wing & the harness
chunks.text: A harness (worn round your waist or seat) has a hook that clips into a harness line , a loop of rope on each side of the boom, so your body weight takes the load instead of your arms. The line needs to straddle the sail's centre of effort. If your front hand is doing most of the work, the force is centred ahead of the lines: move the line forward. If your back hand is, move it back. When it's set right you can hook in and briefly let go with both hands.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: The sail as a wing & the harness
chunks.text: Worked example · how far you lean, 75 kg rider (simplified, illustrative) Sideways pull from the sail Lean from vertical to balance it 219 N (15 kn, standing still) ≈ 17° 316 N (18 kn apparent) ≈ 23° 522 N (23 kn apparent) ≈ 35° Treat yourself as a straight body pivoting at your feet, with the pull at your centre of mass: tan(lean) = pull ÷ weight. 75 × 9.81 ≈ 736 N, so 316 ÷ 736 ≈ 0.43 and arctan 0.43 ≈ 23°. Real riders also bend their legs and move their hips, but the idea holds: more pull, lean further out. The apparent wind rises from 10 to 15 kn. How much more sail force? (15 ÷ 10)² = 2.25 times . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 3

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Steering, fin & daggerboard
chunks.text: No rudder. You steer by moving the sail. The sail's force acts through its centre of effort (CE) . The water's sideways resistance acts through the board's centre of lateral resistance (CLR) , near the fin or daggerboard. If the CE is directly above the CLR the board goes straight. Tilt the rig forward and the CE moves ahead of the CLR: the force turns the nose away from the wind (bearing away). Tilt it back and the tail is pushed away, turning the nose into the wind (heading up).

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Steering, fin & daggerboard
chunks.text: Worked example · a turning moment (illustrative values) Rig tilt CE ahead (+) or behind (−) the CLR Turning moment at 300 N Board turns Upright 0 m 0 N·m Straight Forward +0.3 m 90 N·m Away from the wind Back −0.3 m 90 N·m the other way Into the wind Moment = force × lever arm: 300 N × 0.3 m = 90 N·m. On a planing board, riders also steer by tilting the board onto its rail. Fins and daggerboards are underwater wings. Without them, the sideways part of the sail force would just push the board sideways across the water.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Steering, fin & daggerboard
chunks.text: A fin meets the water at a small angle as the board slips very slightly sideways (leeway), and makes sideways lift with the same formula as the sail, ½ ρ v² A C L , but in water about 840 times denser than air. So a fin a fraction of the sail's size can balance the sail, if the board is moving fast. Worked example · sideways grip from a 0.04 m² fin, C L 0.3 (illustrative) Board speed Fin side force What it means 5 kn ≈ 41 N Too little: a learner's board would slide sideways 10 kn ≈ 163 N Getting there 20 kn ≈ 651 N Plenty: why fast boards need only a fin At 20 kn (10.3 m/s): 0.5 × 1,025 × 10.3² × 0.04 × 0.3 ≈ 651 N.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Steering, fin & daggerboard
chunks.text: Side force grows with speed squared, so halving your speed leaves a quarter of the grip. That's why beginner and racing longboards (such as the Raceboard and Techno 293 classes) carry a daggerboard : a much larger blade through the middle of the board that gives grip at low speed and lets you point upwind. When the board is going fast on a reach, riders pull the daggerboard up. Left down at speed, its own lift tends to tip the board onto its rail. You want to turn towards the wind. Which way do you tilt the rig? Back , towards the tail. ↑ Back to the challenge CH 4

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & foiling
chunks.text: Push water aside, skim over it, or fly above it. A board pushing through the water makes a bow wave. A wave's speed depends on its length, v = √(g L ÷ 2π) , so once the bow wave is as long as the board, going faster means climbing your own wave. That's the hull speed . With enough wind, a light board climbs onto the surface and planes , skimming instead of pushing water aside. A hydrofoil (as on the Olympic iQFOiL) goes further: an underwater wing lifts the whole board clear of the water. Floating first: volume. Standing still, the board floats by buoyancy: it must displace its own weight plus yours in water.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & foiling
chunks.text: Each litre of seawater it pushes under supports about 1 kg, so a 100 kg load of rider plus rig sinks a board to its deck at about 98 litres. Learner boards carry far more volume than that, so they float high and stable while you uphaul (Ch 6). Fast boards carry less, and only work once they're planing. Planing: from floating to skimming. Naval architects compare speed with length using the Froude number , Fr = v ÷ √(g L) . Hull speed is Fr ≈ 0.4. Somewhere above Fr ≈ 1, the flat underside acts like a water-ski: it deflects water downwards, the reaction lifts the board, and most of it rises out of the water.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & foiling
chunks.text: The wetted area shrinks, drag falls, and the board accelerates, which raises the apparent wind (Ch 1) and the sail force (Ch 2). That's why "getting on the plane" feels like a sudden surge. Riders help it happen by bearing away onto a reach, moving back into the footstraps, hooking into the harness, and pumping the sail in marginal wind. Worked example · a 2.5 m board (rules of thumb, illustrative) Regime Froude number Board speed Displacement (hull speed) ≈ 0.4 ≈ 3.8 kn Planing begins (roughly) ≈ 1 ≈ 9.6 kn Hull speed of a 2.5 m board: √(9.81 × 2.5 ÷ 6.28) ≈ 1.98 m/s ≈ 3.8 kn, which is Fr = 1 ÷ √(2π) ≈ 0.4. Fr = 1: √(9.81 × 2.5) ≈ 4.95 m/s ≈ 9.6 kn.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Hull speed, planing & foiling
chunks.text: Real boards vary with shape, weight and rider. Worked example · foil lift, 0.1 m² wing, C L 0.4, 85 kg rider and board (from our Sail Lab, illustrative) Board speed Foil lift Share of weight (834 N) 8 kn ≈ 347 N 42% 10 kn ≈ 543 N 65% 12 kn ≈ 781 N 94% 13 kn ≈ 917 N 110%: flying Foil: 0.5 × 1,025 × (10 × 0.514)² × 0.1 × 0.4 ≈ 543 N. Water is about 800 times denser than air (1,025 ÷ 1.225 ≈ 840), which is why such a small wing can lift a person. Lift grows with speed squared. If the foil just flies at 13 kn, about what share of the lift does it give at 6.5 kn? (6.5 ÷ 13)² = 25% . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 5

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tacking, gybing & VMG
chunks.text: To go upwind, you zig-zag. Angle and speed trade off. No sail can drive you straight into the wind: there's a "no-go zone" on either side of it (Ch 1). To reach a point upwind you sail at an angle, then turn through the wind (a tack ) and sail the other way. Turning with the wind behind you is a gybe . Your upwind progress is the velocity made good , VMG = speed × cos(angle off the wind) . Worked example · pointing high vs sailing fast (illustrative) Angle off the wind Board speed VMG 40° 6 kn ≈ 4.6 kn 45° 8 kn ≈ 5.7 kn 55° 10 kn ≈ 5.7 kn 90° 10 kn 0 kn 8 × cos 45° ≈ 5.7 kn. Pointing higher isn't always better: sailing a little lower and faster can make the same progress.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tacking, gybing & VMG
chunks.text: Beginner courses teach turning the board slowly (Quest's Level 2 introduces tacks and gybes in non-planing conditions). Then comes turning at speed: Quest's Level 3 and its "turning with speed" course cover tacks and gybes in planing conditions, and the RYA scheme runs carve gybe clinics. The carve gybe: a banked turn on water. A planing board turns by tipping onto its inside rail, so the rail and fin carve an arc. Turning in a circle of radius r at speed v takes a sideways (centripetal) force m v² ÷ r towards the centre of the turn. You lean into the turn, like a cyclist, until your weight and that force balance: tan(lean) = v² ÷ (g r) .

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Tacking, gybing & VMG
chunks.text: As you head downwind through the turn, the apparent wind drops and swings behind you (Ch 1), so the rig goes light. That's the moment to flip the sail onto the new side and keep planing out of the turn. Worked example · lean angle in a carve gybe (illustrative) Speed Turn radius Lean from vertical 15 kn 15 m ≈ 22° 15 kn 8 m ≈ 37° 20 kn 10 m ≈ 47° 20 kn = 10.3 m/s: 10.3² ÷ (9.81 × 10) ≈ 1.08, and arctan 1.08 ≈ 47°. Faster or tighter turns need more lean. If you lean too little, the board can't hold the arc and the rail lets go. At 12 kn and 60° off the wind, what's your VMG? 12 × cos 60° = 6 kn . ↑ Back to the challenge CH 6

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Uphaul, waterstart & self-rescue
chunks.text: Know how you'll get up, and how you'd get home without the wind. Uphauling: a lift with your legs. Beginners start standing on a floaty board with the rig lying in the water downwind. You pull the uphaul rope hand over hand, keeping your back straight and leaning back so your body weight and legs do the lifting, not your arms. It's hardest at the start: water lying on the sail adds weight until the top of the mast clears and the water drains. Once the clew (back corner) is out of the water, you're lifting only the rig's own weight and can bring it up to the sailing position. Waterstarting: let the wind lift you. Better sailors skip the uphaul.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Uphaul, waterstart & self-rescue
chunks.text: Floating beside the board, you raise the rig into the wind, put your feet on the board, and let the sail's pull lift you up and on. That only works when the sail can pull hard enough, and sail force grows with the wind speed squared (Ch 2). Quest's Level 3 introduces stronger winds and the steps for beach and water starts, and its waterstart course is about getting up "in windy conditions".

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Uphaul, waterstart & self-rescue
chunks.text: Worked example · pull of a 6 m² sail while you're not moving (C L 1.0, illustrative) True wind Sail force Share of a 75 kg rider's weight (736 N) 8 kn ≈ 62 N ≈ 8% 12 kn ≈ 140 N ≈ 19% 15 kn ≈ 219 N ≈ 30% The water still supports most of you, and the board starts moving as you rise, which raises the apparent wind. But nearly four times the pull at 15 kn as at 8 kn is why waterstarts are taught in stronger wind and uphauling in light wind. Wind and weather. Sail force grows with the square of the wind (Ch 2), so a gust that's 40% stronger nearly doubles it. And wind direction decides where you drift if something goes wrong: offshore wind (land to sea) carries you away from the beach.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Uphaul, waterstart & self-rescue
chunks.text: Learn in steady, moderate wind, ideally cross-shore, with rescue cover. Worked example · the wind at Quest's Palk Bay school Season (Quest) Wind Force on a 6 m² sail (at the wind speed, illustrative) Dec–Mar, afternoons 10–15 kn ≈ 97–219 N Apr–Sep, all day 18–25 kn ≈ 315–608 N 0.5 × 1.225 × (25 × 0.514)² × 6 ≈ 608 N. Stronger seasons suit planing and smaller sails; lighter winds suit first lessons. Self-rescue: if you can't sail back, you can drop or de-rig the sail onto the board and paddle in. Quest's Level 1 course includes self-rescue drills. Swimming: Quest asks Level 1 students to swim 100 m unaided, or 200 m with a personal flotation device. Stay with the board.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Uphaul, waterstart & self-rescue
chunks.text: It floats, and it's easier to spot than a swimmer. Monsoon: on the west coast, Goa's water-sports policy bars water sports in the monsoon, and in 2026 Uttara Kannada (Karwar) banned sea water sports from 1 June to 31 August. Safety Learn with a school Take lessons at a recognised centre with a qualified instructor and a rescue boat, wear a buoyancy aid while learning, and tell someone ashore when you go out. A gust takes the wind from 15 to 21 kn. About how much more sail force? (21 ÷ 15)² ≈ 1.96 times : nearly double. ↑ Back to the challenge 03 · The windsurf ladder

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Start windsurfing → intermediate → planing & advanced → national racing → Olympic iQFOiL → instructor
chunks.text: Indian schools and Karnataka's state adventure academy run their own level courses, and the RYA (UK) scheme is a widely used reference; YAI's own National Windsurfing Scheme is listed as "yet to come". National racing runs under the Yachting Association of India. The steps below show the real content and requirements we found.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: Who sets the rules
chunks.text: Olympic windsurfing comes under World Sailing, and the IWA represents the windsurfing classes; training schemes come from bodies such as the RYA and VDWS; in India, competition runs through the Yachting Association of India, with state associations and Karnataka's state academy running training. We checked each on an official website.

chunks.heading: When to go
chunks.text: Subscribe Copy link Full season calendar → April–September Quest says Palk Bay winds average 18–25 kn all day: planing season. December–March Quest describes afternoon winds of 10–15 kn: good for first lessons. Karwar, Karnataka GETHNAA lists a Basic Aqua Sports Course batch with an introduction to windsurfing on 1–10 Nov 2026. In 2026, sea water sports in Uttara Kannada were banned from 1 June to 31 August. Goa, Mar–Apr 2026 YAI's national windsurfing & kiteboarding championship ran at Morjim, and Sail Goa at Dona Paula. Every session Check the wind direction and gusts; tell someone ashore when you go out.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: When to go
chunks.text: ① First lessons ② Improve ③ Race ④ Instruct You're here if… You've never windsurfed (Step 1). Read Ch 3 and Ch 6 . Ask before you book Is there a rescue boat? Do you provide buoyancy aids and beginner boards? What's the swimming requirement? Quest Adventure Sports Academy · Windsurfing School Near Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu (Palk Bay) Level courses From a 2-hour Discover session (age 10+, swimming not required) to a 2-day Level 1 course and a 4-day Level 1–2 bootcamp, in shallow Palk Bay waters at Pirappanvalasai.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: When to go
chunks.text: quest-asia.com GETHNAA · Karwar Water Sports Centre Mouth of the Kali River near Sadashivgad, Karwar, Uttara Kannada, Karnataka State academy Karnataka's state adventure academy teaches sailing, windsurfing and kayaking here. Its 10-day Basic Aqua Sports Course includes an introduction to windsurfing, with a Karwar batch on 1–10 Nov 2026; it also ran a Wind Surfing & Kayaking summer camp at Karwar in April 2026. Check camp dates, eligibility and fees on GETHNAA's own site. gethnaa.org Aquasail India · Start Windsurfing Grand Hyatt, Bambolim Beach, Goa (also Mumbai and Mandwa) Sailing centre Sailing, windsurfing and kayaking; its Goa centre runs a Start Windsurfing course.

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: When to go
chunks.text: aquasailindia.com Mumbai Sailing Club · Learn to Windsurf Gateway of India, Mumbai Club course Five 2-hour sessions for ages 13–50. mumbaisailingclub.com The Alampara · windsurfing Kottaikadu, near Alamparai Fort, Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu Resort A resort between Chennai and Puducherry that lists windsurfing among its water sports. A place to try it; ask about instruction and rescue cover before you book. thealampara.com You're here if… You can sail back and forth and want to tack, gybe and plane (Steps 2–3). Read Ch 5 and Ch 4 . Ask before you book Which skills does the next level cover? Do you have harness lines and planing boards for intermediates?

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: When to go
chunks.text: Quest · Windsurfing Level 2 & bootcamp Near Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu Courses Level 2 introduces tacks and gybes; the bootcamp takes you from Level 1 to Level 2. quest-asia.com Quest · Level 3, waterstart & turning with speed Near Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu Speciality courses Level 3 brings stronger winds, planing, planing tacks and gybes and the steps for beach and water starts; two-day speciality courses focus on the waterstart and on turning at speed. quest-asia.com RYA Windsurfing Scheme Reference syllabus Start Windsurfing, Intermediate non-planing and planing, then Advanced (waterstart and carve gybe clinics). rya.org.uk You're here if… You plane confidently and want to race (Steps 4–5).

chunks.title: Windsurfing · Physics of Apparent Wind, Sail Force & Planing · Kinetic by Curiosta
chunks.heading: When to go
chunks.text: Ask before you book Which classes run at the nationals? How do I enter through my club or association? Which events count for ranking? YAI All India Windsurfing & Kiteboarding Championship Morjim, Goa · 18–22 Mar 2026 A YAI ranking event with T293, Raceboard and iQFOiL windsurfing classes. yai.org.in Sail Goa 2026 GYA Boat Club, Dona Paula, Goa · 13–17 Apr 2026 A YAI zonal championship and national ranking event for iQFOiL and Techno 293 OD, with open windsurf foil and Raceboard fleets. yai.org.in (Notice of Race) YAI Senior Nationals 2026 INWTC, Colaba, Mumbai · 14–20 Nov 2026 Includes iQFOiL for men and women, with up to 15 races scheduled.

chunks.text: Entries go through YAI membership and the organising club. yai.org.in (Notice of Race) YAI domestic calendar Yachting Association of India Lists national championships and selection trials, including iQFOiL trials at Girgaon Chowpatty, Mumbai, and the CESC Regatta at Pawna Dam, Pune (23–28 Oct 2026) with Techno 293, Raceboard and iQFOiL. yai.org.in Tamil Nadu Sailing Association Chennai Promotes windsurfing on the Chennai coast; the 2024 All India Windsurfing Championships, with Raceboard, Techno 293, RS:X and iQFOiL races, were held at Chennai harbour.

chunks.text: tnsa.in LA28 Olympic windsurfing (iQFOiL) Belmont Shore, Long Beach · 17–20 July 2028 Men's and women's iQFOiL medals are decided the day after the kite events. sailing.org You're here if… You're an experienced windsurfer who wants to teach (Step 6). Ask before you book Which instructor qualification does your centre recognise? What first-aid and powerboat requirements apply? RYA windsurf instructor pathway International reference Instructor Start Windsurfing, Intermediate and Advanced Instructor courses, with minimum ages, logged hours, first aid and RYA Powerboat Level 2.
